cards.explanation: The bilateral margin rules require that margin must not be wrong-way, with a counterparty posting its own bonds or equity as the example. A haircut does not make such margin eligible.
cards.originalText: Under the bilateral margin rules, the European bank may post its own bonds as margin, provided a haircut reflecting their price volatility is applied.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify examples of wrong-way collateral.
cards.statement: High-quality sovereign bonds are free of wrong-way risk by definition, so accepting them prevents a bank from posting margin linked to its own credit quality.
cards.explanation: High-quality sovereign bonds are normally eligible, which is why a CSA may not prevent a bank from posting bonds of its own sovereign, a specific wrong-way case.
cards.originalText: High-quality sovereign bonds are free of wrong-way risk by definition, so accepting them prevents the European bank from posting margin linked to its own credit quality.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify examples of wrong-way collateral.
cards.statement: A bank holding, as margin from another bank, bonds issued by that bank's own sovereign has specific wrong-way margin.
cards.explanation: The credit quality of a bank and of its own sovereign are directly linked, and GARP lists such bonds with a bank's own bonds as a clearly problematic example of specific wrong-way margin.
cards.originalText: A bank holding, as margin from another bank, bonds issued by that bank’s own sovereign: specific wrong-way margin.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify examples of wrong-way collateral.
cards.statement: High-quality government bonds held as margin against a receiver interest rate swap are general wrong-way margin.
cards.explanation: With a receiver swap a fall in rates raises both the exposure and the bond's value, so the margin is right-way rather than wrong-way.
cards.originalText: A dealer holding high-quality government bonds as margin against a receiver interest rate swap: general wrong-way margin.
cards.correction: High-quality government bonds held as margin against a receiver interest rate swap are right-way margin.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify examples of wrong-way collateral.
cards.statement: High-quality government bonds held as margin against a payer interest rate swap are specific wrong-way margin.
cards.explanation: The payer-swap case is general wrong-way margin, driven by market rates, not specific wrong-way margin, which comes from a direct link between the margin and the counterparty's credit quality.
cards.originalText: A dealer holding high-quality government bonds as margin against a payer interest rate swap: specific wrong-way margin.
cards.correction: High-quality government bonds held as margin against a payer interest rate swap are general wrong-way margin.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify examples of wrong-way collateral.
cards.statement: A counterparty's own senior bonds held as margin are general wrong-way margin.
cards.explanation: Own bonds are linked directly to the poster's credit quality, which is the specific wrong-way case, not a general market-driven effect.
cards.originalText: A dealer holding a corporate counterparty’s own senior bonds as margin: general wrong-way margin driven by interest rates.
cards.correction: A counterparty's own senior bonds held as margin are specific wrong-way margin.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Discuss the impact of wrong-way risk on central counterparties (CCPs).
cards.statement: A clearing member's default fund contribution and other loss-allocation exposures form a rather senior second-loss position, behind the defaulter's resources and CCP equity, so losses reach it mainly in systemic scenarios.
cards.explanation: In the CCP loss waterfall the first loss is covered by the defaulter's margin and default fund together with CCP equity. Surviving members' contributions are a second-loss position that corresponds to a relatively unlikely event, like a senior CDO tranche.
cards.originalText: The member’s default fund contribution and other loss-allocation exposures form a rather senior second-loss position, behind the defaulter’s resources and CCP equity, so losses reach it mainly in systemic scenarios.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Discuss the impact of wrong-way risk on central counterparties (CCPs).
cards.statement: A member's default fund contribution is an equity (first-loss) tranche that is hit whenever any member defaults, so its risk is mainly idiosyncratic.
cards.explanation: The equity (first-loss) layer is the defaulter's own resources plus CCP equity. The surviving members' default fund is a more senior second-loss position.
cards.originalText: The member’s default fund contribution is an equity (first-loss) tranche, hit whenever any member defaults, so its risk is mainly idiosyncratic.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Discuss the impact of wrong-way risk on central counterparties (CCPs).
cards.statement: A surviving member's default fund contribution ranks ahead of the defaulter's initial margin in the CCP loss waterfall.
cards.explanation: The defaulter's margin and default fund are used first, so surviving members' contributions rank behind them.
cards.originalText: The member’s default fund contribution ranks ahead of the defaulter’s initial margin, so it absorbs the first losses on any member default.
cards.correction: A surviving member's default fund contribution ranks behind the defaulter's initial margin in the CCP loss waterfall.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Discuss the impact of wrong-way risk on central counterparties (CCPs).
cards.statement: Like a senior CDO tranche, a member's default fund exposure carries little systemic risk because it is diversified across many members.
cards.explanation: Seniority does not mean low systemic risk: senior CDO tranches are known to be heavily concentrated in systemic risk, and so is the surviving members' default fund exposure.
cards.originalText: The member’s exposure through the default fund is diversified across many members, so like a senior CDO tranche it carries little systemic risk.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Discuss the impact of wrong-way risk on central counterparties (CCPs).
cards.statement: Multilateral netting across CCP members breaks the link between a member's default and the value of its cleared portfolio, so wrong-way risk is confined to bilateral trades.
cards.explanation: CCPs are exposed to wrong-way risk because they disassociate credit quality and exposure, and a member's default can coincide with adverse moves in its cleared portfolio. Wrong-way risk is not confined to bilateral trades.
cards.originalText: Multilateral netting across members breaks the link between a member’s default and the value of its cleared portfolio, so wrong-way risk is confined to bilateral trades.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Discuss the impact of wrong-way risk on central counterparties (CCPs).
cards.statement: Because CCP initial margins and default fund contributions are driven mainly by the market risk of each portfolio, the CCP may implicitly ignore wrong-way risk.
cards.explanation: Gregory warns that CCPs are in danger of implicitly ignoring wrong-way risk because margin and default fund contributions disassociate credit quality and exposure.
cards.originalText: Initial margins and default fund contributions are driven mainly by the market risk of each portfolio, so the CCP may implicitly ignore wrong-way risk.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Discuss the impact of wrong-way risk on central counterparties (CCPs).
cards.statement: CCP members may choose to post the eligible margin with the greatest risk relative to its haircut, which may also carry the greatest wrong-way risk to the CCP.
cards.explanation: Members naturally post the margin that has the greatest risk relative to its haircut. This adverse selection can also concentrate wrong-way risk, for example a European bank posting European sovereign debt.
cards.originalText: Members may choose to post the eligible margin with the greatest risk relative to its haircut, which may also carry the greatest wrong-way risk to the CCP.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Discuss the impact of wrong-way risk on central counterparties (CCPs).
cards.statement: The default of a large, highly rated, systemically important CCP member is less likely but would be a bigger shock, so the wrong-way risk it brings is greater.
cards.explanation: Wrong-way risk increases with credit quality, which is why it argues for more margin from systemic members.
cards.originalText: The default of a large, highly rated, systemically important member is less likely but would be a bigger shock, so the wrong-way risk it brings is greater.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the various wrong-way modeling methods including hazard rate approaches, structural approaches, parametric approaches, and jump approaches.
cards.statement: The intensity (hazard rate) approach to wrong-way risk generates only weak dependence between exposure and default even when correlations are close to their limits, so it may underestimate the wrong-way risk effect.
cards.explanation: Correlating a stochastic credit spread with the exposure drivers gives only weak dependence given the correlations used are close to their maximum and minimum values. A modest CVA rise even at high correlation is therefore a property of the method, not proof of low wrong-way risk.
cards.originalText: The result is typical of the intensity (hazard rate) approach, which generates only weak dependence between exposure and default even near its correlation limits, so it may underestimate WWR.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the various wrong-way modeling methods including hazard rate approaches, structural approaches, parametric approaches, and jump approaches.
cards.statement: The intensity (hazard rate) approach captures the full dependence between exposure and default once the correlation approaches 100%.
cards.explanation: The intensity approach does not capture the full dependence even near plus or minus 100% correlation, so a weak response is not proof of weak wrong-way risk.
cards.originalText: The result shows that the payer swaps carry no material WWR, since the approach captures the full dependence once the correlation approaches 100%.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the various wrong-way modeling methods including hazard rate approaches, structural approaches, parametric approaches, and jump approaches.
cards.statement: The structural approach to wrong-way risk gives a weaker effect than the intensity approach at the same correlation.
cards.explanation: The structural approach gives a much stronger effect than the intensity approach, and it samples pre-computed exposures rather than simulating credit spreads.
cards.originalText: The engine must in fact be using a structural approach, which is known to give a weaker effect than the intensity approach at the same correlation.
cards.correction: The structural approach to wrong-way risk gives a stronger effect than the intensity approach at the same correlation.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the various wrong-way modeling methods including hazard rate approaches, structural approaches, parametric approaches, and jump approaches.
cards.statement: The intensity approach to wrong-way risk assumes a jump in interest rates at the default time.
cards.explanation: The intensity approach has no jump at default; jumps belong to the jump approaches.
cards.originalText: The result is caused by the jump in interest rates the approach assumes at the default time, which offsets the correlation effect.
cards.correction: The intensity approach to wrong-way risk has no jump at the default time.

changes.from: assumes a jump in interest rates at the default time
changes.to: has no jump at the default time

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the various wrong-way modeling methods including hazard rate approaches, structural approaches, parametric approaches, and jump approaches.
cards.statement: In the structural approach, which maps the default time and the pre-computed exposure distribution onto a bivariate distribution, the correlation parameter is opaque and hard to calibrate, and the unconditional exposure distribution may not contain all the information needed to define wrong-way risk.
cards.explanation: The structural approach adds wrong-way risk on top of existing exposure simulations without re-running them. The drawback is that the correlation parameter is hard to interpret and calibrate, and the unconditional exposure distribution may not hold all the relevant information.
cards.originalText: Its correlation parameter is opaque and hard to calibrate, and the unconditional exposure distribution may not contain all the information needed to define WWR.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the various wrong-way modeling methods including hazard rate approaches, structural approaches, parametric approaches, and jump approaches.
cards.statement: The structural approach to wrong-way risk requires exposures to be re-simulated on every path where a default occurs, which makes it computationally expensive.
cards.explanation: Re-simulating exposures on default paths is the intensity approach. The structural approach uses pre-computed exposure distributions and needs no re-simulation.
cards.originalText: It requires exposures to be re-simulated on every path where a default occurs, which makes it computationally expensive.
cards.correction: The intensity approach to wrong-way risk requires exposures to be re-simulated on every path where a default occurs, which makes it computationally expensive.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the various wrong-way modeling methods including hazard rate approaches, structural approaches, parametric approaches, and jump approaches.
cards.statement: The structural approach to wrong-way risk produces only weak dependence between exposure and default, so its CVA barely changes with correlation.
cards.explanation: Weak dependence is the weakness of the intensity approach; the structural approach gives a much stronger effect.
cards.originalText: It produces only a weak dependence between exposure and default, so its CVA barely changes with correlation.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the various wrong-way modeling methods including hazard rate approaches, structural approaches, parametric approaches, and jump approaches.
cards.statement: The structural approach to wrong-way risk can only be calibrated by revaluing the portfolio at past dates against the counterparty's historical credit spread.
cards.explanation: Calibration against historical portfolio values and credit spreads describes the parametric approach, not the structural approach.
cards.originalText: It can only be calibrated by revaluing the portfolio at past dates against the counterparty’s historical credit spread.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the various wrong-way modeling methods including hazard rate approaches, structural approaches, parametric approaches, and jump approaches.
cards.statement: Hull and White's parametric approach, which calibrates a dependency parameter from past portfolio values and the counterparty's credit spread, requires that the current portfolio is similar in nature to the one used in the historical calibration and that the history shows a meaningful relationship between portfolio value and spread.
cards.explanation: The calibration is only as reliable as the historical data: the current portfolio must resemble the historical portfolios, and the history must reveal a meaningful relationship between portfolio value and credit spread.
cards.originalText: The current portfolio must be similar in nature to the one used in the historical calibration, and the history must show a meaningful relationship between portfolio value and spread.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe a waterfall structure in a securitization.
cards.statement: In a CLO with an overcollateralisation account, fees are paid first, then the senior coupon, then the mezzanine coupon, then the overcollateralisation account up to its annual cap, and the equity receives the residual.
cards.explanation: Fees typically take priority over coupons, the senior coupon is paid in full before the mezzanine, and only the excess spread left after the coupons is diverted to the account up to its cap. Equity receives what remains.
cards.originalText: Fees; senior coupon; mezzanine coupon; overcollateralization account up to its annual cap; equity residual

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe a waterfall structure in a securitization.
cards.statement: In a CLO waterfall, trustee and management fees are paid after the bond coupons.
cards.explanation: Fees and other costs typically take priority over coupons.
cards.originalText: Senior coupon; mezzanine coupon; fees; equity residual; overcollateralization account
cards.correction: In a CLO waterfall, trustee and management fees are paid before the bond coupons.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe a waterfall structure in a securitization.
cards.statement: In a CLO waterfall, the senior and mezzanine coupons are paid pro rata to their par amounts.
cards.explanation: The senior coupon is paid in full before the mezzanine receives anything, so the coupons are paid sequentially, not pro rata.
cards.originalText: Fees; senior and mezzanine coupons pro rata to their par amounts; equity residual; overcollateralization account
cards.correction: In a CLO waterfall, the senior and mezzanine coupons are paid sequentially, with the senior coupon paid in full first.

changes.from: pro rata to their par amounts
changes.to: sequentially, with the senior coupon paid in full first

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe a waterfall structure in a securitization.
cards.statement: In a CLO waterfall, excess spread is diverted to the overcollateralisation account before the senior and mezzanine coupons are paid.
cards.explanation: Excess spread is only what is left after the coupons. Diverting it to the account first would starve the bonds the account is meant to protect.
cards.originalText: Fees; overcollateralization account up to its annual cap; senior coupon; mezzanine coupon; equity residual
cards.correction: In a CLO waterfall, excess spread is diverted to the overcollateralisation account after the senior and mezzanine coupons are paid.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe a waterfall structure in a securitization.
cards.statement: Excess spread diverted to an overcollateralisation account is hard credit enhancement that, like the equity note, is fully in place when the deal is issued.
cards.explanation: Diverted excess spread is soft credit enhancement: it accrues over time and is not present at initiation. Hard overcollateralisation is collateral par above bond par at issue.
cards.originalText: The diverted excess spread is hard credit enhancement: like the equity note, it is fully in place when the deal is issued.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe a waterfall structure in a securitization.
cards.statement: An overcollateralisation account in a CLO protects only the senior bond and may not be used to pay the mezzanine coupon.
cards.explanation: The account pays interest on the bonds, both the senior and mezzanine tranches, when loan interest is insufficient.
cards.originalText: The account protects the senior bond only: it may not be used to pay the mezzanine coupon, which must be met from loan interest alone.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the prepayment forecasting methodologies and calculate the constant prepayment rate (CPR) and the Public Securities Association (PSA) rate.
cards.statement: The WAL of a pass-through note is quoted under a stated prepayment assumption, and a faster assumed PSA speed shortens it.
cards.explanation: A weighted average life approach incorporates prepayment assumptions, so a WAL is associated with a particular prepayment assumption. Faster prepayment cuts the pool factor sooner, which shortens the WAL.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the prepayment forecasting methodologies and calculate the constant prepayment rate (CPR) and the Public Securities Association (PSA) rate.
cards.statement: For commercial MBS, prepayment speed is measured by the debt service coverage ratio, the ratio of net operating income to debt payments.
cards.explanation: The DSCR is a credit measure of the borrower's ability to repay. Prepayment is measured by SMM, CPR and PSA.
cards.originalText: For commercial MBS, prepayment speed is tracked with the DSCR, the ratio of net operating income to debt payments.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the prepayment forecasting methodologies and calculate the constant prepayment rate (CPR) and the Public Securities Association (PSA) rate.
cards.statement: A pool at 100% PSA prepays at a constant 6% CPR from origination, and faster speeds are multiples of that rate.
cards.explanation: At 100% PSA the CPR starts at 0, rises by 0.2% a month and reaches 6% only at month 30, because mortgages prepay more slowly in their first 30 months.
cards.correction: A pool at 100% PSA starts at 0% CPR, rises by 0.2% a month and reaches 6% CPR only at month 30, and faster speeds are multiples of that rate.

changes.from: prepays at a constant 6% CPR from origination
changes.to: starts at 0% CPR, rises by 0.2% a month and reaches 6% CPR only at month 30

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define and calculate expected loss (EL).
cards.statement: The expected loss on a loan is the product of its probability of default, exposure at default and loss given default.
cards.explanation: Expected loss is the product of the three credit-risk components: PD, exposure amount and loss rate (loss given default).
cards.originalText: The product of the loan’s probability of default, exposure at default, and loss given default.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define and calculate expected loss (EL).
cards.statement: Expected loss is the highest potential loss on a loan under the most adverse economic conditions.
cards.explanation: That describes a worst-case loss, not the expected (average) loss. Unexpected loss is the volatility around expected loss.
cards.originalText: The highest potential loss for the loan under the most adverse economic conditions.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define and calculate expected loss (EL).
cards.statement: Expected loss is the risk that arises from variation in loss levels and therefore justifies the rationale for economic capital.
cards.explanation: That describes unexpected loss, the variation in losses around the expected level, which is what economic capital covers.
cards.originalText: Expected loss is the risk that arises due to the variation in loss levels and therefore justifies the rationale for economic capital
cards.correction: Unexpected loss is the risk that arises from variation in loss levels and therefore justifies the rationale for economic capital.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define and calculate expected loss (EL).
cards.statement: The exposure amount is the standard deviation of credit losses estimated at the end of the horizon, excluding outstanding interest payments.
cards.explanation: Exposure amount is the amount owed at the time of default, including promised interest. The standard deviation of credit losses is the unexpected loss.
cards.originalText: Exposure amount (EA) is the standard deviation of credit losses estimated at the end of the horizon, excluding outstanding interest payments

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define and calculate expected loss (EL).
cards.statement: The probability of default is the probability that a borrower defaults before the end of a predetermined estimation horizon, typically one year.
cards.explanation: PD is defined over a chosen horizon, and one year is the usual choice.
cards.originalText: Probability of default (PD) is the probability that a borrower will default before the end of a predetermined period of time (the estimation horizon typically chosen is one year)

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define and calculate expected loss (EL).
cards.statement: The loss rate is the ratio of the actual loss incurred at default, including all costs of collecting and selling collateral, to the exposure amount.
cards.explanation: The loss rate is the fraction of the exposure lost after recoveries and collection costs.
cards.originalText: Loss rate (LR) represents the ratio of actual losses incurred at the time of default (including all costs associated with the collection and sale of collateral) to the exposure amount

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define and calculate expected loss (EL).
cards.statement: Expected loss at horizon H equals the probability of default up to H multiplied by the exposure amount at H and the loss rate at H.
cards.explanation: Expected loss is the product of the three components: $EL(H) = PD(H) \times EA(H) \times LR(H)$.
cards.originalText: Expected loss (EL) is equal to the product of: the probability of default up to time H (horizon); the exposure amount at time H; and the loss rate experienced at time H; i.e., EL(H) = PD(H)\*EA(H)\*LR(H)

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define and calculate expected loss (EL).
cards.statement: If the recovery rate rises and the probability of default falls, expected loss decreases, all else equal.
cards.explanation: The loss rate equals one minus the recovery rate, so a higher recovery rate lowers it, and a lower PD also lowers expected loss. Both effects work in the same direction.
cards.originalText: EL will decrease.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define and calculate expected loss (EL).
cards.statement: A higher recovery rate raises the loss rate and so increases expected loss.
cards.explanation: The loss rate equals one minus the recovery rate, so a higher recovery rate lowers the loss rate and expected loss.
cards.originalText: EL will increase because a higher RR raises the loss rate.
cards.correction: A higher recovery rate lowers the loss rate and so decreases expected loss.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define and calculate expected loss (EL).
cards.statement: A rising recovery rate and a falling probability of default have offsetting effects on expected loss.
cards.explanation: The effects are not offsetting: a higher recovery rate lowers the loss rate and a lower PD lowers the default probability, so both reduce expected loss.
cards.originalText: EL will be indeterminate because the two changes have offsetting effects.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define and calculate expected loss (EL).
cards.statement: Expected loss depends only on the exposure amount.
cards.explanation: Expected loss is the product of PD, exposure amount and loss rate, so it also depends on the other two components.
cards.originalText: EL will be unchanged because EL depends only on the exposure amount.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.loText: Compare and contrast different approaches to credit risk modeling, such as those related to the Merton model, Credit Risk Plus (CreditRisk+), CreditMetrics, and the Moody’s-KMV model.
cards.reading: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.statement: The Moody's KMV model maps distance to default to a probability of default using an empirical distribution of default frequencies derived from historical data.
cards.explanation: Firms with a given distance to default are grouped in a historical default database and the observed default frequency becomes the EDF. This replaces the Merton normal-distribution mapping.
cards.originalText: By deriving an empirical distribution of default frequencies from historical data.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.loText: Compare and contrast different approaches to credit risk modeling, such as those related to the Merton model, Credit Risk Plus (CreditRisk+), CreditMetrics, and the Moody’s-KMV model.
cards.reading: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.statement: The Moody's KMV model maps distance to default to a probability of default with the standard normal distribution.
cards.explanation: The standard normal mapping, $N(-DD)$, is the Merton approach. KMV deliberately uses an empirical distribution of historical default frequencies instead.
cards.originalText: By applying the standard normal distribution to the distance to default.
cards.correction: The Moody's KMV model maps distance to default to a probability of default with an empirical distribution of historical default frequencies.

changes.to: an empirical distribution of historical default frequencies

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.loText: Compare and contrast different approaches to credit risk modeling, such as those related to the Merton model, Credit Risk Plus (CreditRisk+), CreditMetrics, and the Moody’s-KMV model.
cards.reading: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.statement: The Moody's KMV model maps distance to default to a probability of default with a Poisson distribution based on the firm's past default history.
cards.explanation: A Poisson distribution is the CreditRisk+ choice for default counts. KMV uses an empirical distribution of default frequencies for each distance to default.
cards.originalText: By using a Poisson distribution based on the firm’s past default history.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.loText: Compare and contrast different approaches to credit risk modeling, such as those related to the Merton model, Credit Risk Plus (CreditRisk+), CreditMetrics, and the Moody’s-KMV model.
cards.reading: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.statement: In the Moody's KMV model the default point is all short-term debt plus half of long-term debt.
cards.explanation: This approximates the borrower's actual obligations over the horizon better than the face value of debt used in the Merton model, since long-term obligations are only partly due within the horizon.
cards.originalText: All short‑term debt plus half of long‑term debt.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.loText: Compare and contrast different approaches to credit risk modeling, such as those related to the Merton model, Credit Risk Plus (CreditRisk+), CreditMetrics, and the Moody’s-KMV model.
cards.reading: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.statement: The Moody's KMV model backs out the unobservable asset value and asset volatility from the market value of equity and the volatility of equity.
cards.explanation: Equity is a call option on the firm's assets, so the observed equity value and equity volatility allow the asset value and asset volatility to be solved.
cards.originalText: The market value of equity (market capitalization) and the volatility of equity.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.loText: Compare and contrast different approaches to credit risk modeling, such as those related to the Merton model, Credit Risk Plus (CreditRisk+), CreditMetrics, and the Moody’s-KMV model.
cards.reading: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.statement: The Moody's KMV model backs out asset value and asset volatility from the book value of equity and the volatility of accounting earnings.
cards.explanation: KMV is a market-based approach that relies on the market capitalisation and the market volatility of equity, not on accounting figures.
cards.originalText: The book value of equity and the volatility of accounting earnings.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.loText: Compare and contrast different approaches to credit risk modeling, such as those related to the Merton model, Credit Risk Plus (CreditRisk+), CreditMetrics, and the Moody’s-KMV model.
cards.reading: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.statement: The Moody's KMV model backs out asset value and asset volatility from the borrower's credit rating and a rating transition matrix.
cards.explanation: Ratings and transition matrices are CreditMetrics inputs. KMV uses market equity value and equity volatility.
cards.originalText: The borrower’s credit rating and the rating transition matrix.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.loText: Compare and contrast different approaches to credit risk modeling, such as those related to the Merton model, Credit Risk Plus (CreditRisk+), CreditMetrics, and the Moody’s-KMV model.
cards.reading: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.statement: A limitation of CreditMetrics is its use of fixed interest rates, which ignores interest rate volatility and becomes more problematic the longer the horizon.
cards.explanation: CreditMetrics values the portfolio with fixed interest rates, which does not capture rate volatility. Interest rates can be quite volatile over long periods, so the assumption is most damaging for long-term portfolios.
cards.originalText: The use of fixed interest rates when calculating recovery rates.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.loText: Compare and contrast different approaches to credit risk modeling, such as those related to the Merton model, Credit Risk Plus (CreditRisk+), CreditMetrics, and the Moody’s-KMV model.
cards.reading: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.statement: CreditRisk+ treats the default frequency as a continuous random variable, with rare and independent defaults described by a Poisson distribution.
cards.explanation: CreditRisk+ ignores the borrower's capital structure and equity prices. The Poisson distribution suits it because the mean equals the variance and the model needs only default events and little data.
cards.originalText: It treats default frequency as a continuous random variable described by a Poisson distribution.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.loText: Compare and contrast different approaches to credit risk modeling, such as those related to the Merton model, Credit Risk Plus (CreditRisk+), CreditMetrics, and the Moody’s-KMV model.
cards.reading: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.statement: CreditRisk+ monitors fluctuations in the equity market prices of the borrowers.
cards.explanation: CreditRisk+ ignores the borrower's capital structure and equity prices. Equity-price monitoring belongs to market-based models such as KMV.
cards.originalText: It monitors fluctuations in the equity market prices of the borrowers.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.loText: Compare and contrast different approaches to credit risk modeling, such as those related to the Merton model, Credit Risk Plus (CreditRisk+), CreditMetrics, and the Moody’s-KMV model.
cards.reading: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.statement: CreditRisk+ distinguishes only two credit events, bankruptcy and bad credit condition, so losses arise only on default.
cards.explanation: CreditRisk+ is a default-only model, whereas CreditMetrics captures losses from rating changes as well.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.loText: Compare and contrast different approaches to credit risk modeling, such as those related to the Merton model, Credit Risk Plus (CreditRisk+), CreditMetrics, and the Moody’s-KMV model.
cards.reading: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.statement: CreditRisk+ assesses credit risk from market capitalisation, unlike CreditMetrics.
cards.explanation: CreditRisk+ does not use capital structure or market capitalisation; that is the KMV approach.
cards.originalText: CreditRisk+ assesses credit risk from market capitalization, unlike CreditMetrics.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.loText: Compare and contrast different approaches to credit risk modeling, such as those related to the Merton model, Credit Risk Plus (CreditRisk+), CreditMetrics, and the Moody’s-KMV model.
cards.reading: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.statement: CreditMetrics assesses losses only in bankruptcy, whereas CreditRisk+ considers a broader range of credit events.
cards.explanation: The models are the other way round: CreditMetrics is the broader model, valuing rating migrations as well as default, while CreditRisk+ considers default only.
cards.originalText: CreditMetrics assesses losses only in bankruptcy, while CreditRisk+ considers a broader range of credit events.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.loText: Compare and contrast different approaches to credit risk modeling, such as those related to the Merton model, Credit Risk Plus (CreditRisk+), CreditMetrics, and the Moody’s-KMV model.
cards.reading: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.statement: The Moody's KMV model uses market data so that default probabilities update continuously, maps distance to default to a probability using historical default frequencies, and sets the default point at short-term debt plus half of long-term debt.
cards.explanation: Only KMV combines market-driven inputs, an empirical mapping from distance to default to EDF, and a default point that includes half of long-term debt. Merton uses the normal distribution and the face value of debt.
cards.originalText: Moody’s KMV (EDF) model

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.loText: Compare and contrast different approaches to credit risk modeling, such as those related to the Merton model, Credit Risk Plus (CreditRisk+), CreditMetrics, and the Moody’s-KMV model.
cards.reading: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.statement: Unlike the Merton model, which produces default predictions from asset and liability values, rating agencies' models produce default predictions from a substantially larger set of business factors.
cards.explanation: Merton is a narrow structural model based on asset value and debt, whereas agency ratings blend many qualitative and quantitative factors such as country, industry and competitive position.
cards.originalText: Unlike the Merton model that produces default predictions based on asset and liability values, the agencies’ rating models produce default predictions from a substantially larger set of business factors.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.loText: Compare and contrast different approaches to credit risk modeling, such as those related to the Merton model, Credit Risk Plus (CreditRisk+), CreditMetrics, and the Moody’s-KMV model.
cards.reading: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.statement: The CreditRisk+ model relies on a company's capital structure and credit ratings to predict default of the company.
cards.explanation: CreditRisk+ ignores capital structure and models only default events, not ratings. The statement confuses it with KMV.
cards.originalText: The Credit Risk Plus (CreditRisk+) model relies on the use of a company’s capital structure and credit ratings to predict default of the company.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.loText: Compare and contrast different approaches to credit risk modeling, such as those related to the Merton model, Credit Risk Plus (CreditRisk+), CreditMetrics, and the Moody’s-KMV model.
cards.reading: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.statement: A good rating model is expected to provide accurate borrower default predictions without the need to be backtested.
cards.explanation: Any rating model's performance must be validated by backtesting; no model can be assumed accurate a priori.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.loText: Compare and contrast different approaches to credit risk modeling, such as those related to the Merton model, Credit Risk Plus (CreditRisk+), CreditMetrics, and the Moody’s-KMV model.
cards.reading: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.statement: Moody's KMV defines the default point as short-term debt plus half of long-term debt, while the Merton model uses short-term debt only.
cards.explanation: The two key differences between the models are the default point and the mapping of distance to default to PD, where KMV uses an empirical distribution and Merton the standard normal.
cards.originalText: Moody’s KMV defines the default point as short‑term debt plus half of long‑term debt, while the Merton model uses short‑term debt only.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.loText: Compare and contrast different approaches to credit risk modeling, such as those related to the Merton model, Credit Risk Plus (CreditRisk+), CreditMetrics, and the Moody’s-KMV model.
cards.reading: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.statement: The Merton model uses the market value of the borrower's equity, while Moody's KMV uses its book value.
cards.explanation: Both models use the market value of equity, backed out through option pricing. Book value is not used.
cards.originalText: The Merton model uses the market value of the borrower’s equity, while Moody’s KMV uses its book value.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.loText: Compare and contrast different approaches to credit risk modeling, such as those related to the Merton model, Credit Risk Plus (CreditRisk+), CreditMetrics, and the Moody’s-KMV model.
cards.reading: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.statement: The Merton model is based on an option-pricing framework, while Moody's KMV is based on a rating transition matrix.
cards.explanation: KMV is also a structural, option-based model. The rating transition matrix belongs to CreditMetrics.
cards.originalText: The Merton model is based on an option‑pricing framework, while Moody’s KMV is based on a rating transition matrix.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.loText: Compare and contrast different approaches to credit risk modeling, such as those related to the Merton model, Credit Risk Plus (CreditRisk+), CreditMetrics, and the Moody’s-KMV model.
cards.reading: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.statement: The Merton model uses historical data to derive an empirical distribution of default frequencies, while Moody's KMV maps distance to default using the standard normal distribution.
cards.explanation: The two are reversed: KMV uses the empirical distribution of historical default frequencies and Merton uses the standard normal distribution.
cards.originalText: The Merton model uses historical data to derive an empirical distribution of default frequencies, while Moody’s KMV maps distance to default using the standard normal distribution.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.loText: Compare and contrast different approaches to credit risk modeling, such as those related to the Merton model, Credit Risk Plus (CreditRisk+), CreditMetrics, and the Moody’s-KMV model.
cards.reading: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.statement: CreditMetrics estimates default risk by comparing a borrower with a peer set, using the borrower's credit rating, a rating transition matrix and a mark-to-market valuation of the loan.
cards.explanation: CreditMetrics uses credit ratings, transition probabilities, recovery rates and bond-market spreads to revalue loans. Merton and KMV are structural option-based models, and CreditRisk+ models default events only.
cards.originalText: CreditMetrics model

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.loText: Compare and contrast different approaches to credit risk modeling, such as those related to the Merton model, Credit Risk Plus (CreditRisk+), CreditMetrics, and the Moody’s-KMV model.
cards.reading: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.statement: The CreditRisk+ model uses credit ratings and a rating transition matrix to estimate default risk.
cards.explanation: CreditRisk+ considers only default events and does not use credit ratings.
cards.originalText: CreditRisk+ model

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.loText: Compare and contrast different approaches to credit risk modeling, such as those related to the Merton model, Credit Risk Plus (CreditRisk+), CreditMetrics, and the Moody’s-KMV model.
cards.reading: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.statement: A valid criticism of CreditMetrics is its assumption that all borrowers within a credit grade are homogeneous.
cards.explanation: Treating every obligor in a rating grade as identical ignores differences in individual credit quality.
cards.originalText: The assumption of homogeneity in credit grades within the model.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.loText: Compare and contrast different approaches to credit risk modeling, such as those related to the Merton model, Credit Risk Plus (CreditRisk+), CreditMetrics, and the Moody’s-KMV model.
cards.reading: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.statement: CreditMetrics is unable to assess credit risk in real-time market conditions.
cards.explanation: CreditMetrics is a mark-to-market model that revalues loans using current credit spreads, so it does reflect market conditions.
cards.originalText: The inability of the model to assess credit risk in real‑time market conditions.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.loText: Compare and contrast different approaches to credit risk modeling, such as those related to the Merton model, Credit Risk Plus (CreditRisk+), CreditMetrics, and the Moody’s-KMV model.
cards.reading: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.statement: CreditMetrics lacks a focus on market-based instruments such as derivatives.
cards.explanation: CreditMetrics explicitly accommodates market-based instruments such as swaps and forwards.
cards.originalText: The lack of focus on market‑based instruments like derivatives in the model.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.loText: Compare and contrast different approaches to credit risk modeling, such as those related to the Merton model, Credit Risk Plus (CreditRisk+), CreditMetrics, and the Moody’s-KMV model.
cards.reading: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.statement: CreditMetrics is a mark-to-market model using rating transitions, whereas CreditRisk+ considers only default events and does not use credit ratings.
cards.explanation: CreditMetrics values rating migrations as well as default, while CreditRisk+ is a default-only actuarial model.
cards.originalText: CreditMetrics is a mark‑to‑market model using rating transitions, whereas CreditRisk+ considers only default events and does not use credit ratings.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.loText: Compare and contrast different approaches to credit risk modeling, such as those related to the Merton model, Credit Risk Plus (CreditRisk+), CreditMetrics, and the Moody’s-KMV model.
cards.reading: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.statement: CreditRisk+ uses a rating transition matrix to revalue loans, whereas CreditMetrics considers only bankruptcy.
cards.explanation: The roles are reversed: the transition matrix belongs to CreditMetrics, and the default-only focus belongs to CreditRisk+.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.loText: Compare and contrast different approaches to credit risk modeling, such as those related to the Merton model, Credit Risk Plus (CreditRisk+), CreditMetrics, and the Moody’s-KMV model.
cards.reading: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.statement: CreditMetrics assumes defaults follow a Poisson distribution, whereas CreditRisk+ revalues loans using bond-market spreads.
cards.explanation: The roles are reversed: the Poisson default distribution is a CreditRisk+ feature, and spread-based revaluation belongs to CreditMetrics.
cards.originalText: CreditMetrics assumes defaults follow a Poisson distribution, whereas CreditRisk+ revalues loans using bond‑market spreads.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.loText: Compare and contrast different approaches to credit risk modeling, such as those related to the Merton model, Credit Risk Plus (CreditRisk+), CreditMetrics, and the Moody’s-KMV model.
cards.reading: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.statement: CreditRisk+ requires extensive data on the borrower's capital structure, whereas CreditMetrics requires only default counts.
cards.explanation: CreditRisk+ ignores capital structure and needs little data, whereas CreditMetrics needs ratings, transition probabilities and spreads.
cards.originalText: CreditRisk+ requires extensive data on the borrower’s capital structure, whereas CreditMetrics requires only default counts.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare agencies’ ratings to internal credit rating systems.
cards.statement: Agency ratings are designed to be stable and to rate through the cycle, whereas an internal rating system for small and mid-sized firms can be built on profitability, liquidity and leverage ratios and a cash flow statement derived from the borrower's financial statements.
cards.explanation: Agencies favour long-term stability and cover mainly issuers of public debt, so banks fill the gap for smaller firms with ratio analysis and cash flow analysis.
cards.originalText: Agency ratings are designed to be stable and ’rate through the cycle’, whereas an internal system for small and mid‑sized firms can be built on profitability, liquidity and leverage ratios and a cash flow statement derived from the borrower’s financial statements.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare agencies’ ratings to internal credit rating systems.
cards.statement: Agency ratings change frequently so that they reflect each piece of new market information, whereas internal ratings are updated only at annual reviews.
cards.explanation: Agencies deliberately avoid frequent changes, so their ratings change only when a long-term change in creditworthiness is believed to have occurred.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare agencies’ ratings to internal credit rating systems.
cards.statement: Agencies routinely rate small and mid-sized private firms, so a bank has little need for an internal rating system for these borrowers.
cards.explanation: Agencies generally do not rate small and mid-sized firms without public debt, which is exactly why banks build internal rating systems.
cards.originalText: Agencies routinely rate small and mid‑sized private firms, so a bank has little need for an internal system for these borrowers.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare agencies’ ratings to internal credit rating systems.
cards.statement: Internal rating systems rely mainly on accounting profits, because profits rather than cash are what repay a loan, whereas agency ratings focus on cash flow.
cards.explanation: Cash, not accounting profit, repays a loan, which is why banks convert financial statements into cash flow statements. The claim also wrongly attributes a cash flow focus to agencies.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare agencies’ ratings to internal credit rating systems.
cards.statement: Rating agencies try to rate through the cycle, and stable ratings spare rule-bound bond investors from the heavy trading and transaction costs that frequent rating changes would cause.
cards.explanation: A short-lived rise in near-term default risk with little change over three to five years does not justify a rating change. Bond traders are major users of ratings and many are bound by rating-based rules.
cards.originalText: Agencies try to rate through the cycle, and stable ratings spare rule‑bound bond investors from heavy trading and transaction costs caused by frequent rating changes.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare agencies’ ratings to internal credit rating systems.
cards.statement: Rating agencies measure only the probability of default over the next six months.
cards.explanation: Agency ratings reflect a long-term view of creditworthiness, rated through the cycle, not a six-month horizon.
cards.originalText: Agencies measure only the probability of default over the next six months, which the downturn left unchanged.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare agencies’ ratings to internal credit rating systems.
cards.statement: Rating agencies base their ratings on the issuer's equity price.
cards.explanation: Agency ratings are not equity-price based. Estimates from Moody's KMV and Kamakura use equity prices and respond quickly.
cards.originalText: Agencies base ratings on the issuer’s equity price, which does not respond to short‑term economic conditions.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare agencies’ ratings to internal credit rating systems.
cards.statement: Rating agencies update ratings only at fixed annual reviews and ignore information released between reviews.
cards.explanation: Ratings can change when information is released. Their stability is a deliberate objective, not the result of a fixed review calendar.
cards.originalText: Agencies update ratings only at fixed annual reviews and ignore information released between reviews.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare agencies’ ratings to internal credit rating systems.
cards.statement: Internal credit rating systems for small private borrowers typically score each borrower on profitability, liquidity and solvency measures such as return on equity, the quick ratio and debt-to-equity, and adjust the borrower's financial statements to derive a cash flow statement.
cards.explanation: Agencies typically do not rate small and mid-sized firms, so lenders build their own systems. Borrowings are repaid with cash, so company statements are adjusted to produce a cash flow statement.
cards.originalText: Score each borrower on profitability, liquidity and solvency measures such as return on equity, the quick ratio and debt‑to‑equity, and adjust the borrower’s financial statements to derive a cash flow statement.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare agencies’ ratings to internal credit rating systems.
cards.statement: An unrated small borrower can adopt the rating of the largest rated firm in its industry, since agencies rate whole industries rather than individual issuers.
cards.explanation: Agency ratings are issuer-specific and are not transferable from an industry peer.
cards.originalText: Adopt the rating of the largest rated firm in the same industry, since agencies rate whole industries rather than individual issuers.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare agencies’ ratings to internal credit rating systems.
cards.statement: Equity-market-based default probabilities from a vendor model can be used for small private firms, because such firms have market-traded shares.
cards.explanation: Private firms have no traded equity price, so market-based vendor estimates such as KMV or Kamakura are unavailable for them.
cards.originalText: Use the equity‑market‑based default probability from a vendor model, because small private firms have market‑traded shares.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare agencies’ ratings to internal credit rating systems.
cards.statement: A loan is repaid out of reported accounting profits rather than out of cash.
cards.explanation: Loans are repaid with cash, not accounting profit, which is why a cash flow statement is built in internal rating systems.
cards.originalText: Rely on accounting net income alone, because a loan is repaid out of reported profits rather than out of cash.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the relationship between borrower rating and probability of default.
cards.statement: A CCC/C issuer faces a critical period in the first year or two, and if it survives, its financial health is likely to have improved, so its annual default probability falls over time.
cards.explanation: For poorly rated issuers the next year or two are critical, and survivors are likely to be healthier, so the marginal default probability declines. Investment-grade issuers show the opposite, rising pattern because they can only deteriorate with time.
cards.originalText: A CCC/C issuer faces a critical period in the first year or two; if it survives, its financial health is likely to have improved.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the relationship between borrower rating and probability of default.
cards.statement: Cumulative default rates for CCC/C issuers decline over time, so fewer issuers default in later years.
cards.explanation: Cumulative default rates never decline; only the marginal (annual) default rates for CCC/C issuers decline.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe recovery rates and their dependencies on default rates.
cards.statement: In an economic downturn average recovery rates fall, because the weak economy that raises defaults also depresses the prices of defaulted bonds and collateral.
cards.explanation: Default rates and recovery rates are negatively correlated: the same weak economy produces more defaults and lowers the value of defaulted bonds and collateral, a double hit for lenders.
cards.originalText: Recovery rates fall, because defaults rise with a weak economy that depresses the prices of defaulted bonds and collateral.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe recovery rates and their dependencies on default rates.
cards.statement: In an economic downturn average recovery rates rise, because the larger number of defaults gives lenders more experience to improve their workout strategies.
cards.explanation: Recovery rates are negatively correlated with default rates; the market effect of depressed prices dominates any learning effect.
cards.originalText: Recovery rates rise, because the larger number of defaults gives lenders more experience to improve their workout strategies.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe recovery rates and their dependencies on default rates.
cards.statement: Average recovery rates are unaffected by the economic cycle because they are determined only by the issuer's original credit rating.
cards.explanation: Seniority and rating matter, but average recovery rates also move with the default cycle, falling when defaults rise.
cards.originalText: Recovery rates are unaffected, because they are determined only by the issuer’s original credit rating.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe recovery rates and their dependencies on default rates.
cards.statement: Average recovery rates are unaffected by a downturn because defaulted securities are highly liquid and are always resold at face value.
cards.explanation: Defaulted securities are illiquid and trade at depressed prices in a downturn, and recoveries are not tied to face value.
cards.originalText: Recovery rates are unaffected, because defaulted securities are highly liquid in a downturn and are always resold at face value.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare default probabilities calculated from historical data with those calculated from credit yield spreads.
cards.statement: Hazard rates implied by credit spreads, approximately the spread divided by one minus the recovery rate, are materially higher than hazard rates from historical default data, because spreads also compensate investors for systematic risk and liquidity.
cards.explanation: The gap between the spread-implied and historical hazard rates reflects a risk premium, not under-compensation: defaults are correlated with the economy and bonds are less liquid.
cards.originalText: Historical hazard rate about 0.58% per year versus spread‑implied about 5.00% per year; the spread‑implied rate is much higher, so investors are compensated for more than the expected cost of default (systematic risk, liquidity)

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare default probabilities calculated from historical data with those calculated from credit yield spreads.
cards.statement: A spread-implied hazard rate that is higher than the historical hazard rate shows that investors are under-compensated for default risk.
cards.explanation: The conclusion is reversed: a spread-implied rate above the historical rate means investors are compensated for more than the actuarial cost of default, because spreads include premiums for systematic risk and liquidity.
cards.originalText: Historical hazard rate about 0.58% per year versus spread‑implied about 5.00% per year; the spread‑implied rate is much higher, which shows investors are under‑compensated for default risk
cards.correction: A spread-implied hazard rate that is higher than the historical hazard rate shows that investors are compensated for more than the expected cost of default.

changes.to: compensated for more than the expected cost of default

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Assess the quality of the default probabilities produced by the Merton model, the Moody’s KMV model, and the Kamakura model.
cards.statement: The Merton, Moody's KMV and Kamakura models all produce reliable and reasonably accurate rankings of default probabilities, and the Merton output is in theory a risk-neutral probability that KMV and Kamakura restate as a real-world probability.
cards.explanation: KMV and Kamakura share the empirically good Merton ranking and add a transformation from risk-neutral to real-world probabilities.
cards.originalText: All three produce reliable and reasonably accurate rankings of default probabilities; the Merton output is in theory a risk‑neutral probability, and KMV and Kamakura restate it as a real‑world probability.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Assess the quality of the default probabilities produced by the Merton model, the Moody’s KMV model, and the Kamakura model.
cards.statement: The Merton model produces real-world default probabilities directly, while KMV and Kamakura convert them into risk-neutral probabilities.
cards.explanation: The direction is reversed: Merton's N(-d2) comes from an option pricing model and is in theory risk-neutral, and KMV and Kamakura restate it as a real-world probability.
cards.originalText: The Merton model produces real‑world default probabilities directly, while KMV and Kamakura convert them into risk‑neutral probabilities.
cards.correction: The Merton model produces risk-neutral default probabilities, while KMV and Kamakura convert them into real-world probabilities.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Assess the quality of the default probabilities produced by the Merton model, the Moody’s KMV model, and the Kamakura model.
cards.statement: Only the Moody's KMV and Kamakura models rank default probabilities reliably, and the Merton model's rankings are poor because it ignores market data.
cards.explanation: Merton's ranking is empirically good, and the KMV and Kamakura outputs are built from the Merton ranking.
cards.originalText: Only the KMV and Kamakura models rank default probabilities reliably; the Merton model’s rankings are poor because it ignores market data.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Assess the quality of the default probabilities produced by the Merton model, the Moody’s KMV model, and the Kamakura model.
cards.statement: The Merton, Moody's KMV and Kamakura models all rank default probabilities too poorly to be useful, so agency ratings should be used instead.
cards.explanation: Empirical evidence supports all three models as giving reliable, reasonably accurate rankings of default probabilities.
cards.originalText: None of the three models ranks default probabilities well enough to be useful, so ratings from agencies should be used instead.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Assess the quality of the default probabilities produced by the Merton model, the Moody’s KMV model, and the Kamakura model.
cards.statement: The Merton default probability is in theory risk-neutral, whereas the Moody's KMV and Kamakura probabilities are restated as real-world, so the levels they produce can differ without any model being wrong.
cards.explanation: Risk-neutral and real-world probabilities are different quantities, so a gap in levels is expected. The models are still judged by how well they rank default probabilities.
cards.originalText: The Merton figure is in theory a risk‑neutral probability, whereas the KMV and Kamakura figures are restated as real‑world probabilities, so a somewhat higher Merton figure does not by itself signal that any model is wrong.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Assess the quality of the default probabilities produced by the Merton model, the Moody’s KMV model, and the Kamakura model.
cards.statement: A default probability model that produces the lowest estimate is the most accurate, because it uses market data.
cards.explanation: Accuracy of these models is assessed on the quality of their ranking of default probabilities, not on which produces the lowest number.
cards.originalText: KMV’s estimate is the lowest, so it is the most accurate because it uses market data.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Assess the quality of the default probabilities produced by the Merton model, the Moody’s KMV model, and the Kamakura model.
cards.statement: If the Merton, Moody's KMV and Kamakura models give different default probability estimates for the same issuer, all three models are unreliable and should be discarded.
cards.explanation: The models measure different types of probability (risk-neutral versus real-world), so different levels are expected, and all three rank default probabilities well.
cards.originalText: Because the three estimates differ, all three models are unreliable and should be discarded.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Assess the quality of the default probabilities produced by the Merton model, the Moody’s KMV model, and the Kamakura model.
cards.statement: The Merton, Moody's KMV and Kamakura models all rank default probabilities reliably, but only KMV and Kamakura restate the risk-neutral Merton output as a real-world probability.
cards.explanation: Real-world probabilities are what is needed to estimate the actual frequency of defaults, and only KMV and Kamakura provide them.
cards.originalText: All three rank default probabilities reliably, but only KMV and Kamakura restate the risk‑neutral Merton output as a real‑world probability.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Assess the quality of the default probabilities produced by the Merton model, the Moody’s KMV model, and the Kamakura model.
cards.statement: The Merton model's output is risk-neutral and therefore cannot be used to rank counterparties by default risk.
cards.explanation: Being risk-neutral affects the level of the probability, not the reliability of the ranking, which empirical evidence supports.
cards.originalText: Merton output is risk‑neutral and therefore cannot be used to rank counterparties by default risk.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Assess the quality of the default probabilities produced by the Merton model, the Moody’s KMV model, and the Kamakura model.
cards.statement: Moody's KMV and Kamakura produce more reliable default probability rankings than the Merton model because they do not use the Merton output.
cards.explanation: KMV and Kamakura build on the Merton output, and empirical evidence supports all three models for ranking.
cards.originalText: KMV and Kamakura produce more reliable rankings than Merton because they do not use the Merton output.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Assess the quality of the default probabilities produced by the Merton model, the Moody’s KMV model, and the Kamakura model.
cards.statement: The Merton model's output is a real-world probability, while KMV and Kamakura convert it to a risk-neutral probability for pricing.
cards.explanation: The roles are reversed: Merton's output is risk-neutral, and KMV and Kamakura convert it to a real-world probability.
cards.originalText: Merton output is a real‑world probability, while KMV and Kamakura convert it to a risk‑neutral probability for pricing.
cards.correction: The Merton model's output is a risk-neutral probability, while KMV and Kamakura convert it to a real-world probability.

changes.from: to a risk-neutral probability for pricing

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define and calculate Credit VaR.
cards.statement: Credit VaR is the credit loss over a certain time period that will not be exceeded with a certain confidence level.
cards.explanation: Credit VaR is a percentile of the credit loss distribution over a horizon, often one year, just as VaR is a percentile of the market loss distribution.
cards.originalText: The credit loss over a certain time period that will not be exceeded with a certain confidence level.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define and calculate Credit VaR.
cards.statement: Credit VaR is the average credit loss expected over the horizon and does not depend on any confidence level.
cards.explanation: That describes expected loss, a mean. A VaR is defined by a confidence level.
cards.originalText: The average credit loss expected over the horizon, which does not depend on any confidence level.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define and calculate Credit VaR.
cards.statement: Credit VaR is the loss from adverse market price movements that will not be exceeded over a one-day horizon with a certain confidence level.
cards.explanation: That describes market risk VaR. Credit VaR measures credit losses, typically over a longer horizon such as one year.
cards.originalText: The loss from adverse market price movements that will not be exceeded over a one‑day horizon with a certain confidence level.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define and calculate Credit VaR.
cards.statement: Credit VaR is the total exposure that would be lost if every counterparty in the portfolio defaulted over the horizon.
cards.explanation: That is the maximum possible loss, at 100% confidence with all names defaulting, not a loss at a chosen confidence level.
cards.originalText: The total exposure that would be lost if every counterparty in the portfolio defaulted over the horizon.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define and calculate Credit VaR.
cards.statement: During a period of slowing economic growth, credit correlation and defaults both increase.
cards.explanation: A weak economy raises default probabilities and the tendency of defaults to cluster, because common economic factors drive all firms. Higher correlation raises the risk of a financial institution's credit portfolio.
cards.originalText: An increase in credit correlation and defaults.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define and calculate Credit VaR.
cards.statement: During a period of slowing economic growth, credit correlation and defaults both decrease.
cards.explanation: In a slowdown most companies are adversely affected, so defaults rise and tend to occur together, raising credit correlation.
cards.originalText: A decrease in credit correlation and defaults.
cards.correction: During a period of slowing economic growth, credit correlation and defaults both increase.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define and calculate Credit VaR.
cards.statement: During a period of slowing economic growth, credit correlation decreases while defaults increase.
cards.explanation: Defaults do rise, but credit correlation rises too, because common economic factors drive all firms.
cards.originalText: A decrease in credit correlation and an increase in defaults.
cards.correction: During a period of slowing economic growth, credit correlation increases while defaults increase.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define and calculate Credit VaR.
cards.statement: Credit VaR is the credit loss that will not be exceeded over a given time horizon with a specified confidence level.
cards.explanation: Credit VaR parallels market VaR as a loss quantile over a horizon, typically one year, at the chosen confidence level.
cards.originalText: The credit loss that will not be exceeded over a given time horizon with a specified confidence level.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define and calculate Credit VaR.
cards.statement: Credit VaR is the expected credit loss over a one-day horizon, estimated by historical simulation.
cards.explanation: This confuses credit VaR with expected loss and with market VaR. Credit VaR is a high-percentile loss over a horizon that is typically one year.
cards.originalText: The expected credit loss over a one‑day horizon, estimated by historical simulation.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the Vasicek’s model, Credit Risk Plus (CreditRisk+) model, and the CreditMetrics ways of estimating the probability distribution of losses arising from defaults as well as modeling the default correlation.
cards.statement: Vasicek's model considers only losses from default, and captures default correlation with a one-factor Gaussian copula with a single credit (asset) correlation parameter.
cards.explanation: All borrowers are tied to one systematic factor plus an idiosyncratic factor each, so default correlation is governed by the single parameter rho.
cards.originalText: Losses arise only from defaults, and default correlation is captured by a one‑factor Gaussian copula with a single credit (asset) correlation parameter.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the Vasicek’s model, Credit Risk Plus (CreditRisk+) model, and the CreditMetrics ways of estimating the probability distribution of losses arising from defaults as well as modeling the default correlation.
cards.statement: Vasicek's model considers losses only from default and correlates default events through a multiple-factor Gaussian copula.
cards.explanation: The Vasicek copula is one-factor, not multiple-factor: one common systematic factor drives all borrowers.
cards.originalText: Losses arise only from defaults, and default events are correlated through a multiple‑factor Gaussian copula.
cards.correction: Vasicek's model considers losses only from default and correlates default events through a one-factor Gaussian copula.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the Vasicek’s model, Credit Risk Plus (CreditRisk+) model, and the CreditMetrics ways of estimating the probability distribution of losses arising from defaults as well as modeling the default correlation.
cards.statement: Vasicek's model assumes defaults follow a Poisson distribution and quantifies losses without explicitly modelling default correlation.
cards.explanation: Poisson default counts describe CreditRisk+. Vasicek's model exists to capture default correlation through its Gaussian copula.
cards.originalText: Defaults follow a Poisson distribution, and losses are quantified without explicitly modeling default correlation.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the Vasicek’s model, Credit Risk Plus (CreditRisk+) model, and the CreditMetrics ways of estimating the probability distribution of losses arising from defaults as well as modeling the default correlation.
cards.statement: Vasicek's model treats defaults as independent events, so the loss distribution is estimated separately for each borrower.
cards.explanation: Independence is the opposite of Vasicek's premise: the model uses a common systematic factor to capture credit correlation.
cards.originalText: Defaults are treated as independent events, so the loss distribution is estimated separately for each borrower.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the Vasicek’s model, Credit Risk Plus (CreditRisk+) model, and the CreditMetrics ways of estimating the probability distribution of losses arising from defaults as well as modeling the default correlation.
cards.statement: CreditMetrics relies on a rating transition matrix, together with the credit spread term structure for each rating category, as its central inputs.
cards.explanation: The transition matrix gives one-year migration probabilities, and non-default outcomes are revalued using the credit spread term structure for the new rating. This is what lets CreditMetrics capture downgrades, not only defaults.
cards.originalText: A rating transition matrix (internal or from rating agencies), with the credit spread term structure for each rating category.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the Vasicek’s model, Credit Risk Plus (CreditRisk+) model, and the CreditMetrics ways of estimating the probability distribution of losses arising from defaults as well as modeling the default correlation.
cards.statement: CreditMetrics is built on the worst case default rate at the 99.9% level, computed from each bond's probability of default and a single correlation parameter.
cards.explanation: The worst case default rate from PD and a single correlation is Vasicek's approach, which looks only at defaults.
cards.originalText: The worst case default rate at the 99.9% level, computed from each bond’s PD and a single correlation parameter.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the Vasicek’s model, Credit Risk Plus (CreditRisk+) model, and the CreditMetrics ways of estimating the probability distribution of losses arising from defaults as well as modeling the default correlation.
cards.statement: The Poisson mean number of defaults per year for each rating bucket is a key input to CreditMetrics.
