cards.explanation: The Poisson default mean is a CreditRisk+ input and ignores downgrades.
cards.originalText: The Poisson mean number of defaults per year for each rating bucket.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the Vasicek’s model, Credit Risk Plus (CreditRisk+) model, and the CreditMetrics ways of estimating the probability distribution of losses arising from defaults as well as modeling the default correlation.
cards.statement: Unlike Vasicek's model and Credit Risk Plus, CreditMetrics incorporates mark-to-market revaluation due to credit downgrades.
cards.explanation: Vasicek's model and Credit Risk Plus consider defaults only. CreditMetrics uses a rating transition matrix and credit spreads, so a downgrade lowers the revalued position and creates a loss even without default.
cards.originalText: It incorporates mark‑to‑market revaluations due to credit downgrades.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the Vasicek’s model, Credit Risk Plus (CreditRisk+) model, and the CreditMetrics ways of estimating the probability distribution of losses arising from defaults as well as modeling the default correlation.
cards.statement: In Credit Risk Plus, when there is uncertainty about the default rate, the number of defaults follows a negative binomial distribution.
cards.explanation: If the expected number of defaults is itself uncertain and gamma distributed, mixing it with a Poisson count gives a negative binomial distribution. As the uncertainty falls it converges to the Poisson.
cards.originalText: Negative binomial distribution

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the Vasicek’s model, Credit Risk Plus (CreditRisk+) model, and the CreditMetrics ways of estimating the probability distribution of losses arising from defaults as well as modeling the default correlation.
cards.statement: In Credit Risk Plus, the number of defaults follows a Poisson distribution even when there is uncertainty about the default rate.
cards.explanation: The Poisson applies only when the default rate is known; with an uncertain gamma-distributed default rate the count follows a negative binomial distribution.
cards.originalText: Poisson distribution

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the Vasicek’s model, Credit Risk Plus (CreditRisk+) model, and the CreditMetrics ways of estimating the probability distribution of losses arising from defaults as well as modeling the default correlation.
cards.statement: In Credit Risk Plus, the number of defaults follows a normal distribution when there is uncertainty about the default rate.
cards.explanation: A normal distribution cannot capture the positively skewed, fat-tailed distribution of the number of defaults; Credit Risk Plus uses a negative binomial distribution.
cards.originalText: Normal distribution

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the Vasicek’s model, Credit Risk Plus (CreditRisk+) model, and the CreditMetrics ways of estimating the probability distribution of losses arising from defaults as well as modeling the default correlation.
cards.statement: Credit Risk Plus is an actuarial-style model that uses analytic approximations from the insurance industry, with Poisson default counts and no copula linking borrowers.
cards.explanation: Credit Risk Plus (Credit Suisse Financial Products) uses a negative binomial count if the default rate is uncertain. Vasicek and CreditMetrics both rely on a Gaussian copula.
cards.originalText: Credit Risk Plus

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the Vasicek’s model, Credit Risk Plus (CreditRisk+) model, and the CreditMetrics ways of estimating the probability distribution of losses arising from defaults as well as modeling the default correlation.
cards.statement: Vasicek's model uses a single systematic factor that represents overall economic conditions to model default correlation, affecting all entities in the portfolio.
cards.explanation: Vasicek's model has one Gaussian copula, one systematic factor plus idiosyncratic noise, and one correlation parameter.
cards.originalText: Vasicek’s model uses a single systematic factor that represents overall economic conditions to model default correlations, affecting all entities in the portfolio.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the Vasicek’s model, Credit Risk Plus (CreditRisk+) model, and the CreditMetrics ways of estimating the probability distribution of losses arising from defaults as well as modeling the default correlation.
cards.statement: Vasicek's model applies a Gaussian copula to estimate the worst case default rate (WCDR) of a loan portfolio.
cards.explanation: The worst case default rate from a Gaussian copula is Vasicek's contribution; the portfolio loss percentile is the sum of WCDR times EAD times LGD.
cards.originalText: Vasicek’s model applies a Gaussian copula to estimate the worst case default rate (WCDR) of a loan portfolio.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the Vasicek’s model, Credit Risk Plus (CreditRisk+) model, and the CreditMetrics ways of estimating the probability distribution of losses arising from defaults as well as modeling the default correlation.
cards.statement: CreditMetrics uses a Gaussian copula to calculate the exposure at default of each counterparty from correlated equity returns.
cards.explanation: The copula drives joint rating transitions. Exposure at default is an input to the model, not an output of the copula.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the Vasicek’s model, Credit Risk Plus (CreditRisk+) model, and the CreditMetrics ways of estimating the probability distribution of losses arising from defaults as well as modeling the default correlation.
cards.statement: Credit Risk Plus estimates default probability with a Gaussian copula that combines individual and systematic risk factors.
cards.explanation: Credit Risk Plus uses Poisson and negative binomial default counts, not a Gaussian copula.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the Vasicek’s model, Credit Risk Plus (CreditRisk+) model, and the CreditMetrics ways of estimating the probability distribution of losses arising from defaults as well as modeling the default correlation.
cards.statement: CreditMetrics assumes that the rating changes of different counterparties are independent.
cards.explanation: CreditMetrics explicitly models correlated rating transitions through a Gaussian copula.
cards.originalText: CreditMetrics assumes that rating changes of different counterparties are independent.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the Vasicek’s model, Credit Risk Plus (CreditRisk+) model, and the CreditMetrics ways of estimating the probability distribution of losses arising from defaults as well as modeling the default correlation.
cards.statement: In CreditMetrics, the correlation between the rating transitions of two companies is modelled with a Gaussian copula whose correlation is set equal to the correlation between the companies' equity returns.
cards.explanation: Two standard normal variables are sampled with correlation equal to the equity-return correlation, and each is mapped to a new rating through the transition matrix thresholds.
cards.originalText: Using a Gaussian copula with the correlation set equal to the correlation between the companies’ equity returns

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the Vasicek’s model, Credit Risk Plus (CreditRisk+) model, and the CreditMetrics ways of estimating the probability distribution of losses arising from defaults as well as modeling the default correlation.
cards.statement: CreditMetrics assumes that the rating transitions of different companies are independent.
cards.explanation: Independence is not assumed: ratings momentum and common economic conditions make transitions dependent, and a Gaussian copula models this.
cards.originalText: By assuming independence between all rating transitions

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the Vasicek’s model, Credit Risk Plus (CreditRisk+) model, and the CreditMetrics ways of estimating the probability distribution of losses arising from defaults as well as modeling the default correlation.
cards.statement: CreditMetrics models the correlation between companies' rating transitions through sector-specific Poisson distributions.
cards.explanation: Poisson distributions belong to Credit Risk Plus. CreditMetrics uses a Gaussian copula with equity-return correlations.
cards.originalText: Through sector‑specific Poisson distributions

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the Vasicek’s model, Credit Risk Plus (CreditRisk+) model, and the CreditMetrics ways of estimating the probability distribution of losses arising from defaults as well as modeling the default correlation.
cards.statement: In CreditRisk+, greater uncertainty (volatility) in the default rate raises the probability of a large number of defaults and gives a positively skewed loss distribution.
cards.explanation: Default-rate uncertainty creates correlation among defaults, which fattens the right tail of the loss distribution.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the Vasicek’s model, Credit Risk Plus (CreditRisk+) model, and the CreditMetrics ways of estimating the probability distribution of losses arising from defaults as well as modeling the default correlation.
cards.statement: The Vasicek model and CreditRisk+ both capture losses from rating downgrades as well as from defaults.
cards.explanation: Vasicek's model and CreditRisk+ consider defaults only; only CreditMetrics adds downgrades through a ratings transition matrix.
cards.originalText: Vasicek’s model and CreditRisk+ both capture losses from rating downgrades as well as from defaults.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the Vasicek’s model, Credit Risk Plus (CreditRisk+) model, and the CreditMetrics ways of estimating the probability distribution of losses arising from defaults as well as modeling the default correlation.
cards.statement: In CreditRisk+, as the volatility of the default rate decreases, the distribution of the number of defaults moves further away from the Poisson distribution.
cards.explanation: Lower volatility moves the negative binomial distribution of defaults closer to the Poisson, not further away.
cards.correction: In CreditRisk+, as the volatility of the default rate decreases, the distribution of the number of defaults moves closer to the Poisson distribution.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the Vasicek’s model, Credit Risk Plus (CreditRisk+) model, and the CreditMetrics ways of estimating the probability distribution of losses arising from defaults as well as modeling the default correlation.
cards.statement: CreditMetrics models the rating changes of different counterparties as independent, so no copula is needed.
cards.explanation: CreditMetrics uses a Gaussian copula to correlate rating transitions; assuming independence would ignore credit correlation.
cards.originalText: CreditMetrics models rating changes of different counterparties as independent, so no copula is needed.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the Vasicek’s model, Credit Risk Plus (CreditRisk+) model, and the CreditMetrics ways of estimating the probability distribution of losses arising from defaults as well as modeling the default correlation.
cards.statement: CreditMetrics accounts for both defaults and downgrades.
cards.explanation: CreditMetrics combines a ratings transition matrix with a Gaussian copula, so it captures losses from downgrades as well as defaults.
cards.originalText: CreditMetrics.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the Vasicek’s model, Credit Risk Plus (CreditRisk+) model, and the CreditMetrics ways of estimating the probability distribution of losses arising from defaults as well as modeling the default correlation.
cards.statement: Credit Risk Plus accounts for rating downgrades as well as defaults.
cards.explanation: Credit Risk Plus models only the number of defaults, with no rating migration.
cards.originalText: Credit Risk Plus.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the Vasicek’s model, Credit Risk Plus (CreditRisk+) model, and the CreditMetrics ways of estimating the probability distribution of losses arising from defaults as well as modeling the default correlation.
cards.statement: Vasicek's model accounts for rating downgrades as well as defaults.
cards.explanation: Vasicek's model gives the worst case default rate only; downgrades are ignored.
cards.originalText: Vasicek’s model.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define credit spread risk and assess its impact on calculating credit VaR.
cards.statement: A historical simulation of credit spread changes for issuers that exist today implicitly assumes no probability of default, because those issuers did not default in the sample period, and so may understate tail risk.
cards.explanation: Scenarios are built only from past spread changes of surviving companies, so default losses never appear and the tail of the credit loss distribution is understated.
cards.originalText: Because the issuers are alive today, they did not default in the sample period, so the calculation implicitly assumes no probability of default and may understate tail risk.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define credit spread risk and assess its impact on calculating credit VaR.
cards.statement: Historical simulation of credit spread changes assumes that the changes follow a normal distribution.
cards.explanation: Historical simulation is non-parametric and makes no normality assumption; assuming a normal distribution describes a parametric method.
cards.originalText: It assumes credit spread changes follow a normal distribution, underestimating extreme movements in bond prices.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define credit spread risk and assess its impact on calculating credit VaR.
cards.statement: Historical simulation of credit spread changes fails to capture the correlations between the spread changes of different issuers.
cards.explanation: Applying the same-day spread changes to all issuers preserves their historical correlation, so correlation is captured.
cards.originalText: It fails to capture correlations between the spread changes of different issuers, overstating portfolio losses.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define credit spread risk and assess its impact on calculating credit VaR.
cards.statement: Relative to a buy-and-hold strategy, a constant level of risk strategy reduces the probability of large losses from defaults and increases the probability of losses from small rating changes.
cards.explanation: Rebalancing sells downgraded bonds before they can slide to default, so large default losses become less likely. It also realises small downgrade losses repeatedly through the year, so losses from small rating changes become more likely.
cards.originalText: It reduces the probability of large losses from defaults and increases the probability of losses from small rating changes.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define credit spread risk and assess its impact on calculating credit VaR.
cards.statement: Relative to a buy-and-hold strategy, a constant level of risk strategy increases the probability of large losses from defaults and reduces the probability of losses from small rating changes.
cards.explanation: The effect is the reverse: it is buy-and-hold that leaves bonds exposed to large downgrades and default, while constant level of risk rebalancing lowers the default probability and raises the chance of small downgrade losses.
cards.originalText: It increases the probability of large losses from defaults and reduces the probability of losses from small rating changes.
cards.correction: Relative to a buy-and-hold strategy, a constant level of risk strategy reduces the probability of large losses from defaults and increases the probability of losses from small rating changes.

changes.from: increases the probability of large losses
changes.to: reduces the probability of large losses

changes.from: reduces the probability of losses from small
changes.to: increases the probability of losses from small

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define credit spread risk and assess its impact on calculating credit VaR.
cards.statement: Relative to a buy-and-hold strategy, a constant level of risk strategy increases both the probability of large losses from defaults and the probability of losses from small rating changes.
cards.explanation: Constant level of risk rebalancing does raise the probability of losses from small rating changes, but it lowers, not raises, the probability of large default losses because deteriorating bonds are sold early.
cards.originalText: It increases both the probability of large losses from defaults and the probability of losses from small rating changes.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define credit spread risk and assess its impact on calculating credit VaR.
cards.statement: A constant level of risk strategy has no effect on the probability of losses compared with a buy-and-hold strategy.
cards.explanation: The two strategies produce different outcome probabilities: rebalancing lowers the probability of default and raises the probability of small downgrade losses.
cards.originalText: It has no effect on the probability of losses compared with buy‑and‑hold.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define credit spread risk and assess its impact on calculating credit VaR.
cards.statement: A key limitation of historical simulation for credit VaR is the challenge of capturing jump-to-default risk, which arises from the possibility that a company could default abruptly without prior indication.
cards.explanation: A company that is operating today did not default in the sample period, so a history of its spread changes implicitly assumes no default in the future and omits jump-to-default losses.
cards.originalText: The challenge of capturing jump‑to‑default risk, which arises from the possibility that a company could default abruptly without prior indication.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define credit spread risk and assess its impact on calculating credit VaR.
cards.statement: Historical simulation for credit VaR overestimates credit spread changes because it assumes that spreads increase continuously over time.
cards.explanation: Historical simulation draws scenarios from observed spread changes, which move both up and down, and does not assume continuously rising spreads. Its stated weaknesses are stale spread data and the omission of default events.
cards.originalText: The risk of overestimating credit spread changes due to the assumption of continuously increasing spreads over time.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define credit spread risk and assess its impact on calculating credit VaR.
cards.statement: A historical simulation of credit spread changes is hampered because spreads are not updated daily for all companies, so the data may be of poor quality.
cards.explanation: Credit spreads are not observed daily for every company, so the historical series of spread changes can be stale. This is one of the two stated weaknesses of historical simulation for credit VaR.
cards.originalText: Damian

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define credit spread risk and assess its impact on calculating credit VaR.
cards.statement: Because a company that is operating today has not defaulted in the past, a historical simulation of credit spread changes implicitly assumes no default, whereas a CreditMetrics-type approach using a rating transition matrix brings in downgrades and defaults.
cards.explanation: Surviving firms show no default in their spread history, so historical simulation omits jump-to-default risk. A transition-matrix approach sampled by Monte Carlo adds rating changes and default.
cards.originalText: Tanyth

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define credit spread risk and assess its impact on calculating credit VaR.
cards.statement: To introduce credit correlation in credit VaR, the spread changes for different rating categories should be assumed uncorrelated so that diversification is preserved.
cards.explanation: Credit correlation is introduced through a Gaussian copula for rating changes, or by assuming that spread changes across rating categories are perfectly or very highly correlated. Assuming zero correlation would remove the very dependence being modelled.
cards.originalText: James

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define credit spread risk and assess its impact on calculating credit VaR.
cards.statement: For a bond currently rated A, the highest probability is assigned to the outcome in which the bond keeps its rating.
cards.explanation: In a one-period rating transition matrix the diagonal (no change) entry is by far the largest, because ratings are persistent.
cards.originalText: highest probability to situations where the bond maintains its rating.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define credit spread risk and assess its impact on calculating credit VaR.
cards.statement: In credit VaR analysis of a bond currently rated A, the biggest credit spreads are assigned to scenarios in which the bond's rating increases.
cards.explanation: Spreads rise as credit quality falls, so the biggest spreads go with downgrades, the lowest spreads with upgrades, and intermediate spreads with an unchanged rating.
cards.originalText: biggest spreads to situations where the bond rating increases.
cards.correction: In credit VaR analysis of a bond currently rated A, the biggest credit spreads are assigned to scenarios in which the bond's rating falls.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define credit spread risk and assess its impact on calculating credit VaR.
cards.statement: In credit VaR analysis of a bond currently rated A, the lowest credit spreads are assigned to scenarios in which the bond maintains its rating.
cards.explanation: The lowest spreads go with upgrades. A bond that keeps its rating carries an intermediate spread, and downgrades carry the biggest spreads.
cards.originalText: lowest spreads to situations where the bond maintains its rating.
cards.correction: In credit VaR analysis of a bond currently rated A, the lowest credit spreads are assigned to scenarios in which the bond is upgraded.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define credit spread risk and assess its impact on calculating credit VaR.
cards.statement: A buy-and-hold strategy generally produces larger losses from big downgrades and defaults than a constant level of risk strategy, so its credit VaR tends to be larger.
cards.explanation: Buy-and-hold keeps a downgraded bond through to the horizon, so a multi-notch downgrade or default is fully borne. Constant level of risk replaces deteriorated bonds with bonds of the original rating, so large cumulative losses are less likely.
cards.originalText: Strategy 1 (buy‑and‑hold) generally produces larger losses from big downgrades and defaults, so its credit VaR tends to be larger than under strategy 2.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define credit spread risk and assess its impact on calculating credit VaR.
cards.statement: A constant level of risk strategy generally produces larger losses from big downgrades and defaults than a buy-and-hold strategy, so its credit VaR tends to be larger.
cards.explanation: The strategies are reversed: rebalancing to the original rating reduces exposure to deteriorated credits, so constant level of risk has the smaller credit VaR.
cards.originalText: Strategy 2 (constant level of risk) generally produces larger losses from big downgrades and defaults, so its credit VaR tends to be larger than under strategy 1.
cards.correction: A buy-and-hold strategy generally produces larger losses from big downgrades and defaults than a constant level of risk strategy, so its credit VaR tends to be larger.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define credit spread risk and assess its impact on calculating credit VaR.
cards.statement: A buy-and-hold strategy and a constant level of risk strategy give the same credit VaR because the rating transition matrix is identical.
cards.explanation: The transition matrix is the same for each period, but the strategies apply it differently (held bonds versus bonds rebalanced to the original rating), so their credit VaR differs.
cards.originalText: The two strategies give the same credit VaR because the rating transition matrix is identical.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define and calculate default correlation for credit portfolios.
cards.statement: When two firms' default events are independent, the conditional default probability $\pi_{12}/\pi_{1}$ reduces to $\pi_{2}$ and is therefore not zero.
cards.explanation: Independence means $\pi_{12} = \pi_{1}\pi_{2}$, so the covariance and default correlation are zero. The conditional probability $\pi_{12}/\pi_{1}$ then equals the unconditional default probability $\pi_{2}$, which is positive.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define and calculate default correlation for credit portfolios.
cards.statement: The default correlation of two firms is $\rho_{12} = \frac{\pi_{12} - \pi_{1}\pi_{2}}{\sqrt{\pi_{1}(1 - \pi_{1}) \pi_{2}(1 - \pi_{2})}}$, where $\pi_{12}$ is the joint default probability.
cards.explanation: Each default indicator is Bernoulli with variance $\pi_{i}(1 - \pi_{i})$, and the covariance is $\pi_{12} - \pi_{1}\pi_{2}$. Correlation is the covariance divided by the product of the standard deviations.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define and calculate default correlation for credit portfolios.
cards.statement: The default correlation of two firms is $\rho_{12} = \frac{\pi_{12} - \pi_{1}\pi_{2}}{\pi_{1}(1 - \pi_{1}) \pi_{2}(1 - \pi_{2})}$, where $\pi_{12}$ is the joint default probability.
cards.explanation: The denominator must be the product of the standard deviations, that is, the square root of the product of the variances. Dividing by the variances without the square root is wrong.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define and calculate default correlation for credit portfolios.
cards.statement: The default correlation of two firms is $\rho_{12} = \frac{\pi_{12}}{\sqrt{\pi_{1}(1 - \pi_{1}) \pi_{2}(1 - \pi_{2})}}$, where $\pi_{12}$ is the joint default probability.
cards.explanation: The numerator must be the covariance $\pi_{12} - \pi_{1}\pi_{2}$, not the raw joint default probability $\pi_{12}$.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define and calculate default correlation for credit portfolios.
cards.statement: The default correlation of two firms is $\rho_{12} = \frac{\pi_{12} - \pi_{1}\pi_{2}}{\pi_{1}\pi_{2}}$, where $\pi_{12}$ is the joint default probability.
cards.explanation: The covariance $\pi_{12} - \pi_{1}\pi_{2}$ must be scaled by the product of the standard deviations of the Bernoulli default indicators, not by the product of the default probabilities.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Assess the impact of correlation on a credit portfolio and its Credit VaR.
cards.statement: Default correlation captures the systematic, non-diversifiable component of portfolio credit risk, that is, the tendency for defaults to cluster.
cards.explanation: Default correlation measures how defaults move together because of common drivers, and this co-movement cannot be diversified away by adding more credits.
cards.originalText: Default correlation

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Assess the impact of correlation on a credit portfolio and its Credit VaR.
cards.statement: Expected loss captures the systematic, non-diversifiable component of portfolio credit risk, that is, the tendency for defaults to cluster.
cards.explanation: Expected loss is unaffected by correlation, so it cannot capture the clustering of defaults. Default correlation is the measure of that tendency.
cards.originalText: Expected loss

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Assess the impact of correlation on a credit portfolio and its Credit VaR.
cards.statement: Granularity captures the systematic, non-diversifiable component of portfolio credit risk, that is, the tendency for defaults to cluster.
cards.explanation: Granularity concerns how finely the portfolio is divided into positions, which relates to idiosyncratic concentration, not to common-factor risk.
cards.originalText: Granularity

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Assess the impact of correlation on a credit portfolio and its Credit VaR.
cards.statement: When the credits in a portfolio have a default correlation of 1, the portfolio behaves as if it consisted of just one credit.
cards.explanation: With a default correlation of 1, all credits default together or not at all, so the portfolio has only two outcomes and no diversification benefit.
cards.originalText: The portfolio behaves as if it consisted of just one credit

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Assess the impact of correlation on a credit portfolio and its Credit VaR.
cards.statement: When the credits in a portfolio have a default correlation of 1, the number of defaults is binomially distributed because there is no correlation among the credits.
cards.explanation: A binomial number of defaults describes independent defaults (default correlation of 0). With a correlation of 1 the outcome is two-point: all credits default or none do.
cards.originalText: The number of defaults is binomially distributed because there is no correlation among the credits

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Assess the impact of correlation on a credit portfolio and its Credit VaR.
cards.statement: When the credits in a portfolio have a default correlation of 1, significant credit diversification may be achieved.
cards.explanation: Diversification is greatest at a default correlation of 0 and is absent at a default correlation of 1, where the portfolio acts like a single credit.
cards.originalText: Significant credit diversification may be achieved
cards.correction: When the credits in a portfolio have a default correlation of 1, no credit diversification can be achieved.

changes.from: significant credit diversification may be achieved
changes.to: no credit diversification can be achieved

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Assess the impact of correlation on a credit portfolio and its Credit VaR.
cards.statement: Holding each loan's default probability and loss given default fixed, higher default correlation leaves the portfolio's expected loss unchanged but makes its loss distribution more volatile, with a fatter right tail.
cards.explanation: Expected loss depends only on the individual default probabilities, exposures and loss given default. Higher correlation makes defaults cluster, which raises loss volatility and the extreme quantiles.
cards.originalText: Both have the same expected loss, but Portfolio B has a more volatile loss distribution with a fatter right tail.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Assess the impact of correlation on a credit portfolio and its Credit VaR.
cards.statement: Holding each loan's default probability and loss given default fixed, higher default correlation raises the portfolio's expected loss because correlated loans default more often.
cards.explanation: Correlation does not change each loan's default probability, so expected loss is unchanged. It makes defaults cluster, which changes the shape of the loss distribution, not its mean.
cards.originalText: Portfolio B has a higher expected loss because correlated loans default more often.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Assess the impact of correlation on a credit portfolio and its Credit VaR.
cards.statement: A portfolio with uncorrelated defaults has a higher volatility of loss than an otherwise identical portfolio with highly correlated defaults.
cards.explanation: Independence diversifies and reduces loss volatility. Higher default correlation raises the variance of portfolio loss.
cards.originalText: Portfolio A has the higher volatility of loss because it has more independent sources of default.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Assess the impact of correlation on a credit portfolio and its Credit VaR.
cards.statement: Default correlation affects neither the expected loss nor the volatility of a portfolio's loss.
cards.explanation: Default correlation leaves expected loss unchanged but raises the variance of portfolio loss and fattens the right tail of the loss distribution.
cards.originalText: Both have the same expected loss and the same loss volatility, since default correlation affects neither.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the use of a single factor model to measure portfolio credit risk, including the impact of correlation.
cards.statement: In the single-factor credit model $a_{i} = \beta_{i}m + \sqrt{1 - \beta^{2}_{i}} \epsilon_{i}$, the market factor $m$ and the idiosyncratic shock $\epsilon_{i}$ are independent standard normal variables.
cards.explanation: Independent standard normal $m$ and $\epsilon_{i}$ are the basic assumption of the single-factor model.
cards.originalText: $m$ and $\epsilon_{i}$ are independent standard normal variables.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the use of a single factor model to measure portfolio credit risk, including the impact of correlation.
cards.statement: In the single-factor credit model $a_{i} = \beta_{i}m + \sqrt{1 - \beta^{2}_{i}} \epsilon_{i}$, $m$ and $\epsilon_{i}$ have zero covariance, so the asset return $a_{i}$ is also standard normal.
cards.explanation: The variance of $a_{i}$ is $\beta^{2}_{i} + (1 - \beta^{2}_{i}) = 1$ and its mean is 0, so $a_{i}$ is standard normal.
cards.originalText: Because cov$[m, \epsilon_{i}] = 0$, the asset return $a_{i}$ is also standard normal.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the use of a single factor model to measure portfolio credit risk, including the impact of correlation.
cards.statement: In the single-factor credit model $a_{i} = \beta_{i}m + \sqrt{1 - \beta^{2}_{i}} \epsilon_{i}$, the correlation between the asset returns of firms $i$ and $j$ is $\beta_{i}\beta_{j}$.
cards.explanation: Because the idiosyncratic shocks are independent, the only shared component is the market factor, and the asset correlation between two firms is the product of their loadings $\beta_{i}\beta_{j}$.
cards.originalText: The correlation between the asset returns of firms $i$ and $j$ is $\beta_{i}\beta_{j}$.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the use of a single factor model to measure portfolio credit risk, including the impact of correlation.
cards.statement: In the single-factor credit model $a_{i} = \beta_{i}m + \sqrt{1 - \beta^{2}_{i}} \epsilon_{i}$, conditioning is done by fixing the idiosyncratic shock $\epsilon$ (the single factor), which increases the standard deviation of the default distribution.
cards.explanation: The single factor is the market factor $m$, not the idiosyncratic shock. Conditioning on $m$ shifts the mean to $\beta_{i}m$ and reduces the standard deviation from 1 to $\sqrt{1 - \beta^{2}_{i}}$.
cards.originalText: Conditioning is done by fixing the idiosyncratic shock $\epsilon$ (the single factor), which increases the standard deviation of the default distribution.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the use of a single factor model to measure portfolio credit risk, including the impact of correlation.
cards.statement: In the single-factor credit model, when $\beta = 1$ every firm's asset return equals the market factor, so a fully granular portfolio with 100% loss given default has a loss rate of either 0% or 100%.
cards.explanation: With $\beta = 1$ the idiosyncratic term vanishes, so all firms default together when $m$ falls below the threshold and none default otherwise. Defaults are perfectly correlated and the portfolio is all-or-nothing.
cards.originalText: When $\beta= 1$, the loss rate of the portfolio is either 0% or 100%.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the use of a single factor model to measure portfolio credit risk, including the impact of correlation.
cards.statement: In the single-factor credit model, for a given probability of default, a firm's distance to default is low when its correlation to the market factor is low.
cards.explanation: The default threshold $k = N^{-1}(PD)$ depends only on the probability of default. Correlation changes the shape of the portfolio loss distribution, not the distance to default.
cards.originalText: For a given probability of default, the distance to default of a firm is low when its correlation to the market factor is low.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the use of a single factor model to measure portfolio credit risk, including the impact of correlation.
cards.statement: In the single-factor credit model, when the correlation to the market factor is zero, the loss rate of a fully granular portfolio is typically higher than each firm's probability of default.
cards.explanation: With zero correlation the firms are independent, and in a granular portfolio diversification makes the loss rate converge to the probability of default, not above it.
cards.originalText: When the correlation to the market factor is zero, the portfolio loss rate is typically higher than the firm’s probability of default.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the use of a single factor model to measure portfolio credit risk, including the impact of correlation.
cards.statement: In the single-factor credit model, the correlation of a firm's asset return with the market factor is measured by the square root of $\beta$.
cards.explanation: A firm's correlation with the market factor is $\beta$ itself, and the correlation between two firms is $\beta_{i}\beta_{j}$. The square root of $\beta$ is not used.
cards.originalText: The asset return correlation to the market factor is measured by the square root of $\beta$.
cards.correction: In the single-factor credit model, the correlation of a firm's asset return with the market factor is measured by $\beta$.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the use of a single factor model to measure portfolio credit risk, including the impact of correlation.
cards.statement: In the single-factor model $a_{i} = \beta_{i}m + \sqrt{1 - \beta^{2}_{i}} \epsilon_{i}$, once a value of the market factor $m$ is realized, firm $i$'s asset return has conditional mean $\beta_{i}m$ and standard deviation $\sqrt{1 - \beta^{2}_{i}}$.
cards.explanation: Fixing $m$ leaves only the idiosyncratic term random, so the mean is $\beta_{i}m$ and the dispersion is $\sqrt{1 - \beta^{2}_{i}}$, below the unconditional value of 1.
cards.originalText: Mean $\beta_{i}m$ and standard deviation $\sqrt{1 - \beta^{2}_{i}}$.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the use of a single factor model to measure portfolio credit risk, including the impact of correlation.
cards.statement: In the single-factor model, once a value of the market factor $m$ is realized, firm $i$'s asset return has the same conditional mean of 0 and standard deviation of 1 as its unconditional distribution.
cards.explanation: Conditioning on $m$ shifts the mean to $\beta_{i}m$ and reduces the standard deviation to $\sqrt{1 - \beta^{2}_{i}}$.
cards.originalText: Mean 0 and standard deviation 1, the same as the unconditional distribution.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the use of a single factor model to measure portfolio credit risk, including the impact of correlation.
cards.statement: In the single-factor model, once a value of the market factor $m$ is realized, firm $i$'s asset return has conditional mean $m$ and standard deviation $\beta_{i}$.
cards.explanation: The conditional mean is $\beta_{i}m$, not $m$, and the conditional standard deviation comes from the idiosyncratic loading $\sqrt{1 - \beta^{2}_{i}}$, not from $\beta_{i}$.
cards.originalText: Mean $m$ and standard deviation $\beta_{i}$.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the use of a single factor model to measure portfolio credit risk, including the impact of correlation.
cards.statement: In the single-factor model, once a value of the market factor $m$ is realized, firm $i$'s asset return has conditional mean $\beta_{i}m$ and a standard deviation of $1 - \beta^{2}_{i}$.
cards.explanation: The quantity $1 - \beta^{2}_{i}$ is the conditional variance. The conditional standard deviation is its square root, $\sqrt{1 - \beta^{2}_{i}}$.
cards.originalText: Mean $\beta_{i}m$ and standard deviation $1 - \beta^{2}_{i}$.
cards.correction: In the single-factor model, once a value of the market factor $m$ is realized, firm $i$'s asset return has conditional mean $\beta_{i}m$ and a standard deviation of $\sqrt{1 - \beta^{2}_{i}}$.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Assess the effect of granularity on Credit VaR.
cards.statement: Replacing a few large loans with a larger number of smaller loans increases the granularity of a portfolio, which tends to lower its credit VaR.
cards.explanation: Spreading the same exposure across many smaller loans reduces the weight of each credit, so idiosyncratic defaults diversify away and the loss converges toward the expected loss.
cards.originalText: Granularity would increase as the bank holds a larger number of smaller loans, which tends to lower credit VaR.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Assess the effect of granularity on Credit VaR.
cards.statement: The granularity of a portfolio is not affected by the size of its loans or the number of its borrowers.
cards.explanation: Granularity is defined by the weight of each credit in the portfolio, so it depends on loan size and the number of credits.
cards.originalText: Granularity would not be affected by the loan size or number of borrowers.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Assess the effect of granularity on Credit VaR.
cards.statement: Holding all else constant, increasing granularity by spreading a portfolio over more, smaller positions decreases its credit VaR.
cards.explanation: With more independent positions, the loss quantile moves closer to the expected loss, so credit VaR (the loss quantile less expected loss) falls.
cards.originalText: Increasing granularity from n = 20 to n = 100 positions decreases the 95% credit VaR.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Assess the effect of granularity on Credit VaR.
cards.statement: Holding all else constant, an increase in default correlation increases credit VaR.
cards.explanation: Higher default correlation fattens the tail of the loss distribution and raises extreme quantiles, while expected loss is unchanged, so credit VaR rises.
cards.originalText: An increase in default correlation increases the 95% credit VaR.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Assess the effect of granularity on Credit VaR.
cards.statement: Higher loan granularity in a pool enhances diversification, thereby reducing the probability of tail events and concentration risk.
cards.explanation: More, smaller exposures diversify idiosyncratic default risk, so a single default has a small effect, loss converges toward the expected loss and extreme losses become less likely.
cards.originalText: It enhances diversification, thereby reducing the probability of tail events and concentration risk.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Assess the effect of granularity on Credit VaR.
cards.statement: Higher loan granularity in a pool increases systemic risk because of the higher number of loans.
cards.explanation: Granularity removes idiosyncratic risk and does not raise systemic risk. A larger number of smaller loans lowers the probability of extreme losses.
cards.originalText: It increases the systemic risk due to a higher number of loans.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Assess the effect of granularity on Credit VaR.
cards.statement: Higher loan granularity in a pool reduces the diversification benefit, thus increasing the probability of tail events.
cards.explanation: Higher granularity increases diversification and lowers the probability of tail events and credit VaR.
cards.originalText: It reduces the diversification benefit, thus increasing the probability of tail events.
cards.correction: Higher loan granularity in a pool enhances the diversification benefit, thus reducing the probability of tail events.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the Gaussian copula model for time to default and calculate the probability of default using the one-factor Gaussian copula model.
cards.statement: In a Gaussian copula simulation of default times, a company defaults within a given year if its simulated correlated normal value is below the inverse cumulative normal of its cumulative default probability for that year.
cards.explanation: Each company's cumulative default probability is mapped into a standard normal threshold, and correlated normals are sampled. A sample below the threshold for a horizon, for example $N^{-1}(1\%) = -2.33$ for 1%, means default by that horizon.
cards.originalText: Simulate a value from a multivariate normal distribution for each company. If the value is less than the inverse cumulative normal distribution value at 1% (‑2.33), default occurs within the first year.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the Gaussian copula model for time to default and calculate the probability of default using the one-factor Gaussian copula model.
cards.statement: The Gaussian copula model transforms each company's time to default into a standard normal variable.
cards.explanation: Times to default are not normally distributed, so the model maps each one, percentile to percentile, into a standard normal variable and applies a correlation structure to those variables.
cards.originalText: Times to default.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the Gaussian copula model for time to default and calculate the probability of default using the one-factor Gaussian copula model.
cards.statement: The Gaussian copula model transforms recovery rates into normal variables.
cards.explanation: The copula transforms times to default. Recovery rates are not transformed and enter only in loss calculations such as credit VaR.
cards.originalText: Recovery rates.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-16: Netting, Close-out and Related Aspects
cards.loText: Identify and describe termination events and discuss their potential effects on parties to a transaction.
cards.reading: CR-16: Netting, Close-out and Related Aspects
cards.statement: A break clause (additional termination event) gives a party the option to terminate a long-dated transaction at specified future dates at its replacement value, so that exposure cannot keep growing as the counterparty's credit quality worsens.
cards.explanation: A break clause, also called a liquidity put or early termination option, lets a party exit before the counterparty deteriorates to the point of default.
cards.originalText: A break clause (additional termination event)

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-16: Netting, Close-out and Related Aspects
cards.loText: Identify and describe termination events and discuss their potential effects on parties to a transaction.
cards.reading: CR-16: Netting, Close-out and Related Aspects
cards.statement: A practical weakness of additional termination events and other break clauses is that parties tend to avoid exercising them early to preserve the relationship, so they may not be used until the counterparty's credit quality has already declined substantially.
cards.explanation: This is the banker's paradox: a break clause is most valuable if exercised early, yet relationship concerns delay its use until the weakened counterparty has deteriorated further.
cards.originalText: Parties tend to avoid exercising them early to preserve the relationship, so they may not be used until the counterparty’s credit quality has already declined substantially

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-16: Netting, Close-out and Related Aspects
cards.loText: Identify and describe termination events and discuss their potential effects on parties to a transaction.
cards.reading: CR-16: Netting, Close-out and Related Aspects
cards.statement: Additional termination events and other break clauses can only be exercised after the counterparty has already defaulted.
cards.explanation: Break clauses operate before default, when credit quality declines, so they are not default-only. Their weakness is that they tend to be exercised too late.
cards.originalText: They can only be exercised after the counterparty has already defaulted, so they give no protection

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-16: Netting, Close-out and Related Aspects
cards.loText: Identify and describe termination events and discuss their potential effects on parties to a transaction.
cards.reading: CR-16: Netting, Close-out and Related Aspects
cards.statement: Break clauses are always mandatory, so the trade is terminated whether or not the counterparty has deteriorated.
cards.explanation: Break clauses can be mandatory, optional or trigger-based, so they are not always mandatory.
cards.originalText: They are always mandatory, so the trade is terminated whether or not the counterparty has deteriorated

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-16: Netting, Close-out and Related Aspects
cards.loText: Identify and describe termination events and discuss their potential effects on parties to a transaction.
cards.reading: CR-16: Netting, Close-out and Related Aspects
cards.statement: Termination events give an institution the right to terminate a trade before the counterparty's creditworthiness deteriorates to the point of bankruptcy.
cards.explanation: Termination events let an institution exit a trade ahead of the counterparty's bankruptcy.
cards.originalText: Termination events give an institution the right (option) to terminate a trade prior to their counterparty’s creditworthiness deteriorating to the point of bankruptcy

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-16: Netting, Close-out and Related Aspects
cards.loText: Identify and describe termination events and discuss their potential effects on parties to a transaction.
cards.reading: CR-16: Netting, Close-out and Related Aspects
cards.statement: A break clause, also known as a liquidity put or early termination option, is an agreement to terminate a transaction at pre-specified dates in the future at market rates.
cards.explanation: Break clauses terminate the trade at specified future dates at replacement (market) value.
cards.originalText: A break clause (a.k.a. liquidity put or early termination option) is an agreement to terminate (break) a transaction at pre‑specified dates in the future at market rates

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-16: Netting, Close-out and Related Aspects
cards.loText: Identify and describe termination events and discuss their potential effects on parties to a transaction.
cards.reading: CR-16: Netting, Close-out and Related Aspects
cards.statement: Break clauses are often linked to additional termination events (ATEs), which are not in the standardized ISDA documentation and are therefore the result of negotiation.
cards.explanation: ATEs are not part of the standard ISDA form, so they arise from negotiation between the parties.
cards.originalText: Break clauses are often linked to additional termination events (ATEs), which are not in the standardized ISDA documentation and therefore are a result of negotiations

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-16: Netting, Close-out and Related Aspects
cards.loText: Identify and describe termination events and discuss their potential effects on parties to a transaction.
cards.reading: CR-16: Netting, Close-out and Related Aspects
cards.statement: Walkaway features are part of the standardized ISDA documentation and should be used in almost all transactions because they mitigate counterparty risk.
cards.explanation: Walkaway clauses were common before the 1992 ISDA Master Agreement but are not part of the standard documentation. They do not reduce credit exposure, impose extra costs on the defaulter and should be avoided.
cards.originalText: Walkaway features are parts of the standardized ISDA documentation and ”should be utilized in almost all transactions” as they mitigate counterparty risk

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-16: Netting, Close-out and Related Aspects
cards.loText: Identify and describe termination events and discuss their potential effects on parties to a transaction.
cards.reading: CR-16: Netting, Close-out and Related Aspects
cards.statement: The banker's paradox of a break clause is that the option tends to be used too late, after the weak firm has weakened further.
cards.explanation: A break clause is most valuable if exercised early, but entities avoid early exercise to preserve relationships, so it is often used only after substantial deterioration.
cards.originalText: The break clause option is used too late, and the weak firm gets weaker.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-16: Netting, Close-out and Related Aspects
cards.loText: Identify and describe termination events and discuss their potential effects on parties to a transaction.
cards.reading: CR-16: Netting, Close-out and Related Aspects
cards.statement: For a break clause to be effective, the option should not be exercised too early.
cards.explanation: Effectiveness requires early exercise, before the counterparty's credit quality declines substantially. The banker's paradox is that early exercise is usually avoided.
cards.originalText: To be effective, the break clause option should not be used too early.
cards.correction: For a break clause to be effective, the option should be exercised early.

changes.from: should not be exercised too early

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-16: Netting, Close-out and Related Aspects
cards.loText: Identify and describe termination events and discuss their potential effects on parties to a transaction.
cards.reading: CR-16: Netting, Close-out and Related Aspects
cards.statement: The banker's paradox of a break clause is that the option is used too early and is unlikely to avoid systemic risk issues.
cards.explanation: The paradox concerns use that is too late, not too early, and it is not about systemic risk.
cards.originalText: The break clause option is used too early, and is unlikely to avoid systemic risk issues.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify typical credit exposure profiles for various derivative contracts and combination profiles.
cards.statement: An interest rate swap struck at the market swap rate has zero market value to both parties at inception.
cards.explanation: At the market swap rate the present values of the fixed and floating legs are equal, so the swap starts with zero mark-to-market for both parties and exposure builds from zero.
cards.originalText: The market value would be zero to both X and Y.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify typical credit exposure profiles for various derivative contracts and combination profiles.
cards.statement: An interest rate swap struck at the market swap rate with a notional of USD 50 million has a market value of USD 50 million to both parties at inception.
cards.explanation: Notional is not exchanged in an interest rate swap and is not its value. The parties' values are equal and opposite, and both are zero at inception.
cards.originalText: The market value would be \$50 million to both X and Y.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify typical credit exposure profiles for various derivative contracts and combination profiles.
cards.statement: The potential future exposure of an FX forward rises monotonically over its life and is largest near maturity, driven mainly by FX volatility and the single final exchange of notional.
cards.explanation: An FX forward has one payment at maturity and no intermediate cash flows that roll off, so the dispersion of the exchange rate keeps widening with time.
cards.originalText: Monotonically increasing and largest near maturity, driven mainly by FX volatility and the single final exchange of notional.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify typical credit exposure profiles for various derivative contracts and combination profiles.
cards.statement: The potential future exposure of an FX forward is bell-shaped, peaking part-way through its life and falling toward zero at maturity because payments roll off.
cards.explanation: That peaked shape describes an interest rate swap. An FX forward has no periodic payments, so its exposure keeps increasing until maturity.
cards.originalText: Bell‑shaped, peaking at about one year and falling toward zero at maturity because payments roll off.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify typical credit exposure profiles for various derivative contracts and combination profiles.
cards.statement: The potential future exposure of an FX forward is flat at roughly 100% of notional throughout its life, as for a loan or repo.
cards.explanation: A flat profile near the notional describes bonds, loans and repos. A forward struck at market starts with zero exposure and builds over time.
cards.originalText: Flat at roughly 100% of notional throughout, as for a loan or repo.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify typical credit exposure profiles for various derivative contracts and combination profiles.
cards.statement: The potential future exposure of an FX forward struck at the market forward rate is highest at inception and declines thereafter as its time value decays.
cards.explanation: A forward struck at market has zero mark-to-market at inception, so its exposure starts at zero and grows toward maturity.
cards.originalText: Highest at inception and declining thereafter as the forward’s time value decays.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify typical credit exposure profiles for various derivative contracts and combination profiles.
cards.statement: A plain vanilla interest rate swap has a bell-shaped (peaked) potential future exposure profile over time.
cards.explanation: Growing uncertainty about rates raises exposure early, while the roll-off of remaining payments brings it back toward zero at maturity, producing a peak.
cards.originalText: Plain vanilla interest rate swap

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify typical credit exposure profiles for various derivative contracts and combination profiles.
cards.statement: An equity-linked note has a bell-shaped (peaked) potential future exposure profile over time.
cards.explanation: An equity-linked note is a bond-like claim whose exposure is about its notional, not a peaked profile.
cards.originalText: Equity‑linked note

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify typical credit exposure profiles for various derivative contracts and combination profiles.
cards.statement: The maximum exposure of a bought-protection single-name CDS is one minus the recovery rate, as a fraction of notional, reached on default of the reference entity.
cards.explanation: On a credit event the protection buyer receives the payout of $1 - R$ of notional, which is the maximum exposure of the position.
cards.originalText: The maximum exposure of the position is 70% of notional, reached on default of the reference entity.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify typical credit exposure profiles for various derivative contracts and combination profiles.
cards.statement: For a given confidence level, potential future exposure is less than or equal to expected shortfall at that level, since expected shortfall is the average exposure beyond the PFE quantile.
cards.explanation: Expected shortfall averages exposures beyond the PFE quantile, so by construction it is at least as large as the PFE at the same confidence level.
cards.originalText: For a given confidence level, PFE is less than or equal to expected shortfall at that level, since ES is the average exposure beyond the PFE quantile.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify typical credit exposure profiles for various derivative contracts and combination profiles.
cards.statement: For a bought-protection single-name CDS, the gradual early increase in exposure corresponds to scenarios in which the CDS spread widens.
cards.explanation: Spread widening raises the replacement value of protection bought earlier, which produces the gradual rise before any default.
cards.originalText: The gradual early increase in exposure corresponds to scenarios in which the CDS spread widens.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify typical credit exposure profiles for various derivative contracts and combination profiles.
cards.statement: The abrupt jump in the high-confidence PFE of a single-name CDS is caused by the wrong-way risk correlation parameter, so setting that correlation to zero would remove the jump.
cards.explanation: The jump comes from the discrete default payoff: once the reference entity's default probability exceeds one minus the confidence level, the quantile falls in the default scenarios. Zero correlation would not remove it.
cards.originalText: The abrupt jump in the 98% PFE is caused by the wrong‑way risk correlation parameter; setting it to zero would remove the jump.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify typical credit exposure profiles for various derivative contracts and combination profiles.
cards.statement: A long call option position has unbounded potential future credit exposure when the underlying price can rise without limit.
cards.explanation: Credit exposure arises only when the position has positive value. A long call gains without bound as the underlying rises, whereas a long put or short forward gain is capped because the underlying cannot fall below zero.
cards.originalText: Long call

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify typical credit exposure profiles for various derivative contracts and combination profiles.
cards.statement: For a cross-currency swap, paying in the currency with the lower interest rate (receiving the higher-rate currency) tends to decrease both the expected exposure and the potential future exposure.
cards.explanation: Paying the lower-rate currency creates a negative drift in the swap's value, so the swap is increasingly likely to have negative value and exposure is much lower.
cards.originalText: Paying in the currency with the lower interest rate (receiving the higher‑rate currency)

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify typical credit exposure profiles for various derivative contracts and combination profiles.
cards.statement: For a cross-currency swap, paying in the currency with the higher interest rate (receiving the lower-rate currency) tends to decrease both the expected exposure and the potential future exposure.
cards.explanation: Paying the higher-rate currency gives a positive drift and significant exposure, because the large coupons paid are expected to be offset by gains on the final notional exchange.
cards.originalText: Paying in the currency with the higher interest rate (receiving the lower‑rate currency)

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify typical credit exposure profiles for various derivative contracts and combination profiles.
cards.statement: For a cross-currency swap, a longer maturity tends to decrease both the expected exposure and the potential future exposure.
cards.explanation: A longer maturity adds more payments and more time for exchange rates to move, so exposure rises.
cards.originalText: A longer maturity

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify typical credit exposure profiles for various derivative contracts and combination profiles.
cards.statement: For a cross-currency swap, higher foreign exchange volatility tends to decrease both the expected exposure and the potential future exposure.
cards.explanation: Higher FX volatility widens the distribution of the final notional exchange and raises exposure.
cards.originalText: Higher foreign exchange (FX) volatility

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify typical credit exposure profiles for various derivative contracts and combination profiles.
cards.statement: For a long-protection single-name CDS, the 99% PFE profile jumps abruptly once the reference entity's default probability exceeds 1%, because the 99th percentile scenario then includes default.
cards.explanation: PFE is a percentile, so it jumps to the default payoff of $1 - R$ once the default probability exceeds one minus the confidence level. Expected exposure is an average, so the rare default is diluted and no jump appears.
cards.originalText: From year 3 on, the default probability of the reference entity exceeds 1 minus the PFE confidence level (PD > 1%), so the 99th percentile scenario includes default

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify typical credit exposure profiles for various derivative contracts and combination profiles.
cards.statement: The key parameter that determines the shape of the expected exposure profile of a single-name CDS is the recovery rate.
cards.explanation: Recovery sets the height of the PFE jump, $1 - R$. The shape of the expected exposure profile follows spread movements.
cards.originalText: The key parameter that determines the shape of the EE profile is the recovery rate

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify typical credit exposure profiles for various derivative contracts and combination profiles.
cards.statement: The expected exposure profile of a long-protection single-name CDS should show the same abrupt jump as its high-confidence PFE profile.
cards.explanation: Expected exposure is an average, so the low-probability default scenarios are averaged away and the profile stays swap-like without a jump.
cards.originalText: The EE profile is incorrectly drawn; it should also show an abrupt jump like the PFE

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify typical credit exposure profiles for various derivative contracts and combination profiles.
cards.statement: The potential future exposure of a cross-currency swap rises monotonically to its maximum at final maturity, mainly because of uncertainty about the large final notional exchange driven by FX volatility, with a smaller contribution from interest-rate payments.
cards.explanation: A cross-currency swap combines an FX forward, which dominates and rises monotonically, with a smaller interest rate swap component, so its profile lies above that of a plain FX forward.
cards.originalText: PFE of a cross‑currency swap

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify typical credit exposure profiles for various derivative contracts and combination profiles.
cards.statement: The potential future exposure of an interest rate swap rises monotonically to its maximum at final maturity.
cards.explanation: An interest rate swap profile is peaked: it rises with diffusion, peaks at roughly one-third of maturity and falls to zero as payments roll off.
cards.originalText: PFE of an interest rate swap

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify typical credit exposure profiles for various derivative contracts and combination profiles.
cards.statement: For a simple forward contract with independent and identically distributed returns on the underlying market variable, the exposure profile is approximately proportional to the square root of time.
cards.explanation: With i.i.d. returns the standard deviation of a forward's value grows with $\sqrt{t}$, so exposure follows a square-root-of-time rule.
cards.originalText: For a simple forward contract with i.i.d. returns on the underlying market variable, the exposure profile is approximately proportional to the square root of time

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify typical credit exposure profiles for various derivative contracts and combination profiles.
cards.statement: As with market VaR, in most uses of counterparty exposure quantification (xVA) the drift of the risk factor can safely be assumed to be zero.
cards.explanation: Drift can be ignored over the short horizon of market VaR but matters over the long horizons used for exposure.
cards.originalText: As with market VaR, in most uses of counterparty exposure quantification (xVA) the drift of the risk factor can safely be assumed to be zero

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify typical credit exposure profiles for various derivative contracts and combination profiles.
cards.statement: For a single-name CDS, expected exposure generally decreases as spread volatility rises.
cards.explanation: Higher spread volatility widens the distribution of the CDS value and increases expected exposure.
cards.originalText: For a single‑name CDS, expected exposure generally decreases as spread volatility rises

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify typical credit exposure profiles for various derivative contracts and combination profiles.
cards.statement: For an interest rate swap with an upward-sloping yield curve, the floating-rate payer has a positive expected future value and the greater credit exposure.
cards.explanation: With an upward-sloping curve it is the fixed-rate payer, not the floating-rate payer, that has the greater expected positive exposure.
cards.originalText: For an interest rate swap with an upward‑sloping yield curve, the floating‑rate payer has a positive expected future value and the greater credit exposure

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify typical credit exposure profiles for various derivative contracts and combination profiles.
cards.statement: The expected exposure profile of an interest rate swap peaks at about one-third of the swap's maturity.
cards.explanation: Swap exposure is roughly proportional to $(T - t)\sqrt{t}$, which is maximised at $t = T/3$, about 3.33 years for a 10-year swap.
cards.originalText: Because the swap’s maturity is ten years, the exposure peaks at about $\frac{1}{3} \times10 = 3.33$ years

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify typical credit exposure profiles for various derivative contracts and combination profiles.
cards.statement: With a typical upward-sloping yield curve, the receiver swap (the counterparty who pays floating) has greater exposure than the payer swap (the counterparty who pays fixed).
cards.explanation: The receiver of fixed expects positive net cash flows early, giving it a lower expected positive exposure. It is the payer swap that has the greater exposure.
cards.originalText: With a typical upward‑sloping yield curve, the receiver swap (counterparty who pays floating) has greater exposure than the payer swap (counterparty who pays fixed)

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify typical credit exposure profiles for various derivative contracts and combination profiles.
cards.statement: The initial increase in the exposure profile of an interest rate swap is due to the $\sqrt{t}$ term, called the diffusion effect.
cards.explanation: Early on, the growing uncertainty of rates, which scales with $\sqrt{t}$, dominates and exposure rises.
cards.originalText: The profile initially increases because of the $\sqrt{t}$ term, called the diffusion effect

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify typical credit exposure profiles for various derivative contracts and combination profiles.
cards.statement: The later decrease in the exposure profile of an interest rate swap is due to the $(T - t)$ term, called the amortization effect.
cards.explanation: Later, the shrinking remaining maturity as payments are made dominates, so exposure falls toward zero at maturity.
cards.originalText: The profile later decreases because of the $(T - t)$ term, called the amortization effect

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify typical credit exposure profiles for various derivative contracts and combination profiles.
cards.statement: The exposure profile of a cross-currency swap can be represented as a combination of an interest rate swap profile, an FX forward profile and an assumption about the correlation between interest rates and the FX rate.
cards.explanation: A cross-currency swap is essentially an interest rate swap combined with an FX forward, and the correlation between rates and the FX rate also affects the combined exposure.
cards.originalText: The profile can be represented as a combination of an interest rate swap profile, an FX forward profile, and an assumption about the correlation between the interest rates and the FX rate.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify typical credit exposure profiles for various derivative contracts and combination profiles.
cards.statement: In a cross-currency swap, the FX forward component contributes more to the total exposure than the interest rate swap component.
cards.explanation: The FX component dominates because of high FX volatility and the final exchange of notional.
cards.originalText: The FX forward component contributes more to the total exposure than the interest rate swap component.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify typical credit exposure profiles for various derivative contracts and combination profiles.
cards.statement: Because the potential future exposure of a cross-currency swap does not fall back toward zero at maturity, the swap must have had a significantly positive value at inception.
cards.explanation: The exposure stays high because the final notional exchange is still outstanding and FX uncertainty keeps growing. A par cross-currency swap with zero initial value has the same shape.
cards.originalText: Because the PFE does not fall back toward zero at maturity, the swap must have had a significantly positive value at inception.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify typical credit exposure profiles for various derivative contracts and combination profiles.
cards.statement: An increase in the assumed FX volatility increases the exposure of a cross-currency swap.
cards.explanation: Greater FX volatility widens the distribution of the exchange rate and raises the potential future exposure.
cards.originalText: An increase in the assumed FX volatility would increase the exposure.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify typical credit exposure profiles for various derivative contracts and combination profiles.
cards.statement: Swaps tend to have a peaked potential future exposure profile, because periodic payments roll off over time while uncertainty keeps growing.
cards.explanation: Exposure rises with uncertainty (roughly $\sqrt{t}$) and falls as remaining payments shrink (roughly remaining maturity), so it peaks part-way through the life and declines to zero at maturity.
cards.originalText: Swap.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify typical credit exposure profiles for various derivative contracts and combination profiles.
cards.statement: A long option position tends to have a peaked potential future exposure profile.
cards.explanation: A long option has no periodic cash flows to reverse its exposure, so its potential exposure keeps increasing with time.
cards.originalText: Long option position.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify typical credit exposure profiles for various derivative contracts and combination profiles.
cards.statement: A 10-year loan with a floating-rate payment tends to have a peaked potential future exposure profile.
cards.explanation: A loan's exposure is approximately its notional throughout, because the lender is owed principal until the end, so it is not peaked.
cards.originalText: 10‑year loan with a floating rate payment.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain how payment frequencies and exercise dates affect the exposure profile of various securities.
cards.statement: In an interest rate swap, receiving payments more frequently than paying them lowers a party's potential future exposure relative to equal payment frequencies, while paying more frequently than receiving raises it.
cards.explanation: When amounts owed to a party are settled sooner than the amounts it owes, less value accumulates unpaid and exposure falls. When it pays out sooner while its receipts lag, exposure is higher.
cards.originalText: Swap 2 shows lower exposure and Swap 3 shows higher exposure.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain how payment frequencies and exercise dates affect the exposure profile of various securities.
cards.statement: Before the exercise date, a swap-settled European swaption has greater exposure than a forward swap on the same underlying swap, and after the exercise date the forward swap has greater exposure.
cards.explanation: Before exercise the option value is never negative, so the swaption exposure is at least that of the forward swap. Afterwards the forward swap is live in every scenario, including those where the swaption was not exercised.
cards.originalText: Before the exercise date the swaption has greater exposure, and after the exercise date the forward swap has greater exposure.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain how payment frequencies and exercise dates affect the exposure profile of various securities.
cards.statement: A swap-settled European swaption and a forward swap on the same underlying swap have identical exposure at all times.
cards.explanation: The two are identical only in scenarios where the swaption is exercised. In other scenarios the swaption is not exercised while the forward swap remains live.
cards.originalText: The two have identical exposure at all times, because the swaption is exercised into the same underlying swap.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain how payment frequencies and exercise dates affect the exposure profile of various securities.
cards.statement: Before the exercise date, a forward swap has greater exposure than a swap-settled European swaption on the same underlying swap, and after the exercise date the swaption has greater exposure.
cards.explanation: The relationship is the reverse: before exercise the swaption holder can only gain, so its exposure is greater, and afterwards the forward swap has the greater exposure.
cards.originalText: Before the exercise date the forward swap has greater exposure, and after the exercise date the swaption has greater exposure.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain how payment frequencies and exercise dates affect the exposure profile of various securities.
cards.statement: A cash-settled swaption and a physically settled swaption on the same swap have identical exposure until the exercise date, after which the cash-settled swaption has zero exposure while the physically settled one retains exposure on the underlying swap.
cards.explanation: Cash settlement ends the contract at exercise with a single payment. Physical settlement leaves the underlying swap in place, so exposure continues with the usual swap profile until maturity.
cards.originalText: The two have identical exposure until the exercise date; afterwards Swaption X has zero exposure while Swaption Y retains exposure on the underlying swap.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain how payment frequencies and exercise dates affect the exposure profile of various securities.
cards.statement: Before the exercise date, a cash-settled swaption has greater exposure than a physically settled swaption on the same swap because the cash settlement amount is certain.
