cards.explanation: Only expected future value is additive. EPE is sub-additive because $\max(\sum v_i, 0) \le \sum \max(v_i, 0)$, and that gap is the netting benefit.
cards.originalText: Expected future value and expected positive exposure are both additive across transactions, so the EPE of a netting set equals the sum of the EPEs of its trades.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the general impact of aggregation on exposure, and the impact of aggregation on exposure when there is correlation between transaction values.
cards.statement: Expected negative exposure is the driver of the credit value adjustment that a bank charges its counterparty.
cards.explanation: Expected positive exposure drives CVA. Expected negative exposure is the exposure from the counterparty's point of view and drives the bank's own DVA.
cards.originalText: Expected negative exposure is the exposure seen from the counterparty’s point of view, so it drives the credit value adjustment the bank charges that counterparty.
cards.correction: Expected positive exposure is the driver of the credit value adjustment that a bank charges its counterparty.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the general impact of aggregation on exposure, and the impact of aggregation on exposure when there is correlation between transaction values.
cards.statement: Doubling the volatility of future value, with expected future value unchanged, lowers expected positive exposure.
cards.explanation: Exposure is option-like, so higher volatility raises EPE while the expected future value is unchanged.
cards.originalText: Doubling the volatility of future value leaves the expected future value unchanged but lowers expected positive exposure, because more scenarios end below zero.
cards.correction: Doubling the volatility of future value, with expected future value unchanged, raises expected positive exposure.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the general impact of aggregation on exposure, and the impact of aggregation on exposure when there is correlation between transaction values.
cards.statement: A new trade whose value is highly positively correlated with an existing netting set can still have an incremental EPE well below its standalone EPE when the netting set is deep out of the money, because the netting set is unlikely to turn positive unless the market moves a long way.
cards.explanation: Aggregation benefits come from relative moneyness as well as from structural correlation. A deeply negative portfolio absorbs most of the new trade's positive value.
cards.originalText: Although the values are highly correlated, the netting set is unlikely to have positive value unless rates rise a long way, so the incremental EPE will be well below the new trade’s standalone EPE.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the general impact of aggregation on exposure, and the impact of aggregation on exposure when there is correlation between transaction values.
cards.statement: Because a new trade is highly positively correlated with the existing trades in a netting set, aggregation gives no benefit and its incremental EPE equals its standalone EPE.
cards.explanation: Positive correlation of values does not mean the positive parts move together: if the portfolio is deeply negative, it offsets much of the new trade's positive exposure.
cards.originalText: Because the new trade is highly positively correlated with the existing swaps, aggregation gives no benefit and the incremental EPE equals the new trade’s standalone EPE.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the general impact of aggregation on exposure, and the impact of aggregation on exposure when there is correlation between transaction values.
cards.statement: Because expected future value is additive, the EPE of a netting set equals the standalone EPE of a new trade plus the existing portfolio's expected future value.
cards.explanation: EFV is additive but EPE is not, so an EPE cannot be found by adding an EFV to a standalone EPE.
cards.originalText: Because EFV is additive and the portfolio’s EFV is negative, the netting set’s EPE equals the new trade’s standalone EPE plus the portfolio’s EFV.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the general impact of aggregation on exposure, and the impact of aggregation on exposure when there is correlation between transaction values.
cards.statement: An out-of-the-money portfolio raises the incremental exposure of any new trade added to its netting set.
cards.explanation: An out-of-the-money portfolio dampens the incremental exposure of a new trade, because it must recover before the netting set has positive value.
cards.originalText: An out-of-the-money portfolio raises the incremental exposure of any new trade, because the bank already owes the client money.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the differences between funding exposure and credit exposure.
cards.statement: A positive portfolio value is at risk if the counterparty defaults and is also an asset that must be funded while the counterparty survives; margin received against it reduces both the counterparty risk and the funding cost.
cards.explanation: The positive value has a credit dimension (loss on default) and a funding dimension (an asset to be funded). Reusable margin held against it reduces both.
cards.originalText: A positive portfolio value is at risk if the counterparty defaults and is also an asset that must be funded while the counterparty survives; margin received against it reduces both the counterparty risk and the funding cost.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the differences between funding exposure and credit exposure.
cards.statement: A positive portfolio value creates a funding cost only if the counterparty defaults.
cards.explanation: Funding arises in the scenarios where the counterparty survives. On default the exposure is lost, which is the credit risk.
cards.originalText: A positive portfolio value creates a funding cost only if the counterparty defaults, since funding needs arise from the close-out of the transactions.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the differences between funding exposure and credit exposure.
cards.statement: A negative derivatives portfolio value creates a funding cost for the bank.
cards.explanation: A negative value is a source of funding and so a funding benefit, not a cost.
cards.originalText: A negative portfolio value creates a funding cost, because the bank must eventually pay the amount it owes to the counterparty.
cards.correction: A negative derivatives portfolio value creates a funding benefit for the bank.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the differences between funding exposure and credit exposure.
cards.statement: Margin posted by a bank against a negative portfolio value increases the bank's funding benefit.
cards.explanation: Posted margin reduces the bank's funding benefit, because it must give up the funding that the negative value provided.
cards.originalText: Margin posted by the bank against a negative value increases the bank’s funding benefit and reduces the counterparty’s exposure to the bank’s default.
cards.correction: Margin posted by a bank against a negative portfolio value reduces the bank's funding benefit.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the differences between funding exposure and credit exposure.
cards.statement: Liquid bonds such as gilts can be repoed, so the repo cash largely offsets their funding cost, whereas derivatives cannot be repoed; because funding is assessed at portfolio level, negative-value derivatives provide a funding benefit that offsets part of the cost of positive-value ones.
cards.explanation: Costs and benefits partly cancel because funding needs to be considered only at portfolio level, where values are additive across counterparties.
cards.originalText: The gilts can be repoed, so the repo cash largely offsets their funding cost; the swaps cannot be repoed, but because funding is assessed at portfolio level the negative values provide a benefit that offsets part of the cost of the positive values.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the differences between funding exposure and credit exposure.
cards.statement: Funding exposure is assessed counterparty by counterparty, like credit exposure, so negative-value swaps with one counterparty provide no funding offset to positive-value swaps with another.
cards.explanation: Netting-set aggregation belongs to credit exposure. Funding applies at portfolio level, where values are additive across counterparties.
cards.originalText: Funding is assessed counterparty by counterparty, like credit exposure, so the negative swaps provide no offset to the positive swaps.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the differences between funding exposure and credit exposure.
cards.statement: A derivatives portfolio with a negative value creates a funding cost that adds to the funding cost of positive-value portfolios.
cards.explanation: A negative value is a funding benefit that offsets part of the funding cost of positive values.
cards.originalText: The negative swaps create a funding cost equal to their value, which adds to the cost of funding the positive swaps.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the differences between funding exposure and credit exposure.
cards.statement: Credit exposure is measured netting set by netting set, so a positive value with one counterparty is not offset by a negative value with another without a netting agreement, whereas funding is assessed at portfolio level, where values are additive.
cards.explanation: Close-out netting applies only within a netting agreement. For funding, an asset with one counterparty and a liability with another offset, leaving a roughly flat funding position.
cards.originalText: Credit exposure is USD 40 million to X, while the funding position across the two sets is roughly flat, because funding is assessed at portfolio level, where values are additive.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the differences between funding exposure and credit exposure.
cards.statement: Funding, like credit exposure, is assessed netting set by netting set.
cards.explanation: Netting-set aggregation belongs to credit exposure. Funding is assessed at portfolio level, where values are additive.
cards.originalText: Credit exposure is USD 40 million to X and the funding requirement is USD 40 million, because funding, like credit exposure, is assessed netting set by netting set.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the differences between funding exposure and credit exposure.
cards.statement: CVA is measured over a margin period of risk that assumes the counterparty has defaulted and stopped posting margin, leaving residual exposure, whereas funding uses the normal, much shorter posting delay, and reusable cash margin offsets the value to be funded.
cards.explanation: This is one reason why a collateralised derivative can have a material CVA but an FVA close to zero.
cards.originalText: CVA is measured over a margin period of risk that assumes the dealer has defaulted and stopped posting, leaving residual exposure; funding uses the normal, much shorter posting delay, and the reusable cash margin offsets the value to be funded.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the differences between funding exposure and credit exposure.
cards.statement: Funding and credit exposure use the same margin period of risk, so the FVA of a collateralised derivative should equal its CVA.
cards.explanation: The two use different periods: CVA uses the margin period of risk, which assumes the counterparty has stopped posting, while funding uses the normal posting frequency. A material CVA with a near-zero FVA is therefore expected.
cards.originalText: The FVA should equal the CVA, because funding and credit exposure use the same margin period of risk; the FVA calculation is therefore in error.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the motivation for and the challenges of pricing counterparty risk.
cards.statement: CVA matters to any institution with significant OTC derivatives, including corporates that hedge economic risks, and it became a key topic because of volatile credit spreads and the related accounting and capital requirements.
cards.explanation: GARP names three drivers: credit spread volatility, accounting requirements (IFRS 13) and capital requirements (Basel III). The calculation is a major concern for banks but also for other financial institutions and corporations.
cards.originalText: CVA matters to any institution with significant OTC derivatives, including corporates that hedge economic risks; it became a key topic because of volatile credit spreads and the related accounting and capital requirements.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the motivation for and the challenges of pricing counterparty risk.
cards.statement: CVA is relevant only to banks and has no role in a corporate's accounts.
cards.explanation: CVA is a fair-value (accounting) adjustment as well as a capital topic, and it applies to corporations and other institutions with significant OTC derivatives.
cards.originalText: CVA matters only to banks, because it was introduced by Basel III as a regulatory capital charge and has no role in a corporate’s accounts.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the motivation for and the challenges of pricing counterparty risk.
cards.statement: Netting and collateral remove counterparty risk entirely, so CVA is relevant only for trades outside a netting agreement.
cards.explanation: Netting and collateral reduce CVA, and must be reflected in it, but they do not remove counterparty risk entirely.
cards.originalText: CVA matters only for trades outside a netting agreement, because netting and collateral remove counterparty risk entirely and leave nothing to price.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the motivation for and the challenges of pricing counterparty risk.
cards.statement: CVA needs to be computed only after a counterparty has been downgraded; until then the risk-free value of a derivative is its fair value.
cards.explanation: Default can happen at any time and spreads move continuously, so CVA is part of fair value from the trade date, not something triggered by a downgrade.
cards.originalText: CVA needs to be computed only after a counterparty has been downgraded; until then the risk-free value of the derivative is its fair value.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the motivation for and the challenges of pricing counterparty risk.
cards.statement: Most counterparties have no liquid single-name CDS and so need proxy credit spread curves in CVA calculations; the market-implied default probabilities are well above real-world ones and generally cannot be hedged, yet accounting standards still generally require credit spreads.
cards.explanation: GARP lists three objections to market-implied probabilities: they are well above real-world ones, default cannot in general be hedged, and banks warehouse credit risk. In practice the objections are somewhat academic because accounting standards require credit spreads.
cards.originalText: Most counterparties need proxy credit spread curves; the implied default probabilities are well above real-world ones and usually cannot be hedged, yet accounting standards generally still require credit spreads.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the motivation for and the challenges of pricing counterparty risk.
cards.statement: For counterparties without liquid CDS, accounting standards require a switch to historical default probabilities, so no proxy curves are needed.
cards.explanation: The standard response to missing CDS is a proxy credit spread curve. Historical default probabilities are used only in rare cases, not by rule.
cards.originalText: For counterparties without liquid CDS, accounting standards require the desk to switch to historical default probabilities, so no proxy curves are needed.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the motivation for and the challenges of pricing counterparty risk.
cards.statement: Market-implied default probabilities are generally lower than real-world default probabilities.
cards.explanation: Market-implied default probabilities are significantly higher than real-world ones, so CVA based on credit spreads is larger than the actuarial expected loss.
cards.originalText: Market-implied default probabilities are generally lower than real-world estimates, so CVA based on credit spreads understates the actuarial expected loss.
cards.correction: Market-implied default probabilities are generally higher than real-world default probabilities.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the motivation for and the challenges of pricing counterparty risk.
cards.statement: A bank that warehouses credit risk rather than hedging it is exposed only to risk-neutral default risk.
cards.explanation: A bank that warehouses credit risk bears real-world default risk. GARP uses this as an argument against using market-implied default probabilities.
cards.originalText: Because the dealer warehouses its credit risk rather than hedging it, it is exposed only to risk-neutral default risk, which is the main argument for market-implied default probabilities.
cards.correction: A bank that warehouses credit risk rather than hedging it is exposed only to real-world default risk.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the motivation for and the challenges of pricing counterparty risk.
cards.statement: Valuing exotic trades inside an exposure simulation may itself need Monte Carlo, so approximations are common (for example, treating a Bermudan swaption as a European one), and path-dependent exposure needs the whole path to each date.
cards.explanation: Nested simulation is expensive, so approximations are used, such as treating a swaption as a forward swap or a Bermudan payoff as a European one. For collateralised netting sets the margin already called depends on the path to each date.
cards.originalText: Valuing exotics inside an exposure simulation may itself need Monte Carlo, so approximations are common (for example, a Bermudan treated as a European), and path-dependent exposure needs the whole path to each date.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the motivation for and the challenges of pricing counterparty risk.
cards.statement: Exotic and path-dependent trades affect only the counterparty's default probability and leave the exposure model unchanged.
cards.explanation: Exotic trades and collateral change the exposure profile, not the counterparty's default probability, so the exposure model must handle them.
cards.originalText: Exotic and path-dependent trades change only the counterparty’s default probability, so the team should recalibrate the credit curve and leave the exposure model unchanged.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the motivation for and the challenges of pricing counterparty risk.
cards.statement: Margin removes the exposure on collateralised netting sets entirely, so they can be dropped from the CVA calculation.
cards.explanation: Margin reduces CVA but does not remove it, because the margin period of risk leaves residual exposure.
cards.originalText: Collateralised netting sets can be dropped from the CVA calculation because margin removes the exposure, so only the Bermudan swaptions need to be simulated.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe credit value adjustment (CVA).
cards.statement: CVA is the difference between the value of a derivatives portfolio with and without counterparty default; in Gregory's convention it is negative, so the risky value equals the risk-free value plus CVA.
cards.explanation: Either way the risky value is below the risk-free value. Some sources quote CVA as a positive cost and subtract it.
cards.originalText: CVA is the difference between the value of a derivatives portfolio with and without counterparty default; in Gregory’s convention it is negative, so the risky value is the risk-free value plus CVA.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe credit value adjustment (CVA).
cards.statement: CVA is the 99th percentile loss from counterparty default over one year, held as capital against a derivatives portfolio.
cards.explanation: A 99th percentile loss is a capital or risk measure. CVA is an expected value, a price.
cards.originalText: CVA is the 99th percentile loss from counterparty default over one year, held as capital against the derivatives portfolio.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe credit value adjustment (CVA).
cards.statement: CVA is the value to the bank of its own possible default on derivative liabilities, computed from its expected negative exposure and its own default probability.
cards.explanation: That describes DVA. CVA is based on the expected positive exposure to the counterparty and the counterparty's default probability.
cards.originalText: CVA is the value to the bank of its own possible default on derivative liabilities, computed from its expected negative exposure and its own default probability.
cards.correction: DVA is the value to the bank of its own possible default on derivative liabilities, computed from its expected negative exposure and its own default probability.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe credit value adjustment (CVA).
cards.statement: CVA is the sum of the standalone adjustments of each trade with the counterparty, so it is unaffected by netting and collateral agreements.
cards.explanation: Netting and collateral reduce the CVA of a netting set, so it is not the sum of standalone trade adjustments.
cards.originalText: CVA is the sum of the standalone adjustments of each trade with the counterparty, so it is unaffected by netting and collateral agreements.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe credit value adjustment (CVA).
cards.statement: The CVA formula that multiplies LGD, expected positive exposure and marginal default probabilities, with a single average LGD, assumes that default time, exposure at default and LGD are independent, that is, no wrong-way risk.
cards.explanation: If the three components are independent, the expectation of their product splits into the product of expectations: a single average LGD, the unconditional EPE at each date and the marginal default probability.
cards.originalText: It assumes default time, exposure at default and LGD are independent (no wrong-way risk), which lets the expectation split into EPE times marginal PD with one average LGD.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe credit value adjustment (CVA).
cards.statement: The CVA formula that multiplies LGD, expected positive exposure and marginal default probabilities assumes a constant hazard rate, so it cannot be used when the credit curve is upward sloping or inverted.
cards.explanation: The marginal default probabilities can come from any credit curve shape; a constant hazard rate is a convenience, not an assumption of the formula.
cards.originalText: It assumes the counterparty’s hazard rate is constant, so it cannot be used when the credit curve is upward sloping or inverted.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe credit value adjustment (CVA).
cards.statement: The CVA formula that multiplies LGD, expected positive exposure and marginal default probabilities assumes that exposure and default are positively dependent, so each EPE is measured conditional on the counterparty defaulting at that date.
cards.explanation: That describes the wrong-way risk extension with conditional EPE. The simple form leaves wrong-way risk out by assuming independence.
cards.originalText: It assumes exposure and default are positively dependent, so each EPE is measured conditional on the counterparty defaulting at that date.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe credit value adjustment (CVA).
cards.statement: The CVA formula that multiplies LGD, expected positive exposure and marginal default probabilities assumes that LGD is zero on collateralised trades, so only uncollateralised netting sets enter the sum.
cards.explanation: Collateral reduces the EPE; it does not set LGD to zero or remove netting sets from the CVA calculation.
cards.originalText: It assumes the LGD is zero on collateralised trades, so only uncollateralised netting sets need to enter the sum.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe credit value adjustment (CVA).
cards.statement: When a position is very deep in the money, its EPE can be approximated by its expected future value, so the CVA calculation converges to a simpler, bond-like discounting calculation.
cards.explanation: EPE averages $\max(V, 0)$. If $V$ is almost never negative, $\max(V, 0) \approx V$, so EPE is close to the expected future value; the discounting approach must still allow for LGD.
cards.originalText: When a position is very in the money, its EPE can be approximated by its expected future value, so the CVA calculation converges to a simpler, bond-like discounting calculation.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe credit value adjustment (CVA).
cards.statement: The CVA of a deeply in-the-money position should be based on potential future exposure at a high percentile rather than on expected positive exposure.
cards.explanation: CVA always uses the expected exposure; PFE is a limit-setting measure whatever the moneyness of the position.
cards.originalText: Because the swap is deeply in the money, CVA should be based on its potential future exposure at a high percentile rather than on its EPE.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe credit value adjustment (CVA).
cards.statement: For a deeply in-the-money position, CVA no longer depends on the loss given default.
cards.explanation: LGD still scales the loss. Dropping it would treat the entire exposure as lost on default.
cards.originalText: Because the exposure is almost certain to stay positive, CVA no longer depends on the loss given default and equals the expected future value times the cumulative default probability.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain how netting can be incorporated into the CVA calculation.
cards.statement: The netting benefit in CVA is large when the trades in a netting set offset each other and small when they are all in the same direction: same-direction trades give a netting-set EPE close to the sum of standalone EPEs, while offsetting trades make it far lower.
cards.explanation: Aggregation reduces exposure only in scenarios where trade values have opposite signs. Trades in the same direction rarely have opposite signs.
cards.originalText: The netting benefit is large for Y and small for X: X’s netting-set CVA is close to the sum of its standalone CVAs, while Y’s offsetting trades make its netting-set EPE far lower than the sum of standalone EPEs.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain how netting can be incorporated into the CVA calculation.
cards.statement: The netting benefit in CVA depends only on the number of trades in the netting set.
cards.explanation: The benefit depends on the correlation, or sign pattern, of the trade values and not on the number of trades.
cards.originalText: The netting benefit is the same for both, because it depends only on the number of trades in the netting set.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain how netting can be incorporated into the CVA calculation.
cards.statement: The netting benefit in CVA is larger when the trades in the netting set are all in the same direction.
cards.explanation: Same-direction trades reinforce each other and offset least, so netting has little to cancel; the benefit is larger when trades offset.
cards.originalText: The netting benefit is larger for X, because trades in the same direction reinforce each other’s exposure and netting removes this concentration.
cards.correction: The netting benefit in CVA is larger when the trades in the netting set are in offsetting directions.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain how netting can be incorporated into the CVA calculation.
cards.statement: Netting lowers the counterparty's probability of default, which is why it reduces CVA.
cards.explanation: Netting acts on the exposure, path by path, and leaves the default probability unchanged.
cards.originalText: The netting benefit is larger for Y, because netting lowers Y’s default probability, which depends on its offsetting positions.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain how netting can be incorporated into the CVA calculation.
cards.statement: To incorporate netting into CVA, EPE is computed separately for each legally enforceable netting set by netting trade values before taking the positive part; trades without an enforceable netting agreement are each treated as their own netting set; the netting-set CVAs are then added, using the same PD and LGD.
cards.explanation: A netting set is the group of trades under one legally enforceable netting agreement, and there may be more than one with a counterparty. Where netting is not enforceable, each trade's gross positive exposure counts.
cards.originalText: Compute EPE separately for each enforceable netting set, netting trade values before taking the positive part; treat each trade in group (3) as its own netting set; then add the CVAs, using the same PD and LGD throughout.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain how netting can be incorporated into the CVA calculation.
cards.statement: All trades with a counterparty can be netted into a single exposure for CVA because CVA depends on the counterparty's single default probability.
cards.explanation: Netting is a legal right within an enforceable agreement, not a consequence of the counterparty having one default probability.
cards.originalText: Net all the trades with the counterparty into a single exposure, because CVA depends on the counterparty’s one default probability.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain how netting can be incorporated into the CVA calculation.
cards.statement: When the two parties have equal credit spreads and LGDs, BCVA without survival adjustments depends on EPE plus ENE, which equals the expected future value; because that is additive across trades, the CVA and DVA effects of netting offset and there is no incremental netting benefit.
cards.explanation: With equal marginal default probabilities the BCVA is proportional to $\text{EPE} + \text{ENE} = \text{EFV}$, and the EFV is additive across trades.
cards.originalText: The trader is wrong: with equal spreads and LGDs, BCVA depends on EPE plus ENE, which is the expected future value; that is additive across trades, so the CVA and DVA effects of netting offset and there is no incremental netting benefit.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain how netting can be incorporated into the CVA calculation.
cards.statement: Adding an offsetting swap to a netting set reduces the CVA leg of BCVA while leaving the DVA leg unaffected.
cards.explanation: The offset shrinks the expected negative exposure as well, so the DVA leg falls too.
cards.originalText: The trader is right: the offsetting swap lowers the netting set’s EPE, so the CVA leg shrinks while the DVA leg is unaffected, giving a large BCVA benefit.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain how netting can be incorporated into the CVA calculation.
cards.statement: Netting increases the size of both the EPE and the ENE of a netting set.
cards.explanation: Netting reduces the size of both the expected positive exposure and the expected negative exposure.
cards.originalText: The trader is wrong: netting raises both EPE and ENE in size, so the new swap makes BCVA more negative.
cards.correction: Netting reduces the size of both the EPE and the ENE of a netting set.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain how netting can be incorporated into the CVA calculation.
cards.statement: Netting lowers the DVA leg of BCVA but leaves the CVA leg unchanged.
cards.explanation: Netting reduces both the CVA leg and the DVA leg, not only the DVA leg.
cards.originalText: The trader is right: netting lowers the DVA leg but leaves the CVA leg unchanged, so BCVA becomes less negative.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the implications of central clearing on wrong-way risk.
cards.statement: Margin mitigates wrong-way risk at a CCP only if exposure builds gradually before a default; jumps and higher volatility during the margin period of risk can exhaust initial margin, and the margin-posting members are mostly systemic banks whose defaults bring the most extreme wrong-way risk.
cards.explanation: If exposure increases gradually before default, margin can be received; a jump in exposure makes margin useless. Initial margin set at normal coverage can be exhausted in a stressed close-out.
cards.originalText: Disagree: margin mitigates WWR only if exposure builds gradually before a default; jumps and higher volatility during the margin period of risk can exhaust initial margin, and the members that post margin are mostly systemic banks whose defaults bring the most extreme WWR.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the implications of central clearing on wrong-way risk.
cards.statement: Margin removes wrong-way risk at a CCP, because variation margin is received continuously as the exposure to a member rises.
cards.explanation: Margin arrives with a lag and cannot keep up with a jump in exposure at default, so it mitigates wrong-way risk but does not remove it.
cards.originalText: Agree: margin removes WWR at a CCP, because variation margin is received continuously as the exposure to a member rises.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the implications of central clearing on wrong-way risk.
cards.statement: Wrong-way risk matters only for uncollateralised counterparties such as corporates, not for margin-posting clearing members.
cards.explanation: The members that actively post margin are mainly banks, which are highly systemic and face the most extreme wrong-way risk.
cards.originalText: Agree: WWR matters only for uncollateralised counterparties such as corporates, and corporates are not clearing members.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the implications of central clearing on wrong-way risk.
cards.statement: Margin posted by a clearing member increases wrong-way risk because it always loses its value when that member defaults.
cards.explanation: Only specific collateral, such as a member's own bonds, is linked to its default. Margin in general still reduces exposure.
cards.originalText: Disagree: margin increases WWR, because collateral posted by a member always loses its value when that member defaults.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the implications of central clearing on wrong-way risk.
cards.statement: Ideally cleared products carry no wrong-way risk, but a clearing member's default can be adversely linked to the value of the CDSs it has traded, so values can move sharply just as it defaults, complicating default management and the wrong-way risk part of margin and default funds.
cards.explanation: A member that has sold protection on names correlated with itself, such as other financials or its sovereign, owes much more exactly when it defaults. This is why single-name CDSs are hard to clear.
cards.originalText: Ideally cleared products carry no WWR, but a member’s default can be adversely linked to the value of the CDSs it has traded (for example, protection sold on correlated financials), so values can move sharply just as it defaults, complicating default management and the WWR part of margin and default funds.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the implications of central clearing on wrong-way risk.
cards.statement: Because CDSs are illiquid by construction, a CCP cannot compute variation margin on them at all.
cards.explanation: Liquidity is a clearability criterion, but CDSs are cleared with variation margin; illiquidity is not the reason they are hard to clear.
cards.originalText: CDSs are illiquid by construction, so a CCP cannot compute variation margin on them at all.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the implications of central clearing on wrong-way risk.
cards.statement: Once CDSs are cleared they carry no wrong-way risk, because multilateral netting offsets protection bought and sold across members.
cards.explanation: Netting offsets market risk across members, but the CCP still faces each member's default, so wrong-way risk remains.
cards.originalText: Once cleared, CDSs carry no WWR, because multilateral netting offsets protection bought and sold across members, so the diﬀiculty is purely operational.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the implications of central clearing on wrong-way risk.
cards.statement: Central clearing does not eliminate wrong-way risk: a CCP's book is matched only while all members perform, a member's default leaves it unmatched just when wrong-way risk bites, and losses beyond the defaulter's resources and the CCP's equity fall on surviving members.
cards.explanation: The CCP has conditional market risk: after a member default it has an unmatched book to hedge and auction, and the defaulter's positions move sharply against it at that moment. Defaulter-pays resources come first, and any excess loss is mutualised.
cards.originalText: Disagree: the book is matched only while all members perform; a default leaves it unmatched just when WWR bites, and losses beyond the defaulter’s resources and CCP equity fall on surviving members.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the implications of central clearing on wrong-way risk.
cards.statement: After novation a CCP has no net market risk in any circumstances, so a member's default cannot produce wrong-way losses for anyone.
cards.explanation: The book is matched only while every member performs. A default leaves the CCP with an unmatched book, which is exactly when wrong-way risk matters.
cards.originalText: Agree: after novation the CCP has no net market risk in any circumstances, so a member’s default cannot produce wrong-way losses for anyone.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the implications of central clearing on wrong-way risk.
cards.statement: Initial margin is designed to cover every possible close-out loss on a defaulting clearing member's positions.
cards.explanation: Initial margin is set to a confidence level, not to cover every loss, so the defaulter-pays resources may prove insufficient under wrong-way risk.
cards.originalText: Agree: the wrong-way risk now sits entirely in the defaulting member’s own initial margin, which by design covers every possible close-out loss.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the implications of central clearing on wrong-way risk.
cards.statement: Clearing increases wrong-way risk mainly because the CCP must post initial margin to its members, which it loses when a member defaults.
cards.explanation: Members post initial margin to the CCP, not the reverse. The risk comes from the defaulter's positions and the mutualised default fund.
cards.originalText: Disagree: clearing increases wrong-way risk mainly because the CCP must post initial margin to its members, which it loses when a member defaults.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
cards.loText: Differentiate among current exposure, peak exposure, expected exposure, and expected positive exposure.
cards.reading: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
cards.statement: For the minimum capital requirement, expected positive exposure is the time-weighted average of the expected exposures over the first year, each weighted by the share of the year that its interval represents.
cards.explanation: With reporting dates at 1, 3, 6 and 12 months the intervals are unequal (1, 2, 3 and 6 months), so weights of 1/12, 2/12, 3/12 and 6/12 apply rather than equal weights.
cards.originalText: The time-weighted average of the expected exposures over the first year, each weighted by the share of the year that its interval represents.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
cards.loText: Differentiate among current exposure, peak exposure, expected exposure, and expected positive exposure.
cards.reading: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
cards.statement: For the minimum capital requirement, expected positive exposure is the simple average of all the expected exposures over the life of the netting set, with each reporting date counted once.
cards.explanation: The capital EPE is taken over the first year, and unequal reporting intervals need time weights, not equal weights.
cards.originalText: The simple average of all the expected exposures out to year 7, with each reporting date counted once.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
cards.loText: Differentiate among current exposure, peak exposure, expected exposure, and expected positive exposure.
cards.reading: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
cards.statement: Expected positive exposure is the highest 95th-percentile exposure reported over the first year.
cards.explanation: That describes a maximum peak exposure, a tail statistic. EPE is a weighted average of expected exposures.
cards.originalText: The highest 95th-percentile exposure reported over the first year.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
cards.loText: Differentiate among current exposure, peak exposure, expected exposure, and expected positive exposure.
cards.reading: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
cards.statement: For the minimum capital requirement, expected positive exposure is the expected exposure at the one-year date.
cards.explanation: The one-year expected exposure is a single point of the expected exposure profile. EPE is the time-weighted average of the profile.
cards.originalText: The expected exposure at the one-year date, since capital is held for one year.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
cards.loText: Explain the treatment of counterparty credit risk (CCR) both as a credit risk and as a market risk and describe its implications for trading activities and risk management for a financial institution.
cards.reading: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
cards.statement: When counterparty credit risk is viewed as a credit risk, its measures are current exposure, peak exposure and expected exposure; when it is viewed as a market risk, they are CVA and the variability of CVA, for example the VaR of CVA.
cards.explanation: Exposures belong to the credit view, while CVA and its changes belong to the market view.
cards.originalText: Credit-risk view: current exposure, peak exposure and expected exposure; market-risk view: CVA and the variability of CVA, for example the VaR of CVA.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
cards.loText: Explain the treatment of counterparty credit risk (CCR) both as a credit risk and as a market risk and describe its implications for trading activities and risk management for a financial institution.
cards.reading: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
cards.statement: CVA and peak exposure are measures of counterparty credit risk viewed as a credit risk, while current exposure and expected exposure belong to the market-risk view.
cards.explanation: CVA is the market view's measure, whereas current, peak and expected exposure are all credit-view measures.
cards.originalText: Credit-risk view: CVA and peak exposure; market-risk view: current exposure and expected exposure.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
cards.loText: Explain the treatment of counterparty credit risk (CCR) both as a credit risk and as a market risk and describe its implications for trading activities and risk management for a financial institution.
cards.reading: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
cards.statement: A bank that treats counterparty credit risk purely as a credit risk can still be exposed to changes in CVA as credit spreads and exposures move, which can produce balance-sheet surprises unless CVA is included in the valuation of its derivatives.
cards.explanation: Limits, collateral and netting manage the default side of CCR. They do not capture changes in the fair value of counterparty risk.
cards.originalText: Changes in the market value of counterparty risk (CVA) as credit spreads and exposures move, which can produce balance-sheet surprises.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
cards.loText: Explain the treatment of counterparty credit risk (CCR) both as a credit risk and as a market risk and describe its implications for trading activities and risk management for a financial institution.
cards.reading: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
cards.statement: Collateral and netting remove every source of counterparty risk except wrong-way risk.
cards.explanation: Collateral and netting do not remove CVA risk, and wrong-way risk is not the only residual risk.
cards.originalText: Wrong-way risk only, since collateral and netting remove every other source of counterparty risk.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
cards.loText: Explain the treatment of counterparty credit risk (CCR) both as a credit risk and as a market risk and describe its implications for trading activities and risk management for a financial institution.
cards.reading: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
cards.statement: Limits, collateral and netting together capture all counterparty risk in a derivatives portfolio.
cards.explanation: Adopting the credit view alone leaves a bank blind to the market view, including changes in CVA.
cards.originalText: None of significance, since limits, collateral and netting together capture all counterparty risk in a derivatives portfolio.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
cards.loText: Explain the treatment of counterparty credit risk (CCR) both as a credit risk and as a market risk and describe its implications for trading activities and risk management for a financial institution.
cards.reading: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
cards.statement: A dealer that treats counterparty risk as a credit risk must replace all of a defaulting counterparty's trades in the market at once at default, whereas a dealer that treats it as a market risk and manages CVA dynamically has already moved trades to other counterparties in proportion to the rising probability of default.
cards.explanation: For the market-view dealer the default is therefore close to a non-event.
cards.originalText: K must replace all of the defaulting counterparty’s trades in the market at once at default; M has already moved trades to other counterparties in proportion to the rising probability of default, so the default is close to a non-event for M.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
cards.loText: Explain the treatment of counterparty credit risk (CCR) both as a credit risk and as a market risk and describe its implications for trading activities and risk management for a financial institution.
cards.reading: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
cards.statement: A dealer that treats counterparty risk as a credit risk replaces the counterparty's trades gradually, in proportion to its probability of default, so the default is a non-event for it.
cards.explanation: That describes the market-risk view. The credit-view dealer must replace all the trades at once at default.
cards.originalText: K replaces the counterparty’s trades gradually, in proportion to its probability of default, so the default is a non-event for K; M must replace all the trades at once at default.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
cards.loText: Explain the treatment of counterparty credit risk (CCR) both as a credit risk and as a market risk and describe its implications for trading activities and risk management for a financial institution.
cards.reading: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
cards.statement: Under both the credit-risk and the market-risk view of counterparty risk, it can be managed only at inception and not before default.
cards.explanation: This is true only of the credit view. The market view acts before default by moving trades as the probability of default rises.
cards.originalText: Neither dealer can act before default, because under both views counterparty risk can be managed only at inception.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
cards.loText: Explain the treatment of counterparty credit risk (CCR) both as a credit risk and as a market risk and describe its implications for trading activities and risk management for a financial institution.
cards.reading: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
cards.statement: Treating counterparty credit risk as a credit risk was the predominant framework from 2000 to 2006 and the basis of Basel II capital, while the market-risk treatment was largely confined to pricing CVA until the 2007-08 financial crisis.
cards.explanation: Potential exposure and EPE models are the hallmark of the credit view, which was established as the basis for regulatory capital under Basel II.
cards.originalText: Treating CCR as a credit risk was the predominant framework from 2000 to 2006 and the basis of Basel II capital, while the market-risk treatment was largely confined to pricing CVA until the 2007-08 crisis.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
cards.loText: Explain the treatment of counterparty credit risk (CCR) both as a credit risk and as a market risk and describe its implications for trading activities and risk management for a financial institution.
cards.reading: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
cards.statement: Stress testing of counterparty credit risk evolved faster than the statistical measures of counterparty credit risk.
cards.explanation: Statistical measures of CCR progressed faster than stress testing.
cards.originalText: Stress testing of CCR evolved faster than the statistical measures of CCR, which is why the chapter builds the statistical measures on top of stress tests.
cards.correction: Stress testing of counterparty credit risk evolved more slowly than the statistical measures of counterparty credit risk.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
cards.loText: Explain the treatment of counterparty credit risk (CCR) both as a credit risk and as a market risk and describe its implications for trading activities and risk management for a financial institution.
cards.reading: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
cards.statement: Before the 2007-08 financial crisis, CVA was a large and volatile part of bank derivative valuations.
cards.explanation: Before the crisis credit spreads were stable and CVA was a small part of valuations.
cards.originalText: Before the crisis CVA was a large and volatile part of bank derivative valuations, which prompted the FAS 157 accounting requirement.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
cards.loText: Explain the treatment of counterparty credit risk (CCR) both as a credit risk and as a market risk and describe its implications for trading activities and risk management for a financial institution.
cards.reading: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
cards.statement: During the 2007-08 crisis, swings in credit spreads and exposures produced large CVA losses but no gains.
cards.explanation: The crisis produced both large losses and large, unusual gains on CVA, because spreads and exposures moved in both directions.
cards.originalText: During the crisis the combined swings in credit spreads and exposures produced large CVA losses but no gains, since credit spreads only widened.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
cards.loText: Describe a stress test that can be performed on a loan portfolio, and on a derivative portfolio.
cards.reading: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
cards.statement: A table of stressed current exposures shows which counterparties would owe the bank most in a scenario, but it cannot say which counterparty is the greater concern, because stressed current exposure ignores credit quality.
cards.explanation: Stressed current exposure ranks exposure, not loss, and omits each counterparty's willingness or ability to pay.
cards.originalText: The table shows which counterparties would owe the bank most if equities fell 25%, but it cannot say whether C or D is the greater concern, because stressed current exposure ignores credit quality.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
cards.loText: Describe a stress test that can be performed on a loan portfolio, and on a derivative portfolio.
cards.reading: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
cards.statement: The sum of the stressed current exposures across counterparties is the loss the bank would suffer in the stress scenario.
cards.explanation: The sum would be the loss only if every counterparty defaulted in the scenario.
cards.originalText: The equity crash would cost the bank about US\$539 million, the sum of the stressed current exposures.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
cards.loText: Describe a stress test that can be performed on a loan portfolio, and on a derivative portfolio.
cards.reading: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
cards.statement: A counterparty with a larger stressed current exposure is necessarily a greater concern than one with a smaller exposure, whatever their credit quality.
cards.explanation: Stressed current exposure ignores credit quality, so a larger exposure to a strong counterparty need not be the greater concern than a smaller exposure to a weak one.
cards.originalText: Counterparty C is a greater concern than counterparty D in this scenario, because its stressed current exposure is larger.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
cards.loText: Describe a stress test that can be performed on a loan portfolio, and on a derivative portfolio.
cards.reading: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
cards.statement: A counterparty whose trades are fully collateralised today needs no further attention in a stress scenario.
cards.explanation: The stressed exposure is measured before any further collateral is collected, so a fully collateralised counterparty can still show a large stressed exposure.
cards.originalText: Counterparty D needs no further attention in this scenario, because its trades are fully collateralised today.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
cards.loText: Describe a stress test that can be performed on a loan portfolio, and on a derivative portfolio.
cards.reading: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
cards.statement: In the expected-loss stress test of a loan portfolio, EAD and LGD are held fixed, each PD is modelled as a function of variables such as the unemployment rate or an important exchange rate, those variables are set to stressed values, and expected loss is recomputed with the stressed PDs.
cards.explanation: The stress loss is the stressed expected loss minus the base expected loss, where expected loss is the sum of PD times EAD times LGD across the pool.
cards.originalText: Hold EAD and LGD fixed, model each PD as a function of variables such as the unemployment rate or an important exchange rate, set those variables to stressed values, and recompute expected loss with the stressed PDs.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
cards.loText: Describe a stress test that can be performed on a loan portfolio, and on a derivative portfolio.
cards.reading: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
cards.statement: The stress test of a loan portfolio holds PDs fixed and stresses each EAD through instantaneous shocks to equity prices and swap rates.
cards.explanation: Loan exposures are insensitive to market variables; the loan stress works through the probability of default.
cards.originalText: Hold the PDs fixed and stress each EAD through instantaneous shocks to equity prices and swap rates, since the loans’ exposures move with market variables.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
cards.loText: Describe a stress test that can be performed on a loan portfolio, and on a derivative portfolio.
cards.reading: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
cards.statement: In the stress test of a loan portfolio, each EAD is replaced with alpha times EPE.
cards.explanation: Alpha times EPE replaces EAD only for derivatives, whose exposure is stochastic. For loans, EAD is taken as deterministic.
cards.originalText: Replace each EAD with alpha times EPE, and stress EPE by re-running the exposure simulation after a market shock.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
cards.loText: Describe a stress test that can be performed on CVA.
cards.reading: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
cards.statement: An instantaneous market shock applied in a CVA stress test changes today's market values, so the expected exposures in all later periods must be recalculated, and the marginal default probabilities are restated from the shocked credit spread.
cards.explanation: Stresses to the marginal probability of default are usually derived from credit spread shocks.
cards.originalText: The shock changes today’s market values, so the expected exposures in all later periods must be recalculated, and the marginal default probabilities are restated from the shocked credit spread.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
cards.loText: Describe a stress test that can be performed on CVA.
cards.reading: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
cards.statement: In a CVA stress test, an instantaneous shock changes only the expected exposure in the first time bucket, while later buckets keep their base values.
cards.explanation: The shock is applied today but affects every later expected exposure, so the whole expected exposure profile has to be recalculated.
cards.originalText: Only the expected exposure in the first time bucket changes, because the shock is instantaneous; later buckets keep their base values.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
cards.loText: Describe a stress test that can be performed on CVA.
cards.reading: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
cards.statement: In a CVA stress test the expected exposures are left unchanged and only LGD is stressed.
cards.explanation: The scenario's main effects are on the exposures and the default probabilities; LGD can also be stressed, but not alone.
cards.originalText: The expected exposures are left unchanged and only the LGD is stressed, since CVA is linear in LGD.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
cards.loText: Describe a stress test that can be performed on CVA.
cards.reading: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
cards.statement: Replacing each period's expected exposure with the stressed current exposure gives the same stressed CVA at lower cost.
cards.explanation: Current exposure is not a substitute for expected exposure; using it is a common pitfall in stress testing CCR.
cards.originalText: The desk replaces each period’s expected exposure with the stressed current exposure, which gives the same answer at lower cost.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
cards.loText: Describe a stress test that can be performed on CVA.
cards.reading: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
cards.statement: A CVA stress uses risk-neutral values, losses over the life of the transactions and a market-based model of default probability, whereas the expected-loss stress of counterparty credit risk uses physical values over a specified horizon.
cards.explanation: Both stresses rely on expected loss being the product of LGD, exposure and probability of default, but the inputs differ.
cards.originalText: The CVA stress uses risk-neutral values, losses over the life of the transactions and a market-based model of default probability, while the expected-loss stress uses physical values over a specified horizon.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
cards.loText: Describe a stress test that can be performed on CVA.
cards.reading: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
cards.statement: The CVA stress and the expected-loss stress of counterparty credit risk both use physical default probabilities over a one-year horizon and differ only in the exposure measure.
cards.explanation: The CVA stress uses risk-neutral default probabilities over the life of the trades, so the two differ in more than the exposure measure.
cards.originalText: Both use physical default probabilities over a one-year horizon; they differ only in the exposure measure.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
cards.loText: Describe a stress test that can be performed on CVA.
cards.reading: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
cards.statement: The expected-loss stress of counterparty credit risk uses default probabilities implied from CDS spreads, while the CVA stress uses historical default rates.
cards.explanation: This swaps the two views: spread-implied probabilities belong to the CVA stress, and the expected-loss stress uses physical probabilities.
cards.originalText: The expected-loss stress uses default probabilities implied from CDS spreads, while the CVA stress uses historical default rates.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
cards.loText: Describe a stress test that can be performed on CVA.
cards.reading: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
cards.statement: The CVA stress and the expected-loss stress give the same stress loss for the same scenario, because both are products of LGD, exposure and default probability.
cards.explanation: The two share a structure but use different inputs, so their values will be quite different.
cards.originalText: Because both are products of LGD, exposure and default probability, the two exercises give the same stress loss for the same scenario.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
cards.loText: Describe a stress test that can be performed on CVA.
cards.reading: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
cards.statement: When CVA is computed with market-implied default probabilities and a model that correlates exposure with default probability, a recommended additional stress test is to stress that correlation, to see the profit-and-loss impact if the correlation is wrong.
cards.explanation: Since the correlation is highly uncertain, institutions should run stress tests to see the impact if it is wrong (Hull and White, 2012).
cards.originalText: A stress of the correlation between exposure and the default probability, to see the profit-and-loss impact if the correlation is wrong.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
cards.loText: Describe a stress test that can be performed on CVA.
cards.reading: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
cards.statement: The DVA term of bilateral CVA captures wrong-way risk.
cards.explanation: DVA reflects the bank's own default and does not capture wrong-way risk. Wrong-way risk comes from the correlation between exposure and the counterparty's default probability.
cards.originalText: A stress of the bank’s own default probability, since the DVA term captures wrong-way risk.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
cards.loText: Describe the common pitfalls in stress testing CCR.
cards.reading: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
cards.statement: For a linear derivative with no intermediate payments, the error from using the change in stressed current exposure in place of the change in expected exposure is largest when the position is close to at the money.
cards.explanation: Current exposure is a hinge at zero, so its change jumps from 0 to the full shock over a narrow band, whereas expected exposure averages over future scenarios and moves smoothly.
cards.originalText: Close to at the money, where the difference between the two changes is almost half the value of the shock.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
cards.loText: Describe the common pitfalls in stress testing CCR.
cards.reading: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
cards.statement: The error from using stressed current exposure in place of expected exposure is largest for a position that is deep in the money.
cards.explanation: Deep in the money both exposures rise by almost the full shock, so the gap is small.
cards.originalText: Deep in the money, because current exposure then takes the full shock while expected exposure takes almost none of it.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
cards.loText: Describe the common pitfalls in stress testing CCR.
cards.reading: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
cards.statement: The error from using stressed current exposure in place of expected exposure is largest for a position that is deep out of the money.
cards.explanation: Deep out of the money both exposures barely move, so the gap is small.
cards.originalText: Deep out of the money, because current exposure stays at zero while expected exposure takes almost all of the shock.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
cards.loText: Describe the common pitfalls in stress testing CCR.
cards.reading: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
cards.statement: More integrated CCR stress tests come from combining the credit-risk view of CCR with the loan portfolio and the market-risk view with the trading book, but combining default stresses and fair-value stresses into one comprehensive test remains the true difficulty.
cards.explanation: The two integrations are the end points of the credit and market views; the remaining difficulty is producing a single comprehensive stress test.
cards.originalText: More integrated stress tests come from combining the credit-risk view of CCR with the loan portfolio and the market-risk view with the trading book, but combining default stresses and fair-value stresses into one comprehensive test remains the true diﬀiculty.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
cards.loText: Describe the common pitfalls in stress testing CCR.
cards.reading: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
cards.statement: The more CCR stress tests a bank runs, the clearer its view of the risk, so the programme should report every available stress result.
cards.explanation: Too many stress tests can hide the risk of a portfolio; a fair number is needed, not every possible result.
cards.originalText: The more CCR stress tests the bank runs, the clearer its view of the risk, so the programme should report every available stress result.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
cards.loText: Describe the common pitfalls in stress testing CCR.
cards.reading: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
cards.statement: A bank that manages counterparty credit risk purely as a credit risk avoids fair-value losses, so it needs to stress only default losses.
cards.explanation: Fair value losses and default losses can occur no matter how a financial institution manages its CCR.
cards.originalText: A bank that manages CCR purely as a credit risk avoids fair-value losses, so it needs to stress only default losses.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
cards.loText: Describe the common pitfalls in stress testing CCR.
cards.reading: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
cards.statement: Central clearing has removed the need for CCR stress testing.
cards.explanation: Regulators moved derivatives to central clearing just as CCR management was advancing; clearing does not make stress testing unnecessary.
cards.originalText: Central clearing has removed the need for CCR stress testing, which is why the chapter describes the recent advances in CCR management as ironic.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
cards.loText: Describe the common pitfalls in stress testing CCR.
cards.reading: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
cards.statement: Running PD and market stresses through expected positive exposure scaled by alpha in the expected-loss framework allows derivative stress losses to be added to loan stress losses.
cards.explanation: Alpha times EPE allows CCR exposures to be placed in a portfolio credit model along with loans, so both are measured in the same units on the same physical-PD basis.
cards.originalText: Run the PD and market stresses through expected positive exposure scaled by alpha in the expected-loss framework, so that derivative stress losses can be added to the loan stress losses.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
cards.loText: Describe the common pitfalls in stress testing CCR.
cards.reading: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
cards.statement: The sum of the stressed current exposures across all counterparties in a scenario is the stress loss of the derivatives book and can be compared with the stress loss of the loan book.
cards.explanation: The sum would be the loss only if every counterparty defaulted, and current exposure ignores credit quality, so it cannot be compared with an expected-loss stress on loans.
cards.originalText: Sum the stressed current exposures across all counterparties in each scenario and report that total as the stress loss of the derivatives book for comparison with the loan book.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
cards.loText: Describe the common pitfalls in stress testing CCR.
cards.reading: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
cards.statement: Delta approximations for repricing derivatives under large scenario shocks are most reliable for portfolios close to at the money.
cards.explanation: CCR is highly nonlinear, and at-the-money portfolios with large price moves are especially prone to errors from delta approximations.
cards.originalText: Reprice the derivatives under the large scenario shocks using delta sensitivities, since the linear approximation is most reliable for portfolios that are close to at-the-money.
cards.correction: Delta approximations for repricing derivatives under large scenario shocks are least reliable for portfolios close to at the money.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
cards.loText: Describe the common pitfalls in stress testing CCR.
cards.reading: CR-21: The Evolution of Stress Testing Counterparty Exposures
cards.statement: Including DVA in a CVA stress test can only reduce reported stress losses and never creates a loss from changes in the bank's own credit quality.
cards.explanation: The bilateral formula can produce counterintuitive results, such as losses when the firm's own credit quality improves; the liability side should be included to capture the full impact on CVA profit and loss.
cards.originalText: Leave DVA out of the CVA stress test, since a bilateral view can only reduce reported stress losses and never creates a loss from changes in the bank’s own credit quality.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define implied correlation and describe how it can be measured.
cards.statement: A Gaussian copula correlation calibrated to market tranche prices is an implied credit correlation with no direct economic interpretation, although it equals the correlation of a Gaussian single-factor model.
cards.explanation: Copula correlations are the values entered in the off-diagonal cells of the copula's correlation matrix. The implied credit correlation is an estimate of the copula correlation derived from market prices.
cards.originalText: The parameter is a copula correlation inferred from prices; it has no direct economic interpretation, but it equals the correlation of a Gaussian single-factor model.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define implied correlation and describe how it can be measured.
cards.statement: A copula correlation calibrated to market tranche prices is the constituents' default correlation, the correlation of their default indicators.
cards.explanation: Default correlation, the correlation of default indicators, is a different concept and is not what the calibration produces.
cards.originalText: The parameter is the constituents’ default correlation, the correlation of their default indicators, so it can be checked against historical joint default frequencies.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define implied correlation and describe how it can be measured.
cards.statement: A copula correlation calibrated to market tranche prices is the constituents' asset return correlation, which can be measured directly as the correlation of their equity returns.
cards.explanation: Asset return correlation drives Merton-type models and is only proxied by equity correlation; neither is the calibrated copula parameter.
cards.originalText: The parameter is the constituents’ asset return correlation, so it can be measured directly as the correlation of their equity returns.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define implied correlation and describe how it can be measured.
cards.statement: A copula correlation calibrated to the observed prices of traded tranches is a physical, real-world correlation.
cards.explanation: A parameter calibrated to traded prices, with CDS-implied default probabilities, is risk-neutral rather than physical.
cards.originalText: The parameter is a physical (real-world) correlation, because it is estimated from the observed prices of liquid traded tranches.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define implied correlation and describe how it can be measured.
cards.statement: A standard credit index tranche has a partial spread01 to each constituent of the index, and moves in spreads or in implied correlation cause mark-to-market changes, whereas in a cash CLO changes in default rates and correlation alter fundamental value.
cards.explanation: A standard tranche has risk-neutral partial spread01s rather than a default01, and each spread01 is itself a function of the implied correlation, which varies in its own right.
cards.originalText: A standard tranche has a partial spread01 to each of the 125 constituents, and moves in spreads or in implied correlation cause mark-to-market changes; in a cash CLO, default rate and correlation changes alter fundamental value.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define implied correlation and describe how it can be measured.
cards.statement: A standard credit index tranche is valued with physical default probabilities taken from the constituents' ratings, so its main sensitivity is a default01.
cards.explanation: Standard tranches are valued with risk-neutral default probabilities from CDS spreads, and their sensitivities are partial spread01s. The default01 is the cash CLO's measure.
cards.originalText: A standard tranche is valued with physical default probabilities taken from the constituents’ ratings, so its main sensitivity is a default01, measured by shocking those probabilities by 10 bp.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define implied correlation and describe how it can be measured.
cards.statement: Implied correlation is a pure credit-risk parameter that is fixed when a standard tranche is first traded, so it causes no mark-to-market changes.
cards.explanation: Implied correlation moves with tranche prices and is a market concept, so changes in it are mark-to-market changes.
cards.originalText: Implied correlation is a pure credit-risk parameter that is fixed when a standard tranche is first traded, so it causes no mark-to-market changes in the desk’s positions.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define implied correlation and describe how it can be measured.
cards.statement: The CDX spread premium is reset every day to the fair spread of the constituents, so standard tranche positions carry no exposure to changes in constituent spreads.
cards.explanation: The CDX spread premium is fixed on the initiation date, so later trading exchanges a present value that moves with the constituent spreads.
cards.originalText: The CDX spread premium is reset every day to the fair spread of the constituents, so standard tranche positions carry no exposure to changes in constituent spreads.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define implied correlation and describe how it can be measured.
cards.statement: Implied correlation is estimated from rating-based physical default probabilities, so it is a credit risk parameter rather than a market risk parameter.
