cards.explanation: This holds only for sufficiently high confidence levels. At a low confidence level, such as 50%, PFE can fall below expected exposure.
cards.originalText: Expected exposure is less than potential future exposure at all (any) confidence levels

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe and calculate the following metrics for credit exposure: expected mark-to-market, expected exposure, potential future exposure, expected positive exposure and negative exposure, effective expected positive exposure, and maximum exposure.
cards.statement: Changing the mean of the future mark-to-market distribution has no impact on potential future exposure, because PFE is conditional on gains.
cards.explanation: PFE is a quantile of the whole distribution of future value, like VaR, so it shifts one-for-one with the mean. It is expected exposure, not PFE, that is described as the mean of the positive part.
cards.originalText: If the mean (mu) is zero, there is no impact on PFE, as PFE is conditional on gains

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe and calculate the following metrics for credit exposure: expected mark-to-market, expected exposure, potential future exposure, expected positive exposure and negative exposure, effective expected positive exposure, and maximum exposure.
cards.statement: For a normally distributed future value, the potential future exposure at the 50% confidence level equals the mean.
cards.explanation: The 50th percentile of a normal distribution is its mean, because the z-score at the median is zero.
cards.originalText: At a 50% confidence level, the PFE is 2.0

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe and calculate the following metrics for credit exposure: expected mark-to-market, expected exposure, potential future exposure, expected positive exposure and negative exposure, effective expected positive exposure, and maximum exposure.
cards.statement: The maximum potential future exposure of a position equals the peak of its expected exposure profile.
cards.explanation: Expected exposure is an average, whereas PFE is a high-confidence worst-case exposure. The peak of the EE profile therefore understates the maximum PFE.
cards.originalText: Because the EE profile has a single peak of 0.50, the maximum PFE over the year is also 0.50
cards.correction: The maximum potential future exposure of a position typically exceeds the peak of its expected exposure profile.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe and calculate the following metrics for credit exposure: expected mark-to-market, expected exposure, potential future exposure, expected positive exposure and negative exposure, effective expected positive exposure, and maximum exposure.
cards.statement: Effective expected exposure is the non-decreasing version of the expected exposure profile.
cards.explanation: At each date it is the highest expected exposure reached so far, so it never falls after a peak.
cards.originalText: The effective EE at 0.75 years is 0.50, because effective EE is the non‑decreasing version of EE

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe and calculate the following metrics for credit exposure: expected mark-to-market, expected exposure, potential future exposure, expected positive exposure and negative exposure, effective expected positive exposure, and maximum exposure.
cards.statement: Effective expected positive exposure depends on a confidence level, typically 99%.
cards.explanation: Effective EPE is an average of expected (mean) exposures, so it involves no quantile or confidence level. Only PFE-type measures depend on a confidence level.
cards.originalText: Because EEPE is a weighted average over time, it is a single number, but it depends on a confidence level, typically 99%, which can be set at more conservative levels
cards.correction: Effective expected positive exposure does not depend on a confidence level.

changes.from: depends on a confidence level, typically 99%
changes.to: does not depend on a confidence level

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe and calculate the following metrics for credit exposure: expected mark-to-market, expected exposure, potential future exposure, expected positive exposure and negative exposure, effective expected positive exposure, and maximum exposure.
cards.statement: If expected exposure rises to a peak and then declines toward zero, effective expected positive exposure is greater than expected positive exposure.
cards.explanation: After the peak, effective EE stays at the peak while EE falls, so the average of effective EE exceeds the average of EE.
cards.originalText: If expected exposure (EE) increases over a few months to a peak, then declines toward zero by the end of the year, EEPE must be greater than EPE

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe and calculate the following metrics for credit exposure: expected mark-to-market, expected exposure, potential future exposure, expected positive exposure and negative exposure, effective expected positive exposure, and maximum exposure.
cards.statement: If expected exposure is monotonically increasing, effective expected positive exposure equals expected positive exposure.
cards.explanation: The non-decreasing constraint never binds when EE never falls, so effective EE equals EE at every date.
cards.originalText: If expected exposure (EE) is monotonically increasing, EEPE is identical to EPE

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe and calculate the following metrics for credit exposure: expected mark-to-market, expected exposure, potential future exposure, expected positive exposure and negative exposure, effective expected positive exposure, and maximum exposure.
cards.statement: The non-decreasing constraint in effective expected exposure is intended to capture roll-over risk for transactions close to maturity that are likely to be replaced in practice.
cards.explanation: Short-dated trades are usually rolled over with the same counterparty, so exposure persists even though EE falls towards maturity.
cards.originalText: The intent of the non‑decreasing constraint (in effective EE and EEPE) is to capture roll‑off or rollover risk, for transactions close to maturity that are likely to be replaced in practice

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe and calculate the following metrics for credit exposure: expected mark-to-market, expected exposure, potential future exposure, expected positive exposure and negative exposure, effective expected positive exposure, and maximum exposure.
cards.statement: Maximum potential future exposure is the average of the PFE values across all time horizons over the life of the transaction.
cards.explanation: Maximum PFE is the peak of the PFE profile over the stated time frame. Averaging exposure over time is what EPE and effective EPE do.
cards.originalText: Maximum PFE is the average of the PFE values across all time horizons over the life of the transaction.
cards.correction: Maximum potential future exposure is the highest of the PFE values across all time horizons over the life of the transaction.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe and calculate the following metrics for credit exposure: expected mark-to-market, expected exposure, potential future exposure, expected positive exposure and negative exposure, effective expected positive exposure, and maximum exposure.
cards.statement: Expected positive exposure is the average of the expected exposure profile across time horizons, and is the time-weighted average when the horizons are unequally spaced.
cards.explanation: EPE collapses the EE profile into a single number by averaging it through time.
cards.originalText: Expected positive exposure (EPE) is the average of the expected exposure (EE) profile across time horizons; with unequal spacing it is the time‑weighted average.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe and calculate the following metrics for credit exposure: expected mark-to-market, expected exposure, potential future exposure, expected positive exposure and negative exposure, effective expected positive exposure, and maximum exposure.
cards.statement: Effective expected positive exposure can never be lower than expected positive exposure for the same exposure profile.
cards.explanation: Effective EE is the running maximum of EE, so it is at least EE at every date and its average is at least the average of EE.
cards.originalText: Effective EE is the non‑decreasing version of EE, so effective EPE can never be lower than EPE for the same exposure profile.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe and calculate the following metrics for credit exposure: expected mark-to-market, expected exposure, potential future exposure, expected positive exposure and negative exposure, effective expected positive exposure, and maximum exposure.
cards.statement: Expected future value can be negative, whereas expected exposure, which sets negative values to zero, cannot.
cards.explanation: Expected future value averages gains and losses, so it can be negative. Expected exposure floors each outcome at zero, so it is never negative.
cards.originalText: Expected future value (expected mark‑to‑market) can be negative, whereas EE, which counts only positive values (negative ones set to zero), cannot.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe and calculate the following metrics for credit exposure: expected mark-to-market, expected exposure, potential future exposure, expected positive exposure and negative exposure, effective expected positive exposure, and maximum exposure.
cards.statement: If the mark-to-market of a contract is negative, its credit exposure is zero.
cards.explanation: A negative mark-to-market makes only current exposure zero. Potential future exposure can still be positive, because the contract may turn positive later.
cards.originalText: If the mark‑to‑market (MtM) of a contract is negative, credit exposure is zero
cards.correction: If the mark-to-market of a contract is negative, its current exposure is zero.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe and calculate the following metrics for credit exposure: expected mark-to-market, expected exposure, potential future exposure, expected positive exposure and negative exposure, effective expected positive exposure, and maximum exposure.
cards.statement: The loan equivalent amount is typically based on expected positive exposure (EPE), the time average of the expected exposure profile.
cards.explanation: The loan equivalent represents the average amount effectively lent to the counterparty, which is what EPE measures. A multiplier may then be applied.
cards.originalText: Expected positive exposure (EPE), the average of the EE profile over time

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe and calculate the following metrics for credit exposure: expected mark-to-market, expected exposure, potential future exposure, expected positive exposure and negative exposure, effective expected positive exposure, and maximum exposure.
cards.statement: The loan equivalent amount is typically based on potential future exposure at a high confidence level such as 95%.
cards.explanation: PFE is a worst-case quantile, not an average amount lent. The loan equivalent is based on expected positive exposure.
cards.originalText: Potential future exposure (PFE) at a high confidence level, such as 95%

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe and calculate the following metrics for credit exposure: expected mark-to-market, expected exposure, potential future exposure, expected positive exposure and negative exposure, effective expected positive exposure, and maximum exposure.
cards.statement: Expected positive exposure (EPE) is the average of the expected exposure values across all dates through the life of the trade.
cards.explanation: EPE reduces the whole EE profile to a single number, which is why it is called the loan equivalent exposure.
cards.originalText: Expected positive exposure (EPE).

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe and calculate the following metrics for credit exposure: expected mark-to-market, expected exposure, potential future exposure, expected positive exposure and negative exposure, effective expected positive exposure, and maximum exposure.
cards.statement: Effective expected positive exposure is the average of the raw expected exposure profile.
cards.explanation: Effective EPE averages the effective, non-decreasing EE profile. It is therefore equal to or higher than EPE, which averages the raw EE.
cards.originalText: Effective expected positive exposure (effective EPE).
cards.correction: Effective expected positive exposure is the average of the effective (non-decreasing) expected exposure profile.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe and calculate the following metrics for credit exposure: expected mark-to-market, expected exposure, potential future exposure, expected positive exposure and negative exposure, effective expected positive exposure, and maximum exposure.
cards.statement: Expected exposure and expected positive exposure may underestimate the exposure of short-dated transactions because they do not take roll-over risk into account.
cards.explanation: EE falls as short-dated trades approach maturity, but in practice they are rolled over or replaced. Effective EE and effective EPE were introduced to correct this understatement.
cards.originalText: EE and EPE may underestimate exposure for short‑dated transactions because they do not take into account roll‑over risk.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe and calculate the following metrics for credit exposure: expected mark-to-market, expected exposure, potential future exposure, expected positive exposure and negative exposure, effective expected positive exposure, and maximum exposure.
cards.statement: Expected exposure and expected positive exposure may overestimate the exposure of short-dated transactions because they do not take roll-over risk into account.
cards.explanation: Ignoring roll-over lowers, not raises, the measured exposure, so EE and EPE underestimate it for short-dated trades.
cards.originalText: EE and EPE may overestimate exposure for short‑dated transactions because they do not take into account roll‑over risk.
cards.correction: Expected exposure and expected positive exposure may underestimate the exposure of short-dated transactions because they do not take roll-over risk into account.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe and calculate the following metrics for credit exposure: expected mark-to-market, expected exposure, potential future exposure, expected positive exposure and negative exposure, effective expected positive exposure, and maximum exposure.
cards.statement: Expected exposure and expected positive exposure may underestimate the exposure of long-dated transactions because they do not take roll-over risk into account.
cards.explanation: The roll-over adjustment targets short-dated transactions, typically those under one year, not long-dated ones.
cards.originalText: EE and EPE may underestimate exposure for long‑dated transactions because they do not take into account roll‑over risk.
cards.correction: Expected exposure and expected positive exposure may underestimate the exposure of short-dated transactions because they do not take roll-over risk into account.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe a simulation approach to calculating credit losses for different tranches in a securitization.
cards.statement: To simulate CLO tranche losses, one estimates the default probabilities and the correlation parameter, generates correlated default times for each loan in the collateral pool, and then runs the resulting default counts through the waterfall to compute losses for each tranche in every simulation thread.
cards.explanation: The parameters drive the simulated default times, and the waterfall is applied to each simulated thread to give a loss for every tranche. This produces a distribution of tranche losses.
cards.originalText: Estimate the default probabilities and the correlation parameter, generate correlated default times for each loan in the collateral pool, and then run the resulting default counts through the waterfall to compute losses for each tranche in every simulation thread.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe a simulation approach to calculating credit losses for different tranches in a securitization.
cards.statement: In a CLO simulation, tranche losses are computed by running the waterfall once at the expected default rate and then adjusting each tranche loss upward to reflect the correlation parameter.
cards.explanation: Correlation must enter the simulation itself, through the correlated default times. A single scenario with a correlation add-on gives no distribution of tranche losses.
cards.originalText: Estimate the default probabilities, run the waterfall once at the expected default rate to compute tranche losses, and then adjust each tranche loss upward to reflect the correlation parameter.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe a simulation approach to calculating credit losses for different tranches in a securitization.
cards.statement: In a CLO simulation, default times are generated for the equity tranche only, and the mezzanine and senior tranche losses are inferred from the equity losses.
cards.explanation: Default times are simulated for every loan in the collateral pool, and the pool's cash flows are run through the waterfall to give each tranche's loss.
cards.originalText: Estimate the correlation parameter, generate default times for the equity tranche only, and then infer the losses of the mezzanine and senior tranches from the equity losses.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe a simulation approach to calculating credit losses for different tranches in a securitization.
cards.statement: When there are almost no market data from which to estimate default correlation, a CLO analyst can infer default intensities from spread data and run the simulation across a range of default probability and correlation pairs to see how tranche results change.
cards.explanation: The copula correlation cannot be estimated reliably, so sensitivity analysis over many (default probability, correlation) pairs is used.
cards.originalText: Infer the default intensities from spread data and run the simulation across a range of default probability and correlation pairs to examine how tranche results change.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe a simulation approach to calculating credit losses for different tranches in a securitization.
cards.statement: The correlation parameter of a copula has a direct economic interpretation as the equity return correlation.
cards.explanation: The copula correlation has no direct economic interpretation. Equity correlation is at best a proxy for asset correlation, not the copula parameter itself.
cards.originalText: Use the observed equity return correlation as the copula correlation, because the copula correlation has a direct economic interpretation as an equity relationship.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe a simulation approach to calculating credit losses for different tranches in a securitization.
cards.statement: When default correlation cannot be observed, setting it to zero is an appropriate way to simulate CLO tranche losses.
cards.explanation: Zero correlation understates the clustering of defaults and the risk to the senior tranche, so tranche losses would be mismeasured.
cards.originalText: Set the correlation to zero, since correlation cannot be observed, and rely on the diversification of the pool to produce the tranche loss distribution.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Analyze the differences in the mechanics of issuing securitized products using a trust versus a special purpose vehicle (SPV) and distinguish between the three main SPV structures: amortizing, revolving, and master trust.
cards.statement: The performance of a credit-linked note issued by a special purpose vehicle depends on the performance of the assets sold to the vehicle, not on the sponsoring entity.
cards.explanation: The vehicle is legally separate and owns the assets, so the note is linked to the performance of those assets rather than to the sponsor's credit.
cards.originalText: The note’s performance depends on the performance of assets that have been sold to the SPV, not on the sponsoring entity.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Analyze the differences in the mechanics of issuing securitized products using a trust versus a special purpose vehicle (SPV) and distinguish between the three main SPV structures: amortizing, revolving, and master trust.
cards.statement: The performance of a credit-linked note issued by a special purpose vehicle depends on the credit of the sponsoring entity that set up the vehicle.
cards.explanation: That describes a note issued by the originator directly. The legal separateness of the vehicle, with a true sale and bankruptcy remoteness, delinks the note from the sponsor.
cards.originalText: The note’s performance depends on the credit of the sponsoring entity that set up the SPV.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Analyze the differences in the mechanics of issuing securitized products using a trust versus a special purpose vehicle (SPV) and distinguish between the three main SPV structures: amortizing, revolving, and master trust.
cards.statement: A special purpose vehicle can issue credit-linked notes only if it is not legally separate from the sponsoring entity.
cards.explanation: The vehicle's legal separateness is what delinks the note from the sponsor, so it is a feature of the structure rather than an obstacle.
cards.originalText: The note can only be issued if the SPV is not legally separate from the sponsoring entity.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Analyze the differences in the mechanics of issuing securitized products using a trust versus a special purpose vehicle (SPV) and distinguish between the three main SPV structures: amortizing, revolving, and master trust.
cards.statement: A revolving structure suits an infrequent issuer whose asset pool consists of short-dated assets with a relatively high prepayment speed, such as credit card debt.
cards.explanation: Principal collections buy new receivables during the revolving period, which fits short-dated, fast-prepaying assets. The master trust is reserved for frequent issuers.
cards.originalText: Revolving structure

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Analyze the differences in the mechanics of issuing securitized products using a trust versus a special purpose vehicle (SPV) and distinguish between the three main SPV structures: amortizing, revolving, and master trust.
cards.statement: A master trust is the structure most likely to be used by an infrequent issuer of securities backed by credit card debt.
cards.explanation: A master trust is used by frequent issuers that issue multiple series from one pool.
cards.originalText: Master trust
cards.correction: A master trust is the structure most likely to be used by a frequent issuer of securities backed by credit card debt.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Analyze the differences in the mechanics of issuing securitized products using a trust versus a special purpose vehicle (SPV) and distinguish between the three main SPV structures: amortizing, revolving, and master trust.
cards.statement: An amortizing structure suits short-dated, fast-prepaying revolving receivables such as credit card debt.
cards.explanation: Amortizing (pass-through) structures suit assets with scheduled amortization, such as mortgages and consumer loans, not short-dated revolving receivables.
cards.originalText: Amortizing structure

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Analyze the differences in the mechanics of issuing securitized products using a trust versus a special purpose vehicle (SPV) and distinguish between the three main SPV structures: amortizing, revolving, and master trust.
cards.statement: A special purpose vehicle used in a true sale can give an originator access to cheaper funding if the credit quality of the securitized assets is higher than the credit quality of the originator's balance sheet.
cards.explanation: A true sale places the assets in a separate vehicle, so investors price the credit quality of the asset pool rather than that of the originator.
cards.originalText: The SPV can give the bank access to cheaper funding if the credit quality of the securitized car loan assets is higher than the credit quality of the bank’s balance sheet.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Analyze the differences in the mechanics of issuing securitized products using a trust versus a special purpose vehicle (SPV) and distinguish between the three main SPV structures: amortizing, revolving, and master trust.
cards.statement: The credit quality of securitized assets is enhanced when the principal value of the securities issued exceeds the principal value of the assets.
cards.explanation: Overcollateralisation enhances credit quality when the securities issued are worth less than the assets, so losses are absorbed by the excess assets.
cards.originalText: The credit quality of the securitized car loan assets is enhanced if the principal value of the securities issued is higher than the principal value of the assets.
cards.correction: The credit quality of securitized assets is enhanced when the principal value of the securities issued is less than the principal value of the assets.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Analyze the differences in the mechanics of issuing securitized products using a trust versus a special purpose vehicle (SPV) and distinguish between the three main SPV structures: amortizing, revolving, and master trust.
cards.statement: In a revolving securitization, principal collections during the revolving period are used to purchase new receivables, and investors are later repaid through controlled amortization or a single soft bullet payment.
cards.explanation: Reinvestment of principal collections in new receivables is the defining feature of a revolving structure. Repayment follows after the revolving period.
cards.originalText: During the revolving period, principal collections are used to purchase new receivables, and investors are later repaid through controlled amortization or a single soft bullet payment.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Analyze the differences in the mechanics of issuing securitized products using a trust versus a special purpose vehicle (SPV) and distinguish between the three main SPV structures: amortizing, revolving, and master trust.
cards.statement: In a revolving securitization structure, principal received from the underlying loans is passed through to investors as it is collected.
cards.explanation: Passing principal through as it is collected describes an amortizing (pass-through) structure. In a revolving structure the principal buys new receivables.
cards.originalText: Principal received from the underlying loans is passed through to investors as it is collected.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Analyze the differences in the mechanics of issuing securitized products using a trust versus a special purpose vehicle (SPV) and distinguish between the three main SPV structures: amortizing, revolving, and master trust.
cards.statement: In a revolving securitization structure, the pool of underlying assets is fixed at closing and cannot be replenished.
cards.explanation: A fixed pool that is not replenished is the amortizing case. Revolving pools are replenished with new receivables during the revolving period.
cards.originalText: The pool of underlying assets is fixed at closing and cannot be replenished.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Analyze the differences in the mechanics of issuing securitized products using a trust versus a special purpose vehicle (SPV) and distinguish between the three main SPV structures: amortizing, revolving, and master trust.
cards.statement: In a true-sale securitization, investors are exposed to the credit risk of the originating bank rather than of the underlying loan pool.
cards.explanation: The true sale to a separate vehicle separates the assets from the originator, so investors bear the risk of the asset pool, not of the originator.
cards.originalText: Investors are exposed to the credit risk of the originating bank rather than of the underlying loan pool.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Analyze the differences in the mechanics of issuing securitized products using a trust versus a special purpose vehicle (SPV) and distinguish between the three main SPV structures: amortizing, revolving, and master trust.
cards.statement: Asset-backed securities backed by credit card receivables typically use a revolving structure.
cards.explanation: Credit card receivables are short-dated, prepay quickly and have no fixed amortization schedule, so principal is returned in lump sums and the revolving structure suits them.
cards.originalText: Credit card debt.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Analyze the differences in the mechanics of issuing securitized products using a trust versus a special purpose vehicle (SPV) and distinguish between the three main SPV structures: amortizing, revolving, and master trust.
cards.statement: Asset-backed securities backed by residential mortgages typically use a revolving structure.
cards.explanation: Residential mortgages repay on an amortization schedule, so they typically use the amortizing (pass-through) structure rather than a revolving one.
cards.originalText: Residential mortgage.
cards.correction: Asset-backed securities backed by residential mortgages typically use an amortizing structure.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Analyze the differences in the mechanics of issuing securitized products using a trust versus a special purpose vehicle (SPV) and distinguish between the three main SPV structures: amortizing, revolving, and master trust.
cards.statement: Asset-backed securities backed by commercial mortgages typically use a revolving structure.
cards.explanation: Commercial mortgages likewise amortize on a schedule, so they typically use the amortizing structure rather than a revolving one.
cards.originalText: Commercial mortgage.
cards.correction: Asset-backed securities backed by commercial mortgages typically use an amortizing structure.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe and explain loan loss provisions and loan loss reserves.
cards.statement: A specific provision on a loan classified as loss reduces pre-tax earnings when it is made, whereas the later write-off of that fully provided loan against the loan loss reserve leaves pre-tax earnings unchanged.
cards.explanation: The provision is an income statement expense that also builds the loan loss reserve. Writing the loan off later removes equal amounts from gross loans and from the reserve, so nothing passes through the income statement again.
cards.originalText: Last year’s provision reduced pre-tax earnings by USD 4 million; this year’s write-off leaves them unchanged.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe and explain loan loss provisions and loan loss reserves.
cards.statement: A specific provision leaves pre-tax earnings unchanged when it is made, and the later write-off of the fully provided loan reduces pre-tax earnings by the loan amount.
cards.explanation: The provision is the expense that hits pre-tax earnings, because it is charged to the income statement. The write-off of a fully provided loan only cleans up the balance sheet and does not reduce earnings again.
cards.originalText: Last year’s provision left pre-tax earnings unchanged; this year’s write-off reduces them by USD 4 million.
cards.correction: A specific provision reduces pre-tax earnings when it is made, and the later write-off of the fully provided loan leaves pre-tax earnings unchanged.

changes.from: leaves pre-tax earnings unchanged when it is made
changes.to: reduces pre-tax earnings when it is made

changes.from: reduces pre-tax earnings by the loan amount

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe and explain loan loss provisions and loan loss reserves.
cards.statement: Loan loss provisions, together with general loss reserves that normally count as Tier 2 capital and are not assigned to specific assets, form the basis of a bank's capacity to absorb losses.
cards.explanation: GARP counts both specific provisions and the general reserve toward loss-absorbing capacity. The general reserve, held against losses not yet identified, is the part that normally counts as Tier 2 capital.
cards.originalText: The provisions, together with the general reserve that normally counts as Tier 2 capital, form the basis of the capacity to absorb losses.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe and explain loan loss provisions and loan loss reserves.
cards.statement: Both specific provisions and general loss reserves are normally counted as Tier 2 capital, since both are loss allowances.
cards.explanation: Only general loss reserves, held against presently unidentified losses, normally count as Tier 2 capital. Provisions against identified deterioration of particular assets do not.
cards.originalText: Both the specific provisions and the general reserve are normally counted as Tier 2 capital, since both are loss allowances.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe and explain loan loss provisions and loan loss reserves.
cards.statement: Only specific provisions add to a bank's capacity to absorb losses, because a general loss reserve is not linked to any particular loan.
cards.explanation: A general reserve is exactly the cushion for losses not yet tied to a particular loan, so it adds to loss-absorbing capacity together with the specific provisions.
cards.originalText: Only the specific provisions add to the capacity to absorb losses, because the general reserve is not linked to any loan.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the requirements for estimating expected loss under IFRS 9.
cards.statement: IFRS 9 replaced the incurred loss model of IAS 39 with an expected loss model, so losses are provided for before any default occurs.
cards.explanation: Under the incurred loss model a loan was impaired only after a loss event. IFRS 9 requires even performing loans to carry a 12-month expected loss, so provisions rise on adoption without new defaults.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the requirements for estimating expected loss under IFRS 9.
cards.statement: IFRS 9 kept the incurred loss model of IAS 39 but required the provision on every impaired loan to cover its lifetime losses.
cards.explanation: IFRS 9 did not keep the incurred loss model. It replaced it with an expected loss model, under which even performing loans carry a provision.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the requirements for estimating expected loss under IFRS 9.
cards.statement: IFRS 9 requires every loan to carry a provision equal to its lifetime expected losses from the day it is granted.
cards.explanation: Under IFRS 9 performing (stage 1) loans carry 12-month expected losses, and lifetime expected losses apply only after credit deterioration (stages 2 and 3). Lifetime losses from origination is the approach of the US CECL standard.
cards.originalText: IFRS 9 required every loan to carry a provision equal to its lifetime expected losses from the day it is granted.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the requirements for estimating expected loss under IFRS 9.
cards.statement: IFRS 9 requires loan loss provisions to be counted as Tier 1 capital.
cards.explanation: An accounting standard does not decide regulatory capital, and loan loss provisions are not Tier 1 capital.
cards.originalText: IFRS 9 required provisions to be counted as Tier 1 capital, so the bank built them up to protect its capital ratios.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the requirements for estimating expected loss under IFRS 9.
cards.statement: Under IFRS 9 as described by GARP, a significant change in the credit environment moves a loan to stage 2 even if the borrower has no payment arrears.
cards.explanation: GARP's stage 2 covers assets in arrears or where a significant change in the credit environment has occurred, for example when the original underwriting would now differ materially on price or terms. Waiting for arrears would recognise deterioration too late.
cards.originalText: Stage 2, because a significant change in the credit environment moves a loan to stage 2 even without arrears.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the requirements for estimating expected loss under IFRS 9.
cards.statement: Under IFRS 9, only a missed payment can move a performing loan out of stage 1.
cards.explanation: A missed payment is only one trigger. A significant change in the credit environment can also move a loan to stage 2 without arrears.
cards.originalText: Stage 1, because only a missed payment can move a performing loan out of stage 1.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the requirements for estimating expected loss under IFRS 9.
cards.statement: Under IFRS 9, a current loan that would now be priced on significantly different terms is treated as nonperforming and placed in stage 3.
cards.explanation: Stage 3 is for nonperforming assets. A fully current loan whose credit environment has changed significantly belongs in stage 2.
cards.originalText: Stage 3, because a loan that would now be priced on different terms is treated as nonperforming.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the requirements for estimating expected loss under IFRS 9.
cards.statement: IFRS 9 requires a forward-looking estimate of expected losses, so provisions should reflect current and expected conditions and not past averages alone.
cards.explanation: GARP states that IFRS 9 requires a forward-looking approach to loan loss estimation and provisioning. Historical data remain a legitimate input, but an estimate that ignores a worsening outlook is not forward-looking.
cards.originalText: IFRS 9 requires a forward-looking estimate, so expected losses should reflect current and expected conditions, not past averages alone.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the requirements for estimating expected loss under IFRS 9.
cards.statement: IFRS 9 prohibits any use of historical loss data in estimating expected losses.
cards.explanation: Historical loss data remain a legitimate input to expected loss estimates. IFRS 9 requires that they be combined with current and forward-looking information.
cards.originalText: IFRS 9 prohibits any use of historical loss data, so the ten-year average must be replaced entirely by external credit ratings.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the requirements for estimating expected loss under IFRS 9.
cards.statement: Under IFRS 9, stage 1 loans require a provision for lifetime expected losses.
cards.explanation: Stage 1 loans carry 12-month expected losses. Lifetime expected losses apply from stage 2.
cards.originalText: Stage 1 loans require lifetime expected losses, so the horizon of the model is too short whatever data it uses.
cards.correction: Under IFRS 9, stage 1 loans require a provision for 12-month expected losses.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe a workout procedure for loss assets and compare the following two approaches used to manage loss assets: retaining loss assets and writing off loss assets.
cards.statement: A supervisor assessing the effectiveness of workout procedures for problem loans looks at the unit's organization and staff, its attempted and successful recoveries by number and volume, and its average time to recovery.
cards.explanation: GARP's assessment criteria cover the organization of the workout function, its performance through attempted and successful recoveries by number and volume, and the average time to recovery.
cards.originalText: The unit’s organization and staff, its attempted and successful recoveries by number and volume, and its average time to recovery.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe a workout procedure for loss assets and compare the following two approaches used to manage loss assets: retaining loss assets and writing off loss assets.
cards.statement: The size of the loan loss reserve relative to the loan book, compared with peer banks, is a measure of the effectiveness of a bank's workout procedures.
cards.explanation: The reserve ratio depends heavily on whether a bank retains or writes off loss assets, and on tax rules, so it does not measure workout effectiveness. Recovery rates, recovery time and the unit's organization do.
cards.originalText: The size of the loan loss reserve relative to the loan book, compared with peer banks in the same country.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe a workout procedure for loss assets and compare the following two approaches used to manage loss assets: retaining loss assets and writing off loss assets.
cards.statement: Promptly writing loss assets off against the reserve, as in the US tradition, is more conservative than retaining them on the books, and a write-off does not mean that recovery on the asset is abandoned.
cards.explanation: GARP calls the prompt write-off approach more conservative. Written-off loss assets are considered nonbankable but not necessarily nonrecoverable, so collection can continue.
cards.originalText: Bank W’s approach is the more conservative, and writing a loss asset off does not mean that recovery on it is abandoned.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe a workout procedure for loss assets and compare the following two approaches used to manage loss assets: retaining loss assets and writing off loss assets.
cards.statement: Retaining loss assets on the books until all collection remedies are exhausted, as in the British tradition, is the more conservative approach because the larger loan loss reserve shows more is provided for each loss asset.
cards.explanation: GARP calls the write-off approach more conservative. The larger reserve under retention only reflects loss assets that are still on the books, not more generous provisioning.
cards.originalText: Bank R’s approach is the more conservative, because its larger loan loss reserve shows it provides more for each loss asset.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe a workout procedure for loss assets and compare the following two approaches used to manage loss assets: retaining loss assets and writing off loss assets.
cards.statement: A bank that writes a loss asset off gives up all collection efforts on it, since a write-off declares the asset to be unrecoverable.
cards.explanation: Written-off assets are nonbankable but not necessarily nonrecoverable, so the bank can keep pursuing recovery after the write-off.
cards.originalText: Bank W gives up all collection efforts on written-off assets, since a write-off declares the asset to be unrecoverable.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe a workout procedure for loss assets and compare the following two approaches used to manage loss assets: retaining loss assets and writing off loss assets.
cards.statement: The choice between retaining and writing off loss assets is set by IFRS 9 staging and so does not vary with the national tax treatment of provisions.
cards.explanation: IFRS 9 staging governs expected loss provisioning, not this choice. GARP says the approach used in a country often depends on the taxation applied to provisions.
cards.originalText: The choice between the approaches is set by IFRS 9 staging, so it does not vary with the national tax treatment of provisions.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Differentiate between through-the-cycle credit rating system and point-in-time credit rating system.
cards.statement: Using point-in-time rather than through-the-cycle PDs in an economic capital model makes capital more volatile and procyclical, because a borrower is less likely to keep the same rating under a point-in-time approach.
cards.explanation: Capital calibrated to current conditions falls when the credit environment improves and rises when it deteriorates. The through-the-cycle approach reduces the volatility of economic capital because ratings are more stable.
cards.originalText: Switching the economic capital model from TTC to PIT PDs would make capital more volatile and procyclical, because a borrower is less likely to keep the same rating under a PIT approach.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Differentiate between through-the-cycle credit rating system and point-in-time credit rating system.
cards.statement: Through-the-cycle ratings are updated promptly to reflect any new information about a borrower, which makes them more volatile and more procyclical than point-in-time ratings.
cards.explanation: Prompt updating and higher volatility describe point-in-time ratings. Through-the-cycle ratings are robust to short-term changes and updated less frequently.
cards.originalText: Because TTC ratings are updated promptly to reflect any new information about a borrower, they are the more volatile of the two philosophies and the more procyclical.
cards.correction: Point-in-time ratings are updated promptly to reflect any new information about a borrower, which makes them more volatile and more procyclical than through-the-cycle ratings.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Differentiate between through-the-cycle credit rating system and point-in-time credit rating system.
cards.statement: Through-the-cycle assessments are mainly employed in banks' internal rating systems, while point-in-time assessments are primarily of interest to the major credit rating agencies.
cards.explanation: The roles are reversed. Point-in-time assessments are usually employed in banks' internal systems, while through-the-cycle assessments are primarily of interest to the major rating agencies.
cards.originalText: TTC assessments are mainly employed in banks’ internal systems for short-term loans, while PIT assessments are primarily of interest for the major credit rating agencies.
cards.correction: Point-in-time assessments are mainly employed in banks' internal rating systems, while through-the-cycle assessments are primarily of interest to the major credit rating agencies.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Differentiate between through-the-cycle credit rating system and point-in-time credit rating system.
cards.statement: Research shows that point-in-time assessments have unambiguously higher predictive power than through-the-cycle assessments, so point-in-time PDs should be used for every purpose, including economic capital.
cards.explanation: Findings from existing research are mixed, so the choice depends on the scope of the analysis. Through-the-cycle PDs are the usual choice for economic capital.
cards.originalText: Research shows that PIT assessments have unambiguously higher predictive power than TTC assessments, so the bank should use PIT PDs for every purpose, including economic capital.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe rating agencies’ assignment methodologies for issue and issuer ratings, and identify the main criticisms of the credit rating agencies’ ratings.
cards.statement: Rating agencies combine analytical and judgmental assessment of a wide range of inputs, gathered from proprietary databases, industry and market reports, and on-site meetings between agency analysts and the rated company's executives.
cards.explanation: GARP describes agency ratings as combining analytical and judgmental approaches over many input data. The judgmental element also underlies the transparency criticism of ratings.
cards.originalText: The rating will combine analytical and judgmental assessment of a wide range of inputs, gathered from proprietary databases, industry and market reports, and on-site meetings between the agency’s analysts and the company’s executives.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe rating agencies’ assignment methodologies for issue and issuer ratings, and identify the main criticisms of the credit rating agencies’ ratings.
cards.statement: A credit rating agency's rating is the output of an automated scoring model applied to the latest financial ratios, with no meeting with management and no qualitative factors.
cards.explanation: That describes an automated internal credit score. Agency ratings combine analytical and judgmental approaches and include on-site meetings with the rated company's executives.
cards.originalText: The rating will be the output of an automated scoring model applied to the latest financial ratios, so no meeting with management is involved and qualitative factors are excluded.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe rating agencies’ assignment methodologies for issue and issuer ratings, and identify the main criticisms of the credit rating agencies’ ratings.
cards.statement: Rating agencies publish one rating on a single scale for all horizons, since short-term and long-term credit risk are measured identically.
cards.explanation: Agencies issue short-term ratings (typically one year) and medium- and long-term ratings, and may adopt different rating scales for different horizons.
cards.originalText: The agency will publish one rating on a single scale for all horizons, since short-term and long-term credit risk are measured identically.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe rating agencies’ assignment methodologies for issue and issuer ratings, and identify the main criticisms of the credit rating agencies’ ratings.
cards.statement: Agency credit ratings are updated in real time as the rated company's share price moves, in the same way as a bank's point-in-time internal score.
cards.explanation: Agency ratings are through-the-cycle in character and updated infrequently. Real-time movement is the point-in-time profile.
cards.originalText: The rating will be updated in real time as the company’s share price moves, in the same way as a bank’s point-in-time internal score.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-7: Credit Scoring and Retail Credit Risk Management
cards.loText: Explain the differences between retail credit risk and corporate credit risk.
cards.reading: CR-7: Credit Scoring and Retail Credit Risk Management
cards.statement: Under Basel II and III, retail banks set aside a relatively small amount of capital, but must provide PD, LGD and EAD for clearly differentiated segments, segmented by credit score or an equivalent measure and by vintage.
cards.explanation: Regulators view retail credit risk as relatively predictable and mortgages as safer, so retail attracts less capital than corporate lending. In return banks must supply PD, LGD and EAD statistics for clearly differentiated segments.
cards.originalText: Retail banks set aside a relatively small amount of capital, but must provide PD, LGD and EAD for clearly differentiated segments, segmented by credit score or an equivalent measure and by vintage.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-7: Credit Scoring and Retail Credit Risk Management
cards.loText: Explain the differences between retail credit risk and corporate credit risk.
cards.reading: CR-7: Credit Scoring and Retail Credit Risk Management
cards.statement: Loans to small businesses can never be managed as retail exposures, because Basel's retail definition covers consumer loans only.
cards.explanation: Small business loans can be treated as retail exposures if the total exposure to the borrower is below EUR 1 million.
cards.originalText: Loans to small businesses can never be managed as retail exposures, because Basel’s retail definition covers consumer loans only.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-7: Credit Scoring and Retail Credit Risk Management
cards.loText: Explain the differences between retail credit risk and corporate credit risk.
cards.reading: CR-7: Credit Scoring and Retail Credit Risk Management
cards.statement: Retail exposures attract more capital than corporate loans of the same size, because retail losses are harder to predict.
cards.explanation: Retail exposures attract relatively less capital than corporate loans under Basel, because retail credit risk is viewed as relatively predictable.
cards.originalText: Retail exposures attract more capital than corporate loans of the same size, because the dark side makes retail losses harder to predict.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-7: Credit Scoring and Retail Credit Risk Management
cards.loText: Explain the differences between retail credit risk and corporate credit risk.
cards.reading: CR-7: Credit Scoring and Retail Credit Risk Management
cards.statement: Basel applies one capital formula to all retail exposures, so a mortgage and a credit card with the same PD carry the same capital requirement.
cards.explanation: Basel treats three retail subsectors (residential mortgages, qualifying revolving credit and other retail) with three different formulas.
cards.originalText: Basel applies one formula to all retail exposures, so a mortgage and a credit card with the same PD carry the same capital requirement.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-7: Credit Scoring and Retail Credit Risk Management
cards.loText: Explain the differences between retail credit risk and corporate credit risk.
cards.reading: CR-7: Credit Scoring and Retail Credit Risk Management
cards.statement: Keeping a single interest rate for all card applicants is likely to cause adverse selection, attracting mainly high-risk customers, and the extent of this may only become apparent when the economic climate deteriorates.
cards.explanation: A one-price-fits-all policy in a competitive market attracts high-risk customers and discourages low-risk ones. This is the case for risk-based pricing by score band.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-7: Credit Scoring and Retail Credit Risk Management
cards.loText: Explain the differences between retail credit risk and corporate credit risk.
cards.reading: CR-7: Credit Scoring and Retail Credit Risk Management
cards.statement: The dark side of retail credit is mainly the risk that a loss on a single large customer exceeds its expected level in a downturn.
cards.explanation: Large single-name exposures define corporate portfolios. The dark side of retail credit is an unforeseen systematic risk factor that influences the behaviour of many credits at once.
cards.originalText: Because retail credit losses are relatively predictable, the dark side of retail credit is mainly the risk that a loss on a single large customer exceeds its expected level in a downturn.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-7: Credit Scoring and Retail Credit Risk Management
cards.loText: Explain the differences between retail credit risk and corporate credit risk.
cards.reading: CR-7: Credit Scoring and Retail Credit Risk Management
cards.statement: Because a retail portfolio behaves like a well-diversified portfolio, its expected loss can be priced in and the bank need not hold any capital against retail unexpected losses.
cards.explanation: Expected loss can be priced in, but regulators still require a relatively small amount of risk capital for retail, because losses can rise to unexpected levels.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-7: Credit Scoring and Retail Credit Risk Management
cards.loText: Explain the differences between retail credit risk and corporate credit risk.
cards.reading: CR-7: Credit Scoring and Retail Credit Risk Management
cards.statement: Under tiered pricing above the cutoff score, the higher a customer's score band, the higher the interest rate charged.
cards.explanation: Under tiered pricing the higher the score, the lower the price.
cards.originalText: Under tiered pricing above the cutoff score, the higher a customer’s score band, the higher the interest rate charged, since high-scoring customers tend to use their credit lines more.
cards.correction: Under tiered pricing above the cutoff score, the higher a customer's score band, the lower the interest rate charged.

changes.from: the higher the interest rate charged
changes.to: the lower the interest rate charged

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-7: Credit Scoring and Retail Credit Risk Management
cards.loText: Discuss the “dark side” of retail credit risk and the measures that attempt to address the problem.
cards.reading: CR-7: Credit Scoring and Retail Credit Risk Management
cards.statement: One prime cause of the dark side of retail credit risk is an operational issue in credit assessment that has a systematic effect on the whole consumer portfolio.
cards.explanation: Consumer credit runs as a semiautomated decision process rather than a series of tailored decisions. An operational error in credit assessment can therefore affect the entire consumer portfolio at once.
cards.originalText: An operational issue in credit assessment that has a systematic effect on the whole consumer portfolio.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-7: Credit Scoring and Retail Credit Risk Management
cards.loText: Discuss the measurement and monitoring of a scorecard performance including the use of cumulative accuracy profile (CAP) and the accuracy ratio (AR) techniques.
cards.reading: CR-7: Credit Scoring and Retail Credit Risk Management
cards.statement: A scorecard is better the closer its cumulative accuracy profile lies to the 45-degree line, which is the benchmark a good model should track.
cards.explanation: The 45-degree line is the random model. The closer a CAP curve sits to it, the worse the scorecard; a better scorecard lies closer to the perfect-model line.
cards.originalText: Y is the better scorecard, because its CAP lies closer to the 45-degree line, which is the benchmark a good model should track.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-7: Credit Scoring and Retail Credit Risk Management
cards.loText: Discuss the measurement and monitoring of a scorecard performance including the use of cumulative accuracy profile (CAP) and the accuracy ratio (AR) techniques.
cards.reading: CR-7: Credit Scoring and Retail Credit Risk Management
cards.statement: The accuracy ratios of two scorecards cannot be compared unless the bank's cutoff score is known.
cards.explanation: A CAP is built from the whole population sorted by score and involves no cutoff, so the accuracy ratios of two scorecards on the same cohort are directly comparable.
cards.originalText: The accuracy ratios of X and Y cannot be compared, because the bank’s cutoff score has not been given.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-7: Credit Scoring and Retail Credit Risk Management
cards.loText: Discuss the measurement and monitoring of a scorecard performance including the use of cumulative accuracy profile (CAP) and the accuracy ratio (AR) techniques.
cards.reading: CR-7: Credit Scoring and Retail Credit Risk Management
cards.statement: A CAP curve that drifts towards the 45-degree line signals deteriorating scorecard performance, which can come from changes in the characteristics or the behaviour of the scored population.
cards.explanation: A curve moving towards the diagonal means the scorecard ranks defaulters less well. GARP attributes such deterioration to changes in the population's characteristics and/or behaviour over time.
cards.originalText: The drift signals deterioration, which can come from changes in the population’s characteristics or behaviour, and the switch to credit cards changes the target population enough to justify a new custom scorecard.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-7: Credit Scoring and Retail Credit Risk Management
cards.loText: Discuss the measurement and monitoring of a scorecard performance including the use of cumulative accuracy profile (CAP) and the accuracy ratio (AR) techniques.
cards.reading: CR-7: Credit Scoring and Retail Credit Risk Management
cards.statement: Scorecard performance usually changes abruptly, so the CAP should be recomputed daily and the scorecard replaced the first time its accuracy ratio falls.
cards.explanation: Scorecard performance tends to deteriorate gradually rather than abruptly, and GARP suggests monitoring it quarterly.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-7: Credit Scoring and Retail Credit Risk Management
cards.loText: Discuss the measurement and monitoring of a scorecard performance including the use of cumulative accuracy profile (CAP) and the accuracy ratio (AR) techniques.
cards.reading: CR-7: Credit Scoring and Retail Credit Risk Management
cards.statement: A scorecard built for one product, such as auto loans, can be reused for a new product such as credit cards, because a scorecard's accuracy ratio depends only on the bank's own default rate.
cards.explanation: A scorecard is built for a particular population. A new product brings a different population and calls for a new custom scorecard.
cards.originalText: The auto-loan scorecard can be reused for the credit card, because a scorecard’s accuracy ratio depends only on the bank’s own default rate.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-7: Credit Scoring and Retail Credit Risk Management
cards.loText: Discuss the measurement and monitoring of a scorecard performance including the use of cumulative accuracy profile (CAP) and the accuracy ratio (AR) techniques.
cards.reading: CR-7: Credit Scoring and Retail Credit Risk Management
cards.statement: Monitoring of a scorecard is needed only once the economic cycle turns, because the characteristics and behaviour of a scored population are stable in normal times.
cards.explanation: Populations and their behaviour change over time in any phase of the cycle, so scorecard monitoring has to be continuous.
cards.originalText: Monitoring is needed only once the economic cycle turns, because the characteristics and behaviour of a scored population are stable in normal times.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-7: Credit Scoring and Retail Credit Risk Management
cards.loText: Discuss the benefits of risk-based pricing of financial services.
cards.reading: CR-7: Credit Scoring and Retail Credit Risk Management
cards.statement: In risk-based pricing, the probability of take-up is an external market input that itself depends on the price and credit limit offered, while the cost of equity capital is an internal input.
cards.explanation: Risk-based pricing draws on external market data, such as the probability of take-up, which is a function of price and credit limit. It also draws on internal inputs such as the cost of equity capital.
cards.originalText: The probability of take-up is an external market input that itself depends on the price and credit limit offered, while the cost of equity capital is an internal input.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-7: Credit Scoring and Retail Credit Risk Management
cards.loText: Discuss the benefits of risk-based pricing of financial services.
cards.reading: CR-7: Credit Scoring and Retail Credit Risk Management
cards.statement: Once the PD of a score band is known, the price can be set from the PD alone, since LGD, EAD and allocated capital are the same for every account.
cards.explanation: PD is only one of the inputs to a risk-based price. LGD, EAD and allocated capital differ across accounts and are priced in as well.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-7: Credit Scoring and Retail Credit Risk Management
cards.loText: Discuss the benefits of risk-based pricing of financial services.
cards.reading: CR-7: Credit Scoring and Retail Credit Risk Management
cards.statement: Operating expenses are left out of risk-based pricing, because it prices credit risk only.
cards.explanation: Operating expenses are an explicit input to risk-based pricing, together with take-up probability, PD, LGD, EAD, allocated capital and the cost of equity capital.
cards.originalText: Operating expenses are left out, because risk-based pricing prices credit risk only.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-7: Credit Scoring and Retail Credit Risk Management
cards.loText: Discuss the benefits of risk-based pricing of financial services.
cards.reading: CR-7: Credit Scoring and Retail Credit Risk Management
cards.statement: In risk-based pricing, the probability of take-up is an internal input, estimated from the bank's own default history in each score band.
cards.explanation: Take-up is the probability that the customer accepts the offer, an external market input depending on price and credit limit. It is not estimated from default history.
cards.originalText: The probability of take-up is an internal input, estimated from the bank’s own default history in each score band.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-7: Credit Scoring and Retail Credit Risk Management
cards.loText: Discuss the benefits of risk-based pricing of financial services.
cards.reading: CR-7: Credit Scoring and Retail Credit Risk Management
cards.statement: Risk-based pricing is now mature in retail banking, and banks' key business objectives are generally well reflected in their pricing strategies.
cards.explanation: Risk-based pricing in retail financial services remains in its infancy, and banks' key business objectives are seldom adequately reflected in their pricing.
cards.originalText: Risk-based pricing is now mature in retail banking, and banks’ key business objectives are generally well reflected in their pricing strategies.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-7: Credit Scoring and Retail Credit Risk Management
cards.loText: Discuss the benefits of risk-based pricing of financial services.
cards.reading: CR-7: Credit Scoring and Retail Credit Risk Management
cards.statement: Under risk-based pricing the bank no longer faces a trade-off between growing market share and limiting the rate of bad accounts.
cards.explanation: Pricing is used to balance market share against the rate of bad accounts, so the trade-off remains under risk-based pricing.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-7: Credit Scoring and Retail Credit Risk Management
cards.loText: Discuss the benefits of risk-based pricing of financial services.
cards.reading: CR-7: Credit Scoring and Retail Credit Risk Management
cards.statement: Risk-based pricing suits banks only, and nonbanks that extend credit to consumers should avoid it because it does not apply outside banking.
cards.explanation: GARP says risk-based pricing should also be used when nonbanks offer credit. The obstacle is that many nonbanks lack the logistical and operational infrastructure.
cards.originalText: Risk-based pricing suits banks only; nonbanks that extend credit to consumers should avoid it because it does not apply outside banking.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-8: Country Risk: Determinants, Measures, and Implications
cards.loText: Compare the use of credit ratings, market-based credit default spreads, and CDS spreads in predicting default.
cards.reading: CR-8: Country Risk: Determinants, Measures, and Implications
cards.statement: Default spreads give a more granular and more dynamic view of sovereign default risk than ratings, but they are more volatile and can move with liquidity and investor demand for reasons unrelated to default.
cards.explanation: Market spreads differentiate risk more finely than rating agencies, for example by separating two countries with the same rating. They tend to be far more volatile than ratings and can be affected by liquidity and investor demand.
cards.originalText: Spreads give a more granular and more dynamic view of default risk than ratings, but they are more volatile and can move with liquidity and investor demand for reasons unrelated to default.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-8: Country Risk: Determinants, Measures, and Implications
cards.loText: Compare the use of credit ratings, market-based credit default spreads, and CDS spreads in predicting default.
cards.reading: CR-8: Country Risk: Determinants, Measures, and Implications
cards.statement: Default spreads on sovereign bonds are less volatile than credit ratings.
cards.explanation: Market-based default spreads are far more volatile than ratings, which are updated infrequently.
cards.originalText: Default spreads are less volatile than ratings, because they average the views of many investors.
cards.correction: Default spreads on sovereign bonds are more volatile than credit ratings.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-8: Country Risk: Determinants, Measures, and Implications
cards.loText: Compare the use of credit ratings, market-based credit default spreads, and CDS spreads in predicting default.
cards.reading: CR-8: Country Risk: Determinants, Measures, and Implications
cards.statement: Sovereign default spreads can be compared across countries by measuring each country's local currency bond yield against the US Treasury yield.
cards.explanation: Local currency yields embed expected inflation, so they cannot be compared across countries. A default spread needs a default-free bond in the same currency as the bond being assessed.
cards.originalText: The same comparison could be made with the three countries’ local currency bond yields, provided each is measured against the US Treasury yield.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-8: Country Risk: Determinants, Measures, and Implications
cards.loText: Compare the use of credit ratings, market-based credit default spreads, and CDS spreads in predicting default.
cards.reading: CR-8: Country Risk: Determinants, Measures, and Implications
cards.statement: After a credit event such as a failure to pay, a restructuring or a bankruptcy, the CDS seller either buys the reference bonds at par or pays par minus their market price, and the protection is only as good as the seller's own credit standing.
cards.explanation: The seller settles physically by buying the bonds at par, or in cash by paying par minus the market price. The buyer is exposed to the seller's ability to pay.
cards.originalText: After a failure to pay, a restructuring or a bankruptcy, the seller either buys the bonds at par or pays par minus their market price, and the protection is only as good as the seller’s own credit standing.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-8: Country Risk: Determinants, Measures, and Implications
cards.loText: Compare the use of credit ratings, market-based credit default spreads, and CDS spreads in predicting default.
cards.reading: CR-8: Country Risk: Determinants, Measures, and Implications
cards.statement: If a bond's price falls sharply in a liquidity squeeze while the issuer keeps paying, the CDS protection seller must compensate the buyer for the fall.
cards.explanation: A CDS pays out only after a credit event. A price fall without a credit event is not compensated.
cards.originalText: If the bonds’ price falls sharply in a liquidity squeeze while Colombia keeps paying, the protection seller must compensate the manager for the fall.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-8: Country Risk: Determinants, Measures, and Implications
cards.loText: Compare the use of credit ratings, market-based credit default spreads, and CDS spreads in predicting default.
cards.reading: CR-8: Country Risk: Determinants, Measures, and Implications
cards.statement: A CDS protection buyer carries no exposure to the protection seller when the reference entity is a sovereign.
cards.explanation: The protection buyer is exposed to the seller's ability to pay whatever the reference entity is.
cards.originalText: Because the reference entity is a sovereign, the manager carries no exposure to the protection seller.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-8: Country Risk: Determinants, Measures, and Implications
cards.loText: Compare the use of credit ratings, market-based credit default spreads, and CDS spreads in predicting default.
cards.reading: CR-8: Country Risk: Determinants, Measures, and Implications
cards.statement: Under cash settlement of a CDS, the seller pays the full par value and also takes delivery of the bonds.
cards.explanation: Cash settlement pays par minus the market price of the bonds, with no delivery. Physical settlement pays par against delivery of the bonds.
cards.originalText: Under cash settlement the seller pays the full par value of USD 10 million and also takes delivery of the bonds.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-8: Country Risk: Determinants, Measures, and Implications
cards.loText: Compare the use of credit ratings, market-based credit default spreads, and CDS spreads in predicting default.
cards.reading: CR-8: Country Risk: Determinants, Measures, and Implications
cards.statement: A change in a sovereign rating remains an informational event with a price impact when it occurs, and bond markets draw on ratings just as agencies draw on market data, so ratings remain useful alongside spreads.
cards.explanation: Although market measures lead the agencies, it would be a mistake to conclude that sovereign ratings are useless. Bond markets use ratings and rating changes when pricing bonds.
cards.originalText: A rating change is still an informational event with a price impact when it occurs, and bond markets draw on ratings just as agencies draw on market data, so ratings remain useful alongside spreads.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-8: Country Risk: Determinants, Measures, and Implications
cards.loText: Compare the use of credit ratings, market-based credit default spreads, and CDS spreads in predicting default.
cards.reading: CR-8: Country Risk: Determinants, Measures, and Implications
cards.statement: Credit ratings are better predictors of sovereign default than either market default spreads or CDS spreads.
cards.explanation: Market measures adjust faster than ratings, and changes in CDS spreads are emerging as better predictors of default than ratings.
cards.originalText: Ratings are better predictors of default than either market measure, because each rating is set only after a committee review.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-8: Country Risk: Determinants, Measures, and Implications
cards.loText: Compare the use of credit ratings, market-based credit default spreads, and CDS spreads in predicting default.
cards.reading: CR-8: Country Risk: Determinants, Measures, and Implications
cards.statement: Sovereign default spreads are uncorrelated with credit ratings, so the two measures carry unrelated information.
cards.explanation: Default spreads are correlated with both ratings and actual default.
cards.originalText: Default spreads are uncorrelated with ratings, so the two measures carry unrelated information and both should be kept.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-8: Country Risk: Determinants, Measures, and Implications
cards.loText: Compare the use of credit ratings, market-based credit default spreads, and CDS spreads in predicting default.
cards.reading: CR-8: Country Risk: Determinants, Measures, and Implications
cards.statement: Changes in sovereign CDS spreads tend to lead changes in bond yields and ratings, but a spike may reflect counterparty and liquidity risk rather than higher default risk.
cards.explanation: CDS spreads are the most timely signal. Counterparty and liquidity risk, endemic to the CDS market, can move CDS prices in ways that have little to do with default risk.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-8: Country Risk: Determinants, Measures, and Implications
cards.loText: Compare the use of credit ratings, market-based credit default spreads, and CDS spreads in predicting default.
cards.reading: CR-8: Country Risk: Determinants, Measures, and Implications
cards.statement: Evidence shows sovereign CDS spreads to be clearly superior to default spreads on government bonds as a measure of default risk.
cards.explanation: CDS changes provide information, albeit noisy, but there is little to indicate that they are superior to market default spreads obtained from government bonds.
cards.originalText: Sovereign CDS spreads update continuously, and the evidence shows them to be clearly superior to default spreads on government bonds as a measure of default risk.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-8: Country Risk: Determinants, Measures, and Implications
cards.loText: Compare the use of credit ratings, market-based credit default spreads, and CDS spreads in predicting default.
cards.reading: CR-8: Country Risk: Determinants, Measures, and Implications
cards.statement: Default spreads on sovereign bonds tend to widen only after a rating downgrade, so the bond market confirms agency assessments rather than anticipating them.
cards.explanation: The sovereign bond market leads the rating agencies: default spreads usually climb ahead of a downgrade and drop before an upgrade.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define a credit default swap (CDS) and explain its mechanics including the obligations of both the default protection buyer and the default protection seller.
cards.statement: In a credit default swap, physical settlement has the buyer deliver bonds with a face value equal to the notional and receive that face value, while cash settlement has the seller pay the notional times one minus the auction value of the cheapest deliverable bond per unit of face value.
cards.explanation: Both routes leave the buyer with about the face value: either cash from the seller, or the face value paid for delivered bonds. Cash settlement pays the loss, notional times (1 minus the recovery value).
cards.originalText: Physical settlement: the buyer delivers bonds with a face value equal to the notional and receives their face value; cash settlement: the seller pays the notional times one minus the auction value of the cheapest deliverable bond per unit of face value.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define a credit default swap (CDS) and explain its mechanics including the obligations of both the default protection buyer and the default protection seller.
cards.statement: In a credit default swap, physical settlement has the seller deliver the reference entity's bonds to the buyer at their post-default price, while cash settlement has the seller pay the buyer the market value of the defaulted bonds.
cards.explanation: In physical settlement the buyer delivers the bonds and receives face value. Cash settlement pays the loss (notional times one minus the recovery value), not the recovery value.
cards.originalText: Physical settlement: the seller delivers the reference entity’s bonds to the buyer at their post-default price; cash settlement: the seller pays the buyer the market value of the defaulted bonds.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define a credit default swap (CDS) and explain its mechanics including the obligations of both the default protection buyer and the default protection seller.
cards.statement: In a credit default swap, physical settlement has the reference entity buy back its bonds from the buyer at face value, while cash settlement has the seller pay the buyer the full notional.
cards.explanation: The reference entity is not a party to the CDS. Under physical settlement the seller buys the bonds at face value, and cash settlement pays only the loss, not the full notional.
