cards.originalText: Physical settlement: the reference entity buys back its bonds from the buyer at face value; cash settlement: the seller pays the buyer the full notional.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define a credit default swap (CDS) and explain its mechanics including the obligations of both the default protection buyer and the default protection seller.
cards.statement: When a CDS allowing delivery of several bonds is cash settled through an auction, the auction values the cheapest deliverable bond and the seller pays the notional times one minus that value, so the cheapest-to-deliver option benefits the protection buyer.
cards.explanation: The buyer may deliver any eligible bond and will choose the cheapest, so the cheapest bond sets the payoff. The delivery option therefore belongs to the buyer and makes protection more valuable.
cards.originalText: The auction values the cheapest deliverable bond, the one trading at 35, so the seller pays 65% of notional; the cheapest-to-deliver option benefits the protection buyer.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define a credit default swap (CDS) and explain its mechanics including the obligations of both the default protection buyer and the default protection seller.
cards.statement: The payoff of a cash-settled CDS is based on the average of the prices of the deliverable bonds, so neither party gains from the choice of bond.
cards.explanation: The payoff is not an average. The cheapest deliverable bond sets it, and the choice of bond is an option held by the protection buyer.
cards.originalText: The payoff is based on the average of the three prices, so neither party gains from the choice of bond.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define a credit default swap (CDS) and explain its mechanics including the obligations of both the default protection buyer and the default protection seller.
cards.statement: The payoff of a cash-settled CDS is based on the most expensive deliverable bond, and the choice of bond benefits the protection seller.
cards.explanation: The cheapest deliverable bond sets the payoff, so the option benefits the protection buyer, not the seller.
cards.originalText: The payoff is based on the bond trading at 41, so the seller pays 59% of notional; the choice of bond benefits the protection seller.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define a credit default swap (CDS) and explain its mechanics including the obligations of both the default protection buyer and the default protection seller.
cards.statement: When the quoted CDS spread is below the standard fixed coupon, the seller pays the buyer the present value of the difference upfront, and afterwards the buyer pays the fixed coupon until maturity or a credit event.
cards.explanation: Paying a coupon above the market spread overpays the seller, so the seller compensates the buyer upfront. After that the running payment is the standard coupon.
cards.originalText: The seller pays the buyer the present value of the 40 bp a year difference upfront; afterwards the buyer pays the 100 bp coupon until maturity or a credit event.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define a credit default swap (CDS) and explain its mechanics including the obligations of both the default protection buyer and the default protection seller.
cards.statement: No upfront payment is made on a standard-coupon CDS when the quoted spread is below the coupon, and the buyer simply pays the quoted spread each year.
cards.explanation: An upfront payment is needed whenever the quoted spread and the standard coupon differ, and the running payment is the coupon, not the quoted spread.
cards.originalText: No upfront payment is made because the quoted spread is below the coupon; the buyer pays 60 bp a year.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define a credit default swap (CDS) and explain its mechanics including the obligations of both the default protection buyer and the default protection seller.
cards.statement: When the quoted CDS spread is below the standard fixed coupon, the buyer pays the seller the present value of the difference upfront and then pays the coupon.
cards.explanation: When the spread is below the coupon, the seller pays the buyer the upfront amount. The buyer pays upfront only when the quoted spread is above the coupon.
cards.originalText: The buyer pays the seller the present value of the 40 bp a year difference upfront; afterwards the buyer pays the 100 bp coupon.
cards.correction: When the quoted CDS spread is below the standard fixed coupon, the seller pays the buyer the present value of the difference upfront and then the buyer pays the coupon.

changes.from: the buyer pays the seller the present value
changes.to: the seller pays the buyer the present value
and then the buyer pays the coupon

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define a credit default swap (CDS) and explain its mechanics including the obligations of both the default protection buyer and the default protection seller.
cards.statement: The position of a CDS buyer is approximately that of someone long a risk-free bond and short a corporate bond: the buyer gains as the issuer's credit worsens and pays about the credit spread to hold the position.
cards.explanation: A corporate bond plus bought protection is approximately a risk-free bond, so protection is approximately a long risk-free bond plus a short corporate bond.
cards.originalText: A corporate bond plus bought protection is approximately a risk-free bond, so bought protection is approximately a long risk-free bond plus a short corporate bond: the buyer gains as the issuer’s credit worsens and pays about the credit spread to hold the position.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define a credit default swap (CDS) and explain its mechanics including the obligations of both the default protection buyer and the default protection seller.
cards.statement: A CDS buyer gains when the reference entity's credit quality improves, as a holder of its bonds would.
cards.explanation: That describes the CDS seller or a bondholder, who is long the credit. The buyer gains when the reference entity's credit worsens.
cards.originalText: The buyer gains when the reference entity’s credit improves, as a holder of its bonds would.
cards.correction: A CDS seller gains when the reference entity's credit quality improves, as a holder of its bonds would.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define a credit default swap (CDS) and explain its mechanics including the obligations of both the default protection buyer and the default protection seller.
cards.statement: A CDS buyer pays the risk-free rate and receives the corporate yield, so the position earns the credit spread.
cards.explanation: Earning the credit spread is the seller's side. The CDS buyer pays about the credit spread for protection.
cards.originalText: The buyer pays the risk-free rate and receives the corporate yield, so the position earns the credit spread.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define a credit default swap (CDS) and explain its mechanics including the obligations of both the default protection buyer and the default protection seller.
cards.statement: A CDS buyer has no exposure to the reference entity unless it also owns the entity's bonds.
cards.explanation: The buyer's exposure comes from the contract itself, and owning the bonds is not required.
cards.originalText: The statement is false: a CDS buyer has no exposure to the reference entity unless it also owns the entity’s bonds.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define a credit default swap (CDS) and explain its mechanics including the obligations of both the default protection buyer and the default protection seller.
cards.statement: In a credit-linked note issued through an SPV, the investor pays the principal upfront and bears the credit risk of the assets sold to the SPV, with no credit linkage to the sponsoring entity.
cards.explanation: Unlike a note issued directly by the originator, an SPV-issued note is linked to the assets sold to the SPV. Its performance depends on those assets, and the note is funded by the investor's principal.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define a credit default swap (CDS) and explain its mechanics including the obligations of both the default protection buyer and the default protection seller.
cards.statement: In a total return swap used to finance a bond purchase, the total return receiver retains ownership of the bond, and the spread over the floating rate compensates the receiver for the risk that the payer defaults.
cards.explanation: In this structure the total return payer buys and retains ownership of the bond. The spread over the floating rate compensates the payer for the risk that the receiver defaults.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define a credit default swap (CDS) and explain its mechanics including the obligations of both the default protection buyer and the default protection seller.
cards.statement: The buyer of protection in a credit default swap must own bonds of the reference entity, as with an insurance contract.
cards.explanation: Unlike an insurance contract, a CDS does not require the buyer to own the underlying asset. CDS volume on a company can exceed its outstanding debt.
cards.originalText: In a credit default swap, the protection buyer must own bonds of the reference entity, as with an insurance contract, and receives the notional times one minus the auction price after a credit event.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define a credit default swap (CDS) and explain its mechanics including the obligations of both the default protection buyer and the default protection seller.
cards.statement: In a synthetic CDO priced with the one-factor Gaussian copula, base correlation is the correlation that prices each individual tranche, while compound correlation prices the tranche from zero to its detachment point.
cards.explanation: The definitions are reversed. Compound (tranche) correlation prices an individual tranche, while base correlation prices the tranche from zero to its detachment point.
cards.correction: In a synthetic CDO priced with the one-factor Gaussian copula, compound correlation is the correlation that prices each individual tranche, while base correlation prices the tranche from zero to its detachment point.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the significance of estimating default correlation for credit portfolios and distinguish between reduced form and structural default correlation models.
cards.statement: Default correlation is the major reason that risk-neutral default probabilities are greater than real-world default probabilities, because correlated defaults create systematic risk that investors require compensation for.
cards.explanation: Default correlation means credit risk cannot be completely diversified away. Correlated defaults are systematic risk, which is priced into spreads.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the significance of estimating default correlation for credit portfolios and distinguish between reduced form and structural default correlation models.
cards.statement: Credit contagion, where one company's default triggers the default of another, reduces default correlation.
cards.explanation: Contagion, where one default causes another, is a reason default correlation exists, so it increases default correlation.
cards.originalText: Credit contagion, where one company’s default triggers another’s, reduces default correlation, because the surviving companies take over the defaulted company’s business.
cards.correction: Credit contagion, where one company's default triggers the default of another, increases default correlation.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the significance of estimating default correlation for credit portfolios and distinguish between reduced form and structural default correlation models.
cards.statement: In a reduced form model, perfectly correlated hazard rates for two companies make it highly likely that both default within the same short period.
cards.explanation: Even perfectly correlated hazard rates leave joint default in a short period unlikely, which is the main weakness of reduced form models for modelling default correlation.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the significance of estimating default correlation for credit portfolios and distinguish between reduced form and structural default correlation models.
cards.statement: Because default is rare, default correlation can be ignored in a well-diversified portfolio of investment-grade bonds without affecting the tail of the loss distribution.
cards.explanation: Rarity of default does not make correlation negligible. Default correlation drives the tail of the loss distribution, and diversification cannot remove the common component.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe how to estimate credit VaR using the Gaussian copula and the CreditMetrics approach.
cards.statement: Raising the copula correlation lowers the worst case default rate, because more correlated loans behave like fewer independent loans.
cards.explanation: Higher correlation raises the worst case default rate, because clustering of defaults makes the bad years worse.
cards.originalText: Raising the copula correlation from 0.1 to 0.2 lowers the WCDR, because more correlated loans behave like fewer independent loans.
cards.correction: Raising the copula correlation raises the worst case default rate, because more correlated loans behave like fewer independent loans.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe how to estimate credit VaR using the Gaussian copula and the CreditMetrics approach.
cards.statement: In the Gaussian copula credit VaR model, raising the recovery rate lowers the worst case default rate.
cards.explanation: Recovery affects the credit VaR, because each default costs less, but it leaves the worst case default rate unchanged.
cards.originalText: Raising the recovery rate from 60% to 70% lowers the WCDR, because each default then costs less.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe how to estimate credit VaR using the Gaussian copula and the CreditMetrics approach.
cards.statement: With a copula correlation of zero, the worst case default rate at a 99.9% confidence level still exceeds the PD, because the confidence level always adds a tail term.
cards.explanation: With zero correlation the tail term vanishes and the worst case default rate equals the PD, because the law of large numbers removes uncertainty about the default rate.
cards.originalText: With a copula correlation of zero, the WCDR would still exceed the 2% PD, because the 99.9% confidence level always adds a tail term.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe a credit derivative, credit default swap (CDS), total return swap, and collateralized debt obligation (CDO).
cards.statement: An investor in a credit-linked note issued directly by a bank has sold protection on the reference entity in funded form: after a credit event its principal is repaid less the loss, and it is also exposed to the issuing bank's own credit risk.
cards.explanation: The investor pays principal at issue and the coupon spread is its premium for bearing the reference entity's credit risk. Because the issuer holds the cash and repays the note, the investor also bears the issuer's credit risk.
cards.originalText: The insurer has sold protection on Y in funded form: after a credit event its principal is repaid less the loss on Y, and because Bank X issued the note directly the insurer is also exposed to Bank X’s own credit risk.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe a credit derivative, credit default swap (CDS), total return swap, and collateralized debt obligation (CDO).
cards.statement: The investor in a credit-linked note is the protection buyer: if the reference entity suffers a credit event, the issuing bank compensates the investor for the loss.
cards.explanation: The note investor is the protection seller and loses when the reference entity suffers a credit event.
cards.originalText: The insurer is the protection buyer: if Y suffers a credit event, Bank X compensates the insurer for the loss on Y.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe a credit derivative, credit default swap (CDS), total return swap, and collateralized debt obligation (CDO).
cards.statement: Like a seller of CDS protection, a credit-linked note investor pays nothing at inception and pays cash only if the reference entity suffers a credit event.
cards.explanation: That describes an unfunded CDS sale. A credit-linked note is funded, so the investor pays the principal at issue.
cards.originalText: Like a seller of CDS protection, the insurer pays nothing at inception and pays cash only if Y suffers a credit event.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe a credit derivative, credit default swap (CDS), total return swap, and collateralized debt obligation (CDO).
cards.statement: A credit event at the reference entity of a credit-linked note does not reduce the redemption amount, because the coupon spread compensates the investor only for the issuer's own credit risk.
cards.explanation: The redemption amount is reduced by credit losses on the reference entity. That is the credit link of the note.
cards.originalText: Because Bank X holds the insurer’s cash, the coupon spread compensates the insurer for Bank X’s credit risk only, and a credit event at Y would not reduce the redemption amount.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain how to account for credit risk exposure in valuing a CDS.
cards.statement: Re-running the valuation of a regular CDS with a different recovery rate, after re-implying the hazard rate from the same quotes, changes its value very little, whereas a binary CDS on the same name is far more sensitive to the recovery assumption.
cards.explanation: When the hazard rate is implied from market spreads, implied PDs scale roughly with 1/(1-R) while the payoff scales with (1-R), so the effects largely offset for a regular CDS. A binary CDS pays a fixed amount, so it does not offset.
cards.originalText: Re-running the valuation of a regular CDS with a 20% recovery rate, re-implying the hazard rate from the same quotes, changes its value very little; a binary CDS on the same name is far more sensitive to the assumption.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain how to account for credit risk exposure in valuing a CDS.
cards.statement: Leaving out the accrual payment on default lowers the breakeven spread of a CDS.
cards.explanation: Without the accrual term the denominator of the breakeven spread formula shrinks, so the breakeven spread rises.
cards.originalText: Leaving out the accrual payment on default lowers the breakeven spread, because the buyer is then assumed to pay less.
cards.correction: Leaving out the accrual payment on default raises the breakeven spread of a CDS.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain how to account for credit risk exposure in valuing a CDS.
cards.statement: A binary CDS on a name should trade at a lower spread than the regular CDS on the same name, because its payoff is fixed in advance.
cards.explanation: A binary CDS pays the whole notional on default rather than only the loss (1 minus recovery), so it costs more and trades at a higher spread.
cards.originalText: A binary CDS on the same name should trade at a lower spread than the regular CDS, because its payoff is fixed in advance.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain how to account for credit risk exposure in valuing a CDS.
cards.statement: In valuing a CDS, the expected premium payments are weighted by the probability of default in each year, and the expected payoff by the probability of survival to each payment date.
cards.explanation: The weights are swapped. Expected premium payments are weighted by survival probabilities, and the expected payoff by default probabilities.
cards.originalText: The expected premium payments are weighted by the probability of default in each year, and the expected payoff by the probability of survival to each payment date.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain how to account for credit risk exposure in valuing a CDS.
cards.statement: After inception a CDS is revalued at zero, because its spread is reset to the market level.
cards.explanation: A CDS is worth zero only at inception. Its spread is fixed for the life of the contract, so later changes in the market spread give it a positive or negative value.
cards.originalText: Zero: a CDS is revalued at zero after inception because its spread is reset to the market level.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the process of valuing a synthetic CDO using the spread payments approach and the Gaussian copula model of time to default approach.
cards.statement: Raising the copula correlation makes the equity tranche less risky and the senior tranches riskier, so the equity tranche's spread falls and the senior tranche spreads rise, while the index spread is unchanged.
cards.explanation: Each name keeps its hazard rate, so the portfolio's expected loss and the index spread are unchanged. Higher correlation makes both few and many defaults more likely, which helps the equity tranche and hurts the senior tranches.
cards.originalText: The equity tranche becomes less risky and the senior tranches riskier, so the equity tranche’s price for protection falls and the senior tranche spreads rise; the index spread is unchanged.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the process of valuing a synthetic CDO using the spread payments approach and the Gaussian copula model of time to default approach.
cards.statement: Raising the copula correlation raises all tranche spreads, because higher correlation raises each company's probability of default.
cards.explanation: Correlation does not change each name's default probability. It redistributes losses between tranches, lowering the equity spread and raising the senior spreads.
cards.originalText: All tranche spreads rise, because higher correlation raises each company’s probability of default.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the process of valuing a synthetic CDO using the spread payments approach and the Gaussian copula model of time to default approach.
cards.statement: Raising the copula correlation makes the equity tranche riskier and the senior tranches safer.
cards.explanation: The equity tranche gains from clustering of defaults and the senior tranches lose.
cards.originalText: The equity tranche becomes riskier and the senior tranches safer, because defaults become more frequent in every scenario.
cards.correction: Raising the copula correlation makes the equity tranche less risky and the senior tranches riskier.

changes.from: the equity tranche riskier and the senior tranches safer
changes.to: the equity tranche less risky and the senior tranches riskier

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the process of valuing a synthetic CDO using the spread payments approach and the Gaussian copula model of time to default approach.
cards.statement: Raising the copula correlation changes no tranche price, because the expected loss on the whole portfolio does not depend on correlation.
cards.explanation: The expected portfolio loss is unchanged, but correlation changes how losses are distributed across the tranches, so tranche prices do change.
cards.originalText: No tranche price changes, because the expected loss on the whole portfolio does not depend on correlation.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define the two measures of implied correlation: compound (tranche) correlation and base correlation.
cards.statement: For the equity tranche of a CDO, compound correlation and base correlation coincide, because the tranche is both a single tranche and a base tranche.
cards.explanation: The equity tranche from 0 to its detachment point is both the first tranche and a base tranche, so the two implied correlation measures give the same number.
cards.originalText: The compound correlations form a smile, lowest for the 3 to 6% tranche, while the base correlations rise steadily with the detachment point; the two coincide at 3%, where the tranche is both a single tranche and a base tranche.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define the two measures of implied correlation: compound (tranche) correlation and base correlation.
cards.statement: To value a non-standard tranche, GARP's preferred approach is to interpolate the PV of expected loss on the 0 to X% tranches across the standard detachment points, take the difference between the two relevant values, and then imply the tranche's compound correlation and breakeven spread.
cards.explanation: Interpolating the expected losses themselves can respect the no-arbitrage condition, whereas interpolating base correlations often violates it. The quantity that carries the economics is interpolated, not the model parameter.
cards.originalText: Interpolate the PV of expected loss on the 0 to $X$% tranche across the standard detachment points to estimate it for 0 to 4% and 0 to 8%; take the difference as the expected loss on the 4 to 8% tranche, then imply its compound correlation and breakeven spread.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define the two measures of implied correlation: compound (tranche) correlation and base correlation.
cards.statement: Interpolated base correlations always satisfy the no-arbitrage condition on expected losses.
cards.explanation: Interpolating base correlations often violates the condition that the PV of expected loss on the 0 to X% tranche rises with X at a decreasing rate, because base correlation is a nonlinear function of expected loss.
cards.originalText: Interpolate base correlations at 4% and 8% and use them directly, because interpolated base correlations always satisfy the no-arbitrage condition on expected losses.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define the two measures of implied correlation: compound (tranche) correlation and base correlation.
cards.statement: A non-standard mezzanine tranche has the same risk as the whole portfolio and can be quoted at the index spread.
cards.explanation: The index spread prices protection on the whole portfolio. A mezzanine tranche has a very different risk and its own breakeven spread.
cards.originalText: Quote the index spread for the 4 to 8% tranche, because a tranche straddling two standard tranches has the same risk as the index.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify and describe institutions that take on significant counterparty risk.
cards.statement: Bank counterparties contribute little to a dealer's CVA because interbank derivatives are exempt from collateral agreements.
cards.explanation: Banks contribute little CVA because of their good credit quality and collateralisation, not because interbank derivatives are exempt from collateral agreements.
cards.originalText: Bank counterparties contribute little CVA because interbank derivatives are exempt from collateral agreements.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe credit value adjustment (CVA) and compare the use of CVA and credit limits in evaluating and mitigating counterparty risk.
cards.statement: With PFE-based credit limits, a soft limit may be breached through market movements without forcing trades to be unwound, whereas a breach of the hard limit requires remedial action.
cards.explanation: GARP says a soft limit may be breached through market movements but not through new transactions, while a hard limit breach requires remedial action. New trades that would breach a limit are refused unless specifically approved.
cards.originalText: A rise in PFE to USD 12 million caused purely by market moves breaches the soft limit but does not by itself force trades to be unwound, whereas a breach of the hard limit requires remedial action.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe credit value adjustment (CVA) and compare the use of CVA and credit limits in evaluating and mitigating counterparty risk.
cards.statement: A proposed trade is compared with the remaining headroom under a credit limit using its standalone PFE, since netting with existing trades is captured only in CVA.
cards.explanation: The incremental PFE (after minus before the trade) is what counts, and it is smaller than the standalone PFE because of portfolio effects such as netting.
cards.originalText: A proposed trade is compared with the remaining headroom using its standalone PFE, since netting with existing trades is captured only in CVA.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe credit value adjustment (CVA) and compare the use of CVA and credit limits in evaluating and mitigating counterparty risk.
cards.statement: PFE-based credit limits typically step up at longer horizons.
cards.explanation: Limits are often reduced over time, because credit quality may deteriorate over long horizons.
cards.originalText: The limits should step up at longer horizons, because exposures on most derivatives grow with maturity.
cards.correction: PFE-based credit limits typically step down at longer horizons.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe credit value adjustment (CVA) and compare the use of CVA and credit limits in evaluating and mitigating counterparty risk.
cards.statement: Because a soft credit limit can be breached by market moves, new trades that take PFE above the soft limit at a future date can be booked without approval.
cards.explanation: A soft limit may be breached by market movements but not by new transactions. New trades that would breach a limit at any future point are refused unless specifically approved.
cards.originalText: Because the soft limit can be breached by market moves, new trades that take PFE above USD 10 million at a future date can be booked without approval.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe credit value adjustment (CVA) and compare the use of CVA and credit limits in evaluating and mitigating counterparty risk.
cards.statement: The exit-price concept in FAS 157 and IFRS 13 points to risk-neutral default probabilities, and Basel III also defines CVA with respect to credit spreads, although Basel III does not permit DVA.
cards.explanation: Accounting and regulation both point to risk-neutral, spread-based CVA, but they conflict on DVA: accounting recognises it and Basel III does not permit it.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe credit value adjustment (CVA) and compare the use of CVA and credit limits in evaluating and mitigating counterparty risk.
cards.statement: Under the actuarial approach, CVA is the cost of a hedging strategy built from CDS spreads and so already uses market-implied default probabilities.
cards.explanation: The hedging-cost view is the risk-neutral approach. The actuarial view is an expected value based on historical default probabilities, with a risk premium.
cards.originalText: Under the actuarial approach, CVA is the cost of a hedging strategy built from CDS spreads, so it already uses market-implied default probabilities.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe credit value adjustment (CVA) and compare the use of CVA and credit limits in evaluating and mitigating counterparty risk.
cards.statement: Regulators generally accept CVA models based on expected loss from historical default rates, provided the risk premium is excluded.
cards.explanation: Regulators state that models based on expected loss or historical calculations that ignore risk premia are not acceptable.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify and explain the costs of an OTC derivative.
cards.statement: An uncollateralised trade on which a bank makes an upfront payment must be funded, for example by issuing a bond, because the cash flows that repay it arrive later.
cards.explanation: Lenders require compensation for providing that funding, which creates a funding cost. With collateral, the margin offsets the upfront payment and the funding need largely disappears.
cards.originalText: An uncollateralised trade on which the bank makes an upfront payment must be funded, for example by issuing a bond, because the cash flows that repay it arrive later.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify and explain the costs of an OTC derivative.
cards.statement: A collateralised trade on which a bank makes an upfront payment needs funding just like an uncollateralised one, because margin never offsets an upfront payment.
cards.explanation: In a collateralised trade the margin received offsets the upfront payment, so the funding need disappears.
cards.originalText: A collateralised trade on which the bank makes an upfront payment needs funding just like an uncollateralised one, because margin never offsets an upfront payment.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify and explain the costs of an OTC derivative.
cards.statement: Receiving government bonds instead of cash as collateral removes all funding and collateral costs, because bonds can always be converted to cash at no cost.
cards.explanation: A repo rate defines the cost of converting bonds into cash, so the collateral type changes the cost but does not remove it.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify and explain the costs of an OTC derivative.
cards.statement: Funding costs in derivative valuation are fully objective inputs, because the bank can read them from its bond spreads for any maturity it chooses.
cards.explanation: Some funding inputs are subjective, such as the maturity of funding a trade needs and the dividends shareholders will require.
cards.originalText: Funding costs are fully objective inputs, because the bank can read them from its bond spreads for any maturity it chooses.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify and explain the costs of an OTC derivative.
cards.statement: One party's CVA cost is the other party's DVA benefit, but capital and initial margin costs are costs to both parties with no equal and opposite benefit to the counterparty.
cards.explanation: One party's positive value is the other's negative value, so CVA and DVA mirror each other. Capital and initial margin costs are always present and do not provide an equal and opposite benefit to the counterparties.
cards.originalText: The trainee is right for CVA and DVA, since one party’s CVA cost is the other’s DVA benefit, but wrong for capital and initial margin, which are costs to both parties with no offsetting benefit.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify and explain the costs of an OTC derivative.
cards.statement: Every xVA cost borne by one party to a swap is an equal and opposite benefit to the other party, including capital and initial margin costs.
cards.explanation: Symmetry holds for CVA and DVA, but capital and initial margin costs are borne by both parties with no offsetting benefit.
cards.originalText: The trainee is right for every term, because one party’s positive value is always the other’s negative value.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify and explain the costs of an OTC derivative.
cards.statement: CVA and DVA are costs to both parties of a trade.
cards.explanation: DVA is a benefit to the party whose own default risk it reflects. One party's CVA cost is the other party's DVA benefit.
cards.originalText: The trainee is wrong for every term, because CVA and DVA are costs to both parties.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify and explain the costs of an OTC derivative.
cards.statement: One bank's regulatory capital charge on a trade is released as capital relief at its counterparty.
cards.explanation: Each bank's capital is set by its own regulator on its own exposure, so there is no mirror capital relief at the counterparty.
cards.originalText: The trainee is right for capital, because one bank’s regulatory capital charge is released as capital relief at its counterparty.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the components of the X-Value Adjustment (xVA) term.
cards.statement: In GARP's xVA framework, the funding valuation adjustment (FVA) pairs the valuation as its market component with the funding cost as its cost component.
cards.explanation: Each xVA term combines a market component with a cost component. For FVA these are the valuation (funding position) and the funding cost.
cards.originalText: FVA: the valuation (funding position) as the market component and the funding cost as the cost component.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the components of the X-Value Adjustment (xVA) term.
cards.statement: In GARP's xVA framework, CVA pairs credit exposure as its market component with the institution's funding cost as its cost component.
cards.explanation: CVA pairs credit exposure with the counterparty's default probability. Funding cost is the cost component of FVA.
cards.originalText: CVA: credit exposure as the market component and the institution’s funding cost as the cost component.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the components of the X-Value Adjustment (xVA) term.
cards.statement: In GARP's xVA framework, the margin valuation adjustment (MVA) pairs the initial margin amount as its market component with the cost of capital as its cost component.
cards.explanation: MVA pairs the initial margin amount with the funding cost of that margin. The cost of capital belongs to KVA.
cards.originalText: MVA: the initial margin amount as the market component and the cost of capital as the cost component.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the components of the X-Value Adjustment (xVA) term.
cards.statement: In GARP's xVA framework, the capital valuation adjustment (KVA) pairs the valuation as its market component with the counterparty's default probability as its cost component.
cards.explanation: KVA pairs the capital amount with the cost of capital. The default probability is the cost component of CVA and DVA.
cards.originalText: KVA: the valuation as the market component and the counterparty’s default probability as the cost component.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the components of the X-Value Adjustment (xVA) term.
cards.statement: Since own-default risk is widely seen as a funding benefit, DVA and the funding benefit adjustment (FBA) can overlap, so adding both may double count.
cards.explanation: GARP notes potential overlaps between xVA terms, for example between DVA and FBA. Some costs could also be classed as either FVA or ColVA because collateral must be funded.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the components of the X-Value Adjustment (xVA) term.
cards.statement: Every cost belongs to exactly one xVA term, so the xVA terms can always be added without double counting.
cards.explanation: The definitions of xVA terms overlap, so adding them blindly can double count.
cards.originalText: Every cost belongs to exactly one xVA term, so the terms can always be added without double counting.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the components of the X-Value Adjustment (xVA) term.
cards.statement: In GARP's convention for plotting xVA profiles, benefits are shown as positive values and costs as negative values.
cards.explanation: The convention is reversed: costs are shown as positive values and benefits as negative values.
cards.originalText: In GARP’s convention for plotting xVA profiles, benefits are shown as positive values and costs as negative values.
cards.correction: In GARP's convention for plotting xVA profiles, costs are shown as positive values and benefits as negative values.

changes.from: benefits are shown as positive values and costs as negative values
changes.to: costs are shown as positive values and benefits as negative values

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Provide examples of a loss waterfall.
cards.statement: In a CCP default waterfall, the surviving members' initial margin is used before the mutualised default fund.
cards.explanation: Surviving members' initial margin is not part of the loss waterfall, because loss allocation methods do not let a CCP use the initial margin of non-defaulting members. Survivors pay through their default fund contributions.
cards.originalText: The surviving members’ default fund contributions absorb nothing, because the surviving members’ initial margin is applied before the mutualised default fund.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Provide examples of a loss waterfall.
cards.statement: Losses allocated to a CCP's mutualised default fund are shared only among the members that held trades with the defaulted member.
cards.explanation: Mutualisation does not depend on having traded with the defaulter. A member can suffer default losses even if it never traded with the defaulted counterparty.
cards.originalText: The surviving members’ default fund contributions absorb EUR 270 million, shared only among the members that held trades with the defaulter.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Analyze the differences in the mechanics of issuing securitized products using a trust versus a special purpose vehicle (SPV) and distinguish between the three main SPV structures: amortizing, revolving, and master trust.
cards.statement: In a trust securitisation arrangement, the receivables are sold to a master trust that deposits them in a grantor trust, and the notes rest on a beneficial interest, which further distances the originator from the assets.
cards.explanation: The originator sells the receivables to a master trust, which deposits them in a grantor trust and receives a beneficial interest. The notes are backed by that beneficial claim.
cards.originalText: In the trust arrangement the receivables are sold to a master trust that deposits them in a grantor trust; the notes rest on a beneficial interest, which further distances the originator.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Analyze the differences in the mechanics of issuing securitized products using a trust versus a special purpose vehicle (SPV) and distinguish between the three main SPV structures: amortizing, revolving, and master trust.
cards.statement: A company SPV is the usual form in the US market, because US accounting rules are satisfied by a single entity that issues notes directly against its assets.
cards.explanation: The trust is more common in the US market, because a company may not distance the originator enough for accounting purposes. The single-entity company form is the Euromarkets choice.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Analyze the differences in the mechanics of issuing securitized products using a trust versus a special purpose vehicle (SPV) and distinguish between the three main SPV structures: amortizing, revolving, and master trust.
cards.statement: Choosing the trust form removes the need for a true sale, because the trustee then holds the receivables on behalf of the originator.
cards.explanation: A trust is still an SPV that must buy the assets in a true sale. The trustee represents the investors' interests, not the originator's.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Analyze the differences in the mechanics of issuing securitized products using a trust versus a special purpose vehicle (SPV) and distinguish between the three main SPV structures: amortizing, revolving, and master trust.
cards.statement: A company SPV cannot be bankruptcy remote, so investors in its notes keep a claim on the originator if the receivables underperform.
cards.explanation: An SPV, whether a trust or a company, is defined as bankruptcy remote from the sponsor.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define credit risk and explain how it arises using examples.
cards.statement: For a creditor holding a bond, credit risk is the risk that the issuer fails to honor its contractual interest or principal payments, because of inability, unwillingness or delay.
cards.explanation: Credit risk is the loss arising from a counterparty's inability, unwillingness or nontimeliness in honoring its obligation. For a bond this means missed coupon or principal payments.
cards.originalText: The startup fails to honor its contractual interest or principal payments, because of inability, unwillingness or delay.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define credit risk and explain how it arises using examples.
cards.statement: For a bond investor, credit risk is the risk of losing money because the issuer fails to meet its coupon and principal obligations.
cards.explanation: Credit risk is the possibility of loss from the obligor's failure to honor its payment obligations, which for a bond are the coupons and principal.
cards.originalText: The investor loses money because the bank fails to meet its coupon and principal obligations.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define credit risk and explain how it arises using examples.
cards.statement: For a bond investor, the risk that the bond's market value falls because interest rates rise is credit risk.
cards.explanation: A price fall caused by rising interest rates is interest rate (market) risk. It occurs even if the issuer pays in full.
cards.originalText: The market value of the bond falls because interest rates rise.
cards.correction: For a bond investor, the risk that the bond's market value falls because interest rates rise is interest rate risk.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define credit risk and explain how it arises using examples.
cards.statement: The factors most critical in helping creditors assess credit risk are the amount of credit risk (exposure), the probability of counterparty default, and the recovery amount and timing.
cards.explanation: For each credit risk transaction the three fundamental questions are how much can be lost, how likely default is, and how much is recovered, when and at what cost.
cards.originalText: Amount of credit risk, probability of counterparty default, recovery amount and timing.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define credit risk and explain how it arises using examples.
cards.statement: An investor lending through a peer-to-peer platform bears credit risk, the risk that the borrower fails to repay the loan.
cards.explanation: Lending exposes the lender to loss if the borrower is unable, unwilling or late in repaying, which is credit risk by definition.
cards.originalText: Credit risk that the borrower fails to repay the loan.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define credit risk and explain how it arises using examples.
cards.statement: A lender's credit risk on a short-term credit line depends most directly on the likelihood that the client fails to repay, judged from its repayment record and current ability to meet its obligations.
cards.explanation: Credit risk is driven by the borrower's probability of failing to pay. Assessing it means estimating the probability of default from repayment history and present capacity to pay.
cards.originalText: The likelihood that the client fails to repay, based on its repayment record and current ability to meet obligations.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define credit risk and explain how it arises using examples.
cards.statement: A creditor's credit exposure to a borrower increases when the borrower draws on the credit extended, because available credit becomes an outstanding receivable.
cards.explanation: Credit exposure arises for the party that is owed money. A drawdown converts unused credit into an outstanding receivable for the lender.
cards.originalText: Chazz Bank’s credit exposure to Jason increased on January 25, when his purchase drew on the credit extended to him.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define credit risk and explain how it arises using examples.
cards.statement: A borrower who owes money to a bank is the party exposed to credit risk on that debt.
cards.explanation: The obligor owes the money, so the bank, as creditor, is exposed to the risk of non-payment. A debtor does not bear credit risk on its own borrowing.
cards.originalText: Jason became exposed to credit risk on January 25 because he now owes \$2,500 to the bank.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define credit risk and explain how it arises using examples.
cards.statement: A lender has no credit risk on a credit line until the borrower misses a payment due date.
cards.explanation: Credit risk exists from the moment credit is extended, because the risk is the possibility of loss and not its realization.
cards.originalText: Chazz Bank has no credit risk until Jason misses the February 15 due date.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the differences between insolvency, default, and bankruptcy.
cards.statement: A corporation whose liabilities exceed its assets is insolvent, even if it expects to meet its upcoming payments and has not sought court protection.
cards.explanation: Insolvency is a balance-sheet condition (negative equity). It can exist before any payment is missed and before any court filing.
cards.originalText: insolvent.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the differences between insolvency, default, and bankruptcy.
cards.statement: A corporation is bankrupt as soon as its liabilities exceed its assets.
cards.explanation: Bankruptcy is a legal procedure of seeking court protection. Negative equity alone, which is insolvency, does not trigger it.
cards.originalText: bankrupt.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the differences between insolvency, default, and bankruptcy.
cards.statement: A corporation is in default as soon as its liabilities exceed its assets, even if no payment obligation has been missed.
cards.explanation: Default requires a failure to meet a contractual obligation. A firm with negative equity that still expects to pay is insolvent but not in default.
cards.originalText: in default.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the differences between insolvency, default, and bankruptcy.
cards.statement: A company whose liabilities exceed its assets and that has missed scheduled payments is both insolvent and in default, but it is not bankrupt until it files for court protection.
cards.explanation: Insolvency is a balance-sheet condition, default is a failure to meet obligations, and bankruptcy is a court procedure. The company meets only the first two.
cards.originalText: XYZ is both insolvent and in default, but not bankrupt.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the differences between insolvency, default, and bankruptcy.
cards.statement: A corporation that cannot repay a short-term loan when it falls due is in default, and the default could be due to illiquidity.
cards.explanation: Default is a failure to meet a contractual obligation. A shortfall of current assets against current liabilities makes illiquidity a plausible cause.
cards.originalText: Old Crow defaulted on 1/1/2023, and the default could be due to illiquidity.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the differences between insolvency, default, and bankruptcy.
cards.statement: A corporation's default on a loan does not by itself make it bankrupt, because bankruptcy requires seeking court protection.
cards.explanation: Default and bankruptcy are distinct. Bankruptcy is a legal procedure that involves a court.
cards.originalText: Old Crow’s default on 1/1/2023 does not by itself make it bankrupt.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the differences between insolvency, default, and bankruptcy.
cards.statement: A corporation whose total assets exceed its total liabilities is solvent, even if its current assets fall short of its current liabilities.
cards.explanation: Solvency compares total assets with total liabilities. Such a firm is solvent but may be illiquid.
cards.originalText: Old Crow was solvent on 12/31/2022.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the differences between insolvency, default, and bankruptcy.
cards.statement: Bankruptcy of a corporation is a legal procedure, typically following default, in which the corporation seeks court protection and the court negotiates with management and creditors toward liquidation or reorganization.
cards.explanation: The involvement of a court distinguishes bankruptcy from insolvency and default. The outcome is liquidation or reorganization.
cards.originalText: A legal procedure, typically following default, in which the corporation seeks court protection and the court negotiates with management and creditors toward liquidation or reorganization.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the differences between insolvency, default, and bankruptcy.
cards.statement: Bankruptcy is a condition in which a corporation's liabilities exceed its assets.
cards.explanation: That describes insolvency, a balance-sheet state. Bankruptcy is a legal process.
cards.originalText: A condition in which the corporation’s liabilities exceed its assets.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the differences between insolvency, default, and bankruptcy.
cards.statement: Bankruptcy is a failure to meet a contractual obligation, such as a missed payment.
cards.explanation: That describes default. Default usually precedes bankruptcy but is not the same thing.
cards.originalText: A failure to meet a contractual obligation, such as a missed payment.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the differences between insolvency, default, and bankruptcy.
cards.statement: Bankruptcy is an informal, out-of-court agreement between a debtor and its creditors to restructure its debt.
cards.explanation: An out-of-court restructuring involves no court, while bankruptcy is a legal procedure involving a court.
cards.originalText: An informal, out‑of‑court agreement between the debtor and its creditors to restructure its debt.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify and describe transactions that generate credit risk.
cards.statement: In non-recourse receivables financing, the finance company's principal credit exposure is the risk that the account debtors fail to pay their invoices on time or at all.
cards.explanation: With non-recourse terms the finance company cannot claw back losses from the manufacturer, so repayment depends on the buyers paying their invoices.
cards.originalText: Receivables; the risk that the manufacturer’s customers (the account debtors) fail to pay their invoices on time or at all

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify and describe transactions that generate credit risk.
cards.statement: In non-recourse receivables financing, the finance company's principal credit exposure is the deterioration of the financial condition of the manufacturer that sold it the receivables.
cards.explanation: With non-recourse terms the manufacturer's solvency is not the main source of loss. The credit risk sits with the account debtors who owe the invoices.
cards.originalText: Lending to the manufacturer only; the risk that the manufacturer’s own financial condition deteriorates

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify and describe transactions that generate credit risk.
cards.statement: Credit risk arises not only from lending but also from leases, receivables, prepayments, claims on assets held by others such as deposits, contingent claims such as insurance policies, and derivatives.
cards.explanation: A credit sale creates a receivable, a prepayment depends on the supplier delivering, a deposit is a claim on the bank, and an insurance policy is a contingent claim on the insurer.
cards.originalText: All four: the insurance policy, the prepayment, the credit sales and the bank deposit

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify and describe transactions that generate credit risk.
cards.statement: Credit risk arises only from lending money.
cards.explanation: Credit risk also arises from receivables, prepayments, deposits, contingent claims such as insurance, leases and derivatives.
cards.originalText: None of them; credit risk arises only from lending money

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify and describe transactions that generate credit risk.
cards.statement: A lender under a repurchase agreement still bears credit risk, because if the client defaults it may not be able to sell the collateral bonds to cover the full amount lent.
cards.explanation: Collateral reduces but does not remove credit risk, because the bonds' liquidation value is uncertain at the time of default.
cards.originalText: credit risk because if the client defaults, the bank may not be able to sell the bonds to cover the full amount of the repurchase agreement.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify and describe transactions that generate credit risk.
cards.statement: A repurchase agreement carries no credit risk for the lender if the repurchase agreement matures before the collateral bonds do.
cards.explanation: A maturity mismatch is irrelevant to whether exposure exists. The lender is exposed throughout the life of the agreement.
cards.originalText: no credit risk because the repurchase agreement matures before the bonds.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify and describe transactions that generate credit risk.
cards.statement: A repurchase agreement with an investment grade counterparty carries no credit risk, because counterparty default is unlikely.
cards.explanation: Investment grade lowers the probability of default but does not make it zero.
cards.originalText: no credit risk because the client is rated investment grade; therefore, counterparty default is unlikely.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify and describe transactions that generate credit risk.
cards.statement: A repurchase agreement carries no credit risk when the notional value of the collateral bonds exceeds the amount lent.
cards.explanation: Notional (face) value is not realizable market value. A small cushion can be eroded by price falls or illiquidity.
cards.originalText: no credit risk because the notional value of the bonds exceeds the value of the repurchase agreement.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the entities that are exposed to credit risk and explain circumstances under which exposure occurs.
cards.statement: Buying reinsurance creates no credit risk for an insurer.
cards.explanation: Reinsurance replaces insurance risk with credit risk on the reinsurer, because the reinsurance recoverable is only as good as the reinsurer's ability and willingness to pay.
cards.originalText: Warner’s statement about reinsurance.
cards.correction: Buying reinsurance creates credit risk for an insurer.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the entities that are exposed to credit risk and explain circumstances under which exposure occurs.
cards.statement: An insurer that buys reinsurance takes on credit risk on the reinsurer, because the reinsurance recoverable is a contingent claim on the reinsurer.
cards.explanation: Risk transfer is not risk elimination: the recoverable is only collectable if the reinsurer is able and willing to pay, so reinsurance is a credit exposure.
cards.originalText: Ron’s statement about reinsurance.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the entities that are exposed to credit risk and explain circumstances under which exposure occurs.
cards.statement: Holding emerging market debt in its investment portfolio exposes an insurer to credit risk through issuer default.
cards.explanation: Bonds held in the investment portfolio can default, so investments are one of the main sources of credit risk for an insurer, alongside underwriting and reinsurance.
cards.originalText: Ron’s statement about emerging market debt.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the entities that are exposed to credit risk and explain circumstances under which exposure occurs.
cards.statement: When an insurer grants installment terms and grace periods to corporate customers on new policies, it takes on credit risk from premium non-payment.
cards.explanation: Late or missed premium payments create a non-payment risk in underwriting, so originating policies on credit terms is a source of credit risk for an insurer.
cards.originalText: Warner’s statement about originating new policies.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the entities that are exposed to credit risk and explain circumstances under which exposure occurs.
cards.statement: A bank becomes exposed to credit risk when it commits to a credit limit, not only when the borrower draws on it.
cards.explanation: Exposure arises for the party extending credit and starts when the commitment is made. Drawings later turn the undrawn commitment into an actual receivable.
cards.originalText: Chazz Bank became exposed to credit risk on January 21, when it committed to the \$5,000 limit.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the entities that are exposed to credit risk and explain circumstances under which exposure occurs.
cards.statement: A borrower creates credit risk for itself by applying for a credit card.
cards.explanation: Credit risk is borne by the party that may not be paid, namely the lender, not the borrower. An application also creates no commitment, so nobody is exposed yet.
cards.originalText: Jason creates credit risk for himself on January 15 by applying for the card.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the entities that are exposed to credit risk and explain circumstances under which exposure occurs.
cards.statement: A bank's credit risk does not increase when a customer draws on an already approved credit limit.
cards.explanation: A drawing turns the undrawn limit into a drawn receivable, so actual exposure increases even though the limit was already approved.
cards.originalText: Chazz Bank’s credit risk did not increase on January 25 because the card limit was already approved.
cards.correction: A bank's credit risk increases when a customer draws on an already approved credit limit.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the entities that are exposed to credit risk and explain circumstances under which exposure occurs.
cards.statement: Factoring is a standard way for a corporation to mitigate receivables credit risk.
cards.explanation: Selling receivables to another company (factoring) transfers the credit risk on them, so it is one of the standard mitigants alongside insurance and documentary credit.
cards.originalText: Factoring.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the entities that are exposed to credit risk and explain circumstances under which exposure occurs.
cards.statement: Buying insurance on accounts receivable is a standard way for a corporation to mitigate receivables credit risk.
cards.explanation: Corporations typically mitigate receivables credit risk by insuring the receivables, selling them through factoring, or securing foreign sales with documentary credit.
cards.originalText: Insurance.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the entities that are exposed to credit risk and explain circumstances under which exposure occurs.
cards.statement: Documentary credit is a standard way for a corporation to mitigate credit risk on foreign sales.
cards.explanation: Documentary credit is a bank guarantee commonly used to secure foreign transactions, so it is one of the standard receivables credit mitigants.
cards.originalText: Documentary credit.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Discuss the motivations for managing or taking on credit risk.
cards.statement: A seller can increase sales while adding little credit risk by setting up a financing arm that helps customers obtain credit from other sources.
cards.explanation: When outside lenders fund the customer, the seller is paid by the lender and the credit exposure sits with that lender rather than with the seller.
cards.originalText: Set up a financing arm that helps customers secure credit from other sources.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the processes that lead to risk taking including credit origination, credit risk assessment, and credit approval processes.
cards.statement: Credit origination consists of identifying potential credit transactions and understanding client needs.
cards.explanation: Originators source and structure transactions for clients. Creditworthiness analysis and the approve-or-decline decision come in the later assessment and approval processes.
cards.originalText: Identifying potential credit transactions and understanding client needs

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the processes that lead to risk taking including credit origination, credit risk assessment, and credit approval processes.
cards.statement: Credit origination consists of evaluating the financial stability of a client and setting credit limits.
cards.explanation: Evaluating a client's financial strength and setting limits is credit risk assessment, the second process, not origination.
cards.originalText: Evaluating the financial stability of a client and setting credit limits
cards.correction: Credit risk assessment consists of evaluating the financial stability of a client and setting credit limits.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the processes that lead to risk taking including credit origination, credit risk assessment, and credit approval processes.
cards.statement: Credit origination consists of approving or rejecting credit transactions based on risk assessments.
cards.explanation: Approving or rejecting transactions is credit approval, the third process, carried out under delegated authority.
cards.originalText: Approving or rejecting credit transactions based on risk assessments
cards.correction: Credit approval consists of approving or rejecting credit transactions based on risk assessments.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the processes that lead to risk taking including credit origination, credit risk assessment, and credit approval processes.
cards.statement: Credit origination consists of monitoring and reviewing existing credit transactions for compliance.
cards.explanation: Monitoring existing transactions takes place after approval and is not part of origination, which is the front-office activity of sourcing and structuring new transactions.
cards.originalText: Monitoring and reviewing existing credit transactions for compliance

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the processes that lead to risk taking including credit origination, credit risk assessment, and credit approval processes.
cards.statement: Risk management has no approval authority in a bank's credit approval process; it advises decision makers, and its recommendation is required when the criteria in the bank's guidelines are met.
cards.explanation: Approval authority is delegated to the business hierarchy and committees. Risk management advises and gives a recommendation that the guidelines make mandatory for transactions meeting stated size and rating criteria.
cards.originalText: It has no approval authority; it advises decision makers, and its recommendation is required when the criteria in the guidelines are met.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the processes that lead to risk taking including credit origination, credit risk assessment, and credit approval processes.
cards.statement: Risk management holds a veto over every credit transaction.
cards.explanation: Risk managers rarely hold a veto. They recommend and escalate disagreement, while approval authority stays with the business hierarchy and committees.
cards.originalText: It holds a veto over every transaction because it is the second line of defense.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the processes that lead to risk taking including credit origination, credit risk assessment, and credit approval processes.
cards.statement: Risk management approves all credit transactions that fall below the business unit head's limit.
cards.explanation: Risk management is not a delegated approver and has no approval authority; it plays an advisory role.
cards.originalText: It approves all transactions below the business unit head’s limit so that originators are not slowed down.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the processes that lead to risk taking including credit origination, credit risk assessment, and credit approval processes.
cards.statement: Risk management originates credit transactions jointly with the business so that risk is built into the structure from the start.
cards.explanation: Originators source transactions, and joint origination would compromise risk management's independence. Risk management advises on transactions rather than originating them.
cards.originalText: It originates the transaction jointly with the business so that risk is built into the structure from the start.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the processes that lead to risk taking including credit origination, credit risk assessment, and credit approval processes.
cards.statement: Approving a large loan to a new business without a thorough review of its business plan and market viability is a failure of the credit risk assessment process.
cards.explanation: Credit risk assessment should analyse the key risks of a counterparty before a decision is made. Taking a large exposure without that analysis means risk is taken without a basis for judging it.
cards.originalText: A large loan is approved for a new business without a thorough review of the business plan and market viability.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the processes that lead to risk taking including credit origination, credit risk assessment, and credit approval processes.
cards.statement: When originators are paid mainly on loan volume and margin, they tend to push for higher volume and returns and present deals favourably, which increases the number of higher-risk transactions.
cards.explanation: Volume- and margin-based rewards bias originators towards riskier deals and favourable presentation, which is why independent credit assessment and approval are needed.
cards.originalText: Originators tend to push for higher volume and returns and present deals favorably, increasing the number of higher‑risk transactions.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the most common parameters of a credit-sensitive transaction.
cards.statement: Credit quality is a scale or model developed by a firm to summarise the creditworthiness of each of its counterparties.
cards.explanation: Amount of exposure, credit quality and tenor are the three common parameters of a credit-sensitive transaction. Credit quality is the firm's own summary measure of counterparty creditworthiness.
cards.originalText: Credit quality.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the most common parameters of a credit-sensitive transaction.
cards.statement: Amount of exposure is the estimated maximum amount of money a firm can lose on a transaction.
cards.explanation: Amount of exposure is one of the three common parameters of a credit-sensitive transaction; how to compute it depends on the nature of the transaction.
cards.originalText: Amount of exposure.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the most common parameters of a credit-sensitive transaction.
cards.statement: Counterparty diversification is one of the three common parameters of a credit-sensitive transaction.
cards.explanation: The three common parameters are amount of exposure, credit quality and tenor. Counterparty diversification is not one of them.
cards.originalText: Counterparty diversification.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the most common parameters of a credit-sensitive transaction.
cards.statement: Credit quality is the period from the closing of the agreement until the last principal repayment is due.
cards.explanation: That period is the tenor of a transaction. Credit quality is the firm's scale summarising counterparty creditworthiness.
cards.originalText: The period from the closing of the agreement until the last principal repayment is due.
cards.correction: Tenor is the period from the closing of the agreement until the last principal repayment is due.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the most common parameters of a credit-sensitive transaction.
cards.statement: Credit quality is the estimated maximum amount of money a firm can lose on a transaction.
cards.explanation: That is the amount of exposure. Credit quality is the firm's scale summarising counterparty creditworthiness.
cards.originalText: The estimated maximum amount of money the firm can lose on the transaction.
cards.correction: Amount of exposure is the estimated maximum amount of money a firm can lose on a transaction.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the most common parameters of a credit-sensitive transaction.
cards.statement: A counterparty's credit quality is measured by its share of its industry's total revenue.
cards.explanation: Market share is a single business characteristic. Credit quality is the firm's own scale summarising the counterparty's overall creditworthiness.
cards.originalText: The counterparty’s share of its industry’s total revenue.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the roles of the credit committee in an organization.
cards.statement: The primary role of a bank's credit committee is to make the approval decision, approving or declining a high-risk transaction after reviewing the package prepared by the originator.
cards.explanation: The credit committee is the decision-making body for high-profile, high-risk transactions. Originators prepare and market deals, while committee members review and decide.
cards.originalText: Making the approval decision (approve or decline) on the transaction

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the roles of the credit committee in an organization.
cards.statement: A bank's credit committee prepares the credit analysis and approval package for the transactions it considers.
cards.explanation: Preparing the package is the originator's job. The committee reviews the package circulated to it and decides.
cards.originalText: Preparing the credit analysis and approval package for the transaction

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the roles of the credit committee in an organization.
cards.statement: A bank's credit committee negotiates the pricing and terms of loans directly with the client.
cards.explanation: Negotiating with clients is a front-office function and would compromise the committee's objectivity. The committee reviews and decides.
cards.originalText: Negotiating the pricing and terms of the loan directly with the client

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the roles of the credit committee in an organization.
cards.statement: A bank's credit committee provides independent assurance on the bank's credit processes as part of the third line of defense.
cards.explanation: Independent assurance is the role of internal audit, the third line. The credit committee is a decision-making body within the approval process.
cards.originalText: Providing independent assurance on the bank’s credit processes as part of the third line of defense
cards.correction: Internal audit provides independent assurance on the bank's credit processes as part of the third line of defense.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the roles of the credit committee in an organization.
cards.statement: Credit committee members should be senior decision-makers from the key functions (business, risk, tax and accounting, compliance, legal), with only limited ability to delegate their authority.
cards.explanation: A diverse, senior membership ensures no aspect of a deal is overlooked, and limited delegation keeps accountability with the individuals tasked with deciding.
cards.originalText: Members should be senior decision‑makers from the key functions (business, risk, tax and accounting, compliance, legal), with only limited ability to delegate their authority

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the roles of the credit committee in an organization.
cards.statement: Credit committee members should be senior decision-makers from the key functions (business, risk, tax and accounting, compliance, legal) and may delegate attendance to junior staff freely.
cards.explanation: Free delegation to junior staff undermines the committee's expertise and accountability; members should have only limited ability to delegate.
cards.originalText: Members should be senior decision‑makers from the key functions (business, risk, tax and accounting, compliance, legal) and may delegate attendance to junior staff freely
cards.correction: Credit committee members should be senior decision-makers from the key functions (business, risk, tax and accounting, compliance, legal) and may delegate only to a limited extent.

changes.from: may delegate attendance to junior staff freely
changes.to: may delegate only to a limited extent

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the roles of the credit committee in an organization.
cards.statement: Credit committee membership should be limited to risk management and the business unit so that decisions are made quickly.
cards.explanation: Membership should also include other key functions such as tax and accounting, compliance and legal. Speed is not a reason to remove them.
cards.originalText: Membership should be limited to risk management and the business unit so that decisions are made quickly

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the roles of the credit committee in an organization.
cards.statement: Credit committee membership should be filled by the originators of the transactions presented, so that the best product knowledge is available.
cards.explanation: Originators bring the proposal; having them decide their own deals creates a conflict of interest.
cards.originalText: Membership should be filled by the originators of the transactions presented so that the best product knowledge is available

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the roles of the credit committee in an organization.
cards.statement: A credit committee that never declines a transaction is a warning sign, because a well-functioning committee balances business needs with risk and has a track record of both approving and declining transactions.
cards.explanation: The committee's value lies in independent challenge. Originators must understand that the committee can say no, and a committee that never says no is not efficiently managed.
cards.originalText: It is a warning sign, because a well‑functioning committee balances business needs with risk and has a track record of both approving and declining transactions

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the roles of the credit committee in an organization.
cards.statement: The role of a bank's credit committee is limited to ratifying decisions already made by business unit heads.
cards.explanation: The credit committee is the decision-maker on important or high-risk transactions, not a ratifier of earlier decisions.
cards.originalText: It is appropriate, because the committee’s role is limited to ratifying decisions already made by business unit heads

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the roles of the credit committee in an organization.
