cards.statement: Credit committee minutes should be recorded with detail and accuracy and distributed shortly after the meeting, since they are among the first documents management and auditors request if a transaction goes wrong.
cards.explanation: Detailed, timely minutes document the rationale and any dissent and provide the audit trail for later review of the decision.
cards.originalText: Minutes recorded with detail and accuracy and distributed shortly after the meeting, since they are among the first documents management and auditors request if a transaction goes wrong

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the roles of the credit committee in an organization.
cards.statement: A credit committee's record of a meeting should consist of brief notes of the final decision only, kept by the originator.
cards.explanation: Discussions must be recorded in detail and accurately, including the reasoning. The originator should not own the record.
cards.originalText: Brief notes of the final decision only, kept by the originator to avoid delay

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the roles of the credit committee in an organization.
cards.statement: Credit committee minutes should be prepared only for declined transactions, because approvals are documented in the approval package.
cards.explanation: Approved transactions are the ones most likely to be scrutinised later, so all committee discussions must be recorded.
cards.originalText: Minutes prepared only for declined transactions, because approvals are documented in the approval package

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the roles of the credit committee in an organization.
cards.statement: Credit committee minutes should be kept confidential to committee members and never distributed.
cards.explanation: Minutes must be distributed quickly after the meeting; withholding them defeats their purpose as a record for management and auditors.
cards.originalText: Minutes kept confidential to committee members and never distributed, to protect candid discussion

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the roles of the credit committee in an organization.
cards.statement: Credit committee members should receive the approval documents well in advance of the meeting so that they have time to review the package.
cards.explanation: Committee effectiveness depends on adequate time to read the package and request more information. Documents delivered only hours before the meeting risk a rubber-stamp approval of the originator's deal.
cards.originalText: The approval documents should have been distributed well in advance of the meeting.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the roles of the credit committee in an organization.
cards.statement: Credit committee minutes should be distributed before the committee takes its decision rather than after it.
cards.explanation: Minutes record the meeting, including the decision, so they are distributed shortly after the meeting rather than before it.
cards.originalText: The minutes should have been distributed before the decision, not after.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the roles of the credit committee in an organization.
cards.statement: A credit committee should reject a transaction whenever the members' vote is not unanimous.
cards.explanation: Consensus is not required. When it is absent, a vote is the proper mechanism for reaching a decision.
cards.originalText: The vote was not unanimous, so the loan should have been rejected.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the roles of the credit committee in an organization.
cards.statement: When a credit committee lacks consensus, the chair should allow all members to present their views objectively and then call a vote.
cards.explanation: The chair solicits opinions and facilitates the discussion dispassionately; a vote is the prescribed mechanism when consensus is lacking.
cards.originalText: Allow all members to present their views objectively and then call a vote

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the roles of the credit committee in an organization.
cards.statement: A credit committee chair who favours a transaction should close the discussion and record it as approved because the chair's view carries the most weight.
cards.explanation: The chair must be objective and give every member a hearing. Where there is no consensus, the committee votes.
cards.originalText: Close the discussion and record the transaction as approved because the chair’s view carries the most weight

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the roles of the credit committee in an organization.
cards.statement: A credit committee should defer a decision to the CEO to avoid disagreement within the committee.
cards.explanation: The committee is the decision body; escalating to avoid a vote abdicates its role.
cards.originalText: Defer the decision to the CEO to avoid disagreement within the committee

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe key elements of an effective lending or financing policy.
cards.statement: A bank's lending policy should adapt loan terms and products to regional economic conditions and borrower profiles.
cards.explanation: An effective lending policy is flexible and sets terms by type of loan and borrower, adapting to local conditions so that risk is priced and controlled where it arises.
cards.originalText: Adapting loan terms and products to regional economic conditions and borrower profiles.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe key elements of an effective lending or financing policy.
cards.statement: A lending policy should apply the same interest rate to every loan type.
cards.explanation: Rates should cover the cost of funds, supervision, overhead and probable losses, which differ by loan type, so a uniform rate ignores risk differences.
cards.originalText: Applying the same interest rate to every loan type to simplify the portfolio.
cards.correction: A lending policy should set interest rates by loan type.

changes.from: apply the same interest rate to every loan type
changes.to: set interest rates by loan type

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe key elements of an effective lending or financing policy.
cards.statement: Accepting a wider range of hard-to-value assets as collateral without changing advance rates enhances a bank's credit risk management.
cards.explanation: Looser collateral standards without matching advance rates (loan-to-value limits) raise rather than reduce loss given default.
cards.originalText: Accepting a wider range of hard‑to‑value assets as collateral without changing advance rates.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe key elements of an effective lending or financing policy.
cards.statement: A bank should customise its loan pricing to reflect the risk and potential return of different customer segments and loan types.
cards.explanation: Risk-based pricing by segment and loan type compensates the bank for expected losses and costs while allowing it to serve a diverse clientele.
cards.originalText: Customizing loan pricing models to reflect the risk and potential return of different customer segments and loan types.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe key elements of an effective lending or financing policy.
cards.statement: A lending policy should set the same loan maturity for all customer segments.
cards.explanation: Maturities should be set by loan type, with the source of repayment and the life of the collateral in mind, so a uniform maturity ignores these differences.
cards.originalText: Introducing a uniform loan maturity policy across all customer segments to simplify portfolio management.
cards.correction: A lending policy should set loan maturities by loan type.

changes.from: set the same loan maturity for all customer segments
changes.to: set loan maturities by loan type

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe key elements of an effective lending or financing policy.
cards.statement: A credit policy should provide a structured and independent oversight process for managing workouts and high-risk client actions.
cards.explanation: Sound policy prioritises high-risk client actions and provides independent oversight of collections and workouts, giving objective, case-by-case handling.
cards.originalText: Developing a structured and independent oversight process for managing workouts and high‑risk client actions.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe key elements of an effective lending or financing policy.
cards.statement: A bank's credit policy should automatically close every account that becomes delinquent.
cards.explanation: Automatic closure ignores case-by-case workout or restructuring and may destroy recoverable value.
cards.originalText: Implementing an automated system to immediately close accounts that become delinquent.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe key elements of an effective lending or financing policy.
cards.statement: A bank's credit risk management plan should include a classification of risks organised by collectability.
cards.explanation: Lending policies cover limiting credit risk, classifying assets by exposure and collectability, and creating provisions for potential losses.
cards.originalText: classification of risks organized by collectability.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe key elements of an effective lending or financing policy.
cards.statement: A bank's credit risk management plan must include a loan loss provision equal to at least 8% of its loan portfolio.
cards.explanation: No fixed 8% provision rule exists; provisions reflect each bank's risk. The 8% figure is a Basel capital ratio, not a provisioning requirement.
cards.originalText: loan loss provision equal to at least 8% of their loan portfolio.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe key elements of an effective lending or financing policy.
cards.statement: A bank's credit risk management plan should be a rigid set of policies designed to address every possible risk source.
cards.explanation: Credit policies must be flexible and adapt to changing conditions rather than being rigid.
cards.originalText: rigid set of policies designed to address every possible risk source.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe key elements of an effective lending or financing policy.
cards.statement: A bank should regularly adjust the loan-to-value ratio on pledged securities based on their periodic pricing and marketability.
cards.explanation: Periodic repricing and marketability-based margins keep a buffer against falling collateral values.
cards.originalText: Regularly adjusting the LTV ratio based on the periodic pricing and marketability of the securities.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe key elements of an effective lending or financing policy.
cards.statement: A bank should set a higher loan-to-value ratio for less marketable securities pledged as collateral.
cards.explanation: Less marketable securities are harder to liquidate at value, so they warrant a lower loan-to-value ratio (a larger margin).
cards.originalText: Setting a higher LTV ratio for less marketable securities.
cards.correction: A bank should set a lower loan-to-value ratio for less marketable securities pledged as collateral.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe key elements of an effective lending or financing policy.
cards.statement: A bank should apply a uniform loan-to-value ratio across all securities pledged as collateral.
cards.explanation: A uniform ratio ignores differences in volatility and marketability. Margin requirements should be related to the marketability of each type of security.
cards.originalText: Applying a uniform LTV ratio across all securities.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe key elements of an effective lending or financing policy.
cards.statement: A restructured loan on which the bank has granted concessions is measured by reducing its recorded investment to net realizable value, with the reduction charged to the income statement.
cards.explanation: Concessions impair the loan's value, so the carrying amount is written down and the loss is recognised immediately in earnings.
cards.originalText: Measure the restructured loan by reducing its recorded investment to net realizable value, charging the reduction to the income statement.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe key elements of an effective lending or financing policy.
cards.statement: The reduction in the value of a restructured loan is recorded as a deferred charge to be recognised in future financial periods.
cards.explanation: Deferring the reduction delays loss recognition. The charge belongs to the period of the restructuring and goes through the income statement.
cards.originalText: Record the reduction in loan value as a deferred charge, to be recognized in future financial periods.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe key elements of an effective lending or financing policy.
cards.statement: The recorded investment of a restructured loan should be kept unchanged to maintain consistency in the loan portfolio.
cards.explanation: Leaving the carrying amount unchanged ignores the concessions and overstates assets and income; the loan is written down to net realizable value.
cards.originalText: Keep the recorded investment of restructured loans unchanged to maintain consistency in the loan portfolio.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the importance and challenges of setting exposure and concentration limits.
cards.statement: A derivative position with a client, such as a commodity swap, counts toward the bank's exposure to that client under single-client limits.
cards.explanation: Single-client limits cover all credit exposure to the client, including derivative and other off-balance-sheet claims, not just funded loans.
cards.originalText: A commodity swap position with VH3 where the bank is the fixed‑price receiver

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the importance and challenges of setting exposure and concentration limits.
cards.statement: A bank with significant exposure to a few key sectors should manage concentration risk by monitoring the economic health of those sectors and adjusting its lending to manage exposure.
cards.explanation: Sector concentration is managed by setting sector limits, reviewing and reporting them frequently, and monitoring sector conditions, adjusting lending accordingly.
cards.originalText: Monitoring the economic health of key sectors and adjusting lending practices to manage exposure.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the importance and challenges of setting exposure and concentration limits.
cards.statement: A bank limits its credit risk by concentrating its loans in the most profitable local industry.
cards.explanation: Concentrating in one industry adds to concentration risk and exposes the bank to a single sector shock.
cards.originalText: Concentrating loans in the most profitable local industry to maximize returns.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the importance and challenges of setting exposure and concentration limits.
cards.statement: Regulators typically restrict a bank's total credit to related parties to a specified percentage of its Tier 1 capital.
cards.explanation: The standard control is an aggregate cap on related-party credit as a percentage of Tier 1 capital, which bounds exposure however favourable individual terms are.
cards.originalText: Restrict total credit to related parties to a specified percentage of the bank’s Tier 1 capital.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the importance and challenges of setting exposure and concentration limits.
cards.statement: Regulators require banks to exclude all related parties from receiving any form of credit.
cards.explanation: Related-party lending is permitted within limits. Regulators typically cap it at a percentage of capital rather than prohibiting it.
cards.originalText: Exclude all related parties from receiving any form of credit.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the importance and challenges of setting exposure and concentration limits.
cards.statement: Acceptances and letters of credit should be included in a bank's risk exposure to a single client.
cards.explanation: Exposure to a single client includes less direct forms of credit such as acceptances and letters of credit, not just funded loans.
cards.originalText: acceptances and letters of credit should be factored into the risk exposure of a single client.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the importance and challenges of setting exposure and concentration limits.
cards.statement: The term single client, for the purpose of single-client exposure limits, refers only to a legal person.
cards.explanation: A single client can be an individual, a legal person or a connected group whose exposures must be aggregated.
cards.originalText: the term ”single client” only refers to a legal person.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the importance and challenges of setting exposure and concentration limits.
cards.statement: Every bank is subject to the same single-client limit of 10% of capital.
cards.explanation: Single-client limits vary by jurisdiction and are commonly in a range of about 10% to 25% of capital.
cards.originalText: all banks have a limit of 10% of capital for a single client.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the scope and allocation processes of a bank’s credit facility and explain bank-specific policies and actions to reduce credit risk.
cards.statement: A bank's lending policy should require the financial projections of business clients to cover a horizon matching the maturity of their loan.
cards.explanation: Matching the projection horizon to the loan maturity lets the bank judge whether the loan can be repaid from projected cash flow.
cards.originalText: Financial projections from business clients should match the maturity of their loan.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the scope and allocation processes of a bank’s credit facility and explain bank-specific policies and actions to reduce credit risk.
cards.statement: A bank's lending policy should set a single maximum maturity of 10 years for all loans.
cards.explanation: Policy should set clear maximum maturities for each loan type, based on the source of repayment, the loan purpose and the life of the collateral.
cards.originalText: All loans should have a maximum maturity schedule of 10 years.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the scope and allocation processes of a bank’s credit facility and explain bank-specific policies and actions to reduce credit risk.
cards.statement: The Board should approve every individual delinquency workout plan.
cards.explanation: The Board should be informed of delinquencies and of the process for handling them, but a solid policy means it need not approve every individual workout plan.
cards.originalText: The Board should approve all individual delinquency workout plans.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the scope and allocation processes of a bank’s credit facility and explain bank-specific policies and actions to reduce credit risk.
cards.statement: Under a sound lending policy, credit officers may extend any type of credit that a customer needs as long as they judge it a reasonable risk.
cards.explanation: A lending policy should limit the types of credit offered, based on officer expertise, deposit structure and credit demand, and set lending authority limits. Open-ended discretion increases risk.
cards.originalText: Credit officers should have the flexibility to extend any type of credit that a customer needs as long as they find it to be a reasonable risk for the bank.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the scope and allocation processes of a bank’s credit facility and explain bank-specific policies and actions to reduce credit risk.
cards.statement: To reduce credit risk on loans secured by securities, a lending policy should set margin requirements for each type of security based on its marketability and assign responsibility and a timetable for periodic repricing of the collateral.
cards.explanation: Collateral protects the bank only if its current market value covers the loan, so margins must reflect marketability and the collateral must be repriced periodically.
cards.originalText: Set margin requirements (maximum loan‑to‑market‑value of pledged securities) for each type of security based on its marketability, and assign responsibility and a timetable for periodic repricing of the collateral.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the scope and allocation processes of a bank’s credit facility and explain bank-specific policies and actions to reduce credit risk.
cards.statement: For loans held to maturity, pledged securities need to be valued only once at origination.
cards.explanation: Holding a loan to maturity does not stabilise collateral value. Stale valuations hide margin shortfalls when security prices move, so policy should require periodic repricing.
cards.originalText: Value the pledged securities once at origination and rely on that value until maturity, because the loans are held to maturity.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Discuss factors that should be considered during the credit asset classification process.
cards.statement: In assigning credit asset classifications, the primary emphasis is on the borrower's ability and willingness to meet its obligations out of prospective operating cash flow.
cards.explanation: Classification rests chiefly on whether the borrower's prospective operating cash flow can service the debt. Collateral is a secondary source of repayment.
cards.originalText: The borrower’s ability and willingness to meet obligations out of prospective operating cash flow

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Discuss factors that should be considered during the credit asset classification process.
cards.statement: In assigning credit asset classifications, the primary emphasis is on the realizable value of the collateral pledged against the loan.
cards.explanation: Collateral is a secondary source of repayment. Classification emphasises the borrower's prospective operating cash flow as the primary source.
cards.originalText: The realizable value of the collateral pledged against the loan

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify and explain the components of expected loss and differentiate between expected loss and unexpected loss.
cards.statement: Loss given default reflects the type of product used for a loan, such as secured versus unsecured or senior versus subordinated.
cards.explanation: The product drives collateral and seniority, which determine the fraction of exposure lost if default occurs. Probability of default reflects who the borrower is.
cards.originalText: Loss given default.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify and explain the components of expected loss and differentiate between expected loss and unexpected loss.
cards.statement: Probability of default reflects the type of product used for a loan, such as secured versus unsecured or senior versus subordinated.
cards.explanation: Probability of default reflects the quality of the borrower. The product, with its collateral and seniority, drives loss given default.
cards.originalText: Probability of default.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify and explain the components of expected loss and differentiate between expected loss and unexpected loss.
cards.statement: Unexpected loss is a component of expected loss.
cards.explanation: Expected loss is built from probability of default, exposure at default and loss given default. Unexpected loss is the tail loss not captured by expected loss.
cards.originalText: Unexpected loss.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the components of credit risk analysis.
cards.statement: A bank's portfolio-level credit risk analysis should include segmentation of the loan portfolio by currency, maturity, economic sector and borrower category.
cards.explanation: Portfolio analysis summarises and segments the whole book rather than assessing individual obligors.
cards.originalText: Segmentation of the loan portfolio by currency, maturity, economic sector and borrower category.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the components of credit risk analysis.
cards.statement: Portfolio-level credit risk analysis should consist of a loan-by-loan collateral appraisal performed at origination.
cards.explanation: Loan-by-loan collateral appraisal belongs to the lending and appraisal process. Portfolio analysis works at an aggregate level, summarising and segmenting the whole book.
cards.originalText: An appraisal of the collateral held against each individual loan, performed at origination.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the components of credit risk analysis.
cards.statement: Analysing nonperforming loans by the period in which they were granted (vintage) measures loan losses per period of origination, to show whether credit-granting discipline was maintained.
cards.explanation: A vintage with abnormally high losses indicates that credit-granting standards slipped in that period.
cards.originalText: To measure loan losses per period of origination, in order to determine whether the bank’s disciplines for granting credit were maintained.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the components of credit risk analysis.
cards.statement: Analysing nonperforming loans by their year of origination is used to determine how long each loan has been past due.
cards.explanation: How long loans have been past due is the ageing of past-due loans (30, 90, 180, 360 days). Vintage analysis groups loans by period granted to test credit-granting discipline.
cards.originalText: To determine how long each loan has been past due so that it can be assigned to the appropriate asset classification category.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the components of credit risk analysis.
cards.statement: A bank's loan maturity profile shows how long the bank is lending for, may change with shifts in customers and products, and interacts strongly with liquidity risk management.
cards.explanation: The maturity profile answers how long the bank lends, whereas the customer profile answers to whom and the loan distribution profile answers what product.
cards.originalText: It answers the question of how long the bank is lending for, may be driven by the shifts in customers and products, and interacts strongly with liquidity risk management.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the components of credit risk analysis.
cards.statement: A loan portfolio's maturity profile shows to whom the bank is lending.
cards.explanation: The customer profile shows to whom the bank is lending. The maturity profile shows for how long it is lending.
cards.originalText: It shows to whom the bank is lending and should be reported only with the customer profile.
cards.correction: A loan portfolio's customer profile shows to whom the bank is lending.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the components of credit risk analysis.
cards.statement: Loan maturity is relevant to credit risk analysis only for loans on the nonperforming list.
cards.explanation: Maturity structure is part of aggregate portfolio analysis for all loans, not just delinquent ones.
cards.originalText: It matters only for loans on the nonperforming list, because maturity is relevant to credit risk only after delinquency.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the components of credit risk analysis.
cards.statement: Changes in a bank's loan maturity structure reflect macroeconomic trends alone.
cards.explanation: Changes in maturity structure can also result from shifts in customers, lending products and risk factors, not only macro trends.
cards.originalText: It reflects macroeconomic trends alone, because maturity is a contractual feature unaffected by changes in customers or products.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the components of credit risk management capacity, and identify key questions that the board of directors of a bank should ask.
cards.statement: A credit risk management capacity review should include the timeliness of information flows from loan officers to senior management and the Board.
cards.explanation: A capacity review covers three areas: the lending process, staffing and information flows, including whether information reaches the Board in a timely, accurate and cost-effective way.
cards.originalText: the timeliness of information flows from loan officers to senior management and the Board.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the components of credit risk management capacity, and identify key questions that the board of directors of a bank should ask.
cards.statement: A credit risk management capacity review should include the bank's interest rate hedging policy.
cards.explanation: Hedging policy is a market-risk and asset-liability management topic; a capacity review covers the lending process, staffing and information flows.
cards.originalText: the bank’s interest rate hedging policy.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the components of credit risk management capacity, and identify key questions that the board of directors of a bank should ask.
cards.statement: The staffing part of a credit risk management capacity review identifies the staff involved in origination, appraisal, supervision and monitoring, including their number, levels, age, experience and responsibilities, and reviews the quality, frequency and adequacy of their training.
cards.explanation: The review also analyses staff skills and qualifications against the bank's policies and procedures to judge whether staffing is adequate.
cards.originalText: Identify the staff involved in origination, appraisal, supervision and monitoring, including their number, levels, age, experience and responsibilities, and review the quality, frequency and adequacy of their training.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the components of credit risk management capacity, and identify key questions that the board of directors of a bank should ask.
cards.statement: The staffing part of a credit risk management capacity review should confirm only the total headcount of the credit department.
cards.explanation: The review covers number, levels, age, experience, responsibilities and training. Training quality and frequency are good indicators of lending skills.
cards.originalText: Confirm only the total headcount of the credit department, since the quality of lending skills cannot be assessed from staffing data.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the components of credit risk management capacity, and identify key questions that the board of directors of a bank should ask.
cards.statement: The staffing part of a credit risk management capacity review can rely on staff length of service alone, because experience makes a review of training programs unnecessary.
cards.explanation: Training programs are reviewed and their adequacy assessed regardless of experience; tenure is not a substitute for training.
cards.originalText: Assess the staff’s length of service alone, since experience makes a review of training programs unnecessary.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Evaluate a bank’s economic capital relative to its level of credit risk.
cards.statement: Increasing the confidence level at which economic capital is set raises the economic capital required.
cards.explanation: Economic capital equals the capital multiplier times portfolio unexpected loss, and the capital multiplier increases with the confidence level, so higher confidence needs more capital for any portfolio.
cards.originalText: If the confidence level for both banks is increased, the level of economic capital needed will increase for Bank ABC and for Bank XYZ.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Evaluate a bank’s economic capital relative to its level of credit risk.
cards.statement: Two portfolios with the same exposure, duration, rating and expected loss but different average default correlation need the same economic capital at a given confidence level.
cards.explanation: Higher default correlation raises portfolio unexpected loss, so the portfolio with the higher correlation needs more economic capital at the same confidence level.
cards.originalText: If the confidence level for both banks is kept unchanged, the level of economic capital needed for Bank ABC and for Bank XYZ will be equal.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Evaluate a bank’s economic capital relative to its level of credit risk.
cards.statement: When the confidence level is raised and the credit portfolio is unchanged, the capital multiplier applied to unexpected loss increases, so economic capital increases even though unexpected loss is unchanged.
cards.explanation: A higher target rating requires a higher confidence level, which raises the capital multiplier. Unexpected loss depends on the assets, not on the confidence level.
cards.originalText: The capital multiplier applied to unexpected loss increases, so economic capital increases even though unexpected loss is unchanged.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Evaluate a bank’s economic capital relative to its level of credit risk.
cards.statement: Economic capital for credit risk does not depend on the confidence level, only on the riskiness of the credit assets.
cards.explanation: Economic capital depends on both the confidence level and the riskiness of the assets.
cards.originalText: Economic capital is unchanged because the riskiness of the credit assets, not the confidence level, determines the capital requirement.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Evaluate a bank’s economic capital relative to its level of credit risk.
cards.statement: A higher confidence level decreases the capital multiplier applied to unexpected loss.
cards.explanation: A higher confidence level raises the capital multiplier because more of the loss distribution must be covered.
cards.originalText: The capital multiplier applied to unexpected loss decreases, because a larger share of the loss distribution is then covered by expected loss.
cards.correction: A higher confidence level increases the capital multiplier applied to unexpected loss.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Evaluate a bank’s economic capital relative to its level of credit risk.
cards.statement: At the same confidence level, a riskier and more concentrated credit portfolio has a higher unexpected loss than a diversified one and therefore needs more economic capital.
cards.explanation: The same capital multiplier applied to a higher unexpected loss gives higher economic capital.
cards.originalText: Bank N needs more economic capital because its riskier assets produce a higher unexpected loss to which the same capital multiplier is applied.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Evaluate a bank’s economic capital relative to its level of credit risk.
cards.statement: Pricing expected loss into a portfolio's loan interest rates reduces its unexpected loss.
cards.explanation: Unexpected loss is the volatility of losses around expected loss and is what economic capital must cover; pricing in expected loss does not reduce it.
cards.originalText: Bank N needs less economic capital because its higher expected loss is already priced into its loan interest rates, reducing unexpected loss.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify and describe important factors used to calculate economic capital for credit risk: probability of default, exposure, and loss rate.
cards.statement: Pledging substantial collateral, such as real estate and equipment, against a corporate loan lowers its loss rate (loss given default).
cards.explanation: Loss rate is largely a function of collateral: substantial collateral raises recovery and lowers the loss rate.
cards.originalText: The borrower pledges substantial real estate and equipment as collateral for the loan.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify and describe important factors used to calculate economic capital for credit risk: probability of default, exposure, and loss rate.
cards.statement: The key borrower-specific inputs to expected and unexpected credit loss, and hence to economic capital for credit risk, are probability of default, exposure amount and loss rate.
cards.explanation: Expected loss equals probability of default times exposure amount times loss rate.
cards.originalText: Probability of default, exposure amount, and loss rate.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify and describe important factors used to calculate economic capital for credit risk: probability of default, exposure, and loss rate.
cards.statement: The loss rate is the percentage of exposure lost if a borrower defaults.
cards.explanation: Loss rate, also called loss given default, equals 1 minus the recovery rate.
cards.originalText: loss rate.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify and describe important factors used to calculate economic capital for credit risk: probability of default, exposure, and loss rate.
cards.statement: Probability of default measures the percentage of exposure lost if a borrower fails to perform its obligation.
cards.explanation: Probability of default is the likelihood that default occurs, not the severity of loss once it occurs; the percentage lost given default is the loss rate.
cards.originalText: probability of default.
cards.correction: Loss rate measures the percentage of exposure lost if a borrower fails to perform its obligation.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify and describe important factors used to calculate economic capital for credit risk: probability of default, exposure, and loss rate.
cards.statement: Exposure amount is the percentage of exposure lost if a borrower defaults.
cards.explanation: Exposure amount is the amount at risk at default, not a percentage loss; the percentage lost given default is the loss rate.
cards.originalText: exposure amount.
cards.correction: Loss rate is the percentage of exposure lost if a borrower defaults.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain how the credit loss distribution is modeled.
cards.statement: A beta distribution whose two shape parameters $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are equal is symmetric.
cards.explanation: When $\alpha = \beta$ the density is a mirror image about its mean. Unequal parameters produce skewness.
cards.originalText: Symmetric

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain how the credit loss distribution is modeled.
cards.statement: A beta distribution whose two shape parameters satisfy $\alpha = \beta$ is skewed to the left.
cards.explanation: Skewness requires $\alpha \ne \beta$; equal parameters remove the asymmetry.
cards.originalText: Skewed to the left
cards.correction: A beta distribution whose two shape parameters satisfy $\alpha = \beta$ is symmetric.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain how the credit loss distribution is modeled.
cards.statement: The beta distribution is flexible for modelling credit losses because it can be symmetric or skewed depending on the values of its shape parameters.
cards.explanation: The beta distribution is bounded between 0% and 100%, matching loss rates, and its shape flexibility suits the skewed distribution of credit losses.
cards.originalText: It is flexible and can be symmetric or skewed depending on its shape parameter values

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain how the credit loss distribution is modeled.
cards.statement: The beta distribution is used to model credit losses because it is symmetrical and aligns with the normal distribution.
cards.explanation: Credit losses are not normally distributed but highly skewed. The beta is symmetric only when its two shape parameters are equal, and symmetry is not the reason for using it.
cards.originalText: It is symmetrical and so aligns with the normal distribution of events

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain how the credit loss distribution is modeled.
cards.statement: The beta distribution is suited to credit risk analysis because it focuses only on extreme values.
cards.explanation: The beta describes the whole bounded loss distribution; fitting its tail is in fact the difficult part and needs Monte Carlo support.
cards.originalText: It focuses only on extreme values and is therefore suited to credit risk analysis

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain how the credit loss distribution is modeled.
cards.statement: The beta distribution has a fixed mean, which simplifies the calculation of expected loss.
cards.explanation: The mean of the beta is not fixed; it is set to the portfolio's expected loss, EL(P), when the distribution is fitted.
cards.originalText: It has a fixed mean, which simplifies the calculation of expected loss

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain how the credit loss distribution is modeled.
cards.statement: A beta distribution for portfolio credit losses is characterised by the portfolio's expected loss, EL(P), and unexpected loss, UL(P); the challenge is fitting the tail, which depends on the ratio EL(P)/UL(P).
cards.explanation: Two parameters, the mean EL(P) and the standard deviation UL(P), pin down the beta, but how well its tail fits depends on the ratio of the two.
cards.originalText: It is characterized by the portfolio’s expected loss, EL(P), and unexpected loss, UL(P); the challenge is fitting the tail, which depends on the ratio EL(P)/UL(P)

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain how the credit loss distribution is modeled.
cards.statement: The beta distribution is flexible because it has four parameters, one for each moment, which allows precise calibration of kurtosis.
cards.explanation: The beta has two shape parameters, not four, and they are set from the portfolio's expected loss and unexpected loss.
cards.originalText: It is flexible because it has four parameters, one for each moment, allowing precise calibration of kurtosis

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain how the credit loss distribution is modeled.
cards.statement: The most convenient and sufficiently realistic calibration of the beta distribution for credit losses sets its shape parameters $\alpha$ and $\beta$ equal to each other.
cards.explanation: Setting $\alpha = \beta$ forces symmetry, which contradicts the skewed shape of credit losses; the parameters are fitted to EL(P) and UL(P).
cards.originalText: The most convenient and sufficiently realistic calibration sets the shape parameters $\alpha$ and $\beta$ equal to each other

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain how the credit loss distribution is modeled.
cards.statement: Even when accurately fitted, the beta distribution gives no way to determine the capital multiplier, which therefore requires a different distribution.
cards.explanation: Once the tail is fitted, the capital multiplier is read from the chosen quantile of the same beta distribution.
cards.originalText: Even when accurately fitted it gives no way to determine the capital multiplier, which therefore requires a different distribution

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain how the credit loss distribution is modeled.
cards.statement: The beta distribution is symmetric for all values of $\alpha$ and $\beta$ and can be skewed only if a third parameter is added.
cards.explanation: The beta is symmetric only when $\alpha = \beta$; unequal $\alpha$ and $\beta$ already produce skewness, so no third parameter is needed.
cards.originalText: It is symmetric for all values of $\alpha$ and $\beta$ and can be skewed only if a third parameter is added
cards.correction: The beta distribution is symmetric only when $\alpha = \beta$ and is skewed when $\alpha \ne \beta$, with no third parameter needed.

changes.from: is symmetric for all values of $\alpha$ and $\beta$ and can be skewed only if a third parameter is added
changes.to: is symmetric only when $\alpha = \beta$ and is skewed when $\alpha \ne \beta$, with no third parameter needed

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain how the credit loss distribution is modeled.
cards.statement: Monte Carlo simulation is most useful for modelling extreme credit losses, where a standard distribution such as the beta may not fit the tail adequately.
cards.explanation: Economic capital depends on the far tail of the loss distribution. Combining the beta with Monte Carlo simulation is the practical way to fit that tail.
cards.originalText: Modeling extreme credit losses, where a standard distribution such as the beta distribution may not fit the tail adequately

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain how the credit loss distribution is modeled.
cards.statement: Monte Carlo simulation is most useful for liquid assets whose market prices directly reveal risk correlations.
cards.explanation: Credit assets are generally illiquid, with no market prices revealing correlations; simulation is useful for modelling the extreme tail of credit losses.
cards.originalText: Dealing with liquid assets where market prices directly reveal risk correlations

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain how the credit loss distribution is modeled.
cards.statement: A beta distribution is difficult to fit exactly to the tail of a portfolio's credit loss profile, so the tail is best fitted by combining it with Monte Carlo simulation.
cards.explanation: The beta distribution fits the body of the loss distribution analytically but captures the extreme tail poorly. Monte Carlo simulation generates many loss scenarios and so supplements the beta fit in the tail.
cards.originalText: A Monte Carlo simulation

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain how the credit loss distribution is modeled.
cards.statement: The tail of a credit loss distribution fitted with a beta distribution is best improved by combining the beta distribution with a normal distribution.
cards.explanation: A normal distribution is symmetric and thin-tailed, so it understates the skewed tail of credit losses and does not improve the fit. The tail is better fitted by combining the beta with Monte Carlo simulation.
cards.originalText: A normal distribution

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain how the credit loss distribution is modeled.
cards.statement: A beta distribution characterised by a portfolio's expected loss (EL) and unexpected loss (UL) is hard to fit exactly to the tail of the loss distribution, so the tail is fitted by combining it with Monte Carlo simulation.
cards.explanation: Economic capital is driven by the far tail of the loss distribution, which a beta fitted to EL and UL captures imperfectly. A numerical Monte Carlo procedure is therefore combined with the analytical beta solution.
cards.originalText: A beta distribution characterised by the portfolio’s EL and UL is hard to fit exactly to the tail of the loss distribution, so the tail is fitted by combining it with Monte Carlo simulation.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain how the credit loss distribution is modeled.
cards.statement: The beta distribution can only be symmetric, so it cannot represent skewed credit losses.
cards.explanation: The beta distribution is very flexible: it is symmetric only when its two shape parameters are equal and is skewed otherwise, which suits skewed credit losses.
cards.correction: The beta distribution can be skewed, so it can represent skewed credit losses.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain how the credit loss distribution is modeled.
cards.statement: The beta distribution cannot be defined on the 0% to 100% loss range.
cards.explanation: The beta distribution is defined on the interval from 0 to 1, which maps naturally to losses of 0% to 100% of exposure.
cards.correction: The beta distribution can be defined on the 0% to 100% loss range.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain how the credit loss distribution is modeled.
cards.statement: Monte Carlo simulation replaces the need to estimate the portfolio's expected loss and unexpected loss.
cards.explanation: Expected loss and unexpected loss remain the inputs that characterise the beta distribution. Monte Carlo simulation only helps to fit the tail.
cards.originalText: Monte Carlo simulation replaces the need to estimate the portfolio’s expected loss and unexpected loss.
cards.correction: Monte Carlo simulation does not replace the need to estimate the portfolio's expected loss and unexpected loss.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe challenges to quantifying credit risk.
cards.statement: Ideally a bottom-up credit risk model would capture expected and unexpected changes in borrowers' credit quality over several years, but multi-period solutions are very complex, so a one-year horizon is used in practice.
cards.explanation: Credit exposures are multi-period in nature, but modelling multi-year changes in credit quality is cumbersome. Almost all internal credit risk models therefore use a one-year estimation horizon, which is a recognised simplification.
cards.originalText: Ideally the model would capture expected and unexpected changes in borrowers’ credit quality over several years, but multi‑period solutions are very complex, so a one‑year horizon is used in practice.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe challenges to quantifying credit risk.
cards.statement: A one-year estimation horizon is required in credit risk modelling because credit loss distributions cannot be defined over any other period.
cards.explanation: Credit loss distributions can be defined over other horizons. The one-year choice is a practical simplification, not a mathematical requirement.
cards.originalText: A one‑year horizon is required because credit loss distributions cannot be defined over any other period.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe challenges to quantifying credit risk.
cards.statement: A one-year estimation horizon is used in credit risk models because credits are liquid and can be repriced daily, so longer horizons add nothing.
cards.explanation: The bottom-up framework assumes credits are illiquid. The one-year horizon is used because multi-period models are complex, not because credits can be repriced daily.
cards.originalText: A one‑year horizon is used because credits are liquid and can be repriced daily, so longer horizons add nothing.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe challenges to quantifying credit risk.
cards.statement: A one-year estimation horizon prevents a bottom-up credit risk model from reflecting default correlation among borrowers.
cards.explanation: The bottom-up approach does take default correlation into account within credit risk. The one-year horizon is a separate limitation and is unrelated to correlation.
cards.originalText: A one‑year horizon prevents the model from reflecting default correlation among borrowers.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe challenges to quantifying credit risk.
cards.statement: A bottom-up credit risk approach that assumes credits are illiquid measures only each credit's risk contribution to the existing credit portfolio, not its correlation with risk factors as priced in liquid markets.
cards.explanation: Under the illiquidity assumption, risk is measured by each credit's contribution to the credit portfolio. The correlation with market-priced risk factors that matters once loans become liquid and traded is omitted.
cards.originalText: The approach measures only each credit’s risk contribution to the existing credit portfolio, not its correlation with risk factors as priced in liquid markets.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe challenges to quantifying credit risk.
cards.statement: The bottom-up approach to quantifying credit risk ignores default correlation among the borrowers in the credit portfolio.
cards.explanation: The bottom-up approach does take default correlation among borrowers into account. The correlation it omits is with risk factors priced in liquid markets.
cards.originalText: The approach ignores default correlation among the borrowers in the credit portfolio.
cards.correction: The bottom-up approach to quantifying credit risk takes into account default correlation among the borrowers in the credit portfolio.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe challenges to quantifying credit risk.
cards.statement: Expected loss cannot be computed under the bottom-up approach because it requires a quoted market price for each loan.
cards.explanation: Expected loss equals exposure at default times probability of default times loss rate, all of which are internal estimates. No market price is needed.
cards.originalText: The approach cannot compute expected loss because EL requires a quoted market price for each loan.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe challenges to quantifying credit risk.
cards.statement: The bottom-up approach to economic capital assumes that credits are liquid and fully captures their correlation with risk factors as priced in capital markets.
cards.explanation: The bottom-up approach assumes credits are illiquid, so it measures only their contribution to internal portfolio risk. It does not capture their correlation with risk factors priced in liquid markets.
cards.originalText: The approach assumes credits are liquid and fully captures their correlation with risk factors as priced in capital markets.
cards.correction: The bottom-up approach to economic capital assumes that credits are illiquid and does not capture their correlation with risk factors as priced in capital markets.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe challenges to quantifying credit risk.
cards.statement: The bottom-up approach to economic capital assumes that credits are illiquid assets.
cards.explanation: Presuming credits are illiquid means only their internal risk contribution to the portfolio is measured. This is a recognised limitation of the approach.
cards.originalText: The approach assumes that credits are illiquid assets.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe challenges to quantifying credit risk.
cards.statement: Internal credit risk models typically use only a one-year estimation horizon rather than a multi-period horizon.
cards.explanation: Multi-period solutions are very complex, so practitioners settle for a one-year horizon. This is a recognised limitation of the bottom-up approach.
cards.originalText: Internal credit risk models typically use only a one‑year estimation horizon rather than a multi‑period horizon.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe challenges to quantifying credit risk.
cards.statement: Market and operational risk are separated from credit risk in the bottom-up approach and are measured and managed in different departments of the bank.
cards.explanation: Credit, market and operational risk are typically measured and managed in separate departments. This separation is a recognised limitation when quantifying credit risk and economic capital.
cards.originalText: Market and operational risk are separated from credit risk and are measured and managed in different departments of the bank.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.loText: Explain the capital adequacy, asset quality, management, earnings, and liquidity (CAMEL) system used for evaluating the financial condition of a bank.
cards.reading: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.statement: In the CAMEL system, the asset quality component evaluates loan performance and delinquency.
cards.explanation: Asset quality examines whether a bank's loans are performing or showing signs of delinquency.
cards.originalText: Asset quality

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.loText: Explain the capital adequacy, asset quality, management, earnings, and liquidity (CAMEL) system used for evaluating the financial condition of a bank.
cards.reading: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.statement: In the CAMEL system, the liquidity component is the one focused on delinquent loans.
cards.explanation: Liquidity concerns short-term liquidity events and the interest rate and liquidity risk on investments. Delinquent loans are assessed under asset quality.
cards.originalText: Liquidity
cards.correction: In the CAMEL system, the asset quality component is the one focused on delinquent loans.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.loText: Explain the capital adequacy, asset quality, management, earnings, and liquidity (CAMEL) system used for evaluating the financial condition of a bank.
cards.reading: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.statement: In the CAMEL system, the capital adequacy component is the one focused on delinquent loans.
cards.explanation: Capital adequacy compares a bank's capital with the regulatory minimum. Loan performance and delinquency are assessed under asset quality.
cards.originalText: Capital adequacy
cards.correction: In the CAMEL system, the asset quality component is the one focused on delinquent loans.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.loText: Describe quantitative measurements and factors of credit risk, including probability of default, loss given default, exposure at default, expected loss, and time horizon.
cards.reading: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.statement: Credit loss estimates are built from the probability of default (PD), loss given default (LGD) and exposure at default (EAD).
cards.explanation: Expected loss equals PD times EAD times LGD, usually over a one-year horizon. PD gives the likelihood of default, EAD the amount exposed and LGD the fraction lost.
cards.originalText: Probability of default (PD), loss given default (LGD), and exposure at default (EAD).

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.loText: Describe quantitative measurements and factors of credit risk, including probability of default, loss given default, exposure at default, expected loss, and time horizon.
cards.reading: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.statement: The components of a credit loss estimate are probability of default (PD), time value of money (TM) and loss given default (LGD).
cards.explanation: Time value of money is not a component of the expected loss formula. Exposure at default is needed to turn the loss fraction into a dollar loss.
cards.originalText: Probability of default (PD), time value of money (TM), and loss given default (LGD).
cards.correction: The components of a credit loss estimate are probability of default (PD), exposure at default (EAD) and loss given default (LGD).

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.loText: Describe quantitative measurements and factors of credit risk, including probability of default, loss given default, exposure at default, expected loss, and time horizon.
cards.reading: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.statement: The components of a credit loss estimate are loss given default (LGD), exposure at default (EAD) and credit rating (CR).
cards.explanation: A credit rating is an input to estimating the probability of default, not a loss component itself. Expected loss needs PD, EAD and LGD.
cards.originalText: Loss given default (LGD), exposure at default (EAD), and credit rating (CR).
cards.correction: The components of a credit loss estimate are loss given default (LGD), exposure at default (EAD) and probability of default (PD).

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.loText: Describe quantitative measurements and factors of credit risk, including probability of default, loss given default, exposure at default, expected loss, and time horizon.
cards.reading: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.statement: Exposure at default is hard to estimate for a revolving facility such as a home equity line of credit, because the borrower draws and repays at will and the balance at default is uncertain.
cards.explanation: EAD is easy to specify when payment dates and amounts are fixed. For a revolving line the outstanding balance fluctuates with borrower behaviour, so the balance at default is uncertain.
cards.originalText: A home equity line of credit (HELOC) with variable withdrawals and repayments.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.loText: Describe quantitative measurements and factors of credit risk, including probability of default, loss given default, exposure at default, expected loss, and time horizon.
cards.reading: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.statement: Exposure at default is difficult to estimate for a credit card account with a revolving credit facility, because the outstanding balance varies over time.
cards.explanation: A credit card balance varies with spending and repayment, so the amount outstanding at the unknown default date is hard to predict. Loans and bonds with scheduled payments have predictable balances.
cards.originalText: A credit card account with a revolving credit facility and variable outstanding balances.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.loText: Describe quantitative measurements and factors of credit risk, including probability of default, loss given default, exposure at default, expected loss, and time horizon.
cards.reading: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.statement: The time horizon in credit risk modelling is usually one year, consistent with the standard basis for financial reporting, although longer horizons can be used, especially for long-dated exposures where uncertainty rises.
cards.explanation: Expected loss is estimated over a specific period, usually one year to match financial reporting. Longer horizons are possible but carry more uncertainty.
cards.originalText: The horizon is usually one year, consistent with the standard basis for financial reporting, although longer horizons can be used, especially for long‑dated exposures where uncertainty rises.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.loText: Describe quantitative measurements and factors of credit risk, including probability of default, loss given default, exposure at default, expected loss, and time horizon.
cards.reading: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.statement: The time horizon in credit risk modelling must always equal the remaining maturity of each loan, so a one-year horizon is never appropriate.
cards.explanation: One year is the standard horizon even for loans with longer maturities. Maturity-matched horizons are an option, not a rule.
cards.originalText: The horizon must always equal the remaining maturity of each loan, so a one‑year horizon is never appropriate.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.loText: Describe quantitative measurements and factors of credit risk, including probability of default, loss given default, exposure at default, expected loss, and time horizon.
cards.reading: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.statement: The time horizon in credit risk modelling is fixed at 90 days, the period after which a payment is considered in default.
cards.explanation: The 90-days-past-due rule is a common definition of default, not the modelling horizon. The horizon is usually one year.
cards.originalText: The horizon is fixed at 90 days, the period after which a payment is considered in default.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.loText: Describe quantitative measurements and factors of credit risk, including probability of default, loss given default, exposure at default, expected loss, and time horizon.
cards.reading: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.statement: The time horizon has no effect on the estimated probability of default because default probabilities are independent of the period considered.
cards.explanation: A probability of default is defined over a period, so a longer horizon gives a higher cumulative PD.
cards.originalText: The horizon has no effect on the estimated PD because default probabilities are independent of the period considered.
cards.correction: The time horizon affects the estimated probability of default because default probabilities depend on the period considered.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.loText: Describe quantitative measurements and factors of credit risk, including probability of default, loss given default, exposure at default, expected loss, and time horizon.
cards.reading: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.statement: The probability of default is the likelihood that an obligor will not meet scheduled payments over the period, with default commonly defined as a payment delayed 90 days or more.
cards.explanation: PD is the probability of failing to meet scheduled payments over the horizon, and a payment delay of 90 days or more is the common definition of default.
cards.originalText: PD is the likelihood that the obligor will not meet scheduled payments over the period, with default commonly defined as a payment delayed 90 days or more.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.loText: Describe quantitative measurements and factors of credit risk, including probability of default, loss given default, exposure at default, expected loss, and time horizon.
cards.reading: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.statement: Loss given default is a dollar amount equal to the minimum guaranteed recovery on the loan, fixed at origination.
cards.explanation: LGD is the percentage of exposure expected to be lost if default occurs, equal to one minus the recovery rate. It is not a guaranteed dollar recovery fixed at origination.
cards.originalText: LGD is a dollar amount equal to the minimum guaranteed recovery on the loan, fixed at origination.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.loText: Describe quantitative measurements and factors of credit risk, including probability of default, loss given default, exposure at default, expected loss, and time horizon.
cards.reading: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.statement: Exposure at default depends mainly on the borrower's credit rating and is the same for a term loan and a revolving credit card.
cards.explanation: EAD depends mainly on loan characteristics rather than on the obligor. Revolving exposures such as credit cards fluctuate, so their EAD differs from that of a term loan.
cards.originalText: EAD depends mainly on the borrower’s credit rating and is the same for a term loan and a revolving credit card.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.loText: Describe quantitative measurements and factors of credit risk, including probability of default, loss given default, exposure at default, expected loss, and time horizon.
cards.reading: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.statement: Expected loss is estimated solely from the historical default rate and does not depend on exposure or recovery.
cards.explanation: Expected loss is the product of probability of default, exposure at default and loss given default. Exposure and recovery both matter.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.loText: Describe quantitative measurements and factors of credit risk, including probability of default, loss given default, exposure at default, expected loss, and time horizon.
cards.reading: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.statement: Loss given default is the percentage of a loan's exposure that is expected to be lost if the borrower defaults.
cards.explanation: LGD is the fraction of exposure lost given that default occurs, equal to 100% minus the recovery rate.
cards.originalText: Loss given default.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.topic: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.loText: Describe quantitative measurements and factors of credit risk, including probability of default, loss given default, exposure at default, expected loss, and time horizon.
cards.reading: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
cards.statement: Exposure at default is the percentage of a loan that is expected to be lost if the borrower defaults.
cards.explanation: EAD is the dollar exposure at the time of default. The percentage of exposure expected to be lost is the loss given default.
cards.originalText: Exposure at default.
cards.correction: Loss given default is the percentage of a loan that is expected to be lost if the borrower defaults.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare the credit scoring system to the credit rating system in assessing credit quality and describe the different types of each system.
cards.statement: Credit scoring systems are built for internal decision-making by financial institutions using historical data and numerical scores, whereas credit rating agencies produce ordinal grades for public dissemination.
cards.explanation: Credit scores are numerical outputs of internal automated models, while credit ratings are ordinal grades such as AAA or AA that are publicly available.
cards.originalText: Credit scoring systems are crafted for internal decision‑making by financial institutions using historical data and numerical scores, whereas credit rating agencies produce ordinal grades for public dissemination.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare the credit scoring system to the credit rating system in assessing credit quality and describe the different types of each system.
cards.statement: Credit scoring systems are designed for public use and facilitate investors' assessments using ordinal grades, while credit rating systems provide numerical scores for internal use.
cards.explanation: The two systems are reversed here. Scoring produces internal numerical scores, and rating produces public ordinal grades.
cards.originalText: Credit scoring systems are designed for public use and facilitate investors’ assessments using ordinal grades, while credit rating systems provide numerical scores for internal use.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare the credit scoring system to the credit rating system in assessing credit quality and describe the different types of each system.
cards.statement: Both credit scoring and credit rating systems are exclusively used for public dissemination, offering guidance through a combination of automated models and expert judgment.
cards.explanation: Credit scores are used internally rather than publicly disseminated. Scoring relies on automated models, while expert judgment is characteristic of ratings.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare the credit scoring system to the credit rating system in assessing credit quality and describe the different types of each system.
cards.statement: Credit scoring systems commonly assess the creditworthiness of individual consumers and small businesses, whereas credit rating systems are often used to rate corporations, sovereigns and structured finance products.
cards.explanation: Scoring suits high-volume lending to consumers and small businesses. Ratings are applied to corporations, sovereigns and structured finance products.
cards.originalText: Credit scoring systems commonly assess individual consumer and small business creditworthiness, whereas credit rating systems are often utilized to rate corporations, sovereigns, and structured finance products.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare the credit scoring system to the credit rating system in assessing credit quality and describe the different types of each system.
cards.statement: Credit scoring systems broadly evaluate the creditworthiness of entities across numerous markets, while credit rating systems are focused on individual consumers and small businesses.
cards.explanation: The scopes are swapped. Credit scoring targets consumers and small businesses, and credit ratings target corporations, sovereigns and structured finance products.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare the credit scoring system to the credit rating system in assessing credit quality and describe the different types of each system.
cards.statement: Credit scoring systems only evaluate the creditworthiness of large corporate clients, while credit rating systems are applied to consumers, small businesses and large enterprises.
cards.explanation: Scoring is mainly used for consumers and small businesses, not only large corporates. Ratings are not typically applied to consumers.
cards.originalText: Credit scoring systems only evaluate the creditworthiness of large corporate clients, while credit rating systems have a more versatile application, including consumers, small businesses, and large enterprises.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare the credit scoring system to the credit rating system in assessing credit quality and describe the different types of each system.
cards.statement: Credit rating systems evaluate broad categories such as management quality, industry risk and competitive position when forming a rating.
cards.explanation: Ratings blend quantitative analysis with expert judgment on qualitative factors. Credit scoring is automated and data-driven.
cards.originalText: Evaluating broad categories such as management quality, industry risk, and competitive position to inform the rating.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare the credit scoring system to the credit rating system in assessing credit quality and describe the different types of each system.
cards.statement: Credit rating systems focus on assessing individual consumers and small businesses using the internal financial data of the institution.
cards.explanation: Assessing consumers and small businesses with internal institutional data describes credit scoring. Ratings are mainly applied to corporations, sovereigns and structured finance products.
cards.originalText: Focusing on the assessment of individual consumers and small businesses using internal financial institutional data.
cards.correction: Credit scoring systems focus on assessing individual consumers and small businesses using the internal financial data of the institution.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare the credit scoring system to the credit rating system in assessing credit quality and describe the different types of each system.
cards.statement: A credit scoring system enables fast loan evaluations through automated numerical scoring, while a credit rating system facilitates standardized risk reporting for large-scale borrowers that appeals to external stakeholders.
cards.explanation: Scores are fast, automated and internal, which suits retail loans. Ratings give a common, transparent framework for large borrowers and external users.
cards.originalText: The CSS will enable fast personal loan evaluations through automated numerical scoring, while the CRS will facilitate standardized risk reporting for large‑scale borrowers, attracting external stakeholders.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare the credit scoring system to the credit rating system in assessing credit quality and describe the different types of each system.
cards.statement: Credit scoring and credit rating systems both aim to automate the lending process, removing qualitative assessments and reducing the role of risk management in loan approvals.
cards.explanation: Rating involves analytical plus judgmental assessment, so qualitative input is not removed. Neither system removes human oversight or reduces the role of risk management.
cards.originalText: Both CSS and CRS aim to automate the lending process, removing qualitative assessments and reducing risk management’s role in loan approvals.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare the credit scoring system to the credit rating system in assessing credit quality and describe the different types of each system.
cards.statement: A credit rating, rather than a credit score, is the appropriate tool for assessing a large publicly traded firm, and a recognised benefit of rating systems is a lower time and cost of appraisal.
cards.explanation: Large listed firms are rated, and rating systems reduce the time and cost of appraisal. They also reduce subjectivity, aid transparency and enable scenario analysis and stress testing.
cards.originalText: credit rating to reduce the cost of appraisal.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare the credit scoring system to the credit rating system in assessing credit quality and describe the different types of each system.
cards.statement: A credit score is the appropriate tool for assessing the credit risk of a large publicly traded manufacturer.
cards.explanation: Credit scores are designed for individuals and small businesses. A large publicly traded borrower is assessed with a credit rating.
cards.originalText: credit score to reduce subjectivity.
cards.correction: A credit rating is the appropriate tool for assessing the credit risk of a large publicly traded manufacturer.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare the credit scoring system to the credit rating system in assessing credit quality and describe the different types of each system.
cards.statement: Credit rating systems are limited in their ability to support stress testing.
cards.explanation: Rating and scoring systems enable scenario analysis and stress testing. This is one of the recognised benefits of using them.
cards.originalText: credit rating despite the limitations for stress testing.
cards.correction: Credit rating systems support scenario analysis and stress testing.

changes.from: are limited in their ability to support stress testing
changes.to: support scenario analysis and stress testing

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the process for developing credit risk scoring and rating models.
cards.statement: Once a credit rating system is implemented, it is continuously monitored, reviewed and recalibrated as needed to identify any degradation in the quality of the risk estimates it produces.
