cards.originalText: Buy the QuantTech corporate bond and buy CDS protection to earn more than the risk‑free rate.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define and explain CDS-bond basis.
cards.statement: When the CDS spread is below the bond yield spread (a negative CDS-bond basis), selling the corporate bond and buying CDS protection earns more than the risk-free rate.
cards.explanation: Shorting the bond and also buying protection leaves two credit positions that both gain on default and does not hedge anything; the negative-basis arbitrage is to buy the bond and buy protection.
cards.originalText: Sell the QuantTech corporate bond and buy CDS protection to earn more than the risk‑free rate.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define and explain CDS-bond basis.
cards.statement: When the CDS spread is below the bond yield spread (a negative CDS-bond basis), buying the corporate bond and selling CDS protection allows an investor to borrow at less than the risk-free rate.
cards.explanation: Buying the bond and selling protection doubles the long credit exposure instead of hedging it, so it is not an arbitrage; the negative-basis trade is to buy the bond and buy protection.
cards.originalText: Buy the QuantTech corporate bond and sell CDS protection to borrow at less than the risk‑free rate.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define and explain CDS-bond basis.
cards.statement: When the CDS spread is greater than the bond yield spread (a positive CDS-bond basis), an investor can sell the corporate bond and sell CDS protection, effectively borrowing at less than the risk-free rate.
cards.explanation: Shorting the bond is equivalent to borrowing at the bond's yield, while the protection sold earns the higher CDS spread and offsets the credit exposure, so the net financing cost is below the risk-free rate.
cards.originalText: Sell the corporate bond and sell CDS protection.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define and explain CDS-bond basis.
cards.statement: When the CDS spread is greater than the bond yield spread (a positive CDS-bond basis), buying the corporate bond and buying CDS protection is the appropriate arbitrage trade.
cards.explanation: Buying the bond and buying protection is the trade for a negative basis; with a positive basis protection is too expensive, and the arbitrage is to sell the bond and sell protection.
cards.originalText: Buy the corporate bond and buy CDS protection.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define and explain CDS-bond basis.
cards.statement: Counterparty risk in a CDS, because the protection seller may itself default, tends to push the CDS-bond basis in a negative direction.
cards.explanation: Counterparty default risk lowers what a buyer will pay for protection, so the CDS spread falls relative to the bond yield spread and the basis becomes more negative.
cards.originalText: The protection seller in the CDS may itself default, creating counterparty risk for the protection buyer.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define and explain CDS-bond basis.
cards.statement: The restructuring clause of a CDS, which may lead to a payoff even though the bond has not defaulted, tends to push the CDS-bond basis in a negative direction.
cards.explanation: A restructuring clause makes protection more valuable and raises the CDS spread, which pushes the basis in a positive direction.
cards.originalText: The CDS contract’s restructuring clause may lead to a payoff even though the bond has not defaulted.
cards.correction: The restructuring clause of a CDS, which may lead to a payoff even though the bond has not defaulted, tends to push the CDS-bond basis in a positive direction.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define and explain CDS-bond basis.
cards.statement: A cheapest-to-deliver bond option in a CDS tends to push the CDS-bond basis in a negative direction.
cards.explanation: The cheapest-to-deliver option benefits the protection buyer, so the CDS spread is higher and the basis moves in a positive direction.
cards.originalText: The CDS contains a cheapest‑to‑deliver bond option for the protection buyer.
cards.correction: A cheapest-to-deliver bond option in a CDS tends to push the CDS-bond basis in a positive direction.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare market risk value at risk (VaR) with credit VaR in terms of definition, time horizon, and tools for measuring them.
cards.statement: Credit VaR typically uses a shorter horizon than market risk VaR.
cards.explanation: Credit VaR typically uses a longer horizon (often one year) than the one-day horizon of market risk VaR.
cards.originalText: Credit VaR typically uses a shorter horizon than market risk VaR, because defaults and downgrades occur more often than price changes.
cards.correction: Credit VaR typically uses a longer horizon than market risk VaR.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare market risk value at risk (VaR) with credit VaR in terms of definition, time horizon, and tools for measuring them.
cards.statement: Credit VaR normally requires a more elaborate model than the simple historical simulation used for market risk VaR, one that captures credit correlation and, where relevant, rating transitions and credit spread changes.
cards.explanation: Credit correlation is a key feature of credit losses, and a short history of daily changes rarely contains the defaults and correlated credit events that drive credit VaR.
cards.originalText: A more elaborate model that captures credit correlation and, where relevant, rating transitions and credit spread changes.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare market risk value at risk (VaR) with credit VaR in terms of definition, time horizon, and tools for measuring them.
cards.statement: When modelling credit VaR, defaults of different companies can be assumed independent so that each exposure is modelled separately.
cards.explanation: Defaults are not independent; default correlation, which rises in stressed markets, must be modelled or the tail loss is understated.
cards.originalText: Assuming defaults of different companies are independent so that each exposure can be modeled separately.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare market risk value at risk (VaR) with credit VaR in terms of definition, time horizon, and tools for measuring them.
cards.statement: Market risk VaR is mainly calculated by historical simulation, whereas credit VaR usually needs a more elaborate model that captures credit correlation and several types of credit event.
cards.explanation: Credit VaR differs from market VaR in both horizon (about one year versus one day) and tools: it needs a correlation-aware model of defaults, downgrades and spread changes.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare market risk value at risk (VaR) with credit VaR in terms of definition, time horizon, and tools for measuring them.
cards.statement: Credit VaR is the credit loss over a given time period that will not be exceeded with a given level of confidence.
cards.explanation: Credit VaR is defined like market VaR as a loss quantile, for example 99.9% over one year, and may include losses from defaults, downgrades and spread changes.
cards.originalText: The credit loss over a given time period that will not be exceeded with a given level of confidence.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare market risk value at risk (VaR) with credit VaR in terms of definition, time horizon, and tools for measuring them.
cards.statement: Credit VaR is the credit loss over a given time period that is expected to be exceeded with the given level of confidence.
cards.explanation: At 99.9% confidence the loss is exceeded only 0.1% of the time; credit VaR is the loss that will not be exceeded with that confidence.
cards.originalText: The credit loss over a given time period that is expected to be exceeded with the given level of confidence.
cards.correction: Credit VaR is the credit loss over a given time period that will not be exceeded with the given level of confidence.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare market risk value at risk (VaR) with credit VaR in terms of definition, time horizon, and tools for measuring them.
cards.statement: Credit VaR is the average credit loss expected over the long run, regardless of the confidence level chosen.
cards.explanation: The average expected credit loss is expected loss, a mean; credit VaR is a quantile of the loss distribution tied to a confidence level.
cards.originalText: The average credit loss expected over the long run, regardless of the confidence level chosen.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the use of rating transition matrices for calculating credit VaR.
cards.statement: In the CreditMetrics model, the key driver of potential shifts in a bond portfolio's credit risk over the coming year is the probability of changes in the credit ratings of the bonds.
cards.explanation: CreditMetrics revalues each bond under every possible year-end rating, weighted by the rating transition probabilities, to build the loss distribution.
cards.originalText: The probability of changes in credit ratings of the bonds over time.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the use of rating transition matrices for calculating credit VaR.
cards.statement: Credit rating transition matrices are used in credit VaR to estimate the likelihood of rating changes over time, factoring in the potential for defaults and downgrades.
cards.explanation: A transition matrix is a table of migration probabilities (including default) that weight the possible downgrade and default outcomes in the credit VaR calculation.
cards.originalText: To estimate the likelihood of credit rating changes over time, thereby factoring in the potential for defaults or downgrades.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the use of rating transition matrices for calculating credit VaR.
cards.statement: A credit rating transition matrix predicts the exact future credit rating of each bond at the end of the one-year horizon based on historical patterns.
cards.explanation: A transition matrix gives probabilities of migrating to each rating, not the exact future rating of a particular bond.
cards.originalText: To predict the exact future credit ratings of the bonds at the end of the one‑year time horizon based on historical patterns.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the use of rating transition matrices for calculating credit VaR.
cards.statement: Each entry in a one-year ratings transition matrix is the probability that a company starting in a given rating ends the year in a particular rating category, including the same rating and default, estimated from historical data.
cards.explanation: Each row is a set of conditional migration probabilities covering unchanged, upgrade, downgrade and default outcomes, and each row sums to 100%.
cards.originalText: For a company starting in a given rating, the probability of ending the year in each rating category, including the same rating and default, estimated from historical data.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the use of rating transition matrices for calculating credit VaR.
cards.statement: The entries of a ratings transition matrix give, for a bond starting in a given rating, only the probability of default, with no information about other ratings.
cards.explanation: A transition matrix also gives the probabilities of upgrades, downgrades and no change; default is only one column.
cards.originalText: For a bond starting in a given rating, the probability of default only, with no information about other ratings.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the use of rating transition matrices for calculating credit VaR.
cards.statement: In a CreditMetrics-type Monte Carlo credit VaR, each trial samples year-end ratings from the starting rating's row of the transition matrix, each bond is revalued at its sampled rating (or default value), and credit VaR is read from the resulting loss distribution.
cards.explanation: The matrix supplies the sampling probabilities for each trial, and credit VaR is a percentile of the simulated loss distribution rather than a single expected loss.
cards.originalText: Each trial samples year‑end ratings from the BBB row, each bond is revalued at its sampled rating (or default value), and credit VaR is read from the resulting loss distribution.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the use of rating transition matrices for calculating credit VaR.
cards.statement: A one-year credit rating transition matrix can be extended to a two-year horizon by squaring it.
cards.explanation: Assuming rating changes are independent across periods, two successive one-year migrations compound, so the two-year matrix is the one-year matrix multiplied by itself.
cards.originalText: By squaring the one‑year transition matrix to estimate the transition matrix for a two‑year period.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the use of rating transition matrices for calculating credit VaR.
cards.statement: A one-year credit rating transition matrix can be extended to a two-year horizon by computing the geometric mean of the one-year transition probabilities.
cards.explanation: A geometric mean averages values rather than compounding migration paths; the two-year matrix is the square of the one-year matrix.
cards.originalText: By computing the geometric mean of the one‑year transition probabilities.
cards.correction: A one-year credit rating transition matrix can be extended to a two-year horizon by squaring the one-year transition matrix.

changes.from: computing the geometric mean of the one-year transition probabilities

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the use of rating transition matrices for calculating credit VaR.
cards.statement: A three-month transition matrix can be estimated by taking the fourth root of the one-year transition matrix.
cards.explanation: Four three-month matrices multiplied together must equal the one-year matrix, so the three-month matrix is the one-year matrix raised to the power 1/4.
cards.originalText: The fourth root of the one‑year transition matrix should be taken to estimate the transition matrix for a three‑month period.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the use of rating transition matrices for calculating credit VaR.
cards.statement: A three-month transition matrix can be approximated by dividing every entry of the one-year transition matrix by four.
cards.explanation: Dividing every entry by four breaks the row sums (the diagonal would fall far below 100%) and ignores compounding; the matrix root should be used instead.
cards.originalText: The original one‑year transition matrix should be divided by four to approximate the transitions for a three‑month period.
cards.correction: A three-month transition matrix can be approximated by taking the fourth root of the one-year transition matrix.

changes.from: dividing every entry of the one-year transition matrix by four
changes.to: taking the fourth root of the one-year transition matrix

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the use of rating transition matrices for calculating credit VaR.
cards.statement: Assuming rating changes are independent across periods, the five-year transition matrix is the one-year matrix raised to the fifth power, and the one-month matrix is the twelfth root of the one-year matrix.
cards.explanation: Powers of the one-year matrix lengthen the horizon, while roots shorten it.
cards.originalText: Five‑year matrix: raise the one‑year matrix to the fifth power; one‑month matrix: take the twelfth root of the one‑year matrix.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the use of rating transition matrices for calculating credit VaR.
cards.statement: Assuming rating changes are independent across periods, the five-year transition matrix is the fifth root of the one-year matrix, and the one-month matrix is the one-year matrix raised to the twelfth power.
cards.explanation: Powers extend the horizon and roots shorten it: the five-year matrix is the fifth power and the one-month matrix is the twelfth root of the one-year matrix.
cards.originalText: Five‑year matrix: take the fifth root of the one‑year matrix; one‑month matrix: raise it to the twelfth power.
cards.correction: Assuming rating changes are independent across periods, the five-year transition matrix is the one-year matrix raised to the fifth power, and the one-month matrix is the twelfth root of the one-year matrix.

changes.from: the fifth root of the one-year matrix
changes.to: the one-year matrix raised to the fifth power

changes.from: the one-year matrix raised to the twelfth power
changes.to: the twelfth root of the one-year matrix

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify drawbacks in using the correlation-based credit portfolio framework.
cards.statement: Default correlation is hard to measure or estimate from historical default data.
cards.explanation: Default is a rare event, so historical data are thin and estimates vary widely by period and industry.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify drawbacks in using the correlation-based credit portfolio framework.
cards.statement: Because firm defaults are rare events, estimated default correlations vary greatly with the data horizon and industry sampled.
cards.explanation: Defaults are rare, so there is little data to estimate default correlations, which therefore vary widely by time horizon and industry; this is a recognised drawback of the default-correlation framework.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify drawbacks in using the correlation-based credit portfolio framework.
cards.statement: Default correlations are large in magnitude, so the joint default probability of two firms is much larger than their individual default probabilities.
cards.explanation: Default correlations are small in magnitude, and the joint default probability of two firms can never exceed either firm's individual default probability.
cards.originalText: Because default correlations are large in magnitude, the joint default probability of two firms is much larger than their individual default probabilities.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify drawbacks in using the correlation-based credit portfolio framework.
cards.statement: The number of possible default event outcomes grows only linearly with the number of credits.
cards.explanation: With n credits there are 2^n possible default outcomes, so the number grows exponentially, which is one drawback of the default-correlation framework.
cards.originalText: The number of event outcomes grows only linearly with the number of credits, so the model understates portfolio diversification.
cards.correction: The number of possible default event outcomes grows exponentially with the number of credits.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe how Credit VaR can be calculated using a simulation of joint defaults.
cards.statement: In a copula-based credit VaR simulation, the steps are to define the copula function (including the correlation between credits), simulate default times, obtain market values and profit and loss for each scenario from the simulated default times, and then compute portfolio distribution statistics such as the loss percentile.
cards.explanation: Default times can only be simulated once the copula with its correlation is specified, losses can only be valued once default times are simulated, and VaR comes last from the aggregated distribution.
cards.originalText: Define the copula function (including the correlation between credits); simulate default times; obtain market values and profit‑and‑loss for each scenario using the simulated default times; compute portfolio distribution statistics (e.g., the loss percentile) from the summed terminal values.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe how Credit VaR can be calculated using a simulation of joint defaults.
cards.statement: In a copula-based credit VaR simulation, the copula function is defined first, then market values and profit and loss are obtained for each scenario, then default times are simulated, and finally portfolio distribution statistics are computed.
cards.explanation: Scenario profit and loss cannot be obtained until default times have been simulated, so default times must be simulated before the portfolio is valued.
cards.originalText: Define the copula function; obtain market values and profit‑and‑loss for each scenario; simulate default times; compute portfolio distribution statistics.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe how Credit VaR can be calculated using a simulation of joint defaults.
cards.statement: In a normal copula credit VaR simulation, correlated normal draws are generated for the credits and mapped, using each credit's own default probability, to simulated default times; scenario terminal values are summed and the loss percentile is read from the simulated distribution.
cards.explanation: Correlation is built into the simulated draws themselves, so defaults cluster in the same scenarios, and the portfolio statistics come from summing the scenario terminal values.
cards.originalText: Correlated normal draws are generated for the credits and mapped, using each credit’s own default probability, to simulated default times; terminal values for each scenario are then summed and the loss percentile is read from the simulated distribution.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe how Credit VaR can be calculated using a simulation of joint defaults.
cards.statement: In a copula-based credit VaR simulation, independent default times are simulated for each loan and the copula correlation is applied afterward by scaling the sum of the individual losses.
cards.explanation: Correlation must enter the draws that determine default times; applying it afterward to independent simulations does not reproduce joint defaults.
cards.originalText: Independent default times are simulated for each loan, and the copula correlation is applied afterward by scaling the sum of the individual losses.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define credit valuation adjustment (CVA) and debt valuation adjustment (DVA).
cards.statement: CVA increases the value of a derivatives portfolio by accounting for the potential gain from the counterparty's default, while DVA decreases it by considering the bank's own default risk.
cards.explanation: The signs are reversed: CVA is a cost that lowers portfolio value, and DVA is a benefit that raises it.
cards.originalText: CVA increases the portfolio value by accounting for the potential gain from the counterparty’s default, while DVA decreases it by considering the bank’s own default risk.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define credit valuation adjustment (CVA) and debt valuation adjustment (DVA).
cards.statement: Both CVA and DVA decrease the value of a bank's derivatives portfolio, since each adjusts for expected losses from default.
cards.explanation: CVA reduces the portfolio value, but DVA is a benefit to the bank (a cost to the counterparty) and increases it.
cards.originalText: Both CVA and DVA decrease the portfolio value since they both adjust for the losses expected from defaults by the counterparty and the bank, respectively.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define credit valuation adjustment (CVA) and debt valuation adjustment (DVA).
cards.statement: When a bank's own credit spread widens, its DVA increases, which increases the value of its derivatives portfolio with a counterparty.
cards.explanation: DVA depends on the bank's own default probability; a higher probability raises DVA, which is a benefit to the bank and so raises the value of the portfolio.
cards.originalText: DVA increases and portfolio value increases.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define credit valuation adjustment (CVA) and debt valuation adjustment (DVA).
cards.statement: When a bank's own credit spread widens, its DVA decreases and the value of its derivatives portfolio with a counterparty decreases.
cards.explanation: A wider own credit spread implies a higher own default probability, which increases DVA and increases the portfolio's value to the bank.
cards.originalText: DVA decreases and portfolio value decreases.
cards.correction: When a bank's own credit spread widens, its DVA increases and the value of its derivatives portfolio with a counterparty increases.

changes.from: its DVA decreases and the value of its derivatives portfolio with a counterparty decreases
changes.to: its DVA increases and the value of its derivatives portfolio with a counterparty increases

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define credit valuation adjustment (CVA) and debt valuation adjustment (DVA).
cards.statement: A new transaction that is negatively correlated with a counterparty's existing transactions tends to decrease both CVA and DVA.
cards.explanation: A negatively correlated trade reduces the netted exposure of the portfolio, and both CVA and DVA depend on that exposure.
cards.originalText: decrease in both CVA and DVA.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define credit valuation adjustment (CVA) and debt valuation adjustment (DVA).
cards.statement: A new transaction that is negatively correlated with a counterparty's existing transactions tends to increase both CVA and DVA.
cards.explanation: Negative correlation reduces netted exposure and so lowers CVA and DVA; it is positive correlation that tends to raise both.
cards.originalText: increase in both CVA and DVA.
cards.correction: A new transaction that is negatively correlated with a counterparty's existing transactions tends to decrease both CVA and DVA.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe, compare, and contrast various credit risk mitigants and their role in credit analysis.
cards.statement: Downgrade triggers eliminate liquidity risk, because no collateral ever has to be posted when the triggers are in place.
cards.explanation: Downgrade triggers only defer collateral requirements until a rating fall, and the sudden collateral calls that follow (as with AIG in 2008) can create severe liquidity strain.
cards.originalText: Downgrade triggers of the type AIG had eliminate liquidity risk, because no collateral ever has to be posted when the triggers are in place.
cards.correction: Downgrade triggers defer collateral requirements until a rating fall, which can create severe liquidity strain through sudden collateral calls.

changes.from: eliminate liquidity risk, because no collateral ever has to be posted when the triggers are in place
changes.to: defer collateral requirements until a rating fall, which can create severe liquidity strain through sudden collateral calls

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe, compare, and contrast various credit risk mitigants and their role in credit analysis.
cards.statement: Under a collateral agreement, if the counterparty defaults, the non-defaulting party may keep the collateral that the counterparty has posted.
cards.explanation: Derivatives receive favourable treatment in default: the non-defaulting party can retain collateral posted by the defaulter.
cards.originalText: Under a collateral agreement, if the counterparty defaults, the bank may keep the collateral that the counterparty has posted.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe, compare, and contrast various credit risk mitigants and their role in credit analysis.
cards.statement: The value of downgrade triggers is reduced if the counterparty has similar triggers in place with several dealers.
cards.explanation: If several dealers hold triggers, a downgrade produces simultaneous collateral calls that the counterparty may be unable to meet, so each trigger is worth less.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe, compare, and contrast various credit risk mitigants and their role in credit analysis.
cards.statement: Downgrade triggers offer limited protection if a counterparty's rating drops directly to default, and their value is reduced when the counterparty has similar triggers with several dealers.
cards.explanation: A trigger cannot help against a sudden jump from a good rating to default, and widespread triggers across dealers dilute their value, as AIG showed in 2008.
cards.originalText: The trigger offers limited protection if the counterparty’s rating drops directly from A to default, and the value of the trigger is reduced because other dealers hold similar triggers.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe, compare, and contrast various credit risk mitigants and their role in credit analysis.
cards.statement: The value of a downgrade trigger increases as more dealers hold similar triggers with the same counterparty.
cards.explanation: When many dealers hold triggers, a downgrade produces simultaneous collateral calls that the counterparty cannot meet, so each trigger is worth less.
cards.originalText: The trigger becomes more valuable as more dealers hold similar triggers, because the counterparty then has greater incentive to protect its rating.
cards.correction: The value of a downgrade trigger decreases as more dealers hold similar triggers with the same counterparty.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe, compare, and contrast various credit risk mitigants and their role in credit analysis.
cards.statement: If a derivatives counterparty defaults, the non-defaulting dealer may keep the posted collateral only after lengthy legal proceedings establish its claim.
cards.explanation: Derivatives receive favourable treatment in default: the non-defaulting party may keep the collateral without lengthy legal proceedings.
cards.originalText: If the counterparty defaults, the dealer may keep posted collateral only after lengthy legal proceedings establish its claim.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe, compare, and contrast various credit risk mitigants and their role in credit analysis.
cards.statement: A downgrade trigger eliminates a dealer's credit exposure to a counterparty, because collateral or close-out is available as soon as the rating falls below the trigger level.
cards.explanation: Triggers reduce but do not eliminate exposure: they give no protection against a jump straight to default, and exposure can build before the trigger level is reached.
cards.originalText: The trigger eliminates the dealer’s credit exposure, because collateral or close‑out is available as soon as the rating falls below BBB.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify the default probabilities used to value a CDS.
cards.statement: Credit default swaps are valued using risk-neutral default probabilities, implied from market CDS spreads or bond prices.
cards.explanation: A CDS is priced from market prices, so the default probabilities must be consistent with them; they are backed out of quoted CDS spreads or bond prices given an assumed recovery rate.
cards.originalText: Risk‑neutral default probabilities, implied from market CDS spreads or bond prices.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify the default probabilities used to value a CDS.
cards.statement: Credit default swaps are valued using real-world default probabilities estimated from historical default rates for the issuer's rating class.
cards.explanation: CDS valuation uses risk-neutral probabilities implied from market prices, not real-world probabilities from historical default rates.
cards.originalText: Real‑world default probabilities, estimated from historical default rates for the issuer’s rating class.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Evaluate the use of credit indices and fixed coupons in pricing CDS transactions.
cards.statement: The spread quoted for a CDS index such as the CDX NA IG is approximately the average of the CDS spreads of its constituents, so it gauges the general level of credit risk in the market.
cards.explanation: Each constituent is equally weighted with equal protection, so the index spread behaves like an average of the constituent spreads.
cards.originalText: It is approximately the average of the CDS spreads of the 125 constituents, so it gauges the general level of credit risk in the market.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Evaluate the use of credit indices and fixed coupons in pricing CDS transactions.
cards.statement: The spread quoted for a CDS index such as the CDX NA IG is the sum of the CDS spreads of its constituents.
cards.explanation: The quote is a spread per unit of notional and behaves like an average of the constituent spreads, not a sum.
cards.originalText: It is the sum of the 125 constituent CDS spreads.
cards.correction: The spread quoted for a CDS index such as the CDX NA IG is approximately the average of the CDS spreads of its constituents.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Evaluate the use of credit indices and fixed coupons in pricing CDS transactions.
cards.statement: If one of the 125 entities in the CDX NA IG index defaults, the index contract continues with the remaining 124 entities, and the notional principal of each remaining entity stays the same.
cards.explanation: Only the defaulted entity is settled and removed; the other entities and their notionals are untouched.
cards.originalText: continue with 124 entities, and the notional principal of each entity would remain the same.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Evaluate the use of credit indices and fixed coupons in pricing CDS transactions.
cards.statement: If one of the entities in the CDX NA IG index defaults, the index makes a payoff and is discontinued.
cards.explanation: Only the defaulted entity is settled (with the usual 1 minus recovery payoff on its notional); the index continues with the remaining names.
cards.originalText: make a payoff and be discontinued.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define CDS forwards and CDS options.
cards.statement: A CDS forward, which fixes the spread on protection starting at a future date, is appealing to a creditor looking to hedge against potential future credit deterioration.
cards.explanation: The forward locks in today's spread for protection that begins later, shielding the protection buyer from a later widening of spreads.
cards.originalText: A creditor looking to hedge against potential future credit deterioration

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define CDS forwards and CDS options.
cards.statement: A CDS forward is appealing to a speculative trader seeking instantaneous credit exposure.
cards.explanation: A CDS forward only starts at a future date; instantaneous credit exposure requires a standard CDS entered today.
cards.originalText: A speculative trader seeking instantaneous credit exposure

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define CDS forwards and CDS options.
cards.statement: A CDS call option gives the holder the right to buy protection at the strike spread, which is valuable if credit spreads widen.
cards.explanation: The call is exercised if the market CDS spread exceeds the strike, since protection can then be bought below the market spread.
cards.originalText: The right to buy protection at 250 bps, which is valuable if credit spreads widen

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define CDS forwards and CDS options.
cards.statement: A CDS call option gives the holder the right to sell protection at the strike spread, which is valuable if credit quality improves.
cards.explanation: A CDS call is the right to buy protection and pays off when spreads widen; the right to sell protection is a CDS put.
cards.originalText: The right to sell protection at 250 bps, which is valuable if credit quality improves
cards.correction: A CDS call option gives the holder the right to buy protection at the strike spread, which is valuable if credit spreads widen.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define CDS forwards and CDS options.
cards.statement: A CDS call option gives the holder the obligation to buy protection at the strike spread regardless of market spreads.
cards.explanation: An option carries a right but no obligation; an obligation to buy protection at a future date is a CDS forward.
cards.originalText: The obligation to buy protection at 250 bps in one year regardless of market spreads
cards.correction: A CDS call option gives the holder the right to buy protection at the strike spread.

changes.from: the obligation to buy protection at the strike spread regardless of market spreads
changes.to: the right to buy protection at the strike spread

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define CDS forwards and CDS options.
cards.statement: A CDS call option gives its holder the choice, but not the obligation, to enter a CDS as protection buyer in the future.
cards.explanation: A CDS option gives a right rather than an obligation, and the call is the option to enter as protection buyer.
cards.originalText: CDS call option

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define CDS forwards and CDS options.
cards.statement: A CDS forward gives its holder the choice, but not the obligation, to enter a CDS as protection buyer in the future.
cards.explanation: A CDS forward commits both parties to enter the CDS at a future date, which removes the choice; only an option gives the choice.
cards.originalText: CDS forward

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define CDS forwards and CDS options.
cards.statement: A CDS put option gives the holder the right to sell protection at a strike spread, which is valuable if credit quality improves and spreads tighten.
cards.explanation: The holder exercises if the market spread falls below the strike, since protection can then be sold above the market spread.
cards.originalText: CDS put option

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define CDS forwards and CDS options.
cards.statement: CDS options require a premium payment, while CDS forwards entered at market rates do not.
cards.explanation: A forward struck at the market forward spread has zero value at inception, whereas an option gives the holder a right that must be paid for upfront.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define CDS forwards and CDS options.
cards.statement: CDS forwards entered at market rates require a premium payment, while CDS options do not.
cards.explanation: The instruments are the other way round: options carry an upfront premium, while a forward at the market rate has zero initial value.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Discuss alternative approaches used to estimate default correlation.
cards.statement: A heterogeneous CDO model allows different time-to-default distributions for different entities, so the binomial formula for the probability of k defaults can no longer be used and a numerical procedure is needed.
cards.explanation: Heterogeneity destroys the symmetry that makes the binomial formula valid, so valuation requires numerical procedures.
cards.originalText: It allows different time‑to‑default distributions for different entities, so the binomial formula for the probability of k defaults can no longer be used and a numerical procedure is needed.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Discuss alternative approaches used to estimate default correlation.
cards.statement: A heterogeneous CDO model assumes identical default probabilities and copula correlations for all entities, which simplifies implementation.
cards.explanation: That describes the homogeneous model; a heterogeneous model allows entity-specific default distributions.
cards.originalText: It assumes identical default probabilities and copula correlations for all entities, which simplifies implementation.
cards.correction: A homogeneous CDO model assumes identical default probabilities and copula correlations for all entities, which simplifies implementation.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Discuss alternative approaches used to estimate default correlation.
cards.statement: A heterogeneous CDO model allows different time-to-default distributions for different entities, and the binomial formula for the probability of k defaults still applies, so valuation is no harder.
cards.explanation: With different default distributions the binomial formula no longer applies, so a numerical procedure is needed.
cards.originalText: It allows different time‑to‑default distributions for different entities, and the binomial formula for the probability of k defaults still applies, so valuation is no harder.
cards.correction: A heterogeneous CDO model allows different time-to-default distributions for different entities, and the binomial formula for the probability of k defaults can no longer be used, so a numerical procedure is needed.

changes.from: still applies, so valuation is no harder
changes.to: can no longer be used, so a numerical procedure is needed

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Discuss alternative approaches used to estimate default correlation.
cards.statement: In the simplest version of the Hull and White implied copula approach, a single average hazard rate applies to all companies over the life of the CDO, and its probability distribution is implied from current tranche prices.
cards.explanation: The implied copula is analogous to implied volatility: it is backed out of market tranche quotes rather than estimated from historical data.
cards.originalText: A single average hazard rate applies to all companies over the life of the CDO, and its probability distribution is implied from current tranche prices.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Discuss alternative approaches used to estimate default correlation.
cards.statement: In the simplest version of the Hull and White implied copula approach, each company has its own hazard rate, and these individual hazard rates are implied from tranche prices.
cards.explanation: The simplest implied copula uses one common average hazard rate for all companies, and it is the distribution of that rate that is implied from tranche prices.
cards.originalText: Each company has its own hazard rate, and the individual hazard rates are implied from tranche prices.
cards.correction: In the simplest version of the Hull and White implied copula approach, a single average hazard rate applies to all companies, and its probability distribution is implied from tranche prices.

changes.from: each company has its own hazard rate, and these individual hazard rates are implied from tranche prices
changes.to: a single average hazard rate applies to all companies, and its probability distribution is implied from tranche prices

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Discuss alternative approaches used to estimate default correlation.
cards.statement: The structural model of credit risk is a dynamic model, which models the evolution of portfolio loss through time.
cards.explanation: Dynamic models of portfolio loss include structural, reduced-form and top-down types; structural models simulate correlated asset-value processes and declare default when an asset value hits a barrier.
cards.originalText: dynamic model.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define derivatives and explain how derivative transactions create counterparty credit risk.
cards.statement: Derivatives can induce liquidity crises through rating downgrade triggers, which force firms to meet unexpected cash demands for collateral at critical times.
cards.explanation: Downgrade triggers require extra collateral exactly when a firm is weakest, producing unexpected cash demands and liquidity stress that can lead to further downgrades.
cards.originalText: Derivatives can induce liquidity crises due to (rating) downgrade triggers, necessitating firms to meet unexpected cash demands during critical periods.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define derivatives and explain how derivative transactions create counterparty credit risk.
cards.statement: Derivatives necessitate a substantial initial investment, which can tie up significant capital resources.
cards.explanation: Derivatives typically require little or no upfront payment relative to their notional amount, which is the source of their leverage.
cards.originalText: Derivatives, with their inherent counterparty risk, necessitate a substantial initial investment, which can tie up significant capital resources.
cards.correction: Derivatives typically require little or no upfront payment relative to their notional amount.

changes.from: necessitate a substantial initial investment, which can tie up significant capital resources
changes.to: typically require little or no upfront payment relative to their notional amount

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define derivatives and explain how derivative transactions create counterparty credit risk.
cards.statement: A derivative is a financial instrument whose value is contingent upon, or derived from, a specified underlying asset or group of assets, such as stocks, bonds or market indices.
cards.explanation: A derivative is a contract whose value depends on one or more underlying assets, rates or indices.
cards.originalText: A financial instrument whose value is contingent upon, or derived from, a specified underlying asset or group of assets, like stocks, bonds, or market indices.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define derivatives and explain how derivative transactions create counterparty credit risk.
cards.statement: A derivative is a financial instrument whose value is based solely on the market movements of a single underlying stock or bond.
cards.explanation: Underlyings can be groups of assets, indices, rates or commodities, not just one stock or bond.
cards.originalText: A financial instrument whose value is based solely on the market movements of a single underlying stock or bond.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define derivatives and explain how derivative transactions create counterparty credit risk.
cards.statement: A derivative is a financial instrument that directly represents ownership in an underlying asset, such as shares in a company or government-issued debt securities.
cards.explanation: A derivative does not represent ownership of the underlying; that describes a cash security such as an equity or a bond.
cards.originalText: A financial tool that directly represents ownership in an underlying asset, such as shares in a company or government‑issued debt securities.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define derivatives and explain how derivative transactions create counterparty credit risk.
cards.statement: Daisy-chain risk in derivatives is the risk arising from the accumulation of large receivables from interconnected counterparties, potentially leading to systemic risk.
cards.explanation: Derivatives defeat prudent counterparty diversification because large receivables from interconnected counterparties build up, so one default can cascade through the system.
cards.originalText: The risk arising from the accumulation of large receivables from interconnected counterparties, potentially leading to systemic risk.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define derivatives and explain how derivative transactions create counterparty credit risk.
cards.statement: Daisy-chain risk in derivatives is the risk of a single derivative position leading to disproportionate losses exceeding the initial investment.
cards.explanation: That describes leverage-driven loss magnification; daisy-chain risk is the build-up of large receivables from interconnected counterparties.
cards.originalText: The risk of a single derivative position leading to disproportionate losses, exceeding the initial investment.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define derivatives and explain how derivative transactions create counterparty credit risk.
cards.statement: Daisy-chain risk in derivatives is the risk of regulatory changes leading to sudden adjustments in derivative valuations.
cards.explanation: Daisy-chain risk concerns interconnected counterparty exposures, not regulatory changes.
cards.originalText: The risk of regulatory changes leading to sudden adjustments in derivative valuations, impacting the overall financial market.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define derivatives and explain how derivative transactions create counterparty credit risk.
cards.statement: Leverage in derivatives permits institutions to take on positions significantly larger than their initial investment, potentially amplifying both returns and risks.
cards.explanation: Most derivatives require little or no upfront payment relative to notional, so exposure far exceeds the cash invested and both gains and losses are magnified.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Define derivatives and explain how derivative transactions create counterparty credit risk.
cards.statement: Leverage in derivatives mandates a substantial initial investment, thereby minimizing the risk of default and stabilizing the financial market.
cards.explanation: Leverage means a small, not substantial, initial investment, and it raises rather than lowers risk.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare and contrast exchange-traded derivatives and over-the-counter (OTC) derivatives, and discuss the features of their markets.
cards.statement: A key benefit of an OTC derivative is that the contract can be customized to match the unique hedging needs of the client.
cards.explanation: OTC derivatives are privately negotiated, so size, maturity and other terms can be set to fit non-standard exposures that exchange contracts cannot match.
cards.originalText: Ability to customize the contract to match the unique hedging needs of the client.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare and contrast exchange-traded derivatives and over-the-counter (OTC) derivatives, and discuss the features of their markets.
cards.statement: OTC derivatives typically have highly liquid secondary markets.
cards.explanation: OTC contracts are usually not actively traded in a secondary market, so liquidity is a weakness of OTC derivatives.
cards.originalText: Availability of highly liquid secondary markets for the derivative.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare and contrast exchange-traded derivatives and over-the-counter (OTC) derivatives, and discuss the features of their markets.
cards.statement: A main advantage of OTC derivatives is that contract terms can be tailored accurately to the specific needs of the client.
cards.explanation: OTC derivatives are privately negotiated and need not be standardized, and this flexibility supports hedging non-standard exposures and new products such as credit derivatives.
cards.originalText: Contract terms can be tailored accurately to the specific needs of the client.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare and contrast exchange-traded derivatives and over-the-counter (OTC) derivatives, and discuss the features of their markets.
cards.statement: Trading in OTC derivatives is centralized in one place, which raises liquidity and transparency.
cards.explanation: Centralized trading describes an exchange; OTC trading is decentralized and bilateral, with less transparency.
cards.originalText: Trading is centralized in one place, which raises liquidity and transparency.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare and contrast exchange-traded derivatives and over-the-counter (OTC) derivatives, and discuss the features of their markets.
cards.statement: OTC derivative terms are negotiated privately and directly between the two parties, with no exchange as intermediary.
cards.explanation: Bilateral private negotiation gives OTC trades their flexibility but also lower transparency.
cards.originalText: Terms are negotiated privately and directly between the two parties, with no exchange as intermediary.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare and contrast exchange-traded derivatives and over-the-counter (OTC) derivatives, and discuss the features of their markets.
cards.statement: OTC derivative terms are set by an exchange and the trade is guaranteed by a clearing house.
cards.explanation: That describes exchange-traded derivatives, where the exchange sets standardized terms.
cards.originalText: Terms are set by an exchange and the trade is guaranteed by a clearing house.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare and contrast exchange-traded derivatives and over-the-counter (OTC) derivatives, and discuss the features of their markets.
cards.statement: Interest rate swaps are the bespoke OTC derivatives banks widely use to hedge the interest rate risk inherent in lending, since their maturity, payment frequency and reference rate can be matched precisely to a floating-rate loan.
cards.explanation: A swap matched to a loan converts floating payments to fixed (or the reverse), hedging the interest rate risk of the bank's lending business.
cards.originalText: Interest‑rate swaps

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare and contrast exchange-traded derivatives and over-the-counter (OTC) derivatives, and discuss the features of their markets.
cards.statement: Exchange-traded derivatives offer high liquidity and transparent pricing, which allows efficient trading.
cards.explanation: Standardized exchange contracts trade in deep markets with accessible, transparent prices.
cards.originalText: The fund will take advantage of high liquidity and transparent pricing for efficient trading.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare and contrast exchange-traded derivatives and over-the-counter (OTC) derivatives, and discuss the features of their markets.
cards.statement: Exchange-traded derivatives offer customized contracts tailored to a trader's specific strategy.
cards.explanation: Exchange-traded contracts are standardized; customization is a feature of OTC derivatives.
cards.originalText: The fund will benefit from customized contracts tailored to its specific trading strategies.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare and contrast exchange-traded derivatives and over-the-counter (OTC) derivatives, and discuss the features of their markets.
cards.statement: Exchange-traded derivatives expose traders to higher counterparty risk because there are no bilateral agreements.
cards.explanation: Exchange trades are centrally cleared by a clearing house that becomes the counterparty, which reduces rather than raises counterparty risk.
cards.originalText: The fund will face higher counterparty risk due to the lack of bilateral agreements.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare and contrast exchange-traded derivatives and over-the-counter (OTC) derivatives, and discuss the features of their markets.
cards.statement: A position in an exchange-traded futures contract is typically closed before expiry by executing an offsetting trade, that is, selling an identical contract in the liquid market.
cards.explanation: Standardization and liquidity let exchange positions be closed at market prices without negotiating with the original counterparty.
cards.originalText: The investor executes an offsetting trade (sells an identical contract) in the liquid market.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare and contrast exchange-traded derivatives and over-the-counter (OTC) derivatives, and discuss the features of their markets.
cards.statement: An investor in an exchange-traded futures contract must hold the contract to expiry and deliver or take delivery of the underlying.
cards.explanation: Exchange positions can be closed at any time by an offsetting trade, and most are offset before expiry.
cards.originalText: The investor must hold the contract to expiry and deliver or take delivery of the gold.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare and contrast exchange-traded derivatives and over-the-counter (OTC) derivatives, and discuss the features of their markets.
cards.statement: The original counterparty to a custom OTC derivative may demand a premium for unwinding it, capitalizing on its exclusive position.
cards.explanation: A custom OTC contract has no active secondary market, so it can practically be unwound only with the original counterparty, which can quote unfavourable terms.
cards.originalText: The original counterparty may demand a premium for unwinding the derivative, capitalizing on their exclusive position.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare and contrast exchange-traded derivatives and over-the-counter (OTC) derivatives, and discuss the features of their markets.
cards.statement: Unwinding custom OTC derivatives is typically simpler than unwinding standardized products because of their tailored nature.
cards.explanation: Tailored contracts are harder to unwind because there is no liquid market and usually only the original counterparty can take the other side.
cards.originalText: Unwinding these derivatives is typically simpler than standardized products due to their tailored nature.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare and contrast exchange-traded derivatives and over-the-counter (OTC) derivatives, and discuss the features of their markets.
cards.statement: A custom OTC derivative can easily be transferred to a third party at market value without the original counterparty's consent.
cards.explanation: Transferring (novating) an OTC derivative typically requires the original counterparty's consent.
cards.originalText: Custom OTC derivatives can be easily transferred to a third party at market value without the original counterparty’s consent.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare and contrast exchange-traded derivatives and over-the-counter (OTC) derivatives, and discuss the features of their markets.
cards.statement: Exchange-traded futures have standardised terms such as maturity and size, which may leave a hedger with basis risk, whereas an OTC swap can be tailored to the hedger's exact dates and quantities.
cards.explanation: Exchanges fix maturity and size, so a futures hedge may not match the exposure date and leaves basis risk. A bilaterally negotiated OTC swap can be set to the exact dates and amounts needed.
cards.originalText: The futures contract has standardised terms such as maturity and size, which may leave Robot with basis risk, whereas the OTC swap can be tailored to Robot’s exact dates and quantities.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare and contrast exchange-traded derivatives and over-the-counter (OTC) derivatives, and discuss the features of their markets.
cards.statement: A futures contract can be customised to a hedger's exact dates and quantities, whereas an OTC swap must use standardised maturities.
cards.explanation: It is the reverse. Exchange-traded futures have standardised terms, while privately negotiated OTC swaps can be customised.
cards.originalText: The futures contract can be customised to Robot’s exact dates and quantities, whereas the OTC swap must use standardised maturities.
cards.correction: An OTC swap can be customised to a hedger's exact dates and quantities, whereas a futures contract must use standardised maturities.

changes.from: A futures contract can be customised
changes.to: An OTC swap can be customised

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare and contrast exchange-traded derivatives and over-the-counter (OTC) derivatives, and discuss the features of their markets.
cards.statement: A futures contract is traded privately between two parties and is therefore less liquid than an OTC swap.
cards.explanation: Futures trade on an exchange and are typically very liquid. It is OTC trades that are private, bilateral and generally less liquid.
cards.originalText: The futures contract is traded privately between two parties and is therefore less liquid than the OTC swap.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare and contrast exchange-traded derivatives and over-the-counter (OTC) derivatives, and discuss the features of their markets.
cards.statement: An OTC swap is easy to terminate with any third party at a transparent market price, whereas a futures contract can only be terminated with the original counterparty.
cards.explanation: It is the reverse. A futures position is closed by an offsetting trade at transparent exchange prices, whereas an OTC trade is typically unwound only with the original counterparty or novated with its permission.
cards.originalText: The OTC swap is easy to terminate with any third party at a transparent market price, whereas the futures contract can only be terminated with the original counterparty.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare and contrast exchange-traded derivatives and over-the-counter (OTC) derivatives, and discuss the features of their markets.
cards.statement: Standardised futures maturities introduce basis risk into a hedge when the contract maturity does not match the exposure date, a mismatch that a customised OTC derivative could avoid.
cards.explanation: A futures hedge is restricted to the delivery months the exchange offers, so the hedge and the exposure need not move together. A customised OTC contract can be set to mature exactly on the exposure date.
cards.originalText: The futures hedge introduces basis risk because the contract maturity does not match the exposure date, a mismatch a customised OTC derivative could avoid.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare and contrast exchange-traded derivatives and over-the-counter (OTC) derivatives, and discuss the features of their markets.
cards.statement: Exchange-traded futures contracts cannot be used for hedging.
cards.explanation: Exchange-traded futures are widely used for hedging. They are simply less tailored than OTC contracts, so a hedge may carry basis risk.
cards.originalText: The futures hedge cannot be put in place because exchange‑traded contracts cannot be used for hedging.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare and contrast exchange-traded derivatives and over-the-counter (OTC) derivatives, and discuss the features of their markets.
cards.statement: A futures hedge eliminates all risk because standardised maturities guarantee a perfect offset on any date.
cards.explanation: Standardised maturities do not guarantee an offset on any date. When the contract maturity differs from the exposure date, basis risk remains.
cards.originalText: The futures hedge eliminates all risk because standardised maturities guarantee a perfect offset on any date.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare and contrast exchange-traded derivatives and over-the-counter (OTC) derivatives, and discuss the features of their markets.
cards.statement: A futures hedge has higher counterparty risk than an OTC derivative because standardised maturities require a bilateral agreement.
cards.explanation: Standardised exchange contracts are not bilateral agreements and are centrally cleared. Bilateral counterparty risk is a feature of OTC trades, not a result of standard maturities.
cards.originalText: The futures hedge has higher counterparty risk than an OTC derivative because standardised maturities require a bilateral agreement.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare and contrast exchange-traded derivatives and over-the-counter (OTC) derivatives, and discuss the features of their markets.
cards.statement: An exchange encourages market efficiency and boosts liquidity through centralised trading in a single place.
cards.explanation: Centralised trading of standardised contracts gives transparent prices and makes it easy to enter and exit positions. This promotes market efficiency and liquidity.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the process of clearing a derivative transaction.
cards.statement: Clearing houses are always used in futures markets and only sometimes used in OTC derivatives markets.
cards.explanation: Every derivatives exchange has an associated clearing function, so futures are always centrally cleared. Only sufficiently standardised OTC products can be centrally cleared, and a significant portion of OTC trades remains bilaterally cleared.
cards.originalText: Always used in futures markets and sometimes used in OTC markets

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the process of clearing a derivative transaction.
cards.statement: Clearing houses are never used in futures markets and are sometimes used in OTC markets.
cards.explanation: Every derivatives exchange has a clearing function, so futures are always centrally cleared.
cards.originalText: Never used in futures markets and sometimes used in OTC markets
cards.correction: Clearing houses are always used in futures markets and are sometimes used in OTC markets.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the process of clearing a derivative transaction.
cards.statement: Clearing houses are used in OTC markets but not in futures markets.
cards.explanation: Central clearing is universal for exchange-traded futures. It is OTC markets where clearing houses are used only for some products.
cards.originalText: Used in OTC markets, but not in futures markets

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the process of clearing a derivative transaction.
cards.statement: Clearing houses are always used in both futures markets and OTC markets.
cards.explanation: Non-standardised OTC trades cannot be centrally cleared and remain bilaterally cleared, so clearing houses are used only sometimes in OTC markets.
cards.originalText: Always used in both futures markets and OTC markets
cards.correction: Clearing houses are always used in futures markets and sometimes used in OTC markets.

changes.from: always used in both futures markets and OTC markets
changes.to: always used in futures markets and sometimes used in OTC markets

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the process of clearing a derivative transaction.
cards.statement: Under bilateral clearing the two counterparties handle risk management processes themselves, whereas under central clearing a central counterparty (CCP) takes over these functions.
cards.explanation: The key distinction is who performs risk management between execution and settlement. In bilateral clearing it is the two parties, and in central clearing it is the CCP.
cards.originalText: Bilateral clearing requires the counterparties to handle risk management processes themselves, while central clearing involves a central counterparty (CCP) taking over these functions.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the process of clearing a derivative transaction.
cards.statement: Bilateral clearing involves a third party taking responsibility for managing counterparty risk, while central clearing is conducted between the two parties entering a trade.
cards.explanation: The roles are swapped. The third party (the CCP) exists in central clearing, while in bilateral clearing the two parties manage the risk themselves.
cards.correction: Central clearing involves a third party taking responsibility for managing counterparty risk, while bilateral clearing is conducted between the two parties entering a trade.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the process of clearing a derivative transaction.
cards.statement: Bilateral clearing computes payment obligations without the need for netting, while central clearing mandates netting.
cards.explanation: Netting is not what separates the two approaches. Bilateral netting agreements exist, and the distinction is who performs risk management, the counterparties or the CCP.
cards.originalText: Bilateral clearing facilitates the computation of payment obligations without the necessity for netting, while central clearing mandates netting.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the process of clearing a derivative transaction.
cards.statement: In the central clearing of an OTC derivative, the central counterparty takes over the management of counterparty risk and associated components such as collateralization.
cards.explanation: In bilateral clearing the two parties manage counterparty risk themselves. In central clearing the CCP replaces that bilateral relationship and performs the risk management and collateral functions.
cards.originalText: It takes over the management of counterparty risk and associated components such as collateralization.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the process of clearing a derivative transaction.
cards.statement: A central counterparty customises the contract terms to meet the hedging needs of each client.
cards.explanation: Customisation is done by the counterparties when the trade is structured, before clearing. Central clearing in fact requires standardised contracts.
cards.originalText: It customizes the contract terms to meet the hedging needs of each client.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the process of clearing a derivative transaction.
cards.statement: A central counterparty executes the trade on an exchange to provide price discovery.
cards.explanation: Execution and price discovery are trading functions. Clearing, which is what a CCP performs, takes place after execution.
cards.originalText: It executes the trade on an exchange to provide price discovery.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the process of clearing a derivative transaction.
cards.statement: A central counterparty negotiates the contract terms between buyer and seller.
cards.explanation: Contract terms are negotiated bilaterally before clearing. The CCP's role begins after execution and is to manage counterparty risk.
cards.originalText: It negotiates the contract terms between buyer and seller.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the process of clearing a derivative transaction.
cards.statement: Exchange-traded derivatives are centrally cleared, while OTC derivatives have historically been bilaterally cleared and only sufficiently standardised ones can be centrally cleared.
cards.explanation: Every derivatives exchange has an associated CCP. Central clearing of OTC products is growing, but it requires standardisation, so customised OTC products stay bilateral.
cards.originalText: Exchange‑traded derivatives are centrally cleared, while OTC derivatives have historically been bilaterally cleared and only sufficiently standardized ones can be centrally cleared.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the process of clearing a derivative transaction.
cards.statement: Customised OTC derivatives are routinely centrally cleared because their negotiable terms make the CCP process simpler.
cards.explanation: Customisation prevents central clearing, which requires standardised contracts. Customised OTC derivatives therefore remain bilaterally cleared.
cards.originalText: Customized OTC derivatives are routinely centrally cleared because their negotiable terms make the CCP process simpler.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the process of clearing a derivative transaction.
cards.statement: Exchange-traded derivatives are predominantly bilaterally cleared because their standardised terms allow direct agreement between counterparties.
cards.explanation: Exchange-traded derivatives are centrally cleared, not bilaterally cleared. Every exchange has an associated CCP.
cards.originalText: Exchange‑traded derivatives are predominantly bilaterally cleared because their standardized terms allow direct agreement between counterparties.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the process of clearing a derivative transaction.
cards.statement: Exchange-traded derivatives require individually tailored clearing arrangements for each pair of counterparties.
cards.explanation: Exchange clearing is uniform through the CCP. There are no tailored bilateral clearing arrangements for each pair of counterparties.
cards.originalText: Exchange‑traded derivatives require individually tailored clearing arrangements for each pair of counterparties.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the process of clearing a derivative transaction.
cards.statement: The clearing process for OTC derivatives usually spans a longer time horizon, often years or even decades, because of their long maturities.
cards.explanation: Clearing lasts from execution until settlement. Exchange-traded products settle within days or months, whereas OTC derivatives are long-dated, so their clearing period can last years or decades.
cards.originalText: The clearing process for OTC derivatives usually spans a longer time horizon, often years or even decades, due to their long maturities.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the process of clearing a derivative transaction.
cards.statement: OTC derivatives typically settle immediately after trade execution.
cards.explanation: OTC derivatives are long-dated and are not settled for a long time. Their clearing period, between execution and settlement, therefore lasts years or even decades.
cards.originalText: OTC derivatives typically settle immediately after trade execution, increasing the need for efficient clearing processes.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the process of clearing a derivative transaction.
cards.statement: Exchange-traded derivatives have increasingly longer settlement periods, leading to a demand for more complex clearing procedures.
cards.explanation: Exchange-traded settlement is short, from days to at most months, and is not lengthening. It is the long maturity of OTC derivatives that makes their clearing period long.
cards.originalText: Exchange‑traded derivatives have increasingly longer settlement periods, leading to a demand for more complex clearing procedures.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the process of clearing a derivative transaction.
cards.statement: OTC derivatives tend to have shorter maturities than exchange-traded products, so their clearing has become less significant.
cards.explanation: OTC derivatives generally have longer maturities than exchange-traded products, and clearing is becoming more important, not less.
cards.originalText: OTC derivatives tend to have shorter maturities than exchange‑traded products, thus their clearing has become less significant.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the process of clearing a derivative transaction.
cards.statement: A crucial activity in the clearing of a derivative transaction is the calculation, and often netting, of payment obligations between the parties to streamline future settlements.
cards.explanation: Clearing sits between execution and settlement. During it, payment obligations are computed and often netted, and the transaction is managed through margining and cash-flow payments.
cards.originalText: Calculation and often netting of payment obligations between the parties to streamline future settlements.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the process of clearing a derivative transaction.
cards.statement: During the clearing of a derivative transaction the contract's terms are adjusted to reflect market conditions at the time of settlement.
cards.explanation: Contract terms are fixed at execution and are not adjusted during clearing. Market movements are handled through margin, not by changing terms.
cards.originalText: Adjustment of the derivative contract’s terms to reflect market conditions at the time of settlement.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the process of clearing a derivative transaction.
cards.statement: Clearing involves the complete transfer of the underlying securities or cash between the parties to the transaction.
cards.explanation: The transfer of cash or securities is settlement, the stage after clearing. Clearing is the earlier stage in which obligations are computed and managed.
cards.originalText: Complete transfer of the underlying securities or cash between the parties involved in the transaction.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the process of clearing a derivative transaction.
cards.statement: Clearing of a derivative transaction involves initiating a new derivative transaction as a hedge against the one that has just been executed.
cards.explanation: Hedging is a trading decision unrelated to clearing. Clearing computes and nets payment obligations and manages the transaction before settlement.
cards.originalText: Initiation of a new derivative transaction as a hedge against the one that has just been executed.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the process of clearing a derivative transaction.
cards.statement: A customised, non-standardised OTC swap that is not eligible for a CCP is bilaterally cleared: the two counterparties themselves handle risk management processes such as collateral arrangements and bear the counterparty risk.
cards.explanation: Central clearing requires standardisation, so a tailored swap stays outside a CCP. In bilateral clearing the two parties take responsibility for collateral and counterparty risk themselves.
cards.originalText: It will be bilaterally cleared: Lay and the bank themselves handle the risk management processes, such as collateral arrangements, and bear the counterparty risk.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the process of clearing a derivative transaction.
cards.statement: A customised, non-standardised OTC swap is centrally cleared, with a clearinghouse becoming the counterparty to both parties.
cards.explanation: Central clearing requires standardised contracts. A customised swap cannot go to a CCP and is therefore cleared bilaterally.
cards.originalText: It will be centrally cleared, with a clearinghouse becoming the counterparty to both Lay and the bank.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the process of clearing a derivative transaction.
cards.statement: Clearing does not apply to OTC derivatives because they are privately negotiated.
cards.explanation: Clearing applies to every derivative, including OTC ones. For OTC trades that are not centrally cleared it is simply done bilaterally.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the process of clearing a derivative transaction.
cards.statement: A regulator collects margin from both parties for the life of a bilaterally cleared swap and manages the counterparty risk.
cards.explanation: Regulators do not collect or manage margin. In bilateral clearing the two counterparties do so, and in central clearing the CCP does.
cards.originalText: A regulator will collect margin from both parties for the life of the swap and manage the counterparty risk.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the process of clearing a derivative transaction.
cards.statement: Clearing is the process under which margin transactions are facilitated and payment obligations are computed.
cards.explanation: Clearing is the stage between execution and settlement in which margining is carried out and payment obligations are calculated.
cards.originalText: clearing.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the process of clearing a derivative transaction.
cards.statement: Settlement is the process under which margin transactions are facilitated and computed.
cards.explanation: Settlement is the payment and transfer of money when the contract is closed out. Margining and the computation of obligations take place earlier, during clearing.
cards.originalText: settlement.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the process of clearing a derivative transaction.
cards.statement: Execution is the process under which margin transactions are facilitated and computed.
