cards.loText: Explain the different methods of absorbing losses and managing the default of one or more members of a CCP.
cards.statement: Variation margin gains haircutting is a method in which the CCP applies a haircut to the value of securities posted as margin to reflect their price volatility.
cards.explanation: A haircut on posted securities is a collateral valuation risk control. Variation margin gains haircutting allocates default losses to members with gains.
cards.originalText: The CCP applies a haircut to the value of securities posted as margin to reflect their price volatility.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the different methods of absorbing losses and managing the default of one or more members of a CCP.
cards.statement: Variation margin gains haircutting reduces the variation margin owed by all members, both those with gains and those with losses, by the same percentage.
cards.explanation: Haircuts apply only to payouts to members with gains. Members who owe variation margin must pay in full, otherwise the CCP would be unfunded.
cards.originalText: The CCP reduces the variation margin owed by all members, both those with gains and those with losses, by the same percentage.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the different methods of absorbing losses and managing the default of one or more members of a CCP.
cards.statement: A CCP neutralises a defaulted member's market risk by macro-hedging the portfolio against major risk factors, auctioning the sub-portfolios to surviving members and, if the auction does not work, tearing up unmatched contracts.
cards.explanation: Macro-hedging reduces the CCP's market risk first, the auction transfers the hedged sub-portfolios, and tear-up is the fallback to restore a matched book.
cards.originalText: Macro‑hedge the portfolio against major risk factors, auction the sub‑portfolios to surviving members, and if the auction does not work, tear up unmatched contracts.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the different methods of absorbing losses and managing the default of one or more members of a CCP.
cards.statement: A CCP neutralises a defaulted member's market risk by auctioning the entire portfolio as one block and, if no bids are received, haircutting the initial margin of non-defaulting members.
cards.explanation: An unhedged single-block auction is inefficient, and haircutting non-defaulting members' initial margin is not an accepted fallback.
cards.originalText: Auction the entire portfolio as one block; if no bids are received, haircut the initial margin of non‑defaulting members.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain the different methods of absorbing losses and managing the default of one or more members of a CCP.
cards.statement: A CCP neutralises a defaulted member's market risk by tearing up all contracts first, then macro-hedging, then auctioning the remaining positions.
cards.explanation: Tear-up is a fallback after a failed auction, not a first step. The standard sequence is macro-hedge, then auction.
cards.originalText: Tear up all contracts first, then macro‑hedge, then auction the remaining positions.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare bilateral and central clearing.
cards.statement: In bilaterally cleared OTC derivative markets loss absorbency comes mainly from capital, with increasingly some initial margin, whereas in centrally cleared markets it comes mainly from initial margin and default fund contributions.
cards.explanation: A dealer absorbs bilateral counterparty losses mostly with regulatory capital, while CCP members post full collateral including initial margin plus default fund contributions.
cards.originalText: Bilateral: mainly capital (increasingly some initial margin); central clearing: mainly initial margin and default fund contributions.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare bilateral and central clearing.
cards.statement: In bilaterally cleared OTC derivative markets loss absorbency comes mainly from initial margin and default fund contributions, whereas in centrally cleared markets it comes mainly from capital.
cards.explanation: This reverses the two markets. Bilateral markets rely mainly on capital, and central clearing relies mainly on margin and default fund contributions.
cards.originalText: Bilateral: mainly initial margin and default fund contributions; central clearing: mainly capital.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare bilateral and central clearing.
cards.statement: In both bilaterally and centrally cleared OTC derivative markets, loss absorbency comes mainly from capital, because margin only covers current exposure.
cards.explanation: CCPs collateralise with initial margin and default funds, which carry most of the loss-absorbency cost in central clearing.
cards.originalText: Both markets: mainly capital, because margin only covers current exposure.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare bilateral and central clearing.
cards.statement: Central clearing standardizes and mutualizes risk, which can help increase the liquidity of the underlying markets through greater predictability and confidence.
cards.explanation: A CCP replaces many bilateral credit relationships with one standardized counterparty and common margin rules, so positions are easier to offset and close out.
cards.originalText: Central clearing standardizes and mutualizes risk, which can help increase liquidity of the underlying markets through greater predictability and confidence.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare bilateral and central clearing.
cards.statement: Bilateral clearing enhances market liquidity by allowing counterparties to negotiate credit terms tailored to their needs.
cards.explanation: Bespoke credit terms fragment the market and hinder offsetting, so they do not enhance liquidity.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare bilateral and central clearing.
cards.statement: Bilateral clearing inherently provides greater liquidity than central clearing because there are no standard margin requirements tying up capital.
cards.explanation: Bilateral markets are not inherently more liquid, and tailored terms reduce the fungibility of positions.
cards.originalText: Bilateral clearing inherently provides greater liquidity because there are no standard margin requirements tying up capital.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare bilateral and central clearing.
cards.statement: Central clearing restricts market liquidity because the rigid CCP structure cannot adapt to market changes.
cards.explanation: A CCP can improve liquidity through standardization and mutualization, rather than restrict it.
cards.originalText: Central clearing restricts liquidity because the rigid CCP structure cannot adapt to market changes.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare bilateral and central clearing.
cards.statement: A CCP gives a consolidated view of market exposures and can see aggregate risk concentrations, whereas bilateral clearing obscures them because it is decentralized.
cards.explanation: In a bilateral market each pair of counterparties sees only its own trades. A CCP sits in the middle of all cleared trades and sees aggregate positions.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare bilateral and central clearing.
cards.statement: Bilateral clearing promotes transparency because individual agreements let participants directly assess counterparty risk.
cards.explanation: Bilateral parties see only their own relationships, so the market as a whole is opaque.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare bilateral and central clearing.
cards.statement: Bilateral trades are customizable, so market risk assessments are clearer than the homogenized representations in central clearing.
cards.explanation: Customization makes bilateral exposures harder, not easier, to aggregate and assess.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare bilateral and central clearing.
cards.statement: In centrally cleared OTC derivative markets, only standardized, plain-vanilla, liquid products can be cleared, and participants are usually large dealers (clearing members) with others clearing through them.
cards.explanation: A CCP needs standardized, liquid products so it can value and close out positions. Clearing members are usually large dealers, and other entities access the CCP through them.
cards.originalText: Only standardized, plain‑vanilla, liquid products can be cleared, and participants are usually large dealers (clearing members) with others clearing through them.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare bilateral and central clearing.
cards.statement: In centrally cleared OTC derivative markets, any product the two parties agree on can be cleared, and any market participant can become a clearing member.
cards.explanation: This describes the bilateral market. Central clearing restricts both products and participants.
cards.originalText: Any product the two parties agree on can be cleared, and any market participant can become a clearing member.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare bilateral and central clearing.
cards.statement: In centrally cleared OTC derivative markets, only standardized products can be cleared, but any participant can join the CCP directly.
cards.explanation: The product restriction is right, but access is through clearing members, which are usually large dealers.
cards.originalText: Only standardized products can be cleared, but any participant can join the CCP directly.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare bilateral and central clearing.
cards.statement: Complex, bespoke trades are cleared preferentially because CCPs are best able to manage non-standard risk.
cards.explanation: Bespoke trades typically stay bilateral because they are not standard or liquid enough for a CCP to value and close out.
cards.originalText: Complex, bespoke trades are cleared preferentially because CCPs are best able to manage non‑standard risk.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare bilateral and central clearing.
cards.statement: Centrally cleared transactions offer greater transparency and operational efficiency than bilaterally cleared transactions.
cards.explanation: Centralization gives visibility of aggregate exposures and streamlined netting and settlement.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare bilateral and central clearing.
cards.statement: Bilaterally cleared transactions are subject to stricter regulatory oversight than centrally cleared transactions.
cards.explanation: This is reversed. CCPs face heavier regulatory oversight than bilateral markets.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare bilateral and central clearing.
cards.statement: Centrally cleared transactions typically involve higher counterparty risk than bilaterally cleared transactions.
cards.explanation: This is reversed. CCP margining and loss mutualization generally lower counterparty risk.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare bilateral and central clearing.
cards.statement: Bilaterally cleared transactions have standardized margin requirements, while centrally cleared transactions have negotiated margin requirements.
cards.explanation: This is reversed. Bilateral margin is bespoke and negotiated, whereas CCP margin is standardized and enforced by the CCP.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare bilateral and central clearing.
cards.statement: Centrally cleared markets offer more flexibility in contract selection than bilateral markets because of their collateral collecting process.
cards.explanation: Central clearing trades flexibility for standardization. Only standardized, liquid products are cleared, with fixed, nonnegotiable collateral rules.
cards.originalText: offer more flexibility in contract selection because of their collateral collecting process.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare bilateral and central clearing.
cards.statement: Centrally cleared markets formalize the default workout process by using a loss waterfall structure.
cards.explanation: The loss waterfall is a formal, pre-defined default process, unlike an ad hoc bilateral workout.
cards.originalText: formalize the default workout process by using a loss waterfall structure.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare initial margin and default fund requirements for clearing members in relation to loss coverage, cost of clearing, and moral hazard.
cards.statement: If a CCP lowers initial margin and correspondingly raises the size of the default fund, the cost of clearing falls but moral hazard rises, because a larger share of default losses is borne by other members rather than the defaulter.
cards.explanation: Mutualized default fund resources are cheaper than fully funded initial margin. Less margin weakens the link between a member's behaviour and who pays for its default.
cards.originalText: The cost of clearing falls, but moral hazard rises because a larger share of default losses is borne by other members rather than the defaulter.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare initial margin and default fund requirements for clearing members in relation to loss coverage, cost of clearing, and moral hazard.
cards.statement: If a CCP lowers initial margin and correspondingly raises the size of the default fund, the cost of clearing rises, because mutualized default fund contributions must cover every member's default.
cards.explanation: Mutualization lowers the cost of clearing compared with funding losses through larger initial margins.
cards.originalText: The cost of clearing rises, because mutualized default fund contributions must cover every member’s default.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare initial margin and default fund requirements for clearing members in relation to loss coverage, cost of clearing, and moral hazard.
cards.statement: If a CCP lowers initial margin and correspondingly raises the size of the default fund, both the cost of clearing and moral hazard fall, because losses are shared more widely among members.
cards.explanation: The cost of clearing falls, but wider loss sharing weakens the defaulter-pays incentive, so moral hazard rises rather than falls.
cards.originalText: Both the cost of clearing and moral hazard fall, because losses are shared more widely among members.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare initial margin and default fund requirements for clearing members in relation to loss coverage, cost of clearing, and moral hazard.
cards.statement: A CCP's initial margin covers the defaulter's own losses in all but rare, extreme scenarios, and the mutualized default fund absorbs the extreme losses that exceed it.
cards.explanation: Initial margin is member-specific and sized for about 99% confidence. Because a margin breach remains possible and tails are heavy, the default fund covers the excess.
cards.originalText: Initial margin covers the defaulter’s own losses in all but rare, extreme scenarios; the mutualized default fund absorbs the extreme losses that exceed it.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare initial margin and default fund requirements for clearing members in relation to loss coverage, cost of clearing, and moral hazard.
cards.statement: At a CCP, initial margin is pooled across all members, while the default fund is posted by the defaulter alone against its own portfolio.
cards.explanation: The roles are reversed. Initial margin is the defaulter's own, and the default fund is the pooled, mutualized resource.
cards.originalText: Initial margin is pooled across all members, while the default fund is posted by the defaulter alone against its own portfolio.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare initial margin and default fund requirements for clearing members in relation to loss coverage, cost of clearing, and moral hazard.
cards.statement: At a CCP, the default fund absorbs the majority of ordinary losses, and initial margin is used only for small estimation errors.
cards.explanation: The layering is reversed. Margin takes the first and most likely losses, and the default fund takes only the extreme tail.
cards.originalText: The default fund absorbs the majority of ordinary losses, and initial margin is used only for small estimation errors.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare initial margin and default fund requirements for clearing members in relation to loss coverage, cost of clearing, and moral hazard.
cards.statement: A 99% initial margin covers every possible loss from a clearing member's default, so a default fund is unnecessary.
cards.explanation: A 99% margin still leaves a chance of a breach with potentially very large losses, which is exactly why a default fund exists.
cards.originalText: A 99% initial margin covers every possible loss from a default, so a default fund is unnecessary.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare initial margin and default fund requirements for clearing members in relation to loss coverage, cost of clearing, and moral hazard.
cards.statement: Raising initial margin keeps losses closer to the defaulter and lowers moral hazard, but at a higher cost of clearing.
cards.explanation: Initial margin is defaulter-specific, so the defaulter pays first and moral hazard falls, but posting more collateral raises the cost of clearing for members.
cards.originalText: Proposal A adds \$100 million of defaulter‑specific margin, keeping losses closer to the defaulter and lowering moral hazard but at a higher clearing cost; Proposal B adds \$60 million of mutualized resources, which is cheaper but raises moral hazard.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare initial margin and default fund requirements for clearing members in relation to loss coverage, cost of clearing, and moral hazard.
cards.statement: Initial margin has no funding cost for members because it is returned to non-defaulting members.
cards.explanation: Posting collateral is costly even if it is later returned, so larger initial margins increase the cost of clearing.
cards.originalText: Proposal A is cheaper for members, because initial margin is returned to non‑defaulting members and so has no funding cost.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare initial margin and default fund requirements for clearing members in relation to loss coverage, cost of clearing, and moral hazard.
cards.statement: Larger default fund contributions lower moral hazard because they give members more skin in the game.
cards.explanation: Default fund contributions are mutualized, so other members bear a defaulter's losses; this weakens rather than strengthens incentives and raises moral hazard.
cards.originalText: Proposal B lowers moral hazard, because larger default fund contributions give members more skin in the game.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the advantages and disadvantages of central clearing.
cards.statement: A CCP, by providing a guarantee on transactions, may inadvertently encourage market participants to engage in riskier trading practices and underestimate systemic risk.
cards.explanation: Because the CCP absorbs and mutualizes counterparty losses, members have less incentive to monitor credit quality and manage risk carefully; this is the moral hazard problem of central clearing.
cards.originalText: CCPs, by providing a guarantee on transactions, may inadvertently encourage market participants to engage in riskier trading practices, underestimating the systemic risk.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the advantages and disadvantages of central clearing.
cards.statement: Centralization in a CCP allows multilateral offset of opposing positions across members, which lowers margin costs for members.
cards.explanation: A CCP sees many members' trades, so opposing positions can be offset multilaterally, which reduces margin costs and the need to monitor other members.
cards.originalText: Centralization allows multilateral offset of opposing positions across members, which lowers margin costs for members.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the advantages and disadvantages of central clearing.
cards.statement: Centralizing trades in a CCP makes risk harder to assess.
cards.explanation: A CCP sees aggregate risk concentrations, so central clearing makes risk more transparent rather than harder to assess.
cards.originalText: Because a CCP centralizes trades, risk becomes harder to assess, which makes the trading environment more intricate but more secure.
cards.correction: Centralizing trades in a CCP makes risk easier to assess.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the advantages and disadvantages of central clearing.
cards.statement: Central clearing means each member must collect and monitor detailed private credit information about every other member.
cards.explanation: Multilateral offset through a CCP removes the need for members to monitor the creditworthiness of other members.
cards.originalText: Centralization means each member must collect and monitor detailed private credit information about every other member.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the advantages and disadvantages of central clearing.
cards.statement: Central clearing can lead to over-reliance on CCPs and potential neglect of due diligence by market participants.
cards.explanation: Netting, collateralization and loss mutualization weaken members' incentive to vet each other's credit quality; this is moral hazard, a listed disadvantage of central clearing.
cards.originalText: Central clearing prevents bilateral risk assessment, leading to over‑reliance on CCPs and potential neglect of due diligence by market participants.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the advantages and disadvantages of central clearing.
cards.statement: Central clearing simplifies the legal documentation process, leading to a reduction in clarity and an increase in market ambiguity.
cards.explanation: Rules-based clearing minimizes legal costs and improves clarity; legal and operational efficiency is an advantage of central clearing, not a source of ambiguity.
cards.originalText: It simplifies the legal documentation process, leading to a reduction in clarity and an increase in market ambiguity.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the advantages and disadvantages of central clearing.
cards.statement: The aggregated risk exposure at a CCP makes it difficult for the CCP to manage risk effectively, often resulting in higher losses during defaults.
cards.explanation: Aggregation gives the CCP transparency over members' positions, and the loss waterfall formalizes default handling, so this is not a listed disadvantage of central clearing.
cards.originalText: The aggregated risk exposure makes it difficult for CCPs to manage the risk effectively, often resulting in higher losses during defaults.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the advantages and disadvantages of central clearing.
cards.statement: When markets and the economy become more volatile, CCPs generally raise collateral requirements, which can worsen a potential default scenario.
cards.explanation: Raising margin and collateral in stressed markets is procyclicality, a listed disadvantage of central clearing.
cards.originalText: When markets and the economy become more volatile, CCPs generally raise collateral requirements, which can worsen a potential default scenario.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the advantages and disadvantages of central clearing.
cards.statement: Because of a CCP's multilateral offset, members must monitor each other's creditworthiness more closely.
cards.explanation: Multilateral offset removes the need to monitor other members; the actual concern is too little monitoring, which is moral hazard.
cards.originalText: Members must monitor each other’s creditworthiness more closely because of the CCP’s multilateral offset.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the advantages and disadvantages of central clearing.
cards.statement: Loss mutualization through the loss waterfall increases the market impact of a member default.
cards.explanation: Loss mutualization reduces the market impact of a member default and is a listed advantage of central clearing.
cards.originalText: Loss mutualization through the loss waterfall increases the market impact of a member default.
cards.correction: Loss mutualization through the loss waterfall reduces the market impact of a member default.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the advantages and disadvantages of central clearing.
cards.statement: A CCP has less information on members' aggregate exposures than counterparties have in bilateral markets.
cards.explanation: A CCP sees many members' trades and so has more aggregate information than bilateral counterparties; transparency is a listed advantage of central clearing.
cards.originalText: A CCP has less information on aggregate member exposures than counterparties have in bilateral markets.
cards.correction: A CCP has more information on members' aggregate exposures than counterparties have in bilateral markets.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the advantages and disadvantages of central clearing.
cards.statement: Moral hazard is a disadvantage of central clearing: because losses are netted, collateralized and mutualized, clearing members have little incentive to review one another's creditworthiness.
cards.explanation: Netting, collateral and loss mutualization protect members, so they have little reason to vet each other's credit quality; this is the textbook moral hazard disadvantage.
cards.originalText: Clearing members stop reviewing one another’s creditworthiness because losses are netted, collateralized and mutualized: moral hazard (a disadvantage).

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the advantages and disadvantages of central clearing.
cards.statement: A CCP seeing a member's extreme aggregate exposure and limiting its trading illustrates adverse selection, a disadvantage of central clearing.
cards.explanation: This is transparency, an advantage of central clearing; adverse selection is members knowing more about their own risk than the CCP does.
cards.originalText: Total Clear sees a member’s extreme aggregate exposure and limits its trading: adverse selection (a disadvantage).
cards.correction: A CCP seeing a member's extreme aggregate exposure and limiting its trading illustrates transparency, an advantage of central clearing.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the advantages and disadvantages of central clearing.
cards.statement: Clearing only standardized contracts while customized trades stay in the bilateral market illustrates multilateral offset, an advantage of central clearing.
cards.explanation: This is bifurcation of cleared and non-cleared trades, a disadvantage, because it reduces the benefits of multilateral offset.
cards.originalText: Only standardized contracts are cleared, leaving customized trades in the bilateral market: multilateral offset (an advantage).
cards.correction: Clearing only standardized contracts while customized trades stay in the bilateral market illustrates bifurcation, a disadvantage of central clearing.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the advantages and disadvantages of central clearing.
cards.statement: A CCP raising margin requirements as market volatility rises illustrates loss mutualization, an advantage of central clearing.
cards.explanation: Raising collateral requirements in volatile markets is procyclicality, a disadvantage of central clearing; loss mutualization is the sharing of a defaulter's losses among members.
cards.originalText: Total Clear raises margin requirements as market volatility rises: loss mutualization (an advantage).
cards.correction: A CCP raising margin requirements as market volatility rises illustrates procyclicality, a disadvantage of central clearing.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the advantages and disadvantages of central clearing.
cards.statement: Adverse selection is a disadvantage of central clearing because trading desks at major institutions know derivatives products better than the CCP, creating a one-sided information gap that puts the CCP at a disadvantage.
cards.explanation: Members' superior knowledge of pricing and risk lets them selectively trade with CCPs that underprice risk; this asymmetric information is adverse selection.
cards.originalText: The trading desks at major financial institutions know derivatives products inside and out, which may create a one‑sided information gap that puts the CCP at a disadvantage.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the advantages and disadvantages of central clearing.
cards.statement: Adverse selection in central clearing arises when a CCP, in performing extensive member due diligence, omits a member firm in error.
cards.explanation: Adverse selection arises from information asymmetry, with members knowing more about derivatives pricing and risk than the CCP; an error in member screening is an operational matter.
cards.originalText: In performing extensive member due diligence, the CCP may omit a member firm in error.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the advantages and disadvantages of central clearing.
cards.statement: Adverse selection in central clearing arises because only member firms can transact with a CCP, which limits the pool of available transactions.
cards.explanation: Restricting access to members is a design feature of a CCP, not an information problem; adverse selection stems from asymmetric information favouring members over the CCP.
cards.originalText: Only member firms can transact with a CCP, which limits the pool of available transactions.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the advantages and disadvantages of central clearing.
cards.statement: Central clearing enhances market liquidity because multilateral offset and greater transparency make it easier to enter and terminate trades.
cards.explanation: Multilateral offset and transparency make it easier for members to trade, which improves market liquidity; this is a listed advantage of central clearing.
cards.originalText: Market liquidity is enhanced because multilateral offset and greater transparency make it easier to enter and terminate trades.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the advantages and disadvantages of central clearing.
cards.statement: Counterparty risk is eliminated under a CCP structure.
cards.explanation: A CCP reduces and concentrates counterparty risk but does not eliminate it.
cards.originalText: Counterparty risk is eliminated under a CCP structure.
cards.correction: Counterparty risk is reduced under a CCP structure.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the advantages and disadvantages of central clearing.
cards.statement: Loss sharing through the loss waterfall protects members in the event that a CCP fails.
cards.explanation: The loss waterfall allocates the losses from a clearing member's default; it does not protect members if the CCP itself fails.
cards.originalText: Loss sharing through the loss waterfall protects members in the event that a CCP fails.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the advantages and disadvantages of central clearing.
cards.statement: Central clearing gives end users more incentive to monitor the creditworthiness of clearing members.
cards.explanation: Netting and loss mutualization reduce the incentive to monitor creditworthiness, which is moral hazard, a disadvantage of central clearing.
cards.originalText: There is more incentive for end users to monitor the creditworthiness of clearing members.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the advantages and disadvantages of central clearing.
cards.statement: Increased transparency is an advantage of central clearing through a CCP.
cards.explanation: A CCP sees many members' trades and aggregate exposures, which makes risk more transparent.
cards.originalText: Increase transparency.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the advantages and disadvantages of central clearing.
cards.statement: Loss mutualization is an advantage of central clearing through a CCP.
cards.explanation: Mutualizing a defaulter's losses across members through the loss waterfall reduces the market impact of a default.
cards.originalText: Manage loss mutualization.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe the advantages and disadvantages of central clearing.
cards.statement: Improved operational efficiency is an advantage of central clearing through a CCP.
cards.explanation: Legal and operational efficiency is a listed advantage of central clearing.
cards.originalText: Improve operational efficiency.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare the characterization of credit exposure to VaR methods and describe additional considerations used in the determination of credit exposure.
cards.statement: Future exposure is expressed as a distribution (potential future exposure) because past and current exposure are known with certainty, whereas future exposure depends on uncertain market movements and can only be described by probabilistic estimates.
cards.explanation: Exposure is the positive part of portfolio value, which is observable for past and current dates; future exposure depends on random market moves, so it is characterized probabilistically, as VaR does for market risk.
cards.originalText: Past and current exposure are known with certainty, whereas future exposure depends on uncertain future market movements and can only be described by probabilistic estimates.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare the characterization of credit exposure to VaR methods and describe additional considerations used in the determination of credit exposure.
cards.statement: Future exposure can be projected deterministically by extrapolating the trend of past and present exposure.
cards.explanation: Future market moves are random, so future exposure must be described by a distribution such as potential future exposure rather than by a single projected line.
cards.originalText: Future exposure can be projected deterministically by extrapolating the trend of past and present exposure.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare the characterization of credit exposure to VaR methods and describe additional considerations used in the determination of credit exposure.
cards.statement: Past exposure is known with certainty, but current and future exposure are both subject to probabilistic estimation.
cards.explanation: Only future exposure is uncertain; past and current exposure are known once portfolio values are observed.
cards.originalText: Past exposure is known with certainty, but current and future exposure are both subject to probabilistic estimation.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare the characterization of credit exposure to VaR methods and describe additional considerations used in the determination of credit exposure.
cards.statement: Characterizing credit exposure is more complex than characterizing VaR mainly because exposure must be defined over multiple time horizons, often far in the future, whereas VaR uses a short horizon.
cards.explanation: Exposure is needed at many future dates, so ageing of trades, drift and path dependency must be modelled; VaR's short horizon lets these be neglected.
cards.originalText: Exposure must be defined over multiple time horizons, often far in the future, unlike VaR, which uses a short horizon.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare the characterization of credit exposure to VaR methods and describe additional considerations used in the determination of credit exposure.
cards.statement: Credit exposure can take positive and negative values, whereas VaR is always positive.
cards.explanation: Exposure is defined as the positive part of portfolio value (floored at zero), and VaR is a loss quantile; sign is not what makes exposure more complex.
cards.originalText: Exposure can take positive and negative values, whereas VaR is always positive.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare the characterization of credit exposure to VaR methods and describe additional considerations used in the determination of credit exposure.
cards.statement: Future VaR is always known with certainty, but future exposure is not.
cards.explanation: Neither measure is known with certainty for the future; both VaR and exposure are probabilistic.
cards.originalText: Future VaR is always known with certainty, but future exposure is not.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare the characterization of credit exposure to VaR methods and describe additional considerations used in the determination of credit exposure.
cards.statement: Unlike VaR, credit exposure needs to be defined over multiple time horizons, often far in the future, to capture the impact of time and the specifics of the underlying contracts.
cards.explanation: VaR uses a short horizon, whereas exposure is needed at many, often distant, dates.
cards.originalText: Unlike VaR, credit exposure needs to be defined over multiple time horizons (often far in the future) to capture the impact of time and the specifics of the underlying contracts.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare the characterization of credit exposure to VaR methods and describe additional considerations used in the determination of credit exposure.
cards.statement: Unlike VaR, credit exposure often must model complex or subjective factors, including legal interpretations, because of risk mitigants such as netting and collateral.
cards.explanation: Netting and collateral agreements add legal and subjective modelling complexity to exposure that VaR does not face.
cards.originalText: Unlike VaR, credit exposure often must model complex and/or subjective factors (including legal interpretations) because of risk mitigants such as netting and collateral.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare the characterization of credit exposure to VaR methods and describe additional considerations used in the determination of credit exposure.
cards.statement: Unlike VaR, which depends critically on the portfolio's expected future value (drift), credit exposure is measured with a simulation that does not depend on expected future value.
cards.explanation: The relationship is reversed: drift matters for long-horizon credit exposure, whereas it is negligible for short-horizon VaR.
cards.originalText: Unlike VaR, which depends critically on the portfolio’s expected future value (drift), credit exposure is measured with a simulation that does not depend on expected future value.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Compare the characterization of credit exposure to VaR methods and describe additional considerations used in the determination of credit exposure.
cards.statement: VaR is a risk measure only, whereas credit exposure is defined for both risk management and valuation (pricing), which may imply different calculations for each.
cards.explanation: Exposure is used both for risk and for pricing (xVA), so different calculations may be needed; VaR serves only risk.
cards.originalText: VaR is a risk measure only, whereas credit exposure is defined for both risk management and valuation (pricing), which may imply different calculations for each.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify factors that affect the calculation of the credit exposure profile and summarize the impact of collateral on exposure.
cards.statement: For a simple forward contract with a single cash flow on an underlying whose returns are independent and identically distributed, exposure is approximately proportional to the square root of time.
cards.explanation: With i.i.d. returns, the standard deviation of the underlying grows with $\sqrt{t}$, so the exposure of a single-cash-flow forward scales with the square root of time.
cards.originalText: For a simple forward contract with a single cash flow on an underlying whose returns are independent and identically distributed, exposure is approximately proportional to the square root of time

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify factors that affect the calculation of the credit exposure profile and summarize the impact of collateral on exposure.
cards.statement: Quantification of counterparty credit exposure for xVA can safely ignore the drift of the risk factors, since drift is negligible at all horizons.
cards.explanation: Drift can be ignored only in short-horizon VaR; for xVA exposure over long horizons the drift is relevant.
cards.originalText: As in market value‑at‑risk (VaR) measurement, quantification of counterparty credit exposure for xVA can safely ignore the drift of the risk factors, since drift is negligible at all horizons

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify factors that affect the calculation of the credit exposure profile and summarize the impact of collateral on exposure.
cards.statement: For a single-name credit default swap, expected exposure generally decreases as the volatility of the credit spread rises.
cards.explanation: Exposure is an increasing function of spread volatility, because higher volatility raises the chance of large positive values.
cards.originalText: For a single‑name credit default swap, expected exposure generally decreases as the volatility of the credit spread rises
cards.correction: For a single-name credit default swap, expected exposure generally increases as the volatility of the credit spread rises.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify factors that affect the calculation of the credit exposure profile and summarize the impact of collateral on exposure.
cards.statement: For an interest rate swap, exposure rises steadily until maturity, because periodic payments do not reduce future uncertainty.
cards.explanation: Periodic payments reduce the remaining cash flows, so the exposure profile is hump-shaped, peaking mid-life and falling toward zero at maturity.
cards.originalText: For an interest rate swap, exposure rises steadily until maturity, because periodic payments do not reduce future uncertainty

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify factors that affect the calculation of the credit exposure profile and summarize the impact of collateral on exposure.
cards.statement: The granularity effect arises when the minimum transfer amount prevents a party from calling for all of the collateral it is actually owed.
cards.explanation: Collateral parameters such as the minimum transfer amount and rounding mean small exposure increases cannot be called, leaving some exposure uncollateralized.
cards.originalText: The granularity effect: the minimum transfer amount prevents the bank from calling for all of the collateral it is actually owed.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Assess the impact of collateral on counterparty risk and funding, with and without segregation or rehypothecation.
cards.statement: Non-segregated cash and rehypothecable securities provide both counterparty risk reduction and funding benefits, segregated collateral provides only counterparty risk reduction, and a counterparty's own rehypothecable bonds provide only a funding benefit.
cards.explanation: Collateral reduces counterparty risk if it can be monetised on default and gives a funding benefit only if it can be reused. Segregated collateral cannot be reused, and a counterparty's own bonds are near-worthless at its default (wrong-way risk).
cards.originalText: I. and II. provide both counterparty risk reduction and funding benefits; III. provides only counterparty risk reduction benefits; and IV. provides only funding benefit

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe common types of structured products.
cards.statement: Instruments created by securitizing tranches of other CDOs are known as CDO squared.
cards.explanation: A CDO squared repackages tranches of other CDOs, adding a second layer of securitization.
cards.originalText: CDO squared

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe common types of structured products.
cards.statement: Instruments created by securitizing tranches of other CDOs are known as collateralized loan obligations (CLOs).
cards.explanation: A CLO is backed by a pool of corporate loans; securitizing tranches of other CDOs creates a CDO squared.
cards.originalText: Collateralized loan obligations (CLOs)
cards.correction: Instruments created by securitizing tranches of other CDOs are known as CDO squared.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe common types of structured products.
cards.statement: Instruments created by securitizing tranches of other CDOs are known as synthetic CDOs.
cards.explanation: A synthetic CDO obtains its credit exposure through credit derivatives such as CDS; securitizing tranches of other CDOs creates a CDO squared.
cards.originalText: Synthetic CDOs
cards.correction: Instruments created by securitizing tranches of other CDOs are known as CDO squared.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe common types of structured products.
cards.statement: Instruments created by securitizing tranches of other CDOs are known as mortgage-backed securities (MBS).
cards.explanation: An MBS is backed by mortgage loans and is a single-level securitization; securitizing tranches of other CDOs creates a CDO squared.
cards.originalText: Mortgage‑backed securities (MBS)
cards.correction: Instruments created by securitizing tranches of other CDOs are known as CDO squared.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe common types of structured products.
cards.statement: A mortgage pass-through security entitles the investor to a pro rata share of all principal and interest payments made on the underlying pool of mortgage loans.
cards.explanation: Pass-throughs pass the pool's net cash flows pro rata to investors, with no tranching.
cards.originalText: Mortgage pass‑through

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe common types of structured products.
cards.statement: A collateralized mortgage obligation entitles the investor to a pro rata share of all principal and interest payments made on the underlying pool of mortgage loans.
cards.explanation: A CMO divides the pool's cash flows into tranches by predetermined rules such as sequential pay, so investors do not receive a pro rata share.
cards.originalText: Collateralized mortgage obligation
cards.correction: A mortgage pass-through security entitles the investor to a pro rata share of all principal and interest payments made on the underlying pool of mortgage loans.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe common types of structured products.
cards.statement: A covered bond entitles the investor to a pro rata share of all principal and interest payments made on the underlying pool of mortgage loans.
cards.explanation: A covered bond stays on the originator's balance sheet and is paid and guaranteed by the originator, not passed through from the pool.
cards.originalText: Covered bond
cards.correction: A mortgage pass-through security entitles the investor to a pro rata share of all principal and interest payments made on the underlying pool of mortgage loans.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe common types of structured products.
cards.statement: A collateralized debt obligation entitles the investor to a pro rata share of all principal and interest payments made on the underlying pool of mortgage loans.
cards.explanation: A CDO tranches the credit risk of a pool of debt instruments, so holders do not receive pro rata pool cash flows.
cards.originalText: Collateralized debt obligation
cards.correction: A mortgage pass-through security entitles the investor to a pro rata share of all principal and interest payments made on the underlying pool of mortgage loans.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe common types of structured products.
cards.statement: A collateralized debt obligation (CDO) is a true off-balance-sheet securitization that tranches a pool of credit-risky debt so that junior tranches absorb losses first and senior tranches have the lowest probability of write-down.
cards.explanation: Only a CDO combines a true, bankruptcy-remote securitization with tranches ranked by credit-loss priority.
cards.originalText: Collateralized debt obligation (CDO)

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe common types of structured products.
cards.statement: A covered bond is a true off-balance-sheet securitization that tranches a pool of credit-risky debt so that junior tranches absorb losses first and senior tranches have the lowest probability of write-down.
cards.explanation: A covered bond stays on the originator's balance sheet, is backed by the originator's guarantee and is not tranched by credit risk, so it is not a true securitization.
cards.originalText: Covered bond

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe common types of structured products.
cards.statement: A mortgage pass-through security tranches a pool of credit-risky debt so that junior tranches absorb losses first and senior tranches have the lowest probability of write-down.
cards.explanation: A pass-through is a true securitization but has no tranching, so all holders share losses pro rata.
cards.originalText: Mortgage pass‑through security

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe common types of structured products.
cards.statement: A sequential-pay collateralized mortgage obligation (CMO) tranches a pool of debt by credit-loss priority so that junior tranches absorb losses first.
cards.explanation: The tranches of a sequential-pay CMO differ in maturity and prepayment risk rather than in credit-loss priority.
cards.originalText: Sequential‑pay collateralized mortgage obligation (CMO) in which tranches differ in prepayment risk

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe common types of structured products.
cards.statement: A collateralized debt obligation (CDO) issues securities backed by a pool of conventional debt obligations and other securitized assets such as ABS, MBS and CLOs.
cards.explanation: A CDO issues securities against a pool of debt obligations and/or other securitized products.
cards.originalText: Collateralized debt obligation (CDO)

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe common types of structured products.
cards.statement: A mortgage-backed security (MBS) is backed by a mix of debt obligations and other securitized assets such as ABS and CLOs.
cards.explanation: An MBS is backed by a pool of mortgages only; a pool mixing debt obligations and other securitized products backs a CDO.
cards.originalText: Mortgage‑backed security (MBS)

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe common types of structured products.
cards.statement: In a covered bond the cover pool remains on the originator's balance sheet, whereas in a true securitization the assets are removed from it.
cards.explanation: Covered bonds are on-balance-sheet instruments; true securitizations are off-balance-sheet.
cards.originalText: In a covered bond the cover pool remains on the originator’s balance sheet, whereas in a true securitization the assets are removed from it

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe common types of structured products.
cards.statement: Covered bond principal and interest are paid and guaranteed by the originator, whereas in a securitization they depend on the performance of the collateral pool.
cards.explanation: The originator's guarantee is what separates a covered bond from a true securitization.
cards.originalText: Covered bond principal and interest are paid and guaranteed by the originator, whereas in a securitization they depend on the performance of the collateral pool

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe common types of structured products.
cards.statement: A covered bond involves no true sale of assets to a bankruptcy-remote special purpose vehicle, whereas a true securitization does.
cards.explanation: The absence of a true sale to a bankruptcy-remote SPV is why covered bonds are not true securitizations.
cards.originalText: A covered bond involves no true sale of assets to a bankruptcy‑remote special purpose vehicle, whereas a true securitization does

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe common types of structured products.
cards.statement: A covered bond does not issue securities or raise funds in the capital markets, whereas a true securitization does.
cards.explanation: Covered bonds are bonds, so both covered bonds and securitizations issue securities to raise funding; they differ in balance-sheet treatment, recourse and source of payment.
cards.originalText: A covered bond does not issue securities or raise funds in the capital markets, whereas a true securitization does

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe common types of structured products.
cards.statement: The essential difference between a CMO and a pass-through MBS is that a CMO issues classes with different risk, return and cash-flow properties.
cards.explanation: A CMO tranches the mortgage cash flows into classes with different risk and payment priority, whereas pass-through holders share cash flows pro rata.
cards.originalText: CMO issues classes with different risk/return/cash‑flow properties

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe common types of structured products.
cards.statement: A pass-through MBS can shield some investors from prepayment risk.
cards.explanation: Pass-through holders share cash flows pro rata and so bear prepayment risk equally; it is CMO tranching that can shield some classes from prepayment risk.
cards.originalText: The pass‑through MBS can shield some investors from prepayment risk

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe tranching and the distribution of credit losses in a securitization.
cards.statement: The equity tranche of a securitization receives no fixed coupon payment and bears the full brunt of default risk.
cards.explanation: The equity tranche is the first-loss piece and is paid only from residual cash flows after all other claims are satisfied.
cards.originalText: Equity

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe tranching and the distribution of credit losses in a securitization.
cards.statement: The junior debt tranche of a securitization receives no fixed coupon payment and bears the full brunt of default risk.
cards.explanation: Junior (mezzanine) debt absorbs losses only after the equity tranche is exhausted and pays a relatively high fixed coupon or spread.
cards.originalText: Junior debt

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe tranching and the distribution of credit losses in a securitization.
cards.statement: The senior debt tranche of a securitization receives no fixed coupon payment and bears the full brunt of default risk.
cards.explanation: Senior debt has the highest priority, is protected by subordination and receives the lowest coupon, which is still a stated coupon.
cards.originalText: Senior debt

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe tranching and the distribution of credit losses in a securitization.
cards.statement: In a securitization, the equity tranche has only an attachment point, the mezzanine tranche has both, and the senior tranche has only a detachment point.
cards.explanation: The logic is reversed: the equity tranche has nothing below it, so it has only a detachment point, and the senior tranche has nothing above it, so it has only an attachment point.
cards.originalText: Equity: attachment point only; Mezzanine: both; Senior: detachment point only

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe tranching and the distribution of credit losses in a securitization.
cards.statement: In a securitization, the equity tranche has only a detachment point, while the mezzanine and senior tranches each have only an attachment point.
cards.explanation: The mezzanine tranche detaches from the senior tranche above it, so it has both an attachment point and a detachment point.
cards.originalText: Equity: detachment point only; Mezzanine: attachment point only; Senior: attachment point only

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe tranching and the distribution of credit losses in a securitization.
cards.statement: Tranching divides the cash flows generated from a collateral pool into different securities with varying levels of credit risk.
cards.explanation: Tranching slices the pool's cash flows into securities such as equity, mezzanine and senior with different loss priority and therefore different credit risk.
cards.originalText: Dividing the cash flows generated from the collateral pool into different securities with varying levels of credit risk.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe tranching and the distribution of credit losses in a securitization.
cards.statement: Tranching is the process of pooling together different loans or debt securities to create a diversified portfolio.
cards.explanation: Pooling is the collateral side of securitization; tranching splits the pool's cash flows into securities with different credit risk.
cards.originalText: The process of pooling together different loans or debt securities to create a diversified portfolio.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe tranching and the distribution of credit losses in a securitization.
cards.statement: Tranching is the transfer of the default risk of the collateral pool to a third-party guarantor.
cards.explanation: Transferring default risk to a guarantor is credit protection; tranching divides the pool's cash flows into securities with different loss priority.
cards.originalText: Transferring the default risk of the collateral pool to a third‑party guarantor.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe tranching and the distribution of credit losses in a securitization.
cards.statement: Tranching is the process of converting illiquid assets into marketable securities.
cards.explanation: That describes securitization in general; tranching is the splitting of the pool's cash flows into securities with different credit risk.
cards.originalText: The process of converting illiquid assets into marketable securities.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify the key participants in the securitization process and describe conflicts of interest that can arise in the process.
cards.statement: A conflict of interest arises in securitization when a rating agency paid by the issuer gives a high rating to the securitized assets to protect its business relationship with the issuer.
cards.explanation: An issuer-paid rating agency that also shapes the deal structure is tempted to be lenient to keep business, which is the textbook conflict of interest in securitization.
cards.originalText: The rating agency, paid by the issuer, gives a high rating to the securitized assets to protect its business relationship with GFB.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify the key participants in the securitization process and describe conflicts of interest that can arise in the process.
cards.statement: Investors demanding higher yields for buying the senior tranches of securitized assets is an example of a conflict of interest in the securitization process.
cards.explanation: Investors seeking compensation for risk is normal pricing, not a conflict between parties' duties and incentives.
cards.originalText: Investors demand higher yields for buying the senior tranches of the securitized assets.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify the key participants in the securitization process and describe conflicts of interest that can arise in the process.
cards.statement: An originator funding a reserve account to enhance the credit quality of the lower tranches is an example of a conflict of interest in the securitization process.
cards.explanation: Credit enhancement by the originator is a structural feature, and retained risk aligns interests; a lower pool yield is a trade-off, not a conflict.
cards.originalText: GFB, as originator, funds a reserve account to enhance the credit quality of the lower tranches, which may reduce the yield of the pool.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify the key participants in the securitization process and describe conflicts of interest that can arise in the process.
cards.statement: An underwriter performing due diligence on the quality of the mortgage loans in the pool is an example of a conflict of interest in the securitization process.
cards.explanation: Due diligence is the underwriter doing its job and works against, not for, a conflict of interest.
cards.originalText: The underwriter performs due diligence to check the quality of the mortgage loans in the pool.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify the key participants in the securitization process and describe conflicts of interest that can arise in the process.
cards.statement: Trustees and custodians are the economically minor participants in a securitization, tasked with keeping records, verifying documentation, moving cash flows among deal accounts and paying noteholders.
cards.explanation: Trustees and custodians play an administrative back-office role and take no credit or structuring decisions.
cards.originalText: Trustee and custodian

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify the key participants in the securitization process and describe conflicts of interest that can arise in the process.
cards.statement: The rating agency and the underwriter are the economically minor participants in a securitization, tasked with keeping records, verifying documentation, moving cash flows among deal accounts and paying noteholders.
cards.explanation: The rating agency assesses credit quality and shapes subordination, and the underwriter structures, markets and warehouses the deal; both are active, economically important participants.
cards.originalText: Rating agency and underwriter

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify the key participants in the securitization process and describe conflicts of interest that can arise in the process.
cards.statement: The originator and the sponsor are the economically minor participants in a securitization, tasked with keeping records, verifying documentation, moving cash flows among deal accounts and paying noteholders.
cards.explanation: The originator creates the loans and the sponsor supplies most of the collateral; they are the source of the assets, not administrators.
cards.originalText: Originator and sponsor

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify the key participants in the securitization process and describe conflicts of interest that can arise in the process.
cards.statement: The underwriter is the securitization participant most likely to incur warehousing risk.
cards.explanation: The underwriter accumulates the collateral and holds it until the securities are sold, so it bears the risk that the deal is not completed or that the collateral loses value.
cards.originalText: Underwriter

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify the key participants in the securitization process and describe conflicts of interest that can arise in the process.
cards.statement: The rating agency is the securitization participant most likely to incur warehousing risk.
cards.explanation: A rating agency only assesses and assigns ratings and holds no collateral; the underwriter warehouses the pool.
cards.originalText: Rating agency

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify the key participants in the securitization process and describe conflicts of interest that can arise in the process.
cards.statement: The servicer is the securitization participant most likely to incur warehousing risk.
cards.explanation: The servicer collects and distributes cash flows and manages distressed loans; it does not warehouse the pool, which the underwriter does.
cards.originalText: Servicer

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify the key participants in the securitization process and describe conflicts of interest that can arise in the process.
cards.statement: Requiring the manager of a securitization pool to hold a first-loss (equity) portion of the deal helps align the manager's incentives with those of investors.
cards.explanation: First-loss retention gives the manager skin in the game, so poor credit monitoring directly reduces the manager's own payoff.
cards.originalText: Requiring the manager to hold a first‑loss (equity) portion of the deal

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify the key participants in the securitization process and describe conflicts of interest that can arise in the process.
cards.statement: Requiring the manager of a securitization pool to hold a portion of the most senior tranche helps align the manager's incentives with those of investors.
cards.explanation: A senior piece is last to absorb losses and is nearly insulated from pool performance, so it creates little incentive to monitor.
cards.originalText: Requiring the manager to hold a portion of the most senior tranche

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify the key participants in the securitization process and describe conflicts of interest that can arise in the process.
cards.statement: Paying the manager of a securitization pool a fixed fee independent of pool performance helps align the manager's incentives with those of investors.
cards.explanation: A fixed fee unrelated to performance gives the manager no incentive to monitor and worsens the effort problem.
cards.originalText: Paying the manager a fixed fee independent of pool performance

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify the key participants in the securitization process and describe conflicts of interest that can arise in the process.
cards.statement: Because credit rating agencies are paid by the issuer and help determine the deal structure, they have an incentive to require less credit enhancement, allowing the issuer to create a larger set of investment-grade tranches.
cards.explanation: Issuer-pay compensation combined with a role in setting attachment points rewards the agency for requiring less enhancement.
cards.originalText: The agency has an incentive to require less credit enhancement, allowing the issuer to create a larger set of investment‑grade tranches

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify the key participants in the securitization process and describe conflicts of interest that can arise in the process.
cards.statement: Because credit rating agencies are paid by the issuer and help determine the deal structure, they have an incentive to require more credit enhancement so that fewer tranches are rated investment grade.
cards.explanation: The incentive runs the other way: requiring more enhancement would shrink the investment-grade portion and displease issuers.
cards.originalText: The agency has an incentive to require more credit enhancement so that fewer tranches are rated investment grade
cards.correction: Because credit rating agencies are paid by the issuer and help determine the deal structure, they have an incentive to require less credit enhancement so that more tranches are rated investment grade.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify the key participants in the securitization process and describe conflicts of interest that can arise in the process.
cards.statement: When a CMBS servicer extends a distressed loan rather than foreclosing, the risk to the senior bond may increase because a larger property loss erodes credit enhancement, while the junior bond keeps some chance of recovery.
cards.explanation: Resolving a distressed loan redistributes losses across the capital structure: foreclosure favors seniors and extension favors juniors, so any servicer action favors some classes over others.
cards.originalText: Extension may increase the risk to the senior bond because a larger property loss erodes credit enhancement, while it gives the junior bond some chance of recovery

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify the key participants in the securitization process and describe conflicts of interest that can arise in the process.
cards.statement: Foreclosure of a distressed CMBS loan helps the junior bond avoid an immediate writedown, so junior bondholders favor foreclosure.
cards.explanation: Foreclosure can trigger an immediate junior writedown, so junior bondholders prefer extension.
cards.originalText: Foreclosure helps the junior bond avoid an immediate writedown, so juniors favor it

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify the key participants in the securitization process and describe conflicts of interest that can arise in the process.
cards.statement: Foreclosure of a distressed CMBS loan causes an immediate writedown of the senior bond, so senior bondholders favor extension.
cards.explanation: Foreclosure usually brings seniors early principal repayment rather than a writedown, so seniors favor foreclosure.
cards.originalText: Foreclosure causes an immediate writedown of the senior bond, so seniors favor extension

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify the key participants in the securitization process and describe conflicts of interest that can arise in the process.
cards.statement: A CMBS servicer faces no conflict of interest in resolving a distressed loan because it must maximize the loan's present value.
cards.explanation: Maximizing present value is the servicer's obligation, but the action it chooses still favors some bond classes over others, so the conflict persists.
cards.originalText: The servicer faces no conflict because it must maximize the loan’s present value

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify the key participants in the securitization process and describe conflicts of interest that can arise in the process.
cards.statement: Extension of a distressed commercial mortgage loan favors the junior bondholders, who avoid an immediate writedown and keep a chance of recovery, while the senior bondholders risk a larger property loss that erodes their credit enhancement.
cards.explanation: Foreclosure benefits seniors through early par repayment, while extension benefits juniors by avoiding an immediate writedown.
cards.originalText: Extension favors the junior bondholders, who avoid an immediate writedown and keep a chance of recovery, while the senior bondholders risk a larger property loss that erodes their credit enhancement.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify the key participants in the securitization process and describe conflicts of interest that can arise in the process.
cards.statement: Foreclosure of a distressed commercial mortgage loan favors the junior bondholders, because they avoid an immediate writedown while the senior bonds absorb the loss.
cards.explanation: Foreclosure triggers the junior writedown, so it favors seniors, who typically receive early repayment of principal.
cards.originalText: Foreclosure favors the junior bondholders, because they avoid an immediate writedown while the senior bonds absorb the loss.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Identify the key participants in the securitization process and describe conflicts of interest that can arise in the process.
cards.statement: Extension of a distressed commercial mortgage loan favors the senior bondholders, because they receive an earlier-than-anticipated repayment of principal, while the junior bondholders bear the property loss.
cards.explanation: Early principal repayment results from foreclosure, not extension; extension actually puts the senior bondholders' credit enhancement at risk.
cards.originalText: Extension favors the senior bondholders, because they receive an earlier‑than‑anticipated repayment of principal, while the junior bondholders bear the property loss.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain how default sensitivities for tranches are measured.
cards.statement: Default01 is positive for all tranches regardless of the initial default probability or correlation, because equity and bond values decrease monotonically as default probability rises.
cards.explanation: Default01 is quoted as a positive number expressing the decline in value or increase in loss from a 1 bp rise in default probability.
cards.originalText: For all tranches, in all cases, default01 is positive regardless of the initial value of default probability or correlation since equity and bond values decrease monotonically as the default probability rises

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain how default sensitivities for tranches are measured.
cards.statement: Because default01 models correlation as constant, default01 is invariant to different correlation levels.
cards.explanation: Default01 holds correlation fixed while default probability is shocked, but its level and shape depend strongly on the correlation assumed.
cards.originalText: Because default01 ”models correlation as constant according to an implicit ceteris paribus,” default01 is invariant (insensitive) to different correlation levels

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain how default sensitivities for tranches are measured.
cards.statement: Default01 converges to zero for all tranches at very high default rates.
cards.explanation: At very high default rates losses are already large, so marginal defaults matter little for tranche values.
cards.originalText: The default01 sensitivity converges to zero for all the tranches for very high default rates

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain how default sensitivities for tranches are measured.
cards.statement: Default01 is measured by shocking the default probability up and down by 10 bps, reusing the same correlated normal draws, recomputing the default counts and subsequent cash flows, and dividing the difference in mean values or losses by 20.
cards.explanation: Reusing the same random numbers avoids adding simulation noise, and default counts must be recomputed because the shock changes which names default; the 20 is the total width in bps between the up and down shocks.
cards.originalText: Shock the default probability up and down by 10 bps, reuse the same correlated normal draws, recompute the default counts and subsequent cash flows, and divide the difference in mean values or losses by 20.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain how default sensitivities for tranches are measured.
cards.statement: Default01 is reported as a negative number for bonds because their values fall when default probability rises.
cards.explanation: Default01 is expressed as a positive number, representing the decline in value or increase in loss from a 1 bp rise in default probability.
cards.originalText: Shock the default probability by 1 bp, redraw all random numbers for the revaluation, and report the result as a negative number for bonds because their values fall.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain how default sensitivities for tranches are measured.
cards.statement: Default01 is measured by shocking the correlation parameter up and down by 10 bps, redrawing the normal variables for each shock, and dividing the difference in mean losses by 20.
cards.explanation: Default01 shocks the default probability and holds correlation constant; it is not a correlation sensitivity.
cards.originalText: Shock the correlation parameter up and down by 10 bps, redraw the normal variables for each shock, and divide the difference in mean losses by 20.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Explain how default sensitivities for tranches are measured.
cards.statement: Default01 is measured by shocking the default probability up and down by 10 bps, keeping the original default counts fixed, and revaluing each tranche from the existing simulated cash flows.
cards.explanation: Fixed default counts would not respond to the shock and would give zero sensitivity; the default counts and cash flows must be recomputed.
cards.originalText: Shock the default probability up and down by 10 bps, keep the original default counts fixed, and revalue each tranche from the existing simulated cash flows.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe risk factors that impact structured products.
cards.statement: The main concern with tranche thinness is the likelihood of large loss severity within a thin tranche once losses breach its attachment point.
cards.explanation: A thin tranche has a narrow gap between attachment and detachment points, so once collateral losses reach the attachment point the tranche is quickly wiped out.
cards.originalText: The likelihood of large loss severity within thin tranches once a loss event breaches these levels.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe risk factors that impact structured products.
cards.statement: A pool with fewer, larger loans has lower granularity and a greater probability of extreme loss outcomes, so its tranches have greater tail risk than those of a granular pool with the same average default probability, recovery rate and correlation.
cards.explanation: With few large loans, a single default removes a large share of the pool, so losses are lumpy and tail events are more likely.
cards.originalText: Pool Y has lower granularity and a greater probability of extreme loss outcomes, so its tranches have greater tail risk than those of Pool X.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe risk factors that impact structured products.
cards.statement: Two pools with identical average default probability, recovery rate and pairwise default correlation have the same loss distribution and tranche Credit VaR regardless of loan granularity.
cards.explanation: Equal average parameters do not equalize loss distributions; the size of individual loans changes the tail.
cards.originalText: Pool Y has lower granularity, but because the pool parameters are identical the loss distributions and Credit VaR of the tranches are the same.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe risk factors that impact structured products.
cards.statement: A more granular pool exposes its tranches to greater tail risk because defaults are spread across many loans.
cards.explanation: More granular pools are better diversified and have thinner tails, so their tranches face less tail risk.
cards.originalText: Pool X has higher granularity, so its tranches face greater tail risk because defaults are spread across many loans.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe risk factors that impact structured products.
cards.statement: Granularity affects only the expected loss of tranches and has no effect on the tails of the loss distribution.
cards.explanation: Granularity mainly changes the tails of the loss distribution, not the expected loss.
cards.originalText: Granularity affects only the expected loss of the tranches and has no effect on the tails of the loss distribution.

cards.subject: Credit Risk
cards.loText: Describe risk factors that impact structured products.
cards.statement: If pairwise default correlation is high, there is a material probability of a state with an unusually large number of defaults, so a senior bond can suffer a large loss even though the underlying pool is diversified.
